citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint positive operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is a
nonnegative real for every $x$. Then there is a compact self-adjoint positive
operator $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $S^{2}=T$, and it is unique: if
$R\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact and positive
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with $R^{2}=T$,
then $R=S$. The root acts by multiplication by $\sqrt\lambda$ on each positive
eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, $\lambda>0$, and by zero on
$\ker T$; in particular $S$ is the operator denoted $\sqrt T$ or $T^{1/2}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.
This multiplier is bounded: if $t\in\Sigma$ and $u\in E_t$ is a unit vector,
then $0<t=\|Su\|\le\|S\|$, so $|q_\nu(t)|\le\|S\|^\nu$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is
its inverse, whose existence is also supplied by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]].
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies
$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$
When $\Sigma=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field and let $K:X	o Y$ be compact. Write $\kappa:=\|K\|$, $S:=K^*K$, and $|K|:=S^{1/2}$, and let $\Lambda_K$ be zero together with the positive eigenvalues of $|K|$. An admissible spectral index is a bounded function $\psi:\Lambda_K	o[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$. Define $\psi(|K|)$ by the compact spectral multiplier of $S$ with scalar function $t\mapsto\psi(\sqrt t)$. For $ho>0$ define $X_{\psi,ho}(K):=\{\psi(|K|)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\leho\}$. For $
u>0$, $\psi_
u(t)=t^
u$ defines the power source ball $X_{
u,ho}(K)$. If $\kappa>0$ and $q>0$, define the logarithmic spectral-index candidate by $\psi_{\log,q}(0)=0$ and $\psi_{\log,q}(t)=(1+\log(\kappa/t))^{-q}$ for positive $t\in\Lambda_K$; when it is bounded, it defines $X_{\log,q,ho}(K)$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ (Every complete ordered field is Archimedean) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse (Field). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
Every complete ordered field is Archimedean on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

A **Dedekind-complete ordered field** is a commutative field $\mathbb R$ with
identity $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and
the least-upper-bound axiom: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is
bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. Throughout this batch,
all real variables, intervals, limits, derivatives and integrals are taken in
such a field. The integers and rationals are interpreted in their usual
embedded copies. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define $|x|=x$ when $x\ge0$ and
$|x|=-x$ when $x<0$.

derivations.claim: For $0<t\le1$, $1/t\ge1$, so [F8] gives $\log(1/t)\ge\log1=0$. Thus $1+\log(1/t)\ge1$; since $q>0$, the positive power of this base is at least $1$, and its reciprocal $\psi_q(t)$ lies in $(0,1]$. Together with $\psi_q(0)=0$, this verifies that the logarithmic index is bounded and is admissible under [F6].

For $x=(x_j)\in\ell^2$, $\|K_ax\|_2^2=\sum_j j^{-2a}|x_j|^2\le\|x\|_2^2$, so $K_a$ is a well-defined bounded linear map with $\|K_a\|\le1$; $K_ae_1=e_1$ gives $\|K_a\|\ge1$. For $x,y\in\ell^2$, [F2] makes $\sum_j j^{-a}x_jy_j$ absolutely convergent, and the coordinate inner product gives $\langle K_ax,y\rangle=\sum_j j^{-a}x_jy_j=\langle x,K_ay\rangle$. Uniqueness of the adjoint in [F3] yields $K_a^*=K_a$, and $\langle K_ax,x\rangle=\sum_jj^{-a}|x_j|^2\ge0$, so $K_a$ is positive.

For $N\ge1$ define $(K_{a,N}x)_j=j^{-a}x_j$ for $j\le N$ and $0$ for $j>N$. The coordinate estimate from step 1.2 gives $\|K_{a,N}x\|_2\le\|x\|_2$, so $K_{a,N}$ is bounded; its range is contained in $\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_N\}$ and hence it is compact by [F4]. Since $K_a$ is compact, self-adjoint and positive by steps 1.2–2.1, $K_a$ is the unique positive square root of $K_a^*K_a=K_a^2$; [F5] therefore gives $|K_a|=K_a$. Each $e_j$ is an eigenvector of $|K_a|$ with eigenvalue $j^{-a}$. Applying the compact spectral multiplier [F5] coordinatewise yields $(|K_a|^\nu w)_j=j^{-a\nu}w_j$ and $(\psi_q(|K_a|)w)_j=\psi_q(j^{-a})w_j=(1+a\log j)^{-q}w_j$, proving the stated power and logarithmic coordinates.

derivations.claim: For $0<t\le1$, [F8] gives $\log(1/t)\ge0$, so $1+\log(1/t)\ge1$; since $q>0$, $(1+\log(1/t))^q\ge1$ and $\psi_q(t)\le1$. Together with $\psi_q(0)=0$, this verifies that the logarithmic index is bounded and admissible under [F6].

Since $\gamma_j\ge0$, strict increase of the exponential [F10] gives $0<\exp(-\gamma_j)\le1$. Thus for $x=(x_j)\in\ell^2$, $\|K_\gamma x\|_2^2=\sum_j\exp(-2\gamma_j)|x_j|^2\le\|x\|_2^2$, so $K_\gamma$ is bounded with $\|K_\gamma\|\le1$; $K_\gamma e_1=e_1$ gives $\|K_\gamma\|=1$. For $x,y\in\ell^2$, [F2] makes $\sum_j\exp(-\gamma_j)x_jy_j$ absolutely convergent, and the coordinate inner product gives $\langle K_\gamma x,y\rangle=\sum_j\exp(-\gamma_j)x_jy_j=\langle x,K_\gamma y\rangle$. By uniqueness in [F3], $K_\gamma^*=K_\gamma$; moreover $\langle K_\gamma x,x\rangle=\sum_j\exp(-\gamma_j)|x_j|^2\ge0$, so $K_\gamma$ is positive.

Since $\gamma_j\to\infty$, [F9] gives $s_j=\exp(-\gamma_j)\to0$. For $N\ge1$, truncate $K_\gamma$ by $(K_{\gamma,N}x)_j=s_jx_j$ for $j\le N$ and $0$ for $j>N$. By step 1.2, $K_{\gamma,N}$ is bounded; its range lies in $\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_N\}$, so [F4] makes it compact. Since $s_j$ decreases to $0$, $\|K_\gamma-K_{\gamma,N}\|=\sup_{j>N}s_j=s_{N+1}\to0$; [F4] then makes $K_\gamma$ compact, and positivity of each $s_j$ makes it injective. The choices $\gamma_j=j-1$ and $\gamma_j=j(j-1)/2$ are strictly increasing from $0$ to infinity; for the second, $\gamma_j\ge j-1$ for $j\ge2$ and [F8] makes the natural numbers cofinal. Its gaps are $\gamma_{j+1}-\gamma_j=j$, so [F10] gives $s_{j+1}/s_j=\exp(-\gamma_{j+1})/\exp(-\gamma_j)=\exp(-j)\to0$ by [F8]–[F9].

By steps 1.2 and 2.1, $K_\gamma$ is compact, self-adjoint, and positive, so [F5] gives $|K_\gamma|=K_\gamma$. Hence each coordinate vector has singular value $s_j=\exp(-\gamma_j)$; [F5] gives $(|K_\gamma|^\nu w)_j=\exp(-\nu\gamma_j)w_j$ and $(\psi_q(|K_\gamma|)w)_j=(1+\log(1/s_j))^{-q}w_j=(1+\gamma_j)^{-q}w_j$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint positive operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is a
nonnegative real for every $x$. Then there is a compact self-adjoint positive
operator $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $S^{2}=T$, and it is unique: if
$R\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact and positive
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with $R^{2}=T$,
then $R=S$. The root acts by multiplication by $\sqrt\lambda$ on each positive
eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, $\lambda>0$, and by zero on
$\ker T$; in particular $S$ is the operator denoted $\sqrt T$ or $T^{1/2}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.
This multiplier is bounded: if $t\in\Sigma$ and $u\in E_t$ is a unit vector,
then $0<t=\|Su\|\le\|S\|$, so $|q_\nu(t)|\le\|S\|^\nu$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is
its inverse, whose existence is also supplied by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]].
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies
$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$
When $\Sigma=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field and let $K:X	o Y$ be compact. Write $\kappa:=\|K\|$, $S:=K^*K$, and $|K|:=S^{1/2}$, and let $\Lambda_K$ be zero together with the positive eigenvalues of $|K|$. An admissible spectral index is a bounded function $\psi:\Lambda_K	o[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$. Define $\psi(|K|)$ by the compact spectral multiplier of $S$ with scalar function $t\mapsto\psi(\sqrt t)$. For $ho>0$ define $X_{\psi,ho}(K):=\{\psi(|K|)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\leho\}$. For $
u>0$, $\psi_
u(t)=t^
u$ defines the power source ball $X_{
u,ho}(K)$. If $\kappa>0$ and $q>0$, define the logarithmic spectral-index candidate by $\psi_{\log,q}(0)=0$ and $\psi_{\log,q}(t)=(1+\log(\kappa/t))^{-q}$ for positive $t\in\Lambda_K$; when it is bounded, it defines $X_{\log,q,ho}(K)$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, let
$A:X\to Y$ be a compact linear forward map (the closure of $A(B)$ is compact
in $Y$ for every bounded set $B\subseteq X$), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a
bounded linear discretized map with finite-dimensional range. For a datum
$b\in Y$, let $\lambda>0$ be the coefficient of $\|x\|_X^2$ in the Tikhonov
objective $\|Ax-b\|_Y^2+\lambda\|x\|_X^2$. Supply adjoints $A^*:Y\to X$ and
$A_h^*:Y\to X$ satisfying
$\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X$ and
$\langle A_hx,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A_h^*y\rangle_X$, where the inner products
are linear in their first arguments. Assume the shifted normal operators
$A^*A+\lambda I_X$ and $A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X$ are bijective, and define
$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

For a truth $x^\dagger\in X$, data perturbation $e\in Y$, and $\delta\ge0$
with $\|e\|\le\delta$, put
$$y=Ax^\dagger,\qquad y_\delta=y+e,\qquad y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e,\qquad d_h=(A-A_h)x^\dagger=y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}.$$
For any returned output $\widetilde x_h\in X$, define its exact discrete
normal-equation residual by
$$r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}.$$
The five-channel error budget is the ordered tuple
$(b_{\mathrm{bias}},b_{\mathrm{data}},b_{\mathrm{operator}},b_{\mathrm{pre}},b_{\mathrm{solve}})$, where
$$\begin{aligned}b_{\mathrm{bias}}&=x^\dagger-R_\lambda y,\qquad b_{\mathrm{data}}=R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta,\\b_{\mathrm{operator}}&=(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta},\qquad b_{\mathrm{pre}}=R_\lambda d_h,\\b_{\mathrm{solve}}&=R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h.\end{aligned}$$
The five entries are, in order, the truth-bias, data-perturbation,
regularized-operator, pre-inversion, and algebraic-solve error vectors.
The scalar total budget is the sum of the five channel norms. The raw
pre-inversion forward residual is $d_h$; its reconstruction contribution is
$b_{\mathrm{pre}}$. The operator channel measures the difference between the
regularized exact and discretized operators. The solve channel measures the
returned output's difference from the exact discrete Tikhonov output. The
definition supplies no rate or arithmetic residual certificate.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact (hence bounded), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a bounded
discrete operator whose range is a finite-dimensional subspace of $Y$. For
$\lambda>0$,
define

$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

These maps are well-defined by [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Let $x^\dagger\in X$, $y=Ax^\dagger$, $y_\delta=y+e$ with $\|e\|\le\delta$ and $\delta\ge0$, and let $\widetilde x\in X$. Define the exact discrete normal-equation residual

$$r_h=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x-A_h^*y_\delta.$$

Then the following chain is exact:

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +(R_\lambda y_\delta-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) +(R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x).$$

Its norm satisfies

$$\|x^\dagger-\widetilde x\|\le \|x^\dagger-R_\lambda y\|+\frac{\delta}{2\sqrt\lambda} +\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\|+\frac{\|r_h\|}{\lambda}.$$

The first term is regularization bias, the second is data noise, the third is the regularized-operator discretization difference, and the fourth is the solve residual. The third term receives a numerical bound only when an operator-perturbation bound is supplied: if $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$, it is at most $\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. If residual evaluation returns $\widehat r_h$ with a certified $\|r_h-\widehat r_h\|\le\rho_h$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h)/\lambda$. If an algorithm has a specified exact-arithmetic stopping output $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ and returns a computed output $\widetilde x$, the last difference can further split as

$$R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x= (R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-x_{\mathrm{stop}}) +(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-\widetilde x).$$

Writing $r_{\mathrm{stop}}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)x_{\mathrm{stop}} -A_h^*y_\delta$, the first term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the second is the separate returned-output roundoff term. Any bound on that roundoff or on residual-evaluation error requires its own arithmetic hypotheses. For a discretized datum $y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e$ formed before inversion, put $d_h=(A-A_h)x^\dagger=y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}$. Let $\widetilde x_h\in X$ be a computed discrete output. The corresponding exact refinement is

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x_h=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +R_\lambda d_h+(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta} +(R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h),$$

so the forward residual discarded by quadrature or collocation is counted before inversion as $R_\lambda d_h$, with $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. The separate operator discretization and solve terms remain. For this refined chain, define $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}$; then $\|R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h\|\le\|r_{h,h}\|/\lambda$. If its evaluation returns $\widehat r_{h,h}$ with a certified $\|r_{h,h}-\widehat r_{h,h}\|\le\rho_{h,h}$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h})/\lambda$. No rate for $d_h$, no operator perturbation estimate, and no floating-point residual bound is implicit. When $X,Y$ are finite-dimensional and $b=Ax^\dagger+e$, the same identity is the canonical Tikhonov bias/noise formula

$$x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda b=(I-A^\#_\lambda A)x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda e, \qquad A^\#_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*.$$

Here $\lambda$ is the coefficient of $\|x\|^2$ in
$\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2$.

For stored finite matrices, [[lem-computed-augmented-tikhonov-solve-residual-and-output-error]] supplies the concrete augmented-QR or independently certified-residual application: take its $\rho$ as $\rho_h$ with datum $y_\delta$, or as $\rho_{h,h}$ with datum $y_{h,\delta}$. It bounds returned-output roundoff for the exact direct-solve target and retains explicit real/complex realization, square-root representation, successful-operation and nonsingularity conditions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For $\lambda>0$, put
$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*$, which is well-defined by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Then for every $g\in Y$,

$$\|R_\lambda g\|\le\frac{\|g\|}{2\sqrt\lambda},\qquad \|R_\lambda\|\le\frac1{2\sqrt\lambda}.$$

The proof uses the normal equation and the Hilbert-space inner product; it
does not use a compact-operator convergence rate or a source condition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let stored $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ and $y\in\mathbb F^m$ be real or complex, $m,n\ge1$, and let stored real $\lambda>0$. Let $x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*y$. Compute $\alpha=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)>0$ under the successful normal-range square-root model, and solve the stored augmented problem $\min_x\|[A;\alpha I]x-[y;0]\|_2$ by scaled Householder QR and rounded substitution. For complex inputs use the realification described below, so the backend uses only real triangular divisions. Every operation must succeed; failed pivots, invalid operations and out-of-range nonzero intermediates return range-failure.

For any returned $\widehat x$, let $\widehat r$ and $\rho\ge0$ certify $\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho$ for the intended residual $r=(A^*A+\lambda I)\widehat x-A^*y$. One concrete certificate is supplied by [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]] using its successful sequential-dot evaluation, exact norms or certified upper bounds, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. These dimension restrictions concern evaluation on the original $m\times n$ matrix, including for complex data; if evaluating on the realified $2m\times2n$ matrix instead, require $(\max(2m,2n)-1)u<1$. Arithmetic success alone does not imply these restrictions. Then
$$\|\widehat x-x_\lambda\|_2\le\frac{\|\widehat r\|_2+\rho}{\lambda}.$$
This bounds returned-output roundoff relative to the exact direct-solve target $x_{\rm stop}=x_\lambda$. It also certifies the solve term in any larger analytic error chain, irrespective of the backend. The representation of $\sqrt\lambda$ contributes no hidden change of target: $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\le(2u+u^2)\lambda$. If residual evaluation instead uses exact $\alpha^2$, add $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\|\widehat x\|_2$ to its allowance; rounding a computed $\alpha^2$ needs its own scalar error as well.

The backend's nearby least-squares conclusion holds under the completed QR/solve hypotheses and nonsingularity condition of [[thm-computed-full-rank-least-squares-backward-stability]], including $Mu<1$ and $\gamma_{N+3}<1/8$ in the real backend dimensions $(M,N)=(m+n,n)$ or $(2m+2n,2n)$, respectively. In real dimension, write $C=[A;\alpha I]$ and $\epsilon_Q=\beta_Q\|C\|_F$. A sufficient check is $\epsilon_Q<\alpha$ and $\|\Delta R\|_F<\alpha-\epsilon_Q$. An explicit certified nonsingularity check may replace this sufficient margin.

For a Hilbert-space discrete operator, supply isometries $U:\mathbb F^n\to X$ and $V:\mathbb F^m\to Y$ with $A_h=VAU^*$, and return $U\widehat x$. With coefficient datum $y_c=V^*y_\delta$, the exact normal solution lies in $\operatorname{ran}U$ and the coefficient residual lifts isometrically, so the same certificate applies to $r_h$; likewise use $V^*y_{h,\delta}$ for $r_{h,h}$. If a stored coefficient datum $\widehat y_c$ differs from $V^*y$ by at most $\epsilon_y$, add $\|A\|_2\epsilon_y$ to the residual allowance. If the returned output also has an orthogonal component $z\perp\operatorname{ran}U$ of norm at most $\epsilon_\perp$, add $\lambda\epsilon_\perp$. Finite rank alone does not supply these coordinate or output certificates.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:X\to Y$ be compact and $A_h:X\to Y$ be
bounded and finite rank, between real or complex Hilbert spaces. Suppose
$x^\dagger\perp\ker A$, $y=Ax^\dagger$, $y_\delta=y+e$ with
$\|e\|\le\delta$, and $\|A-A_h\|\le\eta$. Form the discretized datum
$y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e$ before inversion. For $\lambda>0$, define
$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)^{-1}A_h^*,$$
and for a computed output $\widetilde x_h$ define its exact normal-equation
residual
$$r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}.$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} \|x^\dagger-\widetilde x_h\|\le{}& \|x^\dagger-R_\lambda y\| +\frac{\delta+\eta\|x^\dagger\|}{2\sqrt\lambda} +\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta}\| +\frac{\|r_{h,h}\|}{\lambda}. \end{aligned}$$
The forward-model term $\eta\|x^\dagger\|$ is counted before inversion and
is amplified by $1/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. The regularized-operator difference is
kept as a separate term; the sequence conclusion below explicitly assumes
that this term tends to zero.

For a sequence of discretizations and outputs, if $\lambda_j\to0$,
$$\frac{\delta_j+\eta_j\|x^\dagger\|}{\sqrt{\lambda_j}}\to0,\qquad \|(R_{\lambda_j}-R_{\lambda_j,h_j})y_{h_j,\delta_j}\|\to0,\qquad \frac{\|r_{h_j,h_j}\|}{\lambda_j}\to0,$$
then $\widetilde x_{h_j}\to x^\dagger$. If a certified residual evaluation
satisfies $\|r_{h,h}-\widehat r_{h,h}\|\le\rho_{h,h}$, its term may be
bounded by $(\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h})/\lambda$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

$M^\perp:=\{z:\langle z,m\rangle=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$ for the
orthogonal complement of a subspace $M$. The kernel $N(K)$ is closed, so the
restriction
$$\widetilde K:=K|_{N(K)^\perp}:N(K)^\perp\to R(K)$$
is a linear bijection. Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$
to have domain
$$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$
and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and
$z\in R(K)^\perp$, set
$$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$

orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero. Boundedness of $K^\dagger$ on
this domain is not part of the definition.

deterministic parameter-choice rule is a function
$\alpha:Y\to(0,\infty)$. It is **noise-level-free** (also called **heuristic**)
when the value $\alpha(z)$ for an observed datum $z\in Y$ uses only $K$, the
fixed family, and $z$; it does not take the exact datum or a noise bound

and a strictly increasing finite grid $0<\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_q$ with

$$x_j=(A^TA+\lambda_j I)^{-1}A^Tb,$$
and the residual $r_j=\|Ax_j-b\|$ and solution norm $s_j=\|x_j\|$.
Discard any index with $r_j=0$ or $s_j=0$. If fewer than three indices
remain, return failure status `insufficient-valid-points`.

For consecutive retained indices $i_0<i_1<i_2$, set
$p_k=(\log r_{i_k},\log s_{i_k})\in\mathbb R^2$, $u=p_1-p_0$,
and $v=p_2-p_1$. Define their discrete curvature by
$$\kappa=\begin{cases} \dfrac{2|\det(u,v)|}{\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|},&\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|>0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$
Assign this curvature to the middle retained index. Among the resulting
$q'-2$ values, return the original grid parameter whose curvature is largest;
if there is a tie, return the tied parameter with the smallest original index.
No uniform-grid spacing is assumed in log parameter. This is a finite-grid
heuristic and carries no universal optimality claim.

index, or the stated failure status. Every step uses a finite loop over the

citations.quote:
Input a real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, data $b\in\mathbb R^m$,
and a strictly increasing finite grid $0<\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_q$ with
$q\ge3$. For each grid point, compute the unique Tikhonov minimizer
$$x_j=(A^TA+\lambda_j I)^{-1}A^Tb,$$
and the residual $r_j=\|Ax_j-b\|$ and solution norm $s_j=\|x_j\|$.
Discard any index with $r_j=0$ or $s_j=0$. If fewer than three indices
remain, return failure status `insufficient-valid-points`.

For consecutive retained indices $i_0<i_1<i_2$, set
$p_k=(\log r_{i_k},\log s_{i_k})\in\mathbb R^2$, $u=p_1-p_0$,
and $v=p_2-p_1$. Define their discrete curvature by
$$\kappa=\begin{cases} \dfrac{2|\det(u,v)|}{\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|},&\|u\|\,\|v\|\,\|u+v\|>0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$
Assign this curvature to the middle retained index. Among the resulting
$q'-2$ values, return the original grid parameter whose curvature is largest;
if there is a tie, return the tied parameter with the smallest original index.
No uniform-grid spacing is assumed in log parameter. This is a finite-grid
heuristic and carries no universal optimality claim.

The output is either a selected $\lambda_j$ with its discrete curvature and
index, or the stated failure status. Every step uses a finite loop over the
input grid.

derivations.claim: Since $A=I_2$, the formula in [F1] gives $x_\lambda=(1+\lambda)^{-1}e_1$, residual norm $r_\lambda=\|Ax_\lambda-b\|_2=\lambda/(1+\lambda)$, and solution norm $s_\lambda=\|x_\lambda\|_2=1/(1+\lambda)$. At the three grid values, $(r_\lambda,s_\lambda)$ equals $(1/10,9/10)$, $(1/2,1/2)$, and $(9/10,1/10)$, respectively. All retained points are valid because both coordinates are positive.

Their log-log points are $p_0=(-\log 10,\log(9/10))$, $p_1=(-\log 2,-\log 2)$, and $p_2=(\log(9/10),-\log 10)$. Thus $u=p_1-p_0=(\log 5,-\log(9/5))$ and $v=p_2-p_1=(\log(9/5),-\log 5)$. Their determinant is $-\log^2 5+\log^2(9/5)\ne0$ because $5>9/5>1$; moreover $\|u\|_2=\|v\|_2>0$ and $u+v=(\log9,-\log9)\ne0$. The algorithm's curvature is therefore well-defined and positive.

There are exactly three retained grid indices, so the only consecutive triple is $(1,2,3)$ and its curvature is assigned to index $2$. This is the only candidate for the maximum, so the selector returns $\lambda_2=1$; no tie-break is needed. The computation supplies no claim about any grid outside this input.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define $Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}
$e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and $0$ elsewhere.

The real sequence space $$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$ with its canonical inner product and norm from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and therefore is a real Hilbert space.
A $\mathbb K$-linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$
The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let $T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).
Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let $T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$ to have domain $$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$ and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and $z\in R(K)^\perp$, set $$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$ Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero.

It is **noise-level-free** (also called **heuristic**) when the value $\alpha(z)$ for an observed datum $z\in Y$ uses only $K$, the fixed family, and $z$; it does not take the exact datum or a noise bound $\delta$ as input.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.
