$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex Hilbert
spaces over the same scalar field, and let $K:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear
operator. Write $R(K):=\{Kx:x\in X\}$ for its range,
$N(K):=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ for its kernel, and
$M^\perp:=\{z:\langle z,m\rangle=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$ for the
orthogonal complement of a subspace $M$. The kernel $N(K)$ is closed, so the
restriction
$$\widetilde K:=K|_{N(K)^\perp}:N(K)^\perp\to R(K)$$
is a linear bijection. Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$
to have domain
$$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$
and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and
$z\in R(K)^\perp$, set
$$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$
Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the
orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero. Boundedness of $K^\dagger$ on
this domain is not part of the definition.

Fix a compact Hilbert inverse model $K:X\to Y$ and a family of reconstruction
maps $(R_\alpha)_{\alpha>0}$, with each $R_\alpha:Y\to X$, both held fixed. A
deterministic parameter-choice rule is a function
$\alpha:Y\to(0,\infty)$. It is **noise-level-free** (also called **heuristic**)
when the value $\alpha(z)$ for an observed datum $z\in Y$ uses only $K$, the
fixed family, and $z$; it does not take the exact datum or a noise bound
$\delta$ as input. Here $\delta\ge0$ is a valid noise bound for $z$ and an
exact datum $y$ when $\|z-y\|_Y\le\delta$. The resulting reconstruction is
$R_{\alpha(z)}z$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

derivations.claim: Coordinatewise linearity gives $K$ and every $K_N$ as linear maps by [F13]. For every $x\in\ell^2$, [F1] gives $\|Kx\|_2^2=\sum_{j\ge1}j^{-2}|x_j|^2\le\|x\|_2^2$ and $\|K_Nx\|_2^2\le\|x\|_2^2$, so [F3] makes both bounded linear operators. For $\|x\|_2\le1$, [F1] also gives $\|(K-K_N)x\|_2^2=\sum_{j>N}j^{-2}|x_j|^2\le(N+1)^{-2}$. Hence [F4] gives $\|K-K_N\|\le1/(N+1)$. The range of $K_N$ is exactly the span of $e_1,\ldots,e_N$: its outputs are supported in these coordinates, and $K_N(je_j)=e_j$ for each $j\le N$ by [F14]. These vectors form an ordered basis by [F5], so each $K_N$ has finite rank.

By [F6], every $K_N$ is compact in the sense of [F9]. By [F2] and [F7], the codomain $\ell^2$ is Banach; [A1] supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of [F8]. Since $\|K-K_N\|\to0$ by step 1.1, [F8] implies that $K$ is compact and hence satisfies the compact-model interface [F10].

The coordinate formula makes $K$ injective. If $y=Kx$, then $x_j=jy_j$ and $(jy_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2$; conversely, whenever $(jy_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2$, taking $x_j=jy_j$ gives $Kx=y$. Thus $R(K)=\{y:(jy_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2\}$. Each $e_j/j=K e_j$ lies in $R(K)$, and these vectors are linearly independent because they have distinct nonzero coordinates by [F14]; hence $R(K)$ is infinite-dimensional. Any vector in $R(K)^\perp$ has every coordinate zero, so $R(K)^\perp=\{0\}$ and $D(K^\dagger)=R(K)$. By [F11], $K^\dagger y=(jy_j)_{j\ge1}$. For each fixed $\alpha>0$, $R_\alpha$ is bounded since its sum has finitely many terms and $\|R_\alpha y\|_2^2\le\lfloor1/\alpha\rfloor^2\|y\|_2^2$. For $y\in D(K^\dagger)$, $R_\alpha y$ is the initial truncation of the square-summable sequence $K^\dagger y$, so as $\alpha\downarrow0$ these truncations converge in $\ell^2$ to $K^\dagger y$. The stated family is therefore pointwise regularizing.

The rule $\alpha$ is positive and depends only on $z$, so it is noise-level-free by [F12]. Take exact datum $y=0$ and noisy datum $z_j=e_j/j=K e_j$. By [F1] and [F14], $\delta_j=\|z_j-y\|_2=1/j\to0$, while $\alpha(z_j)=1/j^2$ and $\lfloor1/\alpha(z_j)\rfloor=j^2$. Therefore $R_{\alpha(z_j)}z_j=e_j$, whereas $K^\dagger y=0$, and the reconstruction error is $1$ for every $j$. The claimed worst-case limit fails at $y=0$, since its supremum is at least $1$ along the null sequence $\delta_j$.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,
surjectivity, or closed-range assumption is included in the model.

Define the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger$ to have domain $$D(K^\dagger):=R(K)\oplus R(K)^\perp$$ and, for the unique decomposition $y=r+z$ with $r\in R(K)$ and $z\in R(K)^\perp$, set $$K^\dagger y:=\widetilde K^{-1}r.$$ Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero.

For a compact operator $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, write $N(K):=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$. For a set $M$ with $0\in M\subseteq N(K)^\perp$ and $\delta\ge0$, define $\varepsilon_K(M,\delta):=\sup\{\|x\|_X:x\in M,\ \|Kx\|_Y\le\delta\}\in[0,+\infty]$.

If $E_y(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$, then $K^\dagger$ is continuous on $D(K^\dagger).$ Thus, when $K^\dagger$ is discontinuous, no such noise-level-free rule yields worst-case convergence over each exact datum's full admissible error balls.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator. The associated compact linear inverse
model has parameter space $X$, data space $Y$, forward map $K$, and admissible
truth class $X$: for a true parameter $x^\dagger\in X$, the exact datum is
$y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse
problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$. No injectivity,

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator between
real or complex Hilbert spaces over one scalar field, with Hilbert-space
Moore–Penrose inverse $K^\dagger:D(K^\dagger)\to X$. Suppose $K^\dagger$ is
discontinuous on $D(K^\dagger)$ with its norm inherited from $Y$. Let
$(R_\alpha)_{\alpha>0}$ be maps $Y\to X$ such that
$R_\alpha y\to K^\dagger y$ for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ as
$\alpha\downarrow0$, and let $\alpha:Y\to(0,\infty)$ be a deterministic
noise-level-free rule. For each exact datum $y\in D(K^\dagger)$ and
$\delta>0$, set $E_y(\delta):=\sup\{\|R_{\alpha(z)}z-K^\dagger y\|_X:z\in Y,\ \|z-y\|_Y\le\delta\}$.
If $E_y(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ for every $y\in D(K^\dagger)$,
then $K^\dagger$ is continuous on $D(K^\dagger).$ Thus, when $K^\dagger$ is
discontinuous, no such noise-level-free rule yields worst-case convergence
over each exact datum's full admissible error balls. The limit is required
separately for each exact datum, not uniformly over $y$. This veto does not
exclude convergence on restricted solution or error classes, stochastic noise
models, or finite-dimensional problems.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.
This multiplier is bounded: if $t\in\Sigma$ and $u\in E_t$ is a unit vector,
then $0<t=\|Su\|\le\|S\|$, so $|q_\nu(t)|\le\|S\|^\nu$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is
its inverse, whose existence is also supplied by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]].

$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies
$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$

A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. **Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is

**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

In the carrier case covered by [F4]–[F5], [F1] supplies independent coordinates with the common standard-normal density and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F5]. Hence [F5] makes the noise coefficient sequence a Borel Gaussian random element of $H(\delta)$; [F4] puts each deterministic signal $Kx$ in the same space. Their sum $Kx+\epsilon W$ is therefore an $H(\delta)$-valued Borel random element, and every continuous linear functional of it is a translate and positive rescaling of the corresponding centered Gaussian functional.

In the infinite-dimensional function-space case, if $Kx+\epsilon W$ were an $H$-valued sample on an event of probability one, then $W=((Kx+\epsilon W)-Kx)/\epsilon$ would also be $H$-valued there, since $Kx\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. This contradicts [F5], so the sample is not $H$-valued.

With $r_N=g-P_Ng$, linearity gives $Y_x(g)-Y_x(P_Ng)=\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(r_N)$. Centering and the covariance identity in [F1] give $\mathbb E Z(r_N)=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z(r_N)^2]=\|r_N\|_H^2$; expanding the square therefore shows that the squared mean-square error is $|\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H|^2+\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$. By step 1.1, for each $g$ and $k\ge1$ the set of integers $N\ge k$ with $\|g-P_Ng\|_H\le2^{-k}$ is nonempty. Its least element $N_k(g)$ is uniquely defined, with no choice and no dependence on $x$, $Kx$ or the observations. do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

Assume countable choice. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the wavelet or trigonometric basis from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $Z_{lk}$ be mutually independent real random variables with density $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Define the formal white-noise coefficient sequence $W=(Z_{lk})$. For every $\delta>1/2$, this sequence is almost surely an element of $H(\delta)$ and is a Borel Gaussian random element there. Its law $N$ is a Borel probability on $H(\delta)$. For an infinite-dimensional basis, white noise is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued random element. Here Gaussian means that each continuous real linear functional has a centered law $N(0,v)$ in the density convention of [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]; in particular, for $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$ its variance is $\sum_jd_j^2$ whenever this pairing is continuous on $H(\delta)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $N$ let $V_N=\operatorname{span}\{u_j:j\in J,\ j\le N\}$ and let $P_Ng=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$. Orthonormality gives $g-P_Ng\perp V_N$. For any $v\in H$, expanding the inner product of $v=P_Nv+(v-P_Nv)$ gives $\|v\|^2=\|P_Nv\|^2+\|v-P_Nv\|^2$, so $\|P_Nv\|\le\|v\|$. Given $\eta>0$, density of the finite span in [F2] gives $w\in V_M$ with $\|g-w\|<\eta$; for $N\ge M$, $P_Nw=w$, so $\|g-P_Ng\|\le\|g-w\|+\|P_N(w-g)\|\le2\|g-w\|<2\eta$. Thus $P_Ng\to g$ in norm, with the finite-basis case eventually equal to $g$.

For distinct indices $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, [F1] gives independent standard-normal variables $Z(u_{j_1}),\ldots,Z(u_{j_m})$. Since $\epsilon>0$, the affine map $z\mapsto\mu_{j_r}+\epsilon z$ and its inverse are continuous, so $Y_x(u_{j_r})$ and its noise coordinate generate the same sigma-algebra; independence therefore transfers. The affine-image definition of $N$ gives each law $N(\mu_{j_r},\epsilon^2)$.

Put $c_j=\langle g,u_j\rangle_H$. The linearity clause in [F1] applied to the finite sum defining $P_Ng$ gives $Z(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}c_jZ(u_j)$; linearity of the inner product gives $\langle Kx,P_Ng\rangle_H=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}c_j\mu_j$. Combining these identities yields $Y_x(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}c_jY_x(u_j)$.

In the carrier case covered by [F4]–[F5], [F1] supplies independent coordinates with the common standard-normal density and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F5]. Hence [F5] makes the noise coefficient sequence a Borel Gaussian random element of $H(\delta)$; [F4] puts each deterministic signal $Kx$ in the same space. Their sum $Kx+\epsilon W$ is therefore an $H(\delta)$-valued Borel random element, and every continuous linear functional of it is a translate and positive rescaling of the corresponding centered Gaussian functional.

In the infinite-dimensional function-space case, if $Kx+\epsilon W$ were an $H$-valued sample on an event of probability one, then $W=((Kx+\epsilon W)-Kx)/\epsilon$ would also be $H$-valued there, since $Kx\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. This contradicts [F5], so the sample is not $H$-valued.

With $r_N=g-P_Ng$, linearity gives $Y_x(g)-Y_x(P_Ng)=\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(r_N)$. Centering and the covariance identity in [F1] give $\mathbb E Z(r_N)=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z(r_N)^2]=\|r_N\|_H^2$; expanding the square therefore shows that the squared mean-square error is $|\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H|^2+\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$. By [F3] and step 1.1, both terms tend to zero, proving the asserted mean-square reconstruction. For any finite list of test vectors, the sum of their finitely many squared errors also tends to zero, so the coordinate reconstructions converge jointly in product mean square.

By step 1.1, for each $g$ and $k\ge1$ the set of integers $N\ge k$ with $\|g-P_Ng\|_H\le2^{-k}$ is nonempty. Its least element $N_k(g)$ is uniquely defined, with no choice and no dependence on $x$, $Kx$ or the observations. For fixed $g,k$, $a_{g,k}$ is a finite linear combination of coordinate evaluations on $\mathbb R^J$, hence is measurable. By [F8], its limsup and liminf are measurable; their equality set, intersected with the set where their common value is finite, is the measurable real-convergence set $A_g$. Defining $T(z)(g)$ to equal that limit on $A_g$ and zero on its complement is measurable: for a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage is $A_g\cap\{\limsup_k a_{g,k}\in B\}$, together with $A_g^c$ if $0\in B$. Thus every evaluation of $T$ is measurable, which makes $T$ measurable into $\mathcal C_H$. Each coordinate of $S$ is a field evaluation, so $S$ is measurable into $\mathcal C_J$ as well.

Fix $x$ and $g$. By steps 1.3 and 2.1, the real random variable $D_k=a_{g,k}(S(Y_x))-Y_x(g)$ satisfies $\mathbb E|D_k|^2\le(\|Kx\|_H^2+\epsilon^2)4^{-k}$. For every positive integer $r$, [F6] applied to $|D_k|^2$ at threshold $r^{-2}$ gives $\mathbb P\{|D_k|\ge1/r\}\le r^2(\|Kx\|_H^2+\epsilon^2)4^{-k}$. The right-hand side is summable in $k$, so [F7] makes $|D_k|<1/r$ eventually almost surely for each $r$. The union over $r\ge1$ of these null exceptional events is null: disjointifying the union and using countable additivity bounds its probability by the sum of zeros. Off that union $D_k\to0$, proving $T(S(Y_x))(g)=Y_x(g)$ almost surely. All limits here concern the explicitly specified representatives at a fixed $x,g$; the $L^2$ equalities used to compute the error hold almost surely and therefore give exactly the same second moments.

The coordinate law $Q_x=S_*P_x$ and the reconstructed law $T_*Q_x$ are probability measures by [F10]; they use only pushforwards of the given process, with no new product-existence assumption. For any finite list $g_1,\ldots,g_n$, intersect the finitely many probability-one events in step 3.1. On that intersection the reconstructed and original evaluation vectors agree, so $T_*Q_x$ and $P_x$ agree on every finite cylinder $\{y:(y(g_1),\ldots,y(g_n))\in B\}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. These cylinders form a generating pi-system for $\mathcal C_H$, and both measures have total mass one, so [F9] gives $T_*Q_x=P_x$ on $\mathcal C_H$. This proves equality of laws without any uncountable intersection of probability-one events.

For every basis index $j$, $N_k(u_j)\ge k\ge j$ once $k\ge j$, so orthonormality gives $a_{u_j,k}(z)=z_j$ then, for every $z\in\mathbb R^J$. Consequently $T(z)(u_j)=z_j$ and $S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R^J}$ everywhere. If $J=\varnothing$, completeness forces $H=\{0\}$, every sum defining $a_{0,k}$ is zero, and $T$ returns the zero field; linearity gives $Y_x(0)=0$ almost surely. If $J$ is nonempty and finite, $P_N=I$ after its last index, so the same construction reduces to the finite linear reconstruction and all preceding arguments apply. Thus the maps in the Statement establish both sampling-law identities in every allowed dimension. The least-index construction spends no choice principle; the only countable-choice use remains step 1.4.

For $g\in H$, set $P_Ng=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$, with $P_N=I$ once all vectors of a finite basis have been included. Then

$$Y_x(g)=L^2(\mathbb P)\text{-}\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j).$$

Thus every finite collection of observation functionals is reconstructed from the coefficient sequence in mean square. This does not assert almost-sure convergence of the full sequence of partial sums, a simultaneous path identity for all test vectors, or an $H$-valued observation.

More precisely, let $\mathcal C_H$ be the cylinder sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^H$, let $\mathcal C_J$ be the sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^J$ generated by its coordinate evaluations, and let $P_x$ be the field sampling law. Define $S:\mathbb R^H\to\mathbb R^J$ by $S(y)_j=y(u_j)$ and $Q_x=S_*P_x$, where a pushforward is $S_*P_x(B)=P_x(S^{-1}(B))$. There is a measurable map $T:(\mathbb R^J,\mathcal C_J)\to(\mathbb R^H,\mathcal C_H)$, depending only on the indexed basis, such that for every parameter $x$,

$$S_*P_x=Q_x,\qquad T_*Q_x=P_x,\qquad S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R^J}.$$

These parameter-independent maps give equivalence of the field cylinder experiment and its coefficient experiment. One such map is the following. For $k\ge1$ and $g\in H$, let $N_k(g)$ be the least integer $N\ge k$ with $\|g-P_Ng\|_H\le2^{-k}$ and put

$$a_{g,k}(z)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N_k(g)}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hz_j,\qquad T(z)(g)=\begin{cases}\lim_{k\to\infty}a_{g,k}(z),&\text{if the limit exists in }\mathbb R,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

For each fixed $x$ and $g$, $T(S(Y_x))(g)=Y_x(g)$ almost surely, and the same holds jointly for each fixed finite list of test vectors. The exceptional event may depend on $x$ and on that list; no intersection over all $g\in H$ is asserted. In dimension zero the coefficient space is a singleton and $T$ returns the field with value zero at $g=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $Q\in[0,\infty)$ and let $a=(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a nondecreasing sequence of positive real numbers, so $0<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots$. The statistical ellipsoid of radius $Q$ and weights $a$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
No assumption that $a_j\to\infty$ is included. In particular, this definition does not assert that the ellipsoid is compact in $\ell^2$.

Input a normalized sequence observation $z=(z_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ from the Gaussian sequence inverse model and a cutoff $D\in\mathbb N_0$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Output the finite-support estimate $\widehat\theta_D(z)\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ defined by
$$\widehat\theta_{D,j}(z)=\begin{cases}z_j,&1\le j\le D,\\0,&j>D.\end{cases}$$
For $D=0$ the output is the zero sequence.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], the model coordinates in [F1] are fixed by the countable-choice SVD branch. If $\epsilon>0$, [F1] and [F3] give $\widehat\theta_{D,j}(Z)-\theta_j=\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ for $j\le D$ and $-\theta_j$ for $j>D$, hence $\|\widehat\theta_D(Z)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}^2=\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2}\xi_j^2+\sum_{j>D}\theta_j^2$. If $\epsilon=0$, the retained error is zero and the omitted error is $-\theta_j$, so the squared error is $\sum_{j>D}\theta_j^2$. In both cases the error is in $\ell^2$ because the estimator has finite support and $\theta\in\ell^2$.

For $\epsilon>0$, taking expectation in the finite random sum of [step 1.1] and using $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$ from [F1] gives $R_\theta(D)=\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2}+\sum_{j>D}\theta_j^2$. For $\epsilon=0$, the deterministic error in [step 1.1] gives the same formula with the first term zero. The deterministic tail is finite because $\theta\in\ell^2$.

For every $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, monotonicity gives $a_j\ge a_{D+1}$ for $j>D$, so $\sum_{j>D}\theta_j^2=\sum_{j>D}a_j^2\theta_j^2a_j^{-2}\le a_{D+1}^{-2}\sum_{j>D}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2/a_{D+1}^2$. Thus [step 2.1] is bounded above by the asserted right-hand side.

The sequence with $\theta^\star_{D+1}=Q/a_{D+1}$ and all other coordinates zero belongs to $\ell^2$ and satisfies $\sum_{j\ge1}a_j^2(\theta^\star_j)^2=Q^2$, including $Q=0$. Its tail squared norm is exactly $Q^2/a_{D+1}^2$, so it attains the upper bound from [step 3.1]. The finite-coordinate variance term in [step 2.1] is independent of $\theta$, hence the same sequence attains the full worst-case risk.
Taking the supremum in [step 2.1], using the universal upper bound [step 3.1] and the attaining sequence [step 4.1], yields the exact equality and the stated zero-cutoff convention.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and let $\epsilon\ge0$. In the Gaussian sequence inverse model with positive singular numbers $(s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$, let $Q\ge0$ and let $(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be positive and nondecreasing. For each $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, define the squared sequence risk of the cutoff estimator at $D\in\mathbb N_0$ by
$$R_\theta(D):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|\widehat\theta_D(Z)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}^2\right].$$
Then its exact worst-case squared sequence risk is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)}R_\theta(D)=\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2},$$
where the sum is $0$ for $D=0$. The supremum is attained by the one-coordinate truth $\theta^\star=(Q/a_{D+1})e_{D+1}$, with $\theta^\star=0$ when $Q=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: The density in the Statement is positive and continuous. The substitution $y=\theta+\sqrt{2}\tau x$ on symmetric finite intervals and [F8] show that its integral is $(\tau\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\sqrt{2}\tau\sqrt{\pi}=1$, so by [F2]–[F3] it defines the scalar sampling probability on the stated Borel sample space.

Write $b=\min\{r,\tau\}$ and $u=b/\tau\in[0,1]$. This location family is the scalar Gaussian coordinate experiment described in [F1]. Under the two-point prior, the likelihood ratio at observation $y$ is $p_{b,\tau}(y)/p_{-b,\tau}(y)=\exp(2by/\tau^2)$. Hence the posterior mean is $b\tanh(by/\tau^2)$ and the posterior variance is $b^2\operatorname{sech}^2(by/\tau^2)$; for any action $a$, its conditional squared loss is the square of its distance from this posterior mean plus that posterior variance. Averaging this identity over any action kernel from [F4] leaves the posterior variance as a lower bound, including the degenerate case $b=0$.

Define $I(u):=\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(x)\operatorname{sech}(ux)\,dx$. Since $\cosh t\ge1$, the integrand lies between $0$ and $\phi(x)$, whose integral is $1$ by [F8] and the affine substitution [F9]; hence $I(u)$ is finite. Since $\cosh$ is even and increasing on $[0,\infty)$ by [F6], $\operatorname{sech}(ux)\ge\operatorname{sech}(x)$ for every real $x$ and $0\le u\le1$. Therefore $I(u)\ge I(1)$, while $e^{-u^2/2}\ge e^{-1/2}$.

For $x\ge0$, [F6] gives $0\le\tanh x$ and $(\tanh x)'\le1$ because $\cosh x\ge1$; with $\tanh0=0$, [F10] yields $\tanh x\le x$. Set $g(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x$. Differentiation using [F6] and [F10] gives $g'(x)=g(x)(\tanh x-x)\le0$, so [F10] implies $g(x)\le g(0)=1$. Evenness extends $\cosh x\le e^{x^2/2}$ to all real $x$. Consequently $\phi(x)\operatorname{sech}x\ge(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2}$, and [F8] gives $I(1)\ge1/\sqrt2$.

The prior predictive density, after $x=y/\tau$, is $\tau^{-1}\phi(x)e^{-u^2/2}\cosh(ux)$, where $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Multiplying by the posterior variance from step 1.2 and changing variables gives Bayes risk $B(r,\tau)=b^2e^{-u^2/2}I(u)$, with $I$ defined in step 1.3.

Steps 2.1, 1.3 and 1.4 give $B(r,\tau)\ge b^2e^{-1/2}/\sqrt2=b^2/\sqrt{2e}=T(r,\tau)/\sqrt{2e}$, where $e=\exp(1)$ by [F7]. Since the prior is supported in $[-r,r]$, the supremum risk of every rule is at least its prior-averaged risk; taking the infimum over rules and using [F4] yields $M(r,\tau)\ge B(r,\tau)$.

The constant estimator $0$ has maximum risk $r^2$, while the identity estimator $y\mapsto y$ has risk $\tau^2$ at every parameter; hence their better maximum risk is $T(r,\tau)=b^2$. This proves the projection-risk claim together with step 3.1.

boundaries.reason: The scalar experiment has no indexed sum or empty family; the risk bound is stated directly for one coordinate.

The item is the one-coordinate Gaussian location case, and step 4.1 checks both scalar estimators.
The degenerate interval r=0 is included through b=0 in steps 1.2 and 3.1.
The prior is supported at the interval endpoints ±b and step 4.1 verifies the endpoint maximum risks.

boundaries.reason: The prior has exactly two explicitly specified atoms (or coincident atoms when $b=0$), so no choice principle is used.
The statement is a lower bound and risk comparison, not an equivalence.
