Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. For supplied finite-valued nonnegative measurable density representatives $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ in the convention of [[def-likelihood-density]], the **root-L2 Hellinger distance** is

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p > 0$. For a natural number $k \ge 1$ write
$\iota(k) = k \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the canonical natural, which is positive
([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and write $k^{p} := \iota(k)^{p}$ for its rational
power ([[def-rational-power]]). Then

$$\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k^{p}} \ \text{converges} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad p > 1 .$$

In particular the harmonic series $\sum_{k \ge 1} 1/k$ diverges, at $p = 1$, and
$\sum_{k \ge 1} 1/k^{2}$ converges, at $p = 2$.

**The index range is not cosmetic.** The series starts at $k = 1$ because
$1/0^{p}$ is undefined: [[def-rational-power]] gives $0^{p} = 0$ for rational
$p > 0$, and $0$ has no inverse. Sequences here are functions on $\mathbb{N}$ and
$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-series]]), so the object named above is a series
from the starting index $1$ in the sense of [[def-series]], not a series of a
sequence on $\mathbb{N}$.

**The exponent is rational, and that is a limitation of this page.** Rational
powers of a positive base are what [[def-rational-power]] supplies; real exponents
require the exponential and the logarithm, which this library develops later. The
statement above is therefore the full $p$-series theorem for every exponent this
page can name.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$ and positive mass on some bounded Borel subset of $D$. Give $D$ the relative norm topology and trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $\Phi,\Phi_N:D\to\mathbb R$ be finite continuous potentials indexed by integers $N\ge1$, let $M_1,M_2:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Borel and nondecreasing, and let $\psi_N\ge0$ satisfy $\psi_N\to0$. Suppose for every $u\in D$ and every $N$,
$$\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X),\qquad \Phi_N(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X),\qquad |\Phi_N(u)-\Phi(u)|\le M_2(\|u\|_X)\psi_N,$$
and
$$J:=\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\bigl(1+M_2(\|u\|_X)^2\bigr)\,\mu_0(du)<\infty.$$
Define the pointwise fixed-data evidences and posterior updates by
$$Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu_0(du),\quad \Pi(du):=Z^{-1}e^{-\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du),\qquad Z_N:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_N(u)}\,\mu_0(du),\quad \Pi_N(du):=Z_N^{-1}e^{-\Phi_N(u)}\mu_0(du).$$
Then $Z,Z_N$ are positive and finite, and there are $C<\infty$ and $N_0$ such that
$$h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N\qquad(N\ge N_0),$$
where $h$ is the library root-L2 Hellinger distance. This is a fixed-data assertion and makes no sampling-law or conditional-law version claim. In a separate branch, if AC is assumed for the library density/total-variation comparison convention, then $\|\Pi-\Pi_N\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N$, where $\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal B(D)}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $0<\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}<\infty$, so $c$ is finite and positive and [F7] makes $\mu_0$ a probability. Each singleton in $\mathbb R$ is closed, so the Borel sigma-algebra contains it and is closed under countable unions; hence $D$ is Borel. Every interval $(n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)$ intersects $D$ in the singleton $\{n\}$, so each singleton is open in $D$ and its relative topology is discrete. Since every subset of a discrete space is open, every real-valued function on $D$, including $\Phi,\Phi_N$, is continuous. The real line with its usual norm is a separable Banach space by [F6]. Thus all $\Phi,\Phi_N$ are finite continuous functions on $D$. They satisfy $\Phi,\Phi_N\ge0$ and $|\Phi_N(n)-\Phi(n)|=n/N=M_2(|n|)\psi_N$. But $\int_D e^{M_1(|u|)}(1+M_2(|u|)^2)\,\mu_0(du)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}(1+n^2)=+\infty,$ since the second summand contributes $c$ for each $n$. This is precisely the integrability hypothesis used by [F4], and it fails here.

The base evidence is $Z=1$. For each $N$, the approximate evidence $Z_N=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}e^{-n/N}$ is positive and at most one, so both posterior updates exist. Moreover $Z_N\to1$: given $\epsilon>0$, choose $m$ with $\sum_{n>m}c/n^2<\epsilon/2$ by [F3]. The finite sum $\sum_{n=1}^m(c/n^2)(1-e^{-n/N})$ tends to zero by continuity of the exponential [F5], while the remaining tail of $1-Z_N$ is at most $\sum_{n>m}c/n^2<\epsilon/2$.

Since $e^{-1}<1$, the number $\alpha:=(1+e^{-1})/2$ is less than one. From $Z_N\to1$, for all sufficiently large $N$ we have $Z_N\ge\alpha$. For $n\ge N$, $\frac{e^{-n/N}}{Z_N}\le\frac{e^{-1}}{\alpha}=\frac{2}{e+1}<1,$ so $1-\sqrt{e^{-n/N}/Z_N}\ge\kappa:=1-\sqrt{2/(e+1)}>0$.

The posterior density of the base law relative to $\mu_0$ is $1$, and that of the approximation is $e^{-n/N}/Z_N$. By [F2] and step 3.1, $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)^2=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{e^{-n/N}}{Z_N}}\right)^2\ge\kappa^2\sum_{n=N}^{2N-1}\frac{c}{n^2}\ge\frac{\kappa^2c}{4N},$ because the block has $N$ terms and each $n$ in it satisfies $n<2N$. Therefore $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\ge(\kappa\sqrt c/2)N^{-1/2}$, while $\psi_N=N^{-1}$. The ratio $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)/\psi_N$ is at least $(\kappa\sqrt c/2)\sqrt N$ and is unbounded, so the claimed $O(\psi_N)$ rate fails.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. For supplied finite-valued nonnegative measurable density representatives $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ in the convention of [[def-likelihood-density]], the **root-L2 Hellinger distance** is

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p > 0$. For a natural number $k \ge 1$ write
$\iota(k) = k \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the canonical natural, which is positive
([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and write $k^{p} := \iota(k)^{p}$ for its rational
power ([[def-rational-power]]). Then

$$\sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{k^{p}} \ \text{converges} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad p > 1 .$$

In particular the harmonic series $\sum_{k \ge 1} 1/k$ diverges, at $p = 1$, and
$\sum_{k \ge 1} 1/k^{2}$ converges, at $p = 2$.

**The index range is not cosmetic.** The series starts at $k = 1$ because
$1/0^{p}$ is undefined: [[def-rational-power]] gives $0^{p} = 0$ for rational
$p > 0$, and $0$ has no inverse. Sequences here are functions on $\mathbb{N}$ and
$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-series]]), so the object named above is a series
from the starting index $1$ in the sense of [[def-series]], not a series of a
sequence on $\mathbb{N}$.

**The exponent is rational, and that is a limitation of this page.** Rational
powers of a positive base are what [[def-rational-power]] supplies; real exponents
require the exponential and the logarithm, which this library develops later. The
statement above is therefore the full $p$-series theorem for every exponent this
page can name.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$ and positive mass on some bounded Borel subset of $D$. Give $D$ the relative norm topology and trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $\Phi,\Phi_N:D\to\mathbb R$ be finite continuous potentials indexed by integers $N\ge1$, let $M_1,M_2:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Borel and nondecreasing, and let $\psi_N\ge0$ satisfy $\psi_N\to0$. Suppose for every $u\in D$ and every $N$,
$$\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X),\qquad \Phi_N(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X),\qquad |\Phi_N(u)-\Phi(u)|\le M_2(\|u\|_X)\psi_N,$$
and
$$J:=\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\bigl(1+M_2(\|u\|_X)^2\bigr)\,\mu_0(du)<\infty.$$
Define the pointwise fixed-data evidences and posterior updates by
$$Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu_0(du),\quad \Pi(du):=Z^{-1}e^{-\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du),\qquad Z_N:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_N(u)}\,\mu_0(du),\quad \Pi_N(du):=Z_N^{-1}e^{-\Phi_N(u)}\mu_0(du).$$
Then $Z,Z_N$ are positive and finite, and there are $C<\infty$ and $N_0$ such that
$$h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N\qquad(N\ge N_0),$$
where $h$ is the library root-L2 Hellinger distance. This is a fixed-data assertion and makes no sampling-law or conditional-law version claim. In a separate branch, if AC is assumed for the library density/total-variation comparison convention, then $\|\Pi-\Pi_N\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N$, where $\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal B(D)}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $0<\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}<\infty$, so $c$ is finite and positive and [F7] makes $\mu_0$ a probability with $\mu_0(D)=1$. By [F6], $D$ is Borel and has the discrete relative topology, so every real-valued function on $D$, including $\Phi,\Phi_N$, is continuous. The real line with its usual norm is a separable Banach space by [F6]. Thus all $\Phi,\Phi_N$ are finite continuous functions on $D$. They satisfy $\Phi,\Phi_N\ge0$ and $|\Phi_N(n)-\Phi(n)|=n/N=M_2(|n|)\psi_N$. But $\int_D e^{M_1(|u|)}(1+M_2(|u|)^2)\,\mu_0(du)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}(1+n^2)=+\infty,$ since the second summand contributes $c$ for each $n$. This is precisely the integrability hypothesis used by [F4], and it fails here.

The base evidence is $Z=1$. For each $N$, the approximate evidence $Z_N=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}e^{-n/N}$ is positive and at most one, so both posterior updates exist. Moreover $Z_N\to1$: given $\epsilon>0$, choose $m$ with $\sum_{n>m}c/n^2<\epsilon/2$ by [F3]. The finite sum $\sum_{n=1}^m(c/n^2)(1-e^{-n/N})$ tends to zero by continuity of the exponential [F5], while the remaining tail of $1-Z_N$ is at most $\sum_{n>m}c/n^2<\epsilon/2$.

Since $e^{-1}<1$, the number $\alpha:=(1+e^{-1})/2$ is less than one. From $Z_N\to1$, for all sufficiently large $N$ we have $Z_N\ge\alpha$. For $n\ge N$, $\frac{e^{-n/N}}{Z_N}\le\frac{e^{-1}}{\alpha}=\frac{2}{e+1}<1,$ so $1-\sqrt{e^{-n/N}/Z_N}\ge\kappa:=1-\sqrt{2/(e+1)}>0$.

The posterior density of the base law relative to $\mu_0$ is $1$, and that of the approximation is $e^{-n/N}/Z_N$. By [F2] and step 3.1, $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)^2=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{e^{-n/N}}{Z_N}}\right)^2\ge\kappa^2\sum_{n=N}^{2N-1}\frac{c}{n^2}\ge\frac{\kappa^2c}{4N},$ because the block has $N$ terms and each $n$ in it satisfies $n<2N$. Therefore $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\ge(\kappa\sqrt c/2)N^{-1/2}$, while $\psi_N=N^{-1}$. The ratio $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)/\psi_N$ is at least $(\kappa\sqrt c/2)\sqrt N$ and is unbounded, so the claimed $O(\psi_N)$ rate fails.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $C$ and order it so the positive eigenvalues are $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. Let $U$ have the corresponding eigenvectors as columns and set $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)$. The zero eigenspace is the orthogonal complement of these columns, so $C=U\Lambda U^T$ and $\operatorname{Ran}(C)=\operatorname{Ran}(U)$. When $r=0$, the eigenbasis gives $C=0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TCv\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$X$ be a random vector with law $N_n(m,C)$, and define
$\mu_X(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. Write
$\operatorname{Ran}(C)=\{Cv:v\in\mathbb R^n\}$, and put
$r=\dim\operatorname{Ran}(C)$. For a Borel probability $\mu$ on
$\mathbb R^n$, define its topological support by
$$ \operatorname{supp}(\mu)=\{x:\mu(B(x,\varepsilon))>0\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}, $$
where $B(x,\varepsilon)$ is the open Euclidean ball. If $r>0$, there are
$U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$ and a symmetric positive-definite
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ with $U^TU=I_r$ such that
$$ C=U\Lambda U^T,\qquad \operatorname{Ran}(C)=\operatorname{Ran}(U),\qquad C^\dagger=U\Lambda^{-1}U^T. $$
Moreover, $X$ has the same law as $m+U\Lambda^{1/2}Z$, where
$Z\sim N_r(0,I_r)$, and
$$ \operatorname{supp}(\mu_X)=m+\operatorname{Ran}(C). $$
Here $C^\dagger$ is the unique matrix satisfying
$CC^\dagger C=C$, $C^\dagger CC^\dagger=C^\dagger$, and such that
$CC^\dagger$ and $C^\dagger C$ are symmetric. If $r=0$, then
$C=0$, $X=m$ almost surely, $C^\dagger=0$, and the support is $\{m\}$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
Rectangular matrix multiplication and the identity matrix $I_n$, including zero-sized shapes and
In orthonormal bases, the matrix of the adjoint is the conjugate transpose of the matrix.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. The **Tikhonov regularised
least-squares objective** is the map

$$ J_\lambda(x):=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb F^n), $$

where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm induced by the standard inner product
([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

The parameter $\lambda$ is part of the problem data. The second term penalises
large norms of $x$, so the regularised problem is not the same optimisation
problem as the unregularised least-squares problem.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume AC and let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$,

$r=\dim\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$. The $r$-dimensional Euclidean Lebesgue
measure on $S_0$ is the pushforward of Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^r$

posterior density with respect to this measure; for $r=0$, the unique point

satisfies
$$ C_0C_0^\dagger C_0=C_0,\qquad C_0^\dagger C_0C_0^\dagger=C_0^\dagger, $$

below is restricted to $S_0$. Then for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$, the unique

$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. The **Tikhonov regularised
least-squares objective** is the map

$$ J_\lambda(x):=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb F^n), $$

where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm induced by the standard inner product
([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

The parameter $\lambda$ is part of the problem data. The second term penalises
large norms of $x$, so the regularised problem is not the same optimisation
problem as the unregularised least-squares problem.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. $$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: Choose the norming family from [F3]. Fix $r>0$, $h\in E$, and $n\ge1$. Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Thus $a_n\perp\ker\Sigma_n$, so $a_n\in S_n:=\operatorname{ran}(\Sigma_n)$, the support subspace of $Y_n$.

In the finite-dimensional space $S_n$, the restriction of $Y_n$ is a nondegenerate Gaussian vector. Let $Q_n=[-r,r]^n$ and $D_n=Q_n\cap S_n$, a closed symmetric convex set. Since $a_n\in S_n$, the event $Y_n-a_n\in Q_n$ is the translate by $a_n$ of $D_n$ inside $S_n$. An invertible linear change of coordinates turns the centered law on $S_n$ into a nondegenerate Gaussian law and preserves symmetry and convexity of $D_n$. Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields
$$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$
If $S_n=\{0\}$, then $Y_n=a_n=0$ almost surely and the same inequality is equality.

Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. The sets $A_n(h)$ decrease with $n$, and [F3] gives $\bigcap_n A_n(h)=\{\|W-ih\|_B\le r\}$; likewise $\bigcap_n A_n(0)=\{\|W\|_B\le r\}$. Apply [F5] to both decreasing sequences and pass to their limits in the finite-dimensional inequalities. This proves the stated ball-mass bound.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: Choose the norming family from [F3]. Fix $r>0$, $h\in E$, and $n\ge1$. Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Thus $a_n\perp\ker\Sigma_n$, so $a_n\in S_n:=\operatorname{ran}(\Sigma_n)$, the support subspace of $Y_n$.

In the finite-dimensional space $S_n$, the restriction of $Y_n$ is a nondegenerate Gaussian vector. Let $Q_n=[-r,r]^n$ and $D_n=Q_n\cap S_n$, a closed symmetric convex set. Since $a_n\in S_n$, the event $Y_n-a_n\in Q_n$ is the translate by $a_n$ of $D_n$ inside $S_n$. An invertible linear change of coordinates turns the centered law on $S_n$ into a nondegenerate Gaussian law and preserves symmetry and convexity of $D_n$. Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields
$$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$
If $S_n=\{0\}$, then $Y_n=a_n=0$ almost surely and the same inequality is equality.

Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. The sets $A_n(h)$ decrease with $n$, and [F3] gives $\bigcap_n A_n(h)=\{\|W-ih\|_B\le r\}$; likewise $\bigcap_n A_n(0)=\{\|W\|_B\le r\}$. Apply [F5] to both decreasing sequences and pass to their limits in the finite-dimensional inequalities. This proves the stated ball-mass bound.

Statement: For h=0, both displayed ball probabilities are identical.

$$ \mu\bigl(\{x\in B:\|x-ih\|_B\le r\}\bigr)\le \mu\bigl(\{x\in B:\|x\|_B\le r\}\bigr). $$

Put $A_r=\overline B_B(0,r)$. By [F4], $\mu(A_r)>0$ because it contains the open ball of radius $r$ about the support point $0$. Let $(\ell_j)$ be the norming family from [F6], and define $A_{r,n}=\bigcap_{j\le n}\{|\ell_j(W)|\le r\}$. The sets decrease to $A_r$. For fixed $n$, the vector $(z_s,\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$ is centered Gaussian: [F3] makes $z_s$ an $L^2$ limit of continuous-linear Gaussian coordinates, so adjoining the finitely many displayed coordinates gives a centered Gaussian limit. Its law is invariant under simultaneous sign reversal, and $A_{r,n}$ is invariant under that reversal. Hence
$$ \mathbb E[e^{z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=\mathbb E[e^{-z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}], \qquad \mathbb E[z_s\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=0. $$
The variables $e^{\pm z_s}$ are integrable by the Gaussian moment formula in [F3]. Dominated convergence as $n\to\infty$ therefore gives conditional symmetry and conditional mean zero on $A_r$. Thus
$$ 1\le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mid A_r]\le e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}. $$
For the lower bound, conditional Jensen applies. For the upper bound, [F3] applied to $-s$ gives
$$ \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mathbf 1_{A_r}] =e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}\,\mu(\overline B_B(is,r)), $$
and [F5] bounds the last probability by $\mu(A_r)$.

For any $h\in E$, choose $\ell_n\in B^*$ with $h_n:=C\ell_n\to h$ in $E$, possible by the completion in [F2], and put $s_n=h-h_n$. The Cameron–Martin formula [F3], applied to the translate by $-h$, gives
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r))}{\mu(A_r)} =e^{-\|h\|_E^2/2}\,\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]. $$
Since $z_{h_n}=\ell_n(W)$ almost surely and $z_h=z_{h_n}+z_{s_n}$, the bound $|\ell_n(W)|\le r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}$ on $A_r$ and step 1.1 imply
$$ e^{-r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}} \le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r] \le e^{r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}}e^{\|s_n\|_E^2/2}. $$
For fixed $n$, let $r\downarrow0$; then let $n\to\infty$, so $\|s_n\|_E\to0$. The two bounds show $\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]\to1$.

Applying step 1.2 separately to $h_1$ and $h_2$ yields
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} =e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} \frac{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_1}}\mid A_r]}{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_2}}\mid A_r]}. $$
Both conditional expectations tend to $1$, so the ratio has the stated limit. Positivity of the denominator follows from [F4], since each closed ball contains the corresponding open neighborhood of a support point.

Put $A_r=\overline B_B(0,r)$. By [F4], $\mu(A_r)>0$ because it contains the open ball of radius $r$ about the support point $0$. Let $(\ell_j)$ be the norming family from [F6], and define $A_{r,n}=\bigcap_{j\le n}\{|\ell_j(W)|\le r\}$. The sets decrease to $A_r$. For fixed $n$, the vector $(z_s,\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$ is centered Gaussian: [F3] makes $z_s$ an $L^2$ limit of continuous-linear Gaussian coordinates, so adjoining the finitely many displayed coordinates gives a centered Gaussian limit. Its law is invariant under simultaneous sign reversal, and $A_{r,n}$ is invariant under that reversal. Hence
$$ \mathbb E[e^{z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=\mathbb E[e^{-z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}], \qquad \mathbb E[z_s\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=0. $$
The variables $e^{\pm z_s}$ are integrable by the Gaussian moment formula in [F3]. Dominated convergence as $n\to\infty$ therefore gives conditional symmetry and conditional mean zero on $A_r$. Thus
$$ 1\le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mid A_r]\le e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}. $$
For the lower bound, conditional Jensen applies. For the upper bound, [F3] applied to $-s$ gives
$$ \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mathbf 1_{A_r}] =e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}\,\mu(\overline B_B(is,r)), $$
and [F5] bounds the last probability by $\mu(A_r)$.

For any $h\in E$, choose $\ell_n\in B^*$ with $h_n:=C\ell_n\to h$ in $E$, possible by the completion in [F2], and put $s_n=h-h_n$. The Cameron–Martin formula [F3], applied to the translate by $-h$, gives
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r))}{\mu(A_r)} =e^{-\|h\|_E^2/2}\,\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]. $$
Since $z_{h_n}=\ell_n(W)$ almost surely and $z_h=z_{h_n}+z_{s_n}$, the bound $|\ell_n(W)|\le r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}$ on $A_r$ and step 1.1 imply
$$ e^{-r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}} \le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r] \le e^{r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}}e^{\|s_n\|_E^2/2}. $$
For fixed $n$, let $r\downarrow0$; then let $n\to\infty$, so $\|s_n\|_E\to0$. The two bounds show $\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]\to1$.

Applying step 1.2 separately to $h_1$ and $h_2$ yields
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} =e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} \frac{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_1}}\mid A_r]}{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_2}}\mid A_r]}. $$
Both conditional expectations tend to $1$, so the ratio has the stated limit. Positivity of the denominator follows from [F4], since each closed ball contains the corresponding open neighborhood of a support point.
