The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- A **separation** of $X$ is an ordered pair $(U, V)$ of **open**, **nonempty**,
  **disjoint** subsets of $X$ with $U \cup V = X$.
- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when
  none does.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **connected subset** of $X$ when the space
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is connected, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the subspace topology
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

Since $U$ and $V$ are complementary in $X$, each of them is closed as well as
open; so a separation is the same thing as a partition of $X$ into two nonempty
clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

**The empty space and the one-point space are connected in this library.**
Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to
those two spaces.

**Connectedness is a property of a space, not of an ambient pair.** The condition
above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is
regarded as a subspace of some other space inducing the same topology on $A$; in
particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). This is why "connected" may be used of a subset
with no ambient space named.

**Spelled out for a subset.** $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when there
are open $U, V \subseteq X$ with

$$A \subseteq U \cup V, \qquad U \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad V \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad U \cap V \cap A = \varnothing,$$

because the open sets of $(A,\mathcal{T}_A)$ are precisely the traces $U \cap A$.
Note the last condition: it asks $U$ and $V$ to be disjoint **on $A$**, not in
$X$. Requiring $U \cap V = \varnothing$ outright is a strictly stronger demand
and is a different notion.

**The two-point discrete space.** Write $\mathbf{2} := \{0,1\}$ with the discrete
topology ([[def-standard-topologies]]), in which every subset is open. A
separation of $X$ is the same datum as a surjective continuous map
$X \to \mathbf{2}$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]): given $(U,V)$, the map sending
$U$ to $0$ and $V$ to $1$ is continuous because the preimage of each of the four
open subsets of $\mathbf{2}$ is one of $\varnothing$, $U$, $V$, $X$; given a
surjective continuous $\chi : X \to \mathbf{2}$, the pair
$(\chi^{-1}[\{0\}], \chi^{-1}[\{1\}])$ is a separation. This reformulation is
proved as a theorem on this page and is recorded here only to name $\mathbf{2}$.

**Separated sets.** Two subsets $A_1, A_2 \subseteq X$ are **separated in $X$**
when

$$\overline{A_1} \cap A_2 = \varnothing \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_1 \cap \overline{A_2} = \varnothing,$$

closures taken in $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]],
[[thm-closure-characterisation-top]]). Separated sets are disjoint, since
$A_1 \subseteq \overline{A_1}$; the converse fails. This is verbatim the
condition [[def-connected-r]] uses on the real line, transported to an arbitrary
space, and the theorem relating it to the definition above is the next lemma on
this page.

**Totally disconnected spaces, and the empty case.** The vocabulary for a space
all of whose connected subsets are single points is fixed later on this page,
together with the components; it is not defined here because it is stated in
terms of components.

reals lies a rational.

and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is

derivations.claim: Let $B\Subset\Omega$ be any open ball and choose concentric balls $B\Subset B'\Subset B''\Subset\Omega$. By [F1] take $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B'')$ equal to one on $B'$, and extend $w:=\chi u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, every mollifier centered at a point of $B$ is supported in $B'$. For such a point $x$, differentiating the convolution gives $\partial_i(w*\rho_\varepsilon)(x)=-\int_{B'}u(y)\partial_{y_i}\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy=0$ by the distributional identity [F2]. Thus $w*\rho_\varepsilon$ is constant on the convex ball $B$ by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem along each segment.

Since $w=u$ on $B'$, the approximate-identity property [F4] gives $w*\rho_{\varepsilon_j}\to u$ in $L^1(B)$ for a sequence $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$. Write each constant from step 1.1 as $c_j$. The $L^1(B)$ convergence makes $(c_j)$ Cauchy because $|B||c_j-c_k|\le\|c_j-u\|_{L^1(B)}+\|c_k-u\|_{L^1(B)}$. Its limit $c_B$ satisfies $u=c_B$ almost everywhere on $B$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, any constant satisfies the conclusion. Otherwise fix one ball and let $c$ be its almost-everywhere value. Let $S$ be the set of points of $\Omega$ having a neighborhood on which $u=c$ almost everywhere. It is nonempty and open. If $x\in\overline S\cap\Omega$, choose a ball $B\Subset\Omega$ containing $x$ and a point of $S$; step 2.1 makes $u$ almost everywhere constant on $B$, and its positive-measure intersection with a neighborhood from $S$ forces that constant to be $c$. Thus $x\in S$, so $S$ is relatively closed. Connectedness [F5] gives $S=\Omega$. By the countable rational base [F6], choose a countable cover of $\Omega$ by rational balls contained in these neighborhoods; the union of their exceptional null sets is null, hence $u=c$ almost everywhere on all of $\Omega$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- A **separation** of $X$ is an ordered pair $(U, V)$ of **open**, **nonempty**,
  **disjoint** subsets of $X$ with $U \cup V = X$.
- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when
  none does.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **connected subset** of $X$ when the space
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is connected, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the subspace topology
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

Since $U$ and $V$ are complementary in $X$, each of them is closed as well as
open; so a separation is the same thing as a partition of $X$ into two nonempty
clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

**The empty space and the one-point space are connected in this library.**
Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to
those two spaces.

**Connectedness is a property of a space, not of an ambient pair.** The condition
above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is
regarded as a subspace of some other space inducing the same topology on $A$; in
particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). This is why "connected" may be used of a subset
with no ambient space named.

**Spelled out for a subset.** $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when there
are open $U, V \subseteq X$ with

$$A \subseteq U \cup V, \qquad U \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad V \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad U \cap V \cap A = \varnothing,$$

because the open sets of $(A,\mathcal{T}_A)$ are precisely the traces $U \cap A$.
Note the last condition: it asks $U$ and $V$ to be disjoint **on $A$**, not in
$X$. Requiring $U \cap V = \varnothing$ outright is a strictly stronger demand
and is a different notion.

**The two-point discrete space.** Write $\mathbf{2} := \{0,1\}$ with the discrete
topology ([[def-standard-topologies]]), in which every subset is open. A
separation of $X$ is the same datum as a surjective continuous map
$X \to \mathbf{2}$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]): given $(U,V)$, the map sending
$U$ to $0$ and $V$ to $1$ is continuous because the preimage of each of the four
open subsets of $\mathbf{2}$ is one of $\varnothing$, $U$, $V$, $X$; given a
surjective continuous $\chi : X \to \mathbf{2}$, the pair
$(\chi^{-1}[\{0\}], \chi^{-1}[\{1\}])$ is a separation. This reformulation is
proved as a theorem on this page and is recorded here only to name $\mathbf{2}$.

**Separated sets.** Two subsets $A_1, A_2 \subseteq X$ are **separated in $X$**
when

$$\overline{A_1} \cap A_2 = \varnothing \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_1 \cap \overline{A_2} = \varnothing,$$

closures taken in $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]],
[[thm-closure-characterisation-top]]). Separated sets are disjoint, since
$A_1 \subseteq \overline{A_1}$; the converse fails. This is verbatim the
condition [[def-connected-r]] uses on the real line, transported to an arbitrary
space, and the theorem relating it to the definition above is the next lemma on
this page.

**Totally disconnected spaces, and the empty case.** The vocabulary for a space
all of whose connected subsets are single points is fixed later on this page,
together with the components; it is not defined here because it is stated in
terms of components.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

derivations.claim: Let $B\Subset\Omega$ be any open ball and choose concentric balls $B\Subset B'\Subset B''\Subset\Omega$. By [F1] take $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B'')$ equal to one on $B'$, and extend $w:=\chi u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, every mollifier centered at a point of $B$ is supported in $B'$. For such a point $x$, differentiating the convolution gives $\partial_i(w*\rho_\varepsilon)(x)=-\int_{B'}u(y)\partial_{y_i}\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy=0$ by the distributional identity [F2]. Thus $w*\rho_\varepsilon$ is constant on the convex ball $B$ by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem along each segment.

Since $w=u$ on $B'$, the approximate-identity property [F4] gives $w*\rho_{\varepsilon_j}\to u$ in $L^1(B)$ for a sequence $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$. Write each constant from step 1.1 as $c_j$. The $L^1(B)$ convergence makes $(c_j)$ Cauchy because $|B||c_j-c_k|\le\|c_j-u\|_{L^1(B)}+\|c_k-u\|_{L^1(B)}$. Its limit $c_B$ satisfies $u=c_B$ almost everywhere on $B$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, any constant satisfies the conclusion. Otherwise fix one ball and let $c$ be its almost-everywhere value. Let $S$ be the set of points of $\Omega$ having a neighborhood on which $u=c$ almost everywhere. It is nonempty and open. If $x\in\overline S\cap\Omega$, choose a ball $B\Subset\Omega$ containing $x$ and a point of $S$; step 2.1 makes $u$ almost everywhere constant on $B$, and its positive-measure intersection with a neighborhood from $S$ forces that constant to be $c$. Thus $x\in S$, so $S$ is relatively closed. Connectedness [F5] gives $S=\Omega$. By the countable rational base [F6], choose a countable cover of $\Omega$ by rational balls contained in these neighborhoods; the union of their exceptional null sets is null, hence $u=c$ almost everywhere on all of $\Omega$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: For $\delta>0$, tile $\mathbb R^n$ by the half-open cubes $Q=\delta(z+[0,1)^n)$, $z\in\mathbb Z^n$, and let $A_\delta v$ equal $\delta^{-n}\int_Qv$ on $Q$. The triangle inequality, followed by [F1] and the substitution $y=x+h$ using [F2], gives $\|v-A_\delta v\|_1\le\delta^{-n}\sum_Q\int_Q\int_Q|v(x)-v(y)|\,dy\,dx\le\delta^{-n}\int_{[-\delta,\delta]^n}\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_1\,dh$. Thus, writing $\omega(r)=\sup_{k,|h|\le r}\|v_k(\cdot+h)-v_k\|_1$, one has $\sup_k\|v_k-A_\delta v_k\|_1\le2^n\omega(\sqrt n\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$.

For each $m\ge1$, only finitely many cubes of side $2^{-m}$ meet a fixed ball containing the common supports; all other cell averages vanish. Enumerate all these cells at all levels by first increasing $m$ and then lexicographic order of their integer coordinates. Each cell-average coefficient $a_j(k)$ is a bounded real sequence, with bound $M$ divided by that cell's volume. There is a deterministically defined nested sequence of infinite subsets $S_m\subseteq\mathbb N$. Set $S_0=\mathbb N$. At stage $m$, partition the bounded ranges of the first $m$ coefficients into finitely many half-open dyadic bins of width $2^{-m}$, adding an endpoint bin if necessary. Among the finitely many vector bins containing infinitely many indices in $S_{m-1}$, take the lexicographically first; let $S_m$ be exactly that infinite set of indices. The finite pigeonhole principle guarantees existence and the specified order gives uniqueness. Ordinary recursion therefore defines $(S_m)$ without an instance of dependent choice. Take $k_m$ to be the least member of $S_m$ larger than $k_{m-1}$. For fixed $j$ and $m\ge j$, all later indices lie in $S_m$, so their $j$th coefficients differ by at most $2^{-m}$. Consequently every coefficient converges and, at each fixed cell level $\ell$, $(A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_m})_m$ is Cauchy in $L^1$, being a finite weighted sum of these coefficients.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a cell level $\ell$ for which $2^n\omega(\sqrt n2^{-\ell})<\varepsilon/3$, using step 1.1. For sufficiently large $a,b$, step 1.2 gives $\|A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_a}-A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon/3$. The two approximation errors from step 1.1 then show $\|v_{k_a}-v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon$. Thus the subsequence is Cauchy.

For completeness at exactly the stated axiom strength, choose representatives of this countable sequence by [A1]. Select a further subsequence $g_j$ with $\|g_{j+1}-g_j\|_1<2^{-j}$, always choosing the least sufficiently late index, which exists by the Cauchy property. By [F1], $\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$ is integrable and finite almost everywhere. Hence $g_j$ has a measurable almost-everywhere limit $g$; moreover $|g|\le|g_1|+\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$, so $g\in L^1$, and $\|g-g_j\|_1\le\sum_{i\ge j}2^{-i}\to0$. The original Cauchy subsequence also converges to this $L^1$ class by the triangle inequality. This proves the assertion using only [A1].

boundaries.reason: The input is a sequence indexed by natural numbers, so an empty family is not an input. Empty common support is the zero-sequence case, covered by steps 1.1–3.1.

boundaries.evidence: If M=0 all sequence classes are zero. The coefficient ranges in step 1.2 consist only of0; their least occupied bins have infinitely many indices, and the constructed subsequence and limit are zero.
For n=1, step 1.1 tiles by half-open intervals and proves the same averaging estimate. Step 1.2 still has finitely many active intervals per level; no higher-dimensional argument is required.

All coefficient values may be equal or repeated. In step 1.2 at least one finite vector bin contains infinitely many indices, so the deterministic least-bin recursion still applies. Bounded common support may have measure zero, giving the zero case.

Step 1.1 uses half-open cells, so adjacent cell boundaries are assigned exactly once. Endpoint bin conventions in step 1.2 assign an extremal coefficient to a definite bin; no coefficient is omitted or divided by its value.

The nonempty sets S_m in step 1.2 are infinite by the finite pigeonhole principle; least qualifying bins and least later indices define ordinary recursion without DC. Only choosing countably many measurable L1 representatives in step 3.1 uses CC.

boundaries.reason: The Statement gives a sufficient condition for subsequence convergence, not a compactness equivalence. Steps 1.1–3.1 prove that sufficient direction directly.
No necessity claim for common bounded support or uniform translation control is asserted, and no metric compactness/sequential compactness equivalence is used.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). Each cell-average coefficient $a_j(k)$ is a bounded real sequence, with bound $M$ divided by that cell's volume. Set $S_0=\mathbb N$ and initialize $k_0=0$. Recursively, at stage $m\ge1$, partition the bounded ranges of the first $m$ coefficients into finitely many half-open dyadic bins of width $2^{-m}$, adding an endpoint bin if necessary. Among the finitely many vector bins containing infinitely many indices in $S_{m-1}$, take the lexicographically first; let $S_m$ be exactly that infinite set of indices. The finite pigeonhole principle guarantees existence and the specified order makes the rule unique. Then let $k_m$ be the least member of $S_m$ larger than $k_{m-1}$; such a member exists because $S_m$ is infinite.    continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

$$\mathcal H^n(B)=c_n\lambda_n(B)\quad(B\text{ Borel}),\qquad \mathcal H^n(A)=c_n\lambda_n^*(A)\quad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n).$$

Here $c_n=\mathcal H^n((0,1]^n)$ and $c_1=1$. For $n\ge2$ no exact identification of $c_n$ is proved here.

$$\mathcal H^s(f(A))=c^s\mathcal H^s(A).$$

This includes isometries and Euclidean translations and dilations. The Hausdorff outer value of a subset of a metric subspace equals its value computed in the ambient metric space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $f:D\subseteq X\to Y$ be an $L$-Lipschitz map between metric spaces and $A\subseteq D$. For finite $s\ge0$ and $L>0$,

$$\mathcal H^s(f(A))\le L^s\mathcal H^s(A).$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.

   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression

If $b$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $[a,d]$, extend it constantly past the endpoints. Its difference quotients are bounded by $L$ and converge to $b'$ almost everywhere by [F1]. For any $a\le s<t\le d$, dominated convergence gives $$\int_s^t b'(r)\,dr=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac1\epsilon\left(\int_t^{t+\epsilon}b(r)\,dr-\int_s^{s+\epsilon}b(r)\,dr\right)=b(t)-b(s).$$ Coordinate difference quotients of $h$ are measurable; [F1] and [F2] show their limits $g_i$ exist almost everywhere, with $|g_i|\le L$. Define them to be zero on the exceptional sets. Applying the preceding identity and one-dimensional integration by parts on each line, then [F2], gives $\int h\partial_i\eta=-\int g_i\eta$ for smooth compactly supported $\eta$. The same line identities hold for every coordinate line of $h$, outside the appropriate line-null exceptional set of derivatives.

For a cube $C$ of side $2r$ and a Lipschitz $w$, join $x$ to $y$ by the $m$ coordinate segments replacing their coordinates in order. Step 1.1 bounds $|w(x)-w(y)|$ by the sum of the line integrals of $|\partial_iw|$. Integrate in $x,y\in C$. For coordinate $i$, the unused coordinates contribute $(2r)^{m-1}$, while the measure of endpoint pairs whose interval contains a fixed coordinate value is at most $(2r)^2$. Thus, after division by $|C|$, the triangle inequality yields $$\int_C|w-w_C|\le 2r\sum_{i=1}^m\int_C|\partial_iw|,$$ where $w_C$ is its mean. Outside a null set, $g=(g_i)$ has strong Lebesgue points: apply [F3] to its coordinates and to $|g-q|$ for every rational vector $q$, then approximate $g(x)$ by such $q$. The countable union of the exceptional null sets is null under Countable Choice. Ball differentiation also gives cube differentiation by the fixed volume comparison. As $w(x)=0$ and $w$ has a fixed Lipschitz bound, a mean with $|w_C|\ge\epsilon r$ would give $|w-w_C|\ge\epsilon r/2$ on a cube of side proportional to $r$ centered at $x$, contradicting this estimate. Hence $\sup_{C(x,r/2)}|w|=o(r)$, proving differentiability with derivative $p$. Difference quotients then give $|p|\le L$. Countably many rational boxes cover $Q$, so the assertion is global.

We prove the area identity first for bounded Borel base sets within one $L$-Lipschitz box. On the differentiability set, for any $0<\epsilon<1/4$, form countably many Borel pieces on each of which $Dh$ lies within $\epsilon$ of a fixed rational vector $p$, the differentiability remainder is at most $\epsilon|z-y|$ whenever $|z-y|<1/k$, and the points lie in one cube of diameter less than $1/k$. Such pieces cover the differentiability set: the remainder condition follows from differentiability, can be tested on countably many rational $z$ by continuity, and is measurable; use increasing integers $k$ and a rational-vector enumeration. Subtract earlier pieces to make them disjoint. For two points $y,z$ of a single piece $E$, set $A_pv=(v,p\cdot v)$. Then $|F(z)-F(y)-A_p(z-y)|\le2\epsilon|z-y|\le2\epsilon|A_p(z-y)|$. Consequently $F\circ A_p^{-1}:A_p(E)\to F(E)$ is at most $(1+2\epsilon)$-Lipschitz, and its inverse is at most $(1-2\epsilon)^{-1}$-Lipschitz. The sets $F(E)$ are Borel because $F$ is a homeomorphism from $Q$ onto its graph.

Choose an orthonormal coordinate system on the range plane of $A_p$. Its square coordinate matrix has determinant of absolute value $J_p=\sqrt{\det(A_p^TA_p)}=\sqrt{1+|p|^2}$. Thus [F4] gives $\sigma_m(A_p(E))=J_p|E|$. The excluded base-null set has graph image of zero $\sigma_m$ by [F4], since $F$ is Lipschitz. Sum the displayed inequalities over the disjoint pieces, using $|p|\le L+\epsilon$. The difference between $\sigma_m(F(B))$ and $\int_B\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ is bounded by $C_{m,L}\epsilon|B|$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves equality. Exhaustion and countable localization extend it to arbitrary Borel $B\subseteq Q$; indicator functions, simple functions and monotone convergence prove the asserted integral formula.

For a compactly supported smooth scalar $b$ in the chart, vertical integration gives $\int_G\partial_zb=-\int_Qb(y,h(y))\,dy$. For a horizontal coordinate put $B_i(y)=\int_{h(y)}^\infty b(y,z)\,dz$. This is Lipschitz and compactly supported in $Q$; step 2.1 and ordinary differentiation of the smooth integral give $\partial_iB_i=\int_{h(y)}^\infty\partial_i b\,dz-b(y,h(y))g_i$ almost everywhere. Its weak derivative integrates to zero by step 1.1 and [F2]. Apply these identities to the components of $\phi$ and sum. Step 4.1 converts the resulting flux into the unit-normal formula. The graph measure is a graph pushforward of the locally bounded measurable density $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}\,dy$; compact and open approximation in the base show it is locally Radon on the graph with its relative topology. The density is between $1$ and $\sqrt{1+L^2}$ on every local box, which also proves the null-set assertion.

**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Every bounded real linear functional $L$ on $C_0(X;\mathbb R)$ can be written $L=L^+-L^-$, where $L^+$ and $L^-$ are bounded positive linear functionals and $\|L^\pm\|\le\|L\|$.
Every Borel subset of a metric space is Carathéodory measurable for every metric outer measure.
For an outer measure $\mu^*$ on $X$, the Carathéodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. If two finite signed Radon measures on $\Omega$ have the same integrals against every function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then the measures are equal.

derivations.claim: First let $P$ be bounded and positive. For relatively open $G\subseteq U$ put $p(G)=\sup\{P(f):f\in C_c(U),\ 0\le f\le1,\ \operatorname{supp}f\subseteq G\}$. Then $0\le p(G)\le\|P\|$, $p(\varnothing)=0$, and $p$ is monotone. If a compact $K$ is covered by open sets $G_j$, finitely many suffice, and there are continuous nonnegative compactly supported functions $b_1,\ldots,b_N$, each supported in one of these sets, whose sum is positive on $K$. Indeed cover $K$ by finitely many balls with doubled closures compactly contained in the relevant $G_j$ and use distance cutoffs on these balls. On a neighborhood of $K$ normalize the $b_i$ by their sum. Thus any $f$ supported on $K$ with $0\le f\le1$ decomposes into finitely many $f_i\ge0$ with $\sum f_i=f$ and each $f_i\le1$ compactly supported in its assigned $G_j$; combine terms assigned to the same $j$. Consequently $p(\bigcup_jG_j)\le\sum_jp(G_j)$. For pairwise disjoint opens, adding finitely many admissible functions gives the reverse inequality for every finite partial sum, so $p$ is countably additive on disjoint open unions. These compact partitions use only finite choices.

Define $\mu^*(A)=\inf\{p(G):A\subseteq G\subseteq U,\ G\text{ open}\}$. For a sequence $(A_j)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [A1] selects open $G_j\supseteq A_j$ with $p(G_j)<\mu^*(A_j)+\varepsilon2^{-j}$; step 1.1 proves countable subadditivity. Zero and monotonicity are immediate, so $\mu^*$ is an outer measure, and $\mu^*(G)=p(G)$ for open $G$. If $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V,W$ in $U$. Every open $G\supseteq A\cup B$ satisfies $p(G)\ge p(G\cap V)+p(G\cap W)\ge\mu^*(A)+\mu^*(B)$, by step 1.1. Taking the infimum and using subadditivity proves the metric condition. By [F2], restriction to Borel sets is a finite measure $\mu$ with $\mu(U)\le\|P\|$.

For an admissible $f$ in the definition of $p(G)$, let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. Every open $V\supseteq K$ admits $f$, hence $\mu(K)=\inf_{V\supseteq K}p(V)\ge P(f)$. Taking the supremum over $f$ proves $\mu(G)=\sup_{K\subseteq G\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$. Outer regularity on every Borel set is the definition of $\mu^*$. Finiteness gives compact inner regularity on every Borel set as well: given Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose compact $H\subseteq U$ with $\mu(U\setminus H)<\varepsilon$ and open $V\supseteq U\setminus A$ with $\mu(V\setminus(U\setminus A))<\varepsilon$. Then $H\setminus V\subseteq A$ is compact and misses at most $2\varepsilon$ of $\mu(A)$. Thus $\mu$ is finite Radon, including regularity on all Borel sets.

If $0\le g\in C_c(U)$ and $g\le\mathbf1_K$ for compact $K$, the argument in step 3.1 gives $P(g)\le\mu(K)$. If instead $g\ge\mathbf1_K$, then for $0<\eta<1$, the open set $G_\eta=\{g>1-\eta\}$ contains $K$ and every admissible $f$ for $p(G_\eta)$ satisfies $f\le g/(1-\eta)$ on all of $U$. Positivity yields $\mu(K)\le p(G_\eta)\le P(g)/(1-\eta)$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $\mu(K)\le P(g)$.

Fix $0\le f\in C_c(U)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, take $N$ with $N\varepsilon\ge\|f\|_\infty$, and put $f_j=\min(\varepsilon,(f-(j-1)\varepsilon)_+)$, $K_0=\operatorname{supp}f$, $K_j=\{f\ge j\varepsilon\}$ for $1\le j\le N$. The sum of the $f_j$ is $f$, and $\varepsilon\mathbf1_{K_j}\le f_j\le\varepsilon\mathbf1_{K_{j-1}}$. Step 4.1 gives the same lower and upper bounds $\varepsilon\mu(K_j)$ and $\varepsilon\mu(K_{j-1})$ for $P(f_j)$ as for $\int f_j\,d\mu$. Summing and telescoping gives $|P(f)-\int f\,d\mu|\le\varepsilon\mu(K_0)$. Hence equality holds for $f\ge0$, then for every real $f\in C_c(U)$ by positive and negative parts. Uniform density [F3], boundedness of $P$, and finiteness of $\mu$ extend the identity to $C_0(U)$.

Apply [F1] to $L=P-Q$ and the preceding construction to $P,Q$, obtaining finite positive Radon measures $\alpha,\beta$. Their difference $\sigma=\alpha-\beta$ represents $L$. Its total variation is dominated by $\alpha+\beta$, hence is regular by compact and open approximation with that finite positive Radon measure. Uniqueness follows from [F3]. All countable selections were the open near-minimizers in step 2.1; all other constructions were explicit or involved finitely many choices.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff and let $f:X\to\mathbb F$ be continuous,
where $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x:f(x)\ne0\}}$. Put
$C_c(X;\mathbb F)=\{f\in C(X;\mathbb F):\operatorname{supp}f\text{ is compact}\}$.
Also $C_0(X;\mathbb F)$ consists of those $f$ for which, for every $\epsilon>0$,
$\{x:|f(x)|\ge\epsilon\}$ is compact. We write $C_c(X)$ for the real space
until the bounded complex $C_0$ theorem is invoked; $C_0(X)$ later means the
complex space when its scalar field matters.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(U;\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure. No Dependent Choice assumption is required.

derivations.claim: Suppose $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and write $\mu=Du$. The distributional derivative identity gives $\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx=-\int_\Omega\varphi\cdot d\mu$. The continuous-field dual formula [F2] bounds the supremum over smooth fields by $|\mu|(\Omega)$. Conversely, for any $f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ with $|f|\le1$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, density [F3] gives one smooth compactly supported $g$ with $\|g-f\|_\infty<\varepsilon$; replacing $g$ by $g/\max(1,\|g\|_\infty)$ keeps the unit bound and changes this error by at most another $\varepsilon$. Finiteness of the coordinate measures bounds the integral error by a fixed constant times $\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ (without selecting a sequence of approximants) shows that the smooth supremum is at least the continuous-field supremum $|\mu|(\Omega)$. Thus $V(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

Assume [A1], let real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$, and suppose $M:=V(u)<\infty$. For each coordinate $i$, define $L_i(\psi):=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\psi\,dx$ on real $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Taking the test vector with only its $i$th component equal to $\psi$ and also its negative shows $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. By density [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on real $C_0(\Omega)$. Apply [F4] directly to this real functional to obtain a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$ representing $D_i u$. Applying [F2] to $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)$ and using [F3] to pass between continuous and smooth unit fields gives $|\mu|(\Omega)=M$. Hence $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)=M$.

If the $L^1$ limit $u$ is already in $BV(\Omega)$, boundedness of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$ gives $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_k\int u_k\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ for each admissible $\varphi$. Each approximating integral is at most $TV(u_k;\Omega)$ by step 1.1, so taking the supremum gives $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$; this branch uses no choice axiom.

If only $L:=\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)<\infty$ is known, choose a subsequence whose variations converge to $L$. The same test-integral limit gives $V(u)\le L$. Under [A1], step 1.2 implies $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)=V(u)\le L$. If $L=+\infty$, the extended inequality is automatic.

boundaries.evidence: For Omega=empty, test integrals, derivative measures and both variation values are zero. Steps 1.1–1.2 and2.1–3.1 remain valid in the zero L1/C0 spaces.

If the test supremum M=0, every coordinate functional L_i in step 1.2 is zero, so its representing measure is zero. The already-BV formula in step 1.1 also includes Du=0 without normalization by its mass.

For n=1 the vector test has a single scalar component. The coordinate extension and real Radon representation in step 1.2 then require only one finite signed measure; all later inequalities are unchanged.

Step 3.1 distinguishes finite liminf L, which implies BV membership under CC, from L=+infinity, which gives only the automatic extended inequality. It does not incorrectly infer finite variation of an arbitrary infinite-liminf limit.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 takes one smooth approximant for each fixed epsilon and then lets epsilon tend to0, preserving the choice-free already-BV formula. Step 1.2 invokes the explicitly CC real Euclidean Radon supplier; no general DC Riesz theorem is used. Subsequence indices in step 3.1 exist by the finite-liminf condition.

For the same characterization, finite V on arbitrary L1 yields bounded coordinate functionals and finite signed Radon derivatives by the CC real representation theorem in step 1.2; equality to vector variation is then established there.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere, its partial derivatives are measurable and are its weak derivatives. On every open region where $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $|Dh|\le L$ almost everywhere. Let $H^m$ denote the repository's unnormalised Hausdorff measure, put $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$, and write $\sigma_m=c_m^{-1}H^m$ also on Euclidean spaces containing $m$-dimensional subsets. The graph map $F(y)=(y,h(y))$ satisfies, for every nonnegative Borel $a$,
$$\int_{F(Q)}a(x)\,d\sigma_m(x)=\int_Qa(F(y))\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}\,dy.$$
For the epigraph $G=\{(y,z):y\in Q,\ z>h(y)\}$, a smooth vector field compactly supported away from the chart sides satisfies
$$\int_G\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_Q\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
Thus its outward normal is $(Dh,-1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ almost everywhere. The sign reverses for a subgraph. The graph surface measure is locally finite and Radon on $F(Q)$ with its relative topology, and its null sets coincide with graph images of Lebesgue-null subsets of the base.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In a graph cylinder $Q\times(a,b)$ with $h\in C^1(Q)$ and $a<h<b$, suppose $\Omega$ locally is $z<h(y)$ and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ is localized with support compactly contained in the cylinder. Then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\int_Q(F_n(y,h(y))-\sum_{i<n}F_i(y,h(y))\partial_i h(y))\,dy$. An interior compactly supported C1 vector field has integral divergence zero.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

If an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is covered by a countable family of open sets $(V_\ell)_{\ell\in I}$, then there is a countable locally finite family of nonnegative functions $(\eta_j)\subset C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ summing to one, with each $\operatorname{supp}\eta_j$ contained in one member $V_\ell$ of the cover. Locally finite means that each point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many supports.

Let $X$ be a locally compact second-countable metric space, let $\lambda$ be a finite positive Radon measure on $X$, and let $
u:X	o\mathbb R^m$ be continuous with $|
u(x)|=1$ for every $x$. Define the vector measure $\mu(A):=\int_A
u\,d\lambda$ on Borel sets. Its partition variation satisfies $|\mu|=\lambda$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The balls with rational centers and radii whose closures lie in $\Omega$ and on which some $\partial_i u$ never vanishes form a countable open cover of $G$ by density and countability [F5]; assign each ball the least such coordinate $i$. Each ball is convex. The map $T_i(x)=(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},u(x),x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n)$ has nonzero Jacobian there; it is injective because along each line parallel to the $i$th axis, $u$ is strictly monotone. Thus [F2] makes it a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its open image. By [F6], choose a locally finite smooth partition of unity $(\eta_j)$ on $G$ subordinate to these chart balls. On a ball assigned coordinate $i$, write $y=x_{\widehat i}$ and $t=u(x)$; the inverse chart has graph form $x_i=h(y,t)$, with $|\det DT_i|=|\partial_i u|$ and $$\sqrt{1+|D_yh|^2}= rac{|
abla u|}{|\partial_i u|}$$ by implicit differentiation. Change of variables [F2] and the surface density [F3], applied to the compactly supported nonnegative weight $\eta_j$, give $$\int_G\eta_j|
abla u|\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{G\cap\{u=t\}}\eta_j\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}\,dt.$$

Sum the chart identities of step 1.1 over $j$. Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ on $G$, Tonelli [F8] gives $$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathcal H^{n-1}(G\cap\{u=t\})\,dt,$$ because $\nabla u=0$ on $\Omega\setminus G$. Sard's theorem [F1] says that outside a null set every point of a level is regular, so the integrand agrees almost everywhere in $t$ with $\mathcal H^{n-1}(\Omega\cap\{u=t\})$. This also establishes measurability of the level-area function as a countable sum of the chart integrals in step 1.1.

Fix a nonzero regular value $t$ for which the area in step 2.1 is finite; throughout the proof $\mathcal H^{n-1}$ denotes the normalized graph measure from [F3], with counting measure if $n=1$. In that case every graph chart is a single point at fixed level, its empty-coordinate Jacobian is one, and the same substitution identity in step 1.1 is the ordinary one-dimensional substitution formula. Then $\Gamma_t:=\Omega\cap\{u=t\}$ is a smooth hypersurface. For a compactly supported smooth test field $\phi$, its intersection with $\Gamma_t$ is compact; local finiteness gives a neighborhood meeting only finitely many chart supports, whose partition sum is one there. Decompose $\phi$ into the finite chart-supported sum and a remainder vanishing near $\Gamma_t$. The remainder has zero divergence integral over either level set because its restriction to that open set extends as a compactly supported smooth field. Each chart term obeys the graph flux formula [F4]. Summing shows that $D\chi_{E_t^+}=+(
abla u/|
abla u|)\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\Gamma_t}$ and $D\chi_{E_t^-}=-(
abla u/|
abla u|)\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\Gamma_t}$. The level $\Gamma_t$ is relatively closed in $\Omega$; hence this measure is finite and Radon by the graph area construction [F3], and [F7] gives its partition variation as exactly $\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\Gamma_t}$. Hence the indicator is BV and its perimeter equals that area. For $t>0$ and $t<0$, respectively, Markov's inequality gives $|E_t^+|\le t^{-1}\|u\|_1$ and $|E_t^-|\le|t|^{-1}\|u\|_1$, so the indicators are in $L^1$. The area integral is finite, so almost every applicable nonzero level is regular and has finite area by step 2.1; the required perimeter equality and almost-everywhere finiteness follow.

For a constant smooth u, gradient is0 and G is empty. Its single possible critical value is excluded by the almost-everywhere assertion in step 2.1; all remaining signed levels have relative perimeter0 in step 3.1.

Step 3.1 explicitly explains n=1: fixed-level charts are points, the empty-coordinate Jacobian is1, and normalized H0 is counting measure. The substitution used in step 1.1 is then one-dimensional substitution.

Critical points/values are handled by G in step 1.1 and Sard in step 2.1. Only regular nonzero levels of finite area are used in step 3.1; infinite-area or critical exceptional levels need no finite-perimeter conclusion.

Step 3.1 uses t>0 or t<0 for the Markov finite-measure bound and excludes t=0. Perimeters are relative to Omega; the divergence remainder vanishing near the level hypersurface contributes zero and no artificial boundary of Omega is added.

Step 1.1 uses a countable rational-ball cover and the least coordinate with nonvanishing derivative, then the explicit locally finite partition supplier. It does not select arbitrary charts for every real level. CC accounts for integration/chart suppliers, while the published Sard theorem is choice-free.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere, its partial derivatives are measurable and are its weak derivatives. On every open region where $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $|Dh|\le L$ almost everywhere. Let $H^m$ denote the repository's unnormalised Hausdorff measure, put $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$, and write $\sigma_m=c_m^{-1}H^m$ also on Euclidean spaces containing $m$-dimensional subsets. The graph map $F(y)=(y,h(y))$ satisfies, for every nonnegative Borel $a$,
$$\int_{F(Q)}a(x)\,d\sigma_m(x)=\int_Qa(F(y))\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}\,dy.$$
For the epigraph $G=\{(y,z):y\in Q,\ z>h(y)\}$, a smooth vector field compactly supported away from the chart sides satisfies
$$\int_G\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_Q\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
Thus its outward normal is $(Dh,-1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ almost everywhere. The sign reverses for a subgraph. The graph surface measure is locally finite and Radon on $F(Q)$ with its relative topology, and its null sets coincide with graph images of Lebesgue-null subsets of the base.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In a graph cylinder $Q\times(a,b)$ with $h\in C^1(Q)$ and $a<h<b$, suppose $\Omega$ locally is $z<h(y)$ and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ is localized with support compactly contained in the cylinder. Then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\int_Q(F_n(y,h(y))-\sum_{i<n}F_i(y,h(y))\partial_i h(y))\,dy$. An interior compactly supported C1 vector field has integral divergence zero.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

If an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is covered by a countable family of open sets $(V_\ell)_{\ell\in I}$, then there is a countable locally finite family of nonnegative functions $(\eta_j)\subset C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ summing to one, with each $\operatorname{supp}\eta_j$ contained in one member $V_\ell$ of the cover. Locally finite means that each point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many supports.

Let $X$ be a locally compact second-countable metric space, let $\lambda$ be a finite positive Radon measure on $X$, and let $
u:X	o\mathbb R^m$ be continuous with $|
u(x)|=1$ for every $x$. Define the vector measure $\mu(A):=\int_A
u\,d\lambda$ on Borel sets. Its partition variation satisfies $|\mu|=\lambda$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ on $G$, Tonelli [F8] gives $$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathcal H^{n-1}(G\cap\{u=t\})\,dt,$$ because $\nabla u=0$ on $\Omega\setminus G$. Sard's theorem [F1] says that outside a null set every point of a level is regular, so the integrand agrees almost everywhere in $t$ with $\mathcal H^{n-1}(\Omega\cap\{u=t\})$. This also establishes measurability of the level-area function as a countable sum of the chart integrals in step 1.1.

Fix a nonzero regular value $t$ for which the area in step 2.1 is finite; throughout the proof $\mathcal H^{n-1}$ denotes the normalized graph measure from [F3], with counting measure if $n=1$. In that case every graph chart is a single point at fixed level, its empty-coordinate Jacobian is one, and the same substitution identity in step 1.1 is the ordinary one-dimensional substitution formula. Then $\Gamma_t:=\Omega\cap\{u=t\}$ is a smooth hypersurface. For a compactly supported smooth test field $\phi$, its intersection with $\Gamma_t$ is compact; local finiteness gives a neighborhood meeting only finitely many chart supports, whose partition sum is one there. Decompose $\phi$ into the finite chart-supported sum and a remainder vanishing near $\Gamma_t$. The remainder has zero divergence integral over either level set because its restriction to that open set extends as a compactly supported smooth field. Each chart term obeys the graph flux formula [F4]. Summing shows that $D\chi_{E_t^+}=+(
abla u/|
abla u|)\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\Gamma_t}$ and $D\chi_{E_t^-}=-(
abla u/|
abla u|)\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\Gamma_t}$. The level $\Gamma_t$ is relatively closed in $\Omega$; hence this measure is finite and Radon by the graph area construction [F3], and [F7] gives its partition variation as exactly $\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\Gamma_t}$. Hence the indicator is BV and its perimeter equals that area. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n\ge1$ and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb R^n$ is a Radon measure, and it is regular in the stronger
compact-inner-regular-on-all-Borel-sets convention.

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

If an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is covered by a countable family of open sets $(V_\ell)_{\ell\in I}$, then there is a countable locally finite family of nonnegative functions $(\eta_j)\subset C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ summing to one, with each $\operatorname{supp}\eta_j$ contained in one member $V_\ell$ of the cover. Locally finite means that each point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many supports.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: By [F6], take a countable locally finite nonnegative smooth partition of unity $(\eta_j)$ on $\Omega$, with each $\eta_j$ compactly supported in $\Omega$.

Extend each $w_j:=\eta_j u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. Fix a nonnegative unit-mass smooth bump $ho$ and its rescalings $ho_\varepsilon$. For each $j$, the approximate-identity property [F2] gives $w_j*ho_\varepsilon	o w_j$ in $L^1$, and also $(u
abla\eta_j)*ho_\varepsilon	o u
abla\eta_j$ in $L^1$. Choose the least nonnegative integer $m_j$ for which $\varepsilon_j:=2^{-m_j}$ is small enough that $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$, the convolution supports remain in $\Omega$, and $\|w_j*ho_{\varepsilon_j}-w_j\|_1+\|(u
abla\eta_j)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}-u
abla\eta_j\|_1<2^{-j}\delta$. Set $u_\delta:=\sum_j w_j*ho_{\varepsilon_j}$. This sum is locally finite: for a compact $C\Subset\Omega$, choose $r>0$ so its closed $r$-neighborhood $C_r$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $\varepsilon_j<r$; if the thickened support of $w_j$ meets $C$, then $\operatorname{supp}\eta_j$ meets $C_r$, and local finiteness of $(\eta_j)$ leaves only finitely many such indices. Thus $u_\delta$ is smooth by [F3]. Summing the first error terms and using $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ gives $\|u_\delta-u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The product rule follows by testing against $C_c^\infty$: $D(\eta_j u)=\eta_jDu+u
abla\eta_j\,dx$. Convolution commutes with distributional derivatives by the defining test pairing and Fubini [F4]. Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$, local finiteness gives $\sum_j u
abla\eta_j=0$. Therefore $
abla u_\delta=\sum_j (\eta_jDu)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}+\sum_j ig((u
abla\eta_j)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}-u
abla\eta_j ig)$. For the first sum, $| (\eta_jDu)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}|\le(\eta_j|Du|)*ho_{\varepsilon_j}$ pointwise, so Tonelli and $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ bound its $L^1$ norm by $|Du|(\Omega)$. The second sum has $L^1$ norm below $\delta$ by the choices in step 2.1. Hence $\int_\Omega|
abla u_\delta|\,dx\le TV(u;\Omega)+\delta$.

Take $\delta_k=1/k$ and set $u_k=u_{\delta_k}$. Step 2.1 gives $u_k\to u$ in $L^1$, while step 3.1 gives $\limsup_k\int_\Omega|\nabla u_k|\,dx\le TV(u;\Omega)$. The choice-free lower-semicontinuity clause of [F5], applied to $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$, gives the reverse inequality. Thus the variations converge. For $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$, choose a smooth cutoff $\chi_R$ equal to one on $B(0,R)$, supported in $B(0,2R)$, and satisfying $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$, using [F7]. Since each $u_{1/(2k)}$ and its gradient are integrable, choose $R_k$ so its $L^1$ tail, gradient tail, and $C\|u_{1/(2k)}\|_1/R_k$ are all below $1/k$. The products $\chi_{R_k}u_{1/(2k)}$ are compactly supported and smooth, converge to $u$ in $L^1$, and have gradient integrals bounded above by $TV(u;\mathbb R^n)+O(1/k)$; lower semicontinuity gives convergence of their variations as well.

boundaries.evidence: If Omega=empty, the partition of unity from F6 is the empty family; the sum in step 2.1 is the zero smooth function and all approximation/variation errors in steps 3.1–4.1 are zero.
For u=0 each w_j and error term in steps 2.1–3.1 is zero. Taking zero approximants gives L1 and variation convergence, including compact support in full space.
Dimension n=1 uses the same locally finite compact-support partition and scalar derivative convolution in steps 1.1–3.1; no n>=2 Sobolev or graph-area claim is needed.
TV(u)=0 is allowed. Step 3.1 bounds the gradient integral by delta, and step 4.1 gives convergence to0. The normalizing/cutoff radii never divide by TV(u).

On a proper open Omega the approximants in the Statement are C-infinity(Omega), not compactly supported there; step 2.1 keeps each localized convolution inside Omega. Compact support is imposed only for full-space approximants by the large-radius cutoff in step 4.1.

Step 1.1 invokes the explicit countable locally finite partition supplier. For each j and delta, step 2.1 chooses the least qualifying dyadic exponent from a nonempty set guaranteed by the actual CC L1 approximate-identity convergence theorem. Step 4.1 takes the fixed sequence delta_k=1/k and finite cutoff radii.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is an approximation existence theorem, not an iff. Steps 2.1–4.1 establish both required convergences for its constructed sequence.
No converse assertion that existence of arbitrary smooth approximants implies BV membership is made here; that separate characterization belongs to the test-field supplier.
