sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

  introduced.**

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits

  introduced.**

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $0<\rho<1$ and $\tau>0$. In real scalar expressions, a natural number denotes its canonical real image. Use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, identifying coordinate label $j$ with library coordinate $j-1$. For $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and $S\subseteq[n]$, let $h_S$ agree with $h$ on $S$ and vanish on $S^c=[n]\setminus S$. The matrix $A$ satisfies the **$\ell^2$ robust nullspace property of order $s$ with constants $(\rho,\tau)$** if
$$\|h_S\|_2\le \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$. This condition applies to all vectors, including vectors with $Ah\ne0$.

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Use one-based labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, identifying label $j$ with library coordinate $j-1$. For $T\subseteq[n]$, let $x_{T^c}$ retain the coordinates outside $T$ and vanish on $T$, where $T^c=[n]\setminus T$. Define the best $s$-term $\ell^1$ approximation error by
$$\sigma_s(x)_1:=\min\{\|x_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}.$$
The indexing family is finite and nonempty, so the displayed minimum exists and is attained.

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$ use the one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. Order the coordinates by decreasing $|x_j|$, breaking ties by increasing $j$, and let $S$ be the first $s$ indices. For every $U\subseteq[n]$, let $x_U$ agree with $x$ on $U$ and vanish on $U^c$. Then for every $T\subseteq[n]$ with $|T|\le s$,
$$\|x_T\|_1\le\|x_S\|_1\quad\text{and}\quad\|x_{S^c}\|_1\le\|x_{T^c}\|_1.$$
Consequently $\sigma_s(x)_1=\|x_{S^c}\|_1$, so the best $s$-term tail error is attained by retaining the first $s$ coordinates in the specified order.

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$. Use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$, and interpret natural numbers in real scalar expressions as their canonical real images. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and suppose that for some $0<\rho<1$ and $\tau>0$,
$$\|h_S\|_2\le\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, where for any vector $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $v_S$ agrees with $v$ on $S$ and vanishes on $S^c=[n]\setminus S$. Let $x^\dagger\in\mathbb R^n$, $\epsilon\ge0$, and $e\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfy $y=Ax^\dagger+e$ and $\|e\|_2\le\epsilon$. Define
$$\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1:=\min\{\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}.$$
The indexing family is finite and nonempty, so this minimum is attained; it also equals the minimum of $\|x^\dagger-z\|_1$ over vectors $z$ with at most $s$ nonzero coordinates. Then the basis-pursuit denoising problem
$$\min_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\|z\|_1\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|Az-y\|_2\le\epsilon$$
has a minimizer. Every minimizer $\widehat x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_2\le C_1\frac{\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1}{\sqrt{s}}+C_2\epsilon,\qquad \|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_1\le C_3\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1+C_4\sqrt{s}\,\epsilon,$$
where
$$C_1=\frac{2(1+2\rho)}{1-\rho},\quad C_2=\frac{6\tau}{1-\rho},\quad C_3=\frac{2(1+\rho)}{1-\rho},\quad C_4=\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}.$$
If the certified finite basis-pursuit denoising procedure returns **success**, its returned vector is a minimizer and satisfies these same bounds. Only reconstruction error is bounded; the theorem asserts neither uniqueness nor support recovery.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $0<\rho<1$ and $\tau>0$. In real scalar expressions, a natural number denotes its canonical real image. Use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, identifying coordinate label $j$ with library coordinate $j-1$. For $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and $S\subseteq[n]$, let $h_S$ agree with $h$ on $S$ and vanish on $S^c=[n]\setminus S$. The matrix $A$ satisfies the **$\ell^2$ robust nullspace property of order $s$ with constants $(\rho,\tau)$** if
$$\|h_S\|_2\le \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$. This condition applies to all vectors, including vectors with $Ah\ne0$.

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Use one-based labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, identifying label $j$ with library coordinate $j-1$. For $T\subseteq[n]$, let $x_{T^c}$ retain the coordinates outside $T$ and vanish on $T$, where $T^c=[n]\setminus T$. Define the best $s$-term $\ell^1$ approximation error by
$$\sigma_s(x)_1:=\min\{\|x_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}.$$
The indexing family is finite and nonempty, so the displayed minimum exists and is attained.

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$ use the one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. Order the coordinates by decreasing $|x_j|$, breaking ties by increasing $j$, and let $S$ be the first $s$ indices. For every $U\subseteq[n]$, let $x_U$ agree with $x$ on $U$ and vanish on $U^c$. Then for every $T\subseteq[n]$ with $|T|\le s$,
$$\|x_T\|_1\le\|x_S\|_1\quad\text{and}\quad\|x_{S^c}\|_1\le\|x_{T^c}\|_1.$$
Consequently $\sigma_s(x)_1=\|x_{S^c}\|_1$, so the best $s$-term tail error is attained by retaining the first $s$ coordinates in the specified order.

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$. Use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$, and interpret natural numbers in real scalar expressions as their canonical real images. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and suppose that for some $0<\rho<1$ and $\tau>0$,
$$\|h_S\|_2\le\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, where for any vector $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $v_S$ agrees with $v$ on $S$ and vanishes on $S^c=[n]\setminus S$. Let $x^\dagger\in\mathbb R^n$, $\epsilon\ge0$, and $e\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfy $y=Ax^\dagger+e$ and $\|e\|_2\le\epsilon$. Define
$$\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1:=\min\{\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}.$$
The indexing family is finite and nonempty, so this minimum is attained; it also equals the minimum of $\|x^\dagger-z\|_1$ over vectors $z$ with at most $s$ nonzero coordinates. Then the basis-pursuit denoising problem
$$\min_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\|z\|_1\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|Az-y\|_2\le\epsilon$$
has a minimizer. Every minimizer $\widehat x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_2\le C_1\frac{\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1}{\sqrt{s}}+C_2\epsilon,\qquad \|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_1\le C_3\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1+C_4\sqrt{s}\,\epsilon,$$
where
$$C_1=\frac{2(1+2\rho)}{1-\rho},\quad C_2=\frac{6\tau}{1-\rho},\quad C_3=\frac{2(1+\rho)}{1-\rho},\quad C_4=\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}.$$
If the certified finite basis-pursuit denoising procedure returns **success**, its returned vector is a minimizer and satisfies these same bounds. Only reconstruction error is bounded; the theorem asserts neither uniqueness nor support recovery.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real vector spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be nonempty, and let $A:X\to Y$ be linear. Supply metrics $d_X$ on $X$ and $d_Y$ on $Y$; for a purely algebraic instance with no specified metrics, use the discrete metrics $d_X(x,x')=0$ if $x=x'$ and $1$ otherwise, and likewise on $Y$. These metrics require no compatibility with the vector operations, and no continuity of $A$ is assumed. The discrete triangle inequality holds because, if two endpoints differ, at least one of the two successive pairs differs. Give $U$ and its subsets their restricted metrics. Thus every pair of real vector spaces still admits this convention. The corresponding metric-space inverse-problem model has admissible truths $U$ and forward map $A|_U$. An **admissible constraint class** is a nonempty subset $C\subseteq U$; its constrained forward map is the restriction $A|_C:C\to Y$. The class $C$ is **identifiable for $A$** if $A|_C$ is injective, meaning $Ax=Ax'$ for $x,x'\in C$ implies $x=x'$. Define the difference set and kernel by

$$C-C:=\{x-x':x,x'\in C\},\qquad \ker A:=\{x\in X:Ax=0_Y\}.$$

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

derivations.claim: Suppose $A|_C$ is injective and take $v\in(C-C)\cap\ker A$. By [F1], write $v=x-x'$ with $x,x'\in C$. By [F2] and [F3], $Ax-Ax'=Av=0_Y$, so $Ax=Ax'$. Injectivity gives $x=x'$, hence $v=0$. Since $C$ is nonempty, choose $x\in C$; then $0=x-x\in C-C$. Linearity also gives $A(0_X)=A(0_X+0_X)=A(0_X)+A(0_X)$, hence $A(0_X)=0_Y$ and $0_X\in\ker A$. Therefore $(C-C)\cap\ker A=\{0\}$.

Conversely, suppose $(C-C)\cap\ker A=\{0\}$ and take $x,x'\in C$ with $Ax=Ax'$. Then $x-x'\in C-C$ by [F1], and $A(x-x')=Ax-Ax'=0_Y$ by [F2], so $x-x'\in\ker A$ by [F3]. Thus $x-x'=0$, hence $x=x'$. Therefore $A|_C$ is injective.

For integers $1\le p\le n$, define the real Stiefel constraint set

$$\operatorname{St}(n,p):=\{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}:X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p\}.$$

Equip $\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with the Frobenius inner product $\langle U,V\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}V)$ and norm $\|U\|_F=\sqrt{\langle U,U\rangle_F}$. Let $H=\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, let $Y$ be a real Hilbert space, let $U\subseteq H$ be open and contain $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, and let $F:U\to Y$ be continuously Fréchet differentiable. Given data $y\in Y$, a reference matrix $X_{\rm ref}\in H$, and $\lambda\ge0$, define the residual and regularized objective by

$$r(X):=\|F(X)-y\|_Y,\qquad \Phi(X):=\tfrac12\|F(X)-y\|_Y^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|X-X_{\rm ref}\|_F^2.$$

Supply an ambient gradient oracle $G:U\to H$ satisfying $D\Phi(X)[Z]=\langle G(X),Z\rangle_F$ for every $X\in U$ and $Z\in H$, an initial frame $X_0\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite integer budget $K\ge0$, and a step schedule $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{K-1}$ with every $\alpha_k>0$. For a square matrix $M$, put $\operatorname{sym}(M):=(M+M^{\mathsf T})/2$. The tangent-projection and metric-dual calculation for this $C^1$ objective, well-definedness of every tangent polar call, and finite-budget feasibility are justified by the finite-budget return and feasibility lemma. No smoothness beyond $C^1$ is required. The procedure is:

1. Set the current frame to $X_0$ and the schedule index to $k=0$. If $r(X)\le\tau$, return $(X,r(X),\texttt{target-met})$.
2. While $k<K$, compute $G(X)$ and the Stiefel gradient $g:=G(X)-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G(X))$. If $g=0$, return $(X,r(X),\texttt{stationary})$.
3. Set $\eta:=-\alpha_k g$ and form the polar-retracted candidate

   $$X_{\rm trial}:=(X+\eta)\bigl((X+\eta)^{\mathsf T}(X+\eta)\bigr)^{-1/2}.$$

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h$ with integrable Fourier transform, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and let $\mu$ be the polar surface measure on $S^1$, with $\mu(E)=2\lambda_2(\{r\theta:\theta\in E,\ 0<r\le1\})$ for Borel $E\subseteq S^1$. The **complete-data filtered-backprojection procedure** takes as input the exact full sinogram $g=Rf$ of some $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$; all oriented normals $\theta\in S^1$ and all offsets $s\in\mathbb R$ are supplied. It returns the function $f_{\mathrm{FBP}}:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$ defined by
$$f_{\mathrm{FBP}}(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^1}q(\theta,x\cdot\theta)\,d\mu(\theta),$$
where the filter output is
$$q(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat{g(\theta,\cdot)}(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
The exact instructions are: (1) for each $\theta$, take the one-dimensional Fourier transform of $g(\theta,\cdot)$ with the negative-sign $2\pi$ convention; (2) multiply that transform by the declared ramp filter $2\pi|\sigma|$ and take its inverse Fourier integral to form $q(\theta,\cdot)$; (3) evaluate $q(\theta,\cdot)$ at $s=x\cdot\theta$ and integrate over the full polar surface measure in $\theta$; (4) divide by $4\pi$. For this input class the slice identity and Schwartz decay make the filter integral absolutely convergent and the backprojection integral well defined. This definition specifies the continuous full-data procedure; it gives no guarantee for finitely sampled, truncated, or noisy measurements. Exact recovery on the stated class is proved by the normal-operator theorem.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$ and $N=2^{m}$. The **radix-two fast Fourier transform** $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ is defined by recursion on $m$ as follows. At $m=0$ the group is $\mathbb Z/1\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{FFT}_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/1}}$. For $m\ge1$, given $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}$ with even and odd parts $e,o\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}}$ ([[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]]), and given $E:=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(e)$ and $O:=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(o)$, extend $E$ and $O$ from $\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb Z$ by $2^{m-1}$-periodicity and set

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k):=E(k)+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}O(k),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$

Then $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k+2^{m})=\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, because $E$ and $O$ are $2^{m-1}$-periodic and $e^{-2\pi i(k+2^{m})/2^{m}}=e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}e^{-2\pi i}=e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); hence $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2^{m}\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{FFT}_m$ is a well-defined map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}$.

**The recursion is legitimate.** Put $\mathcal F_m:=\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^m}$ for each $m\in\mathbb N$, and use the tagged state set $A:=\{(m,g):m\in\mathbb N,\ g:\mathcal F_m\to\mathcal F_m\}$. For a state $(m,g)\in A$ and $f\in\mathcal F_{m+1}$, let $e,o\in\mathcal F_m$ be the even and odd parts supplied by [[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]], and define $g^+(f)\in\mathcal F_{m+1}$ by $g^+(f)([k]_{2^{m+1}}):=g(e)([k]_{2^m})+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m+1}}g(o)([k]_{2^m})$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$. This is well defined on $[k]_{2^{m+1}}$: replacing $k$ by $k+2^{m+1}$ leaves the recursive values unchanged modulo $2^m$ and multiplies the twiddle by $e^{-2\pi i}=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Thus $g^+$ is a total map $\mathcal F_{m+1}\to\mathcal F_{m+1}$, and $T:A\to A$ defined by $T(m,g):=(m+1,g^+)$ is a total step function. Starting from $a:=(0,\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal F_0})$, the recursion theorem [[thm-recursion]] gives a unique $H:\mathbb N\to A$ with $H(0)=a$ and $H(m+1)=T(H(m))$. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-natural-numbers]]) the first coordinate of $H(m)$ is $m$; writing $H(m)=(m,\operatorname{FFT}_m)$ gives $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathcal F_m\to\mathcal F_m$ and exactly the base and combine clauses above. Termination is immediate from recursion on $m$: each recursive call uses level $m-1$, and the base case $m=0$ returns the input. The exponent arithmetic uses $2^{m+1}=2\cdot2^m$ and, for the rescaling below, $2^{-m/2}=(2^m)^{-1/2}$ ([[lem-power-laws]], [[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]).

**What the algorithm computes.** Correctness is proved separately later on this page: $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)$ for every input, where $X$ is the unnormalised transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]; the unitary transform of this page is recovered from the output by the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^{m}$. The operation count is likewise the subject of a later item. At level $m$ the recursion forms the even and odd parts of a length-$2^{m}$ list and performs one combine per output value, reading $E$ and $O$ at their classes and multiplying by the twiddle factors $e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}$.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $N=2^{m}$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $X$ is the unnormalised $N$-point discrete Fourier transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]. Equivalently $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)=2^{m/2}\,\mathcal F_Nf$ for the unitary transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]; consequently the algorithm returns the unitary transform after the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$, and it does so for every input of length $2^{m}$. Correctness is separate from speed: the operation count is the subject of a different theorem, and no floating-point or stability claim is made here.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by

$$X_k(f):=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

the sum being the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] over the representatives $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ of the classes of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]), with $e^z$ the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]]. Comparing with [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]],

$$X_k(f)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k),\qquad (\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] and the two conversions are inverse to each other by $N^{1/2}N^{-1/2}=1$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). So the two transforms determine each other, and the only difference between them is the constant $\sqrt N$.

**The transform is defined on classes and is $N$-periodic.** If $[x]_N=[x']_N$ then $x'=x+mN$ for some integer $m$ and $e^{-2\pi ikx'/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ikm}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, so the summands depend only on classes; and $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, both identities following from the addition law and $\exp(2\pi i\,\cdot)=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Hence $X(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and $X_k(f)$ depends on $k$ only through its class.

**Inverse formulas.** The inversion theorem in its unitary form is the identity $f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ of [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]; substituting $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f)$ and collecting $N^{-1/2}N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]) gives the engineering form

$$f(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_k(f)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.$$

This is the convention in which the radix-two algorithm computes its output. The unitary transform is recovered by the single rescaling $N^{-1/2}=2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^m$. The correctness and complexity theorems refer to this unnormalised output; the convolution lemma is stated in the unitary convention.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

$$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$

the right-hand side being independent of the chosen integer representative of the class $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign transform

$$(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N},\ x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$

and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis anywhere.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$, define $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$, where the absolutely convergent integral is with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ is the space of smooth complex functions for which every seminorm $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, is finite. The parameter $\theta$ is the unit normal to the line, so $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$ represent the same unoriented line. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Lebesgue integral in this definition agrees on compactly supported smooth inputs with the compact-support Riemann line integral, so the normalization is the same.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Fix a derivative multi-index $\beta$ and an integer $N\ge1$, and choose an integer $m\ge N$. Since $(1+|x|)^N\le(1+|x_1|)^m(1+|x_2|)^m$, expanding the right side and using the finite Schwartz seminorms in [F1] gives a finite $C_{\beta,N}(f)$ with $|\partial^\beta f(x)|\le C_{\beta,N}(f)(1+|x|)^{-N}$. For $x=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, orthogonality gives $|x|=(s^2+t^2)^{1/2}\ge(|s|+|t|)/\sqrt2$, so the line integrand is bounded by a constant times $(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N}$. Taking $N>1$ makes this majorant integrable in $t$, proving absolute convergence.

Let $D_\theta=\theta\cdot\nabla$. The chain rule [F4] gives $\partial_s^k f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)=(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Expanding $D_\theta^k$ gives finitely many partial derivatives with coefficients bounded uniformly for $\theta\in S^1$. For the target decay order $N$, apply step 1.1 with spatial decay order $N+2$ to each such derivative. Integrating $(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N-2}$ in $t$ gives $\left|\int_{\mathbb R}(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt\right|\le C'_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N-1}\le C'_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N}$, uniformly in $\theta$ and $s$.

Fix $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and a bounded open interval $I$ containing $s_0$. For each $k\ge0$, set $g_k(t,s)=(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Every slice $g_k(\cdot,s)$ is integrable by step 1.1; it is differentiable in $s$ with derivative $g_{k+1}$ by [F4], and this derivative is measurable. Step 1.1 with spatial decay order $3$ bounds $|g_{k+1}(t,s)|\le C(1+|t|)^{-3}$ uniformly for $s\in I$, an integrable majorant. Thus [F3] proves $\frac{d}{ds}\int g_k(t,s)\,dt=\int g_{k+1}(t,s)\,dt$. To see each resulting derivative is continuous, if $s=s'$ the difference is zero; otherwise apply [F5] to real and imaginary parts on the segment joining $s$ and $s'$. The same majorant gives $|g_k(t,s)-g_k(t,s')|\le C|s-s'|(1+|t|)^{-3}$, and integration proves local continuity. Repeating for all $k$ and using the estimates in step 2.1 shows the offset function is Schwartz.

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open set of line normals, assume $\theta\in\Theta$ if and only if $-\theta\in\Theta$, and assume $S^1\setminus\overline{\Theta}$ contains a nonempty open arc. The measured line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\ell_{\theta,s}=\{y\in\mathbb R^2:y\cdot\theta=s\}$. Identify the nonzero cotangent vectors of the Euclidean plane with pairs $(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^2\times(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\})$. Such a covector is visible from $\Theta$ when $\xi/|\xi|\in\Theta$, and invisible when $\xi/|\xi|\notin\Theta$. The associated measured Fourier wedge is

$$W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\}.$$

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ and, for $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$, define $F(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x_1z_1+x_2z_2)}\,dx$ using the compact-support Riemann integral on any rectangle containing $\operatorname{supp}f$. This value is independent of the containing rectangle. Each coordinate slice of $F$ is entire, with $\frac{\partial F}{\partial z_j}(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(-2\pi ix_j)f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}\,dx$ for $j=1,2$, and the restriction of $F$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is the compact-support Fourier transform in the stated line-normal convention. The proof uses no Countable Choice.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open set of line normals, assume $\theta\in\Theta$ if and only if $-\theta\in\Theta$, and assume $S^1\setminus\overline{\Theta}$ contains a nonempty open arc. The measured line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\ell_{\theta,s}=\{y\in\mathbb R^2:y\cdot\theta=s\}$. Identify the nonzero cotangent vectors of the Euclidean plane with pairs $(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^2\times(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\})$. Such a covector is visible from $\Theta$ when $\xi/|\xi|\in\Theta$, and invisible when $\xi/|\xi|\notin\Theta$. The associated measured Fourier wedge is

$$W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\}.$$

For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$, define $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$, where the absolutely convergent integral is with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ is the space of smooth complex functions for which every seminorm $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, is finite. The parameter $\theta$ is the unit normal to the line, so $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$ represent the same unoriented line. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Lebesgue integral in this definition agrees on compactly supported smooth inputs with the compact-support Riemann line integral, so the normalization is the same.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta\in S^1$, and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the offset variable, using the phase $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$, satisfies $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$, where the two-dimensional transform uses the phase $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. On compactly supported smooth inputs the formula has the same line parameterization and normalization as the Euclidean Radon transform.

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty open set of unit line normals and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. If the line integral $Rf(\theta,s)$ is zero for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, then $f$ is zero everywhere. The assertion holds without Countable Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, [F3] gives the Fourier-slice identity. If the restricted data vanish, their one-dimensional Fourier transforms vanish, so $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)=0$. Every point of $W_\Theta$ has this form, hence $\widehat f$ vanishes on $W_\Theta$.

Now assume $f\in C_c^\infty$ and its restricted data are zero. The compact-support Fourier-slice identity [F4] gives $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)=0$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, so the transform vanishes on the measured wedge. Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open set of line normals, assume $\theta\in\Theta$ if and only if $-\theta\in\Theta$, and assume $S^1\setminus\overline{\Theta}$ contains a nonempty open arc. The measured line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\ell_{\theta,s}=\{y\in\mathbb R^2:y\cdot\theta=s\}$. Identify the nonzero cotangent vectors of the Euclidean plane with pairs $(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^2\times(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\})$. Such a covector is visible from $\Theta$ when $\xi/|\xi|\in\Theta$, and invisible when $\xi/|\xi|\notin\Theta$. The associated measured Fourier wedge is

$$W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\}.$$
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume countable choice. If $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, then $x^\alpha\partial^\beta f\in L^p$ for every $1\le p\le\infty$ and every $\alpha,\beta$. Its norm is bounded by a finite sum of Schwartz seminorms.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta\in S^1$, and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the offset variable, using the phase $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$, satisfies $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$, where the two-dimensional transform uses the phase $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. On compactly supported smooth inputs the formula has the same line parameterization and normalization as the Euclidean Radon transform.

For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ and every $\theta\in S^1$, the defining line integral for $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)$ converges absolutely for every $s\in\mathbb R$, and $s\mapsto R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)$ belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$. For each pair of nonnegative integers $k,N$, its $k$th derivative is bounded by $C_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N}$ with a finite constant $C_{k,N}$ independent of $s$ and $\theta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. For $1\le p<\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_p:=\|f\|_p\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu))$$
   is well defined on the quotient classes.
2. For $p=\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_\infty:=\|f\|_\infty\qquad([f]\in L^\infty(\mu))$$
   is well defined.
3. In either case, with the quotient vector-space operations of
   [[prop-quotient-vector-space-operations-and-projection]], the resulting pair
   $(L^p(\mu),\|\cdot\|_p)$ is a normed space in the sense of
   [[def-norm-and-normed-space]].

Let $(X,d_X)$, $(Y,d_Y)$, and $(Q,d_Q)$ be metric spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth class, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, and let $q:U\to Q$ assign each truth its target class. Let $x_0,x_1\in U$, let $\delta\ge0$, and suppose a single datum $y\in Y$ satisfies

$$d_Y(y,F(x_0))\le\delta\quad\text{and}\quad d_Y(y,F(x_1))\le\delta.$$

For every deterministic data-only estimator, meaning every function $\widehat q:Y\to Q$, the two target-class losses at that datum satisfy

$$\max\{d_Q(\widehat q(y),q(x_0)),d_Q(\widehat q(y),q(x_1))\}\ge\frac12d_Q(q(x_0),q(x_1)).$$

In particular, if $F(x_0)=F(x_1)$ but $q(x_0)\ne q(x_1)$, no data-only estimator exactly recovers both truths. The quantitative bound also holds whenever the radius-$\delta$ data balls around the two forward data share the observed datum $y$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The sector $V$ is a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^2$ because $(r,\omega)\mapsto r\omega$ maps the open parameter set $(1,2)\times J$ to an open polar-coordinate sector. It therefore contains a ball; [F2] supplies a nonzero $q\in C_c^\infty(V)$. This establishes the required bump choice.

By the Fourier definition [F5], the function in the Example is $f(x)=\widehat q(-x)$. Since $q$ is smooth with compact support, every Schwartz seminorm of $q$ is bounded, so $q\in\mathcal S$. By [F3] its transform is Schwartz, and reflection preserves each Schwartz seminorm up to sign, hence $f$ is Schwartz; [F7] gives $f\in L^2\cap L^1$. The reflection substitution [F6] and inversion [F4] give $\widehat f(\eta)=\int\widehat q(-x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}\,dx=\int\widehat q(y)e^{2\pi i y\cdot\eta}\,dy=q(\eta)$. Since $q\ne0$, this identity implies $f$ is nonzero as an $L^1$ and $L^2$ class.

For $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\ne0$, the point $\sigma\theta$ is outside the support of $q$ because every frequency in $V$ has direction in $J$ and $\overline J$ is disjoint from $\overline\Theta$; also $q(0)=0$ since $V$ avoids the origin. Thus [F8] gives $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=q(\sigma\theta)=0$ for all real $\sigma$. By [F9], the offset function is Schwartz, so Fourier inversion [F4] in one dimension gives $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=0$ for every $s$.

Let the parameter and target metric spaces both be $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ with distance $d(g,h)=\|g-h\|_2$, let the admissible truth class be $U=\{0,f\}$, and let the target map $q:U\to L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ be inclusion. Give the data space $Y=L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R)$ its norm metric and define $F:U\to Y$ by the restricted line integrals. The $L^2$ metric axioms follow from [F10] and [F13], and this is an admissible metric-space model by [F12]. Step 1.3 gives $F(0)=F(f)=0$, while step 1.2 gives $d(q(0),q(f))=\|f\|_2>0$. Apply [F11] with shared datum $0$ and radius $0$ to any deterministic estimator $\Phi:Y\to L^2(\mathbb R^2)$; its maximum target loss is at least $\|f\|_2/2$. This proves the asserted lower bound on the stated two-truth class.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. For $x\in\partial M$, let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$ be the outward unit normal. The boundary is **strictly convex** if
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every $x\in\partial M$ and every nonzero $w\in T_x\partial M$. A **Jacobi field** along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ along $\gamma$ satisfying
$$
D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0,
$$
where $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if, on every unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, a Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$ must be identically zero. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple surface** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

The unit tangent bundle is $SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}$. Write $\nu_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$$
\partial_+SM=\{(x,v)\in SM:x\in\partial M,\ g_x(v,\nu_{\mathrm{in}})>0\}
$$
for inward-pointing unit boundary vectors. abla_AQ)e_2=

abla Q=0$ and $n(t)=Q\dot\gamma(t)$ is a parallel unit normal along the whole segment. By [F5], the scalar coefficient $j$ in the Jacobi field $j n$ solves $j''+K(\gamma(t))j=0$. If $\operatorname{supp}f=\varnothing$, then $f=0$ and $u_f=0$, so the transport claim is immediate; assume henceforth that the support is nonempty. The unit circle bundle $SM$ is compact: cover compact $M$ by finitely many smaller coordinate neighborhoods with closures inside charts carrying smooth orthonormal frames; each part of $SM$ over such a closure is homeomorphic to the product of that compact closure with $S^1$, so finitely many compact sets cover $SM$. If $d_g(x,\partial M)<D/4$, the triangle inequality gives $d_g(x,\operatorname{supp}f)>3D/4$; hence a unit-speed curve from $x$ cannot reach the support before time $D/2$, since its length equals elapsed time and endpoint distance is at most length. If $v$ is tangent, step 3.1 gives $\rho''(0)<0$. Away from tangent boundary states, step 3.1 gives transverse exit, so the implicit function theorem and smooth ODE dependence make $u_f$ smooth. The incoming boundary value is $I_0f=0$ and the outgoing value is zero because its future exit time is zero.

The curve convention is [[def-piecewise-c-one-curve-on-a-manifold]] and the norm is [[def-pointwise-norm-and-angle-from-a-riemannian-metric]]. Each integrand is continuous on its closed piece with the one-sided endpoint derivative, hence Riemann integrable and nonnegative. Values chosen at the finitely many corners do not change its integral. For a singleton interval the empty sum is zero; a constant curve also has zero length. Partition independence is established by [[lem-riemannian-length-is-independent-of-piecewise-c-one-subdivision]].

On a connected Riemannian manifold define $d_g(p,q)=\inf\{L_g(\gamma):\gamma\text{ is piecewise }C^1\text{ from }p\text{ to }q\}$.

Lengths are those of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. For each pair $p,q$, [[lem-any-two-points-in-a-connected-smooth-manifold-can-be-joined-by-a-piecewise-c-one-curve]] supplies a curve, so the set of lengths is nonempty, contains a finite real number and is bounded below by zero. Applying the least-upper-bound property [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] to the negatives gives a finite nonnegative infimum. On the empty connected manifold this defines the empty distance function; there are no pairs to evaluate. No minimizing curve is part of this definition.
$d_g$ is a finite metric on a connected Riemannian manifold.
The topology of $d_g$ is the manifold topology on every connected Riemannian manifold.
For every piecewise $C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$, $d_g(\gamma(a),\gamma(b))\le L_g(\gamma)$.

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $n\ge1$. For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, its **support** is
$$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\ne0\}}.$$
The function is **compactly supported** if $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact.

A compactly supported $f$ is **compactly supported Riemann integrable** if there is a nondegenerate closed rectangle $Q$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$ such that $f|_Q$ is Riemann integrable. Its integral over Euclidean space is defined by
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f:=\int_Qf.$$
The value is independent of $Q$ by [[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]]. When the support is empty, $f=0$ and the value is $0$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: If $K=\varnothing$, set $\chi_N=0$ for all $N$; the empty set is a neighborhood of $K$, so every assertion is vacuous. Assume henceforth $K\ne\varnothing$. For each $x\in K$, choose concentric balls $B_{r_x}(x)\Subset B_{R_x}(x)\Subset U$. By [F1], take $b_x\in C_c^\infty(B_{R_x}(x))$ with $0\le b_x\le1$ and $b_x=1$ on $B_{r_x}(x)$. Compactness gives a finite subcover $B_{r_1}(x_1),\ldots,B_{r_m}(x_m)$ of $K$. The smooth function $ g=1-\prod_{j=1}^m(1-b_{x_j}) $ satisfies $0\le g\le1$, equals one on the open set $O=\bigcup_{j=1}^m B_{r_j}(x_j)$ containing $K$, and has compact support $S\Subset U$. This construction uses only finite subcover compactness.

Choose a nonnegative smooth bump $\rho_0$ supported in the unit ball and equal to one on the ball of radius $1/2$, using [F1]. Its compactly supported integral is finite by [F3] and positive because it equals one on a ball. Normalize $\rho=\rho_0/\int\rho_0$, so $\int\rho=1$, $\rho\ge0$, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset\overline B_1(0)$. Since $K\Subset O$ and $S\Subset U$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than one third of each distance $\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(S,U^c)$.

For each $N\ge1$, put $\delta=\varepsilon/N$, $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta)$, and recursively $\eta_1=\rho_\delta$, $\eta_{j+1}=\eta_j*\rho_\delta$ for $1\le j<N$. Compact-rectangle Fubini [F4] and change of variables give $\int\eta_N=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_N\subset\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$; [F4] also permits reassociation of these compact convolution integrals. Define $\chi_N=g*\eta_N$. The integral defining $\chi_N$ is over a fixed compact rectangle. Differentiating the smooth kernel under this compact integral is justified by uniform convergence of its difference quotients on that rectangle, so $\chi_N$ is smooth. Positivity and unit mass give $0\le\chi_N\le1$. If $\operatorname{dist}(x,K)<\varepsilon$, then every $y\in\operatorname{supp}\eta_N$ satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(x-y,K)<2\varepsilon<\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$, hence $g(x-y)=1$ and $\chi_N(x)=1$. Also $\operatorname{supp}\chi_N\subset S+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)\Subset U$.

For smooth compactly supported $f,h$, write $\|h\|_1=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|h|$. Fubini on a rectangle containing their supports and the triangle inequality give $ \|f*h\|_{1}\le\int\!\!\int |f(x-y)||h(y)|\,dy\,dx =\|f\|_{1}\|h\|_{1}. $ Also $\partial_j(f*h)=(\partial_j f)*h=f*(\partial_jh)$ by differentiating under the compact integral and integration by parts; there is no boundary term because the factors have compact support. For $k=|\alpha|\le N$, distribute the $k$ coordinate derivatives to $k$ distinct convolution factors in $\eta_N$. Scaling gives $ \|\partial_j\rho_\delta\|_{1}=\delta^{-1}\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}, $ so repeated use of the preceding inequality yields $ \|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1}\le (AN)^k,\qquad A=\varepsilon^{-1}\max\bigl(1,\max_j\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}\bigr). $ For $k=0$ this is $\|\eta_N\|_{1}=1$.

Since $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, $ |\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)| =|g*(\partial^\alpha\eta_N)(x)| \le \|g\|_\infty\|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1} \le (AN)^{|\alpha|}. $ Thus the lemma holds with $C=1$ (or any larger fixed constant), uniformly for every $|\alpha|\le N$. The cutoffs are smooth and no analytic bump is used.

For each $x\in K$, choose concentric balls $B_{r_x}(x)\Subset B_{R_x}(x)\Subset U$. By [F1], take $b_x\in C_c^\infty(B_{R_x}(x))$ with $0\le b_x\le1$ and $b_x=1$ on $B_{r_x}(x)$. Compactness gives a finite subcover $B_{r_1}(x_1),\ldots,B_{r_m}(x_m)$ of $K$. The smooth function $ g=1-\prod_{j=1}^m(1-b_{x_j}) $ satisfies $0\le g\le1$, equals one on the open set $O=\bigcup_{j=1}^m B_{r_j}(x_j)$ containing $K$, and has compact support $S\Subset U$. This construction uses only finite subcover compactness.

Choose a nonnegative smooth bump $\rho_0$ supported in the unit ball and equal to one on the ball of radius $1/2$, using [F1]. Its compactly supported integral is finite by [F3] and positive because it equals one on a ball. Normalize $\rho=\rho_0/\int\rho_0$, so $\int\rho=1$, $\rho\ge0$, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset\overline B_1(0)$. Since $K\Subset O$ and $S\Subset U$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than one third of each distance $\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(S,U^c)$.

For each $N\ge1$, put $\delta=\varepsilon/N$, $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta)$, and recursively $\eta_1=\rho_\delta$, $\eta_{j+1}=\eta_j*\rho_\delta$ for $1\le j<N$. Compact-rectangle Fubini [F4] and change of variables give $\int\eta_N=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_N\subset\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$; [F4] also permits reassociation of these compact convolution integrals. Define $\chi_N=g*\eta_N$. The integral defining $\chi_N$ is over a fixed compact rectangle. Differentiating the smooth kernel under this compact integral is justified by uniform convergence of its difference quotients on that rectangle, so $\chi_N$ is smooth. Positivity and unit mass give $0\le\chi_N\le1$. If $\operatorname{dist}(x,K)<\varepsilon$, then every $y\in\operatorname{supp}\eta_N$ satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(x-y,K)<2\varepsilon<\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$, hence $g(x-y)=1$ and $\chi_N(x)=1$. Also $\operatorname{supp}\chi_N\subset S+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)\Subset U$.

For smooth compactly supported $f,h$, write $\|h\|_1=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|h|$. Fubini on a rectangle containing their supports and the triangle inequality give $ \|f*h\|_{1}\le\int\!\!\int |f(x-y)||h(y)|\,dy\,dx =\|f\|_{1}\|h\|_{1}. $ Also $\partial_j(f*h)=(\partial_j f)*h=f*(\partial_jh)$ by differentiating under the compact integral and integration by parts; there is no boundary term because the factors have compact support. For $k=|\alpha|\le N$, distribute the $k$ coordinate derivatives to $k$ distinct convolution factors in $\eta_N$. Scaling gives $ \|\partial_j\rho_\delta\|_{1}=\delta^{-1}\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}, $ so repeated use of the preceding inequality yields $ \|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1}\le (AN)^k,\qquad A=\varepsilon^{-1}\max\bigl(1,\max_j\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}\bigr). $ For $k=0$ this is $\|\eta_N\|_{1}=1$.

Since $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, $ |\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)| =|g*(\partial^\alpha\eta_N)(x)| \le \|g\|_\infty\|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1} \le (AN)^{|\alpha|}. $ Thus the lemma holds with $C=1$ (or any larger fixed constant), uniformly for every $|\alpha|\le N$.
