The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
Assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). If $\mu$ is a Radon measure on an LCH space $X$ and $1\le p<\infty$, then $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\xrightarrow{\,g\,}\Omega''\xrightarrow{\,f\,}\Omega'$ be analytically quasiconformal homeomorphisms, with $g$ $K_1$-quasiconformal and $f$ $K_2$-quasiconformal ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]).

(i) **Composition.** The composite $f\circ g$ is analytically $K_1K_2$-quasiconformal, with $K_{f\circ g}\le K_1K_2$, and almost everywhere
$$\mu_{f\circ g}(z)= \frac{g_{\bar z}(z)+\mu_f(g(z))\,\overline{g_z(z)}} {g_z(z)+\mu_f(g(z))\,\overline{g_{\bar z}(z)}}.$$

(ii) **Inverse.** The inverse $f^{-1}$ is $K_2$-quasiconformal, $K_{f^{-1}}=K_f$, and
$$\mu_{f^{-1}}(f(z))=-\mu_f(z)\frac{f_z(z)}{\overline{f_z(z)}}\quad\text{for almost every }z.$$

Consequently quasiconformal homeomorphisms are closed under inverses and composition, and the $1$-quasiconformal self-maps of a domain form a group.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism. The following are equivalent.

(a) $f$ is $1$-quasiconformal, in either the geometric or the analytic sense ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[thm-geometric-and-analytic-quasiconformality-equivalent]]).

(b) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its weak Wirtinger derivative satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere; under this Sobolev hypothesis this is equivalent to $\mu_f=0$ almost everywhere together with $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere on $\{\partial_zf=0\}$ ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]).

(c) $f$ is holomorphic; equivalently, it is a biholomorphism of $\Omega$ onto $\Omega'$ ([[def-biholomorphic-map]]).

Thus the conformal maps in this library's orientation-preserving sense are exactly the $1$-quasiconformal homeomorphisms; in particular, they preserve angles.
Every biholomorphic self-map of the Riemann sphere is Möbius.

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$;
write $\delta_hu=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu)$ and
$Du=(D_1u,\dots,D_nu)$ for the difference-quotient and gradient vectors, with
$$\|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|\delta_h^iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega')},\qquad \|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
(1) If $1\le p\le\infty$ and $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then for every
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$ and every coordinate
direction $i$,
$$\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le n^{|1/p-1/2|}\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
At $p=2$ the vector estimate has constant one. The coordinate bound also
holds on any open $U\subseteq\Omega$ for a fixed $i,h$ for which every
segment $[x,x+he_i]$, $x\in U$, stays in $\Omega$; compact containment
is unnecessary. In particular, $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(H)}\le
\|D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}$ for tangential directions on a half-space $H$.
(2) Conversely, if $1<p<\infty$, $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and there is $C$
with $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$ for every coordinate $i$ and all
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)/2$, then
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega')$ with $D_iu\in L^p(\Omega')$,
$\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$, and
$\delta_h^iu\rightharpoonup D_iu$ weakly in $L^p(\Omega')$ as $h\to0$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, tangential quotients on $H$ also converge strongly:
$\delta_h^iu\to D_iu$ in $L^p(H)$ as $h\to0$.
Both parts are identities of classes and hold without any regularity of
$\partial\Omega$. At $p=1$ the converse in (2) is deliberately not asserted;
the companion remark records why only a measure derivative survives there.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used through the cited Countable-Choice and
Dependent-Choice interfaces (completed-product Fubini, approximate identities,
the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions), for
the countable selections of cutoffs and mollifier scales below, and through the
earlier ACL reconstruction lemma. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For an almost-everywhere class $u$ on $\Omega$ the following are equivalent:

1. $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $u$ has one measurable ACL representative
   $u^*$ whose classical coordinate derivatives $\partial_i u^*$ exist almost
   everywhere, are measurable, and belong to $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

In that case $\partial_i u^*$ is a representative of $D_i u$ for every
$i$, that is, $D_i u=\partial_i u^*$ almost everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is only the zero class, its representative
$u^*=0$ is ACL, and every displayed assertion holds vacuously.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be an orientation-preserving analytically $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism, $K\ge1$, in the sense of [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]. For every Jordan quadrilateral $Q\Subset\Omega$ with either pair of opposite marked sides, write $\Gamma_Q$ for its joining family and $\Gamma_{f(Q)}$ for the corresponding image family ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]). Then
$$K^{-1}\mu(\Gamma_Q)\le\mu(\Gamma_{f(Q)})\le K\mu(\Gamma_Q),$$
equivalently
$$K^{-1}\lambda(\Gamma_Q)\le\lambda(\Gamma_{f(Q)})\le K\lambda(\Gamma_Q).$$
This result supplies quadrilateral bounds; no inverse regularity, inverse null-set property or arbitrary-ring comparison is assumed.

u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open for $d_{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]). Put $V=\Phi[U]$, where $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$ is the bijection of [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]. Then $V$ is open by [[thm-complex-coordinate-isometry-and-topology-transport]]. For $f:U\to\mathbb C$ define $\widetilde f=\Phi\circ f\circ\Phi^{-1}:V\to\mathbb R^2$, with component functions $u=\operatorname{Re}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ and $v=\operatorname{Im}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). All real partial derivatives below are those of $\widetilde f$ on $V$ in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], evaluated at the coordinate point in question. Write $\partial_x f=u_x+iv_x$ and $\partial_y f=u_y+iv_y$ after transport back to $U$.

At a point where the four real partial derivatives exist, define

$$ \partial_z f:=\frac12(\partial_x f-i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x+v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x-u_y), $$

$$ \partial_{\bar z}f:=\frac12(\partial_x f+i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x-v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x+u_y). $$

Real total differentiability means total differentiability of $\widetilde f$ under [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with a real-linear derivative as in [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]. Its transported real-linear map $Df$ is supplied by [[thm-complex-coordinate-map-preserves-real-total-differentiability]]. If $f$ is real totally differentiable, put $A=\partial_x f$ and $B=\partial_y f$. The remainder definition along the two coordinate axes gives $Df(1)=A$ and $Df(i)=B$. Real linearity then gives $Df(s+it)=sA+tB$ for real $s,t$, whereas direct expansion of $\frac12(A-iB)(s+it)+\frac12(A+iB)(s-it)$ gives the same expression. Thus

$$ Df(h)=(\partial_z f)h+(\partial_{\bar z}f)\overline h. $$

A real-differentiable map is **antiholomorphic** on $U$ when $\partial_z f=0$ at every point of $U$. Thus its differential is conjugate-linear at every point; no complex differentiability is asserted unless the other Wirtinger derivative also vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]). Read $f$ as a map into $\mathbb R^2$; continuity makes its components locally square integrable. Recall that $W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) means that the components of $f$ admit weak first partial derivatives ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]) in $L^2_{\rm loc}$; equivalently, their almost-everywhere classes have ACL representatives in both coordinate directions whose measurable classical coordinate derivatives belong to $L^2_{\rm loc}$ ([[def-absolute-continuity-on-almost-every-coordinate-line]], [[thm-acl-characterisation-of-w-one-p]]). ACL alone does not assert this derivative integrability. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is included in AC for the completed-product Fubini interfaces. On almost every coordinate line the continuous map $f$ agrees almost everywhere with its ACL representative, hence everywhere by continuity of both restrictions; its classical line derivatives then represent its weak derivatives.

Let $K\ge1$ and put $k=(K-1)/(K+1)\in[0,1)$. The homeomorphism $f$ is **$K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense** when

(A1) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$; and

(A2) its weak Wirtinger derivatives $\partial_zf,\partial_{\bar z}f$ ([[def-wirtinger-derivatives]]) lie in $L^2_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ and satisfy
$$|\partial_{\bar z}f(z)|\le k|\partial_zf(z)|\qquad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$

The inequality is a statement about $L^2_{\rm loc}$ classes: it is independent of the choice of representative of $f$ and of the Borel representatives of its weak Wirtinger derivatives, since each such representative agrees almost everywhere with its class ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]]). The map is **analytically quasiconformal** if it is $K$-analytically quasiconformal for some finite $K$. Its minimal constant is recovered from the Beltrami coefficient defined later on this page.

**Orientation and the regularity requirement.** Inequality (A2) gives $J_f=|\partial_zf|^2-|\partial_{\bar z}f|^2\ge(1-k^2)|\partial_zf|^2\ge0$ almost everywhere, with respect to planar Lebesgue measure ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). A classical derivative inequality alone does not replace (A1): on $(0,1)^2$, the map $f(x+iy)=x+g(x)+iy$, where $g$ is the Cantor function, is a homeomorphism onto $(0,2)\times(0,1)$ ([[lem-x-plus-the-cantor-function-is-a-homeomorphism-from-zero-one-onto-zero-two]]). The Cantor function is continuous, nonconstant, and locally constant off the null Cantor set, so $g'=0$ almost everywhere ([[thm-cantor-function-properties]], [[cor-cantor-set-is-an-uncountable-lebesgue-null-set]]). Thus the classical Wirtinger derivatives are $\partial_zf=1$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere. But $g$ cannot be absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $(0,1)$: the fundamental theorem would make it constant there, and then continuity would contradict $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=1$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]). Subtracting the identity shows that $f$ fails ACL on every horizontal line and therefore fails (A1). Its classical inequality is not the weak-derivative assertion (A2). Orientation preservation follows from (A1) together with (A2), as proved by the equivalence theorem on this page.

derivations.claim: Define the locally finite Borel measure $\omega(E)=\operatorname{area}(h(E))$. This is a measure because a homeomorphism maps disjoint Borel sets to disjoint Borel sets and respects unions. It is Radon because it is the pushforward of planar area by the homeomorphism $h^{-1}$; compact and open approximation transport through that homeomorphism. The open image $h(B(x,r))$ contains $B(h(x),l(x,r))$: otherwise a segment from $h(x)$ to a point of that smaller disk outside the image would first meet the boundary $h(\partial B(x,r))$, contradicting the definition of $l$. The maximum distance from $h(x)$ in $h(\overline{B(x,r)})$ occurs on its boundary, because distance from a fixed point has no maximum in a nonempty open set. Hence $|h(y)-h(x)|\le L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for $y\in\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\pi l(x,r)^2\le\omega(B(x,r))$.

For $x\in V$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, use step 1.1 with radius $2|t|$ to obtain $|h(x+te_i)-h(x)|^2\le(H^2/\pi)\omega(B(x,2|t|))$. These balls lie in $U$. Tonelli, applied to their incidence indicator, gives $\int_V\omega(B(x,2|t|))\,dx=\int_U|V\cap B(y,2|t|)|\,d\omega(y)\le4\pi t^2\omega(U)$. Combining the two inequalities proves the explicit difference-quotient estimate. All measures in this calculation are locally finite Radon measures and the incidence set is open, so no absolute continuity or null-set preservation of $h$ has been presumed.

Continuity makes $h$ square integrable on every relatively compact $U$. The uniform estimate in step 2.1 and [F1], with $p=2$ and complex-valued functions, give $h\in W^{1,2}(V)$. Exhausting the plane proves local Sobolev regularity. Apply [F2] on a countable collection of rectangles. On almost every coordinate line, its ACL representative agrees with the continuous representative almost everywhere by Fubini, hence everywhere on each compact line interval because both are continuous there. Thus the actual map $h$ is ACL and has finite coordinate partial derivatives almost everywhere, agreeing with the weak derivatives.

By the general-homeomorphism interface [F3], $h$ is totally differentiable almost everywhere. At such a point $x$, write $h(x+v)=h(x)+Av+o(|v|)$; the remainder is uniform over $|v|=r$ after division by $r$. If $A$ has rank one, there are unit vectors $u,v$ with $Au=0$ and $|Av|>0$. Then $l(x,r)=o(r)$ whereas $L(x,r)\ge r|Av|+o(r)$, contradicting the finite circular bound. If $A$ is nonsingular with singular values $s_1\ge s_2>0$, the same uniform expansion gives $L(x,r)/r\to s_1$ and $l(x,r)/r\to s_2$, so $s_1/s_2\le H$. Its determinant is positive by [F3], since $h$ preserves orientation. The remaining possibility is $A=0$.

At almost every point the classical partials of the total derivative equal the weak derivatives by step 3.1. At the nonsingular points, [F5] and step 4.1 give $|h_{\bar z}|/|h_z|\le(H-1)/(H+1)$; at zero derivatives the asserted inequality also holds. Together with $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and ACL regularity, this is exactly analytic $H$-quasiconformality. The proof uses only the locally proved total-differentiability interface [F3]; it does not invoke an infinitesimal metric-to-quasiconformal criterion.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open for $d_{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]). Put $V=\Phi[U]$, where $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$ is the bijection of [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]. Then $V$ is open by [[thm-complex-coordinate-isometry-and-topology-transport]]. For $f:U\to\mathbb C$ define $\widetilde f=\Phi\circ f\circ\Phi^{-1}:V\to\mathbb R^2$, with component functions $u=\operatorname{Re}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ and $v=\operatorname{Im}(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). All real partial derivatives below are those of $\widetilde f$ on $V$ in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], evaluated at the coordinate point in question. Write $\partial_x f=u_x+iv_x$ and $\partial_y f=u_y+iv_y$ after transport back to $U$.

At a point where the four real partial derivatives exist, define

$$ \partial_z f:=\frac12(\partial_x f-i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x+v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x-u_y), $$

$$ \partial_{\bar z}f:=\frac12(\partial_x f+i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x-v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x+u_y). $$

Real total differentiability means total differentiability of $\widetilde f$ under [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with a real-linear derivative as in [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]. Its transported real-linear map $Df$ is supplied by [[thm-complex-coordinate-map-preserves-real-total-differentiability]]. If $f$ is real totally differentiable, put $A=\partial_x f$ and $B=\partial_y f$. The remainder definition along the two coordinate axes gives $Df(1)=A$ and $Df(i)=B$. Real linearity then gives $Df(s+it)=sA+tB$ for real $s,t$, whereas direct expansion of $\frac12(A-iB)(s+it)+\frac12(A+iB)(s-it)$ gives the same expression. Thus

$$ Df(h)=(\partial_z f)h+(\partial_{\bar z}f)\overline h. $$

A real-differentiable map is **antiholomorphic** on $U$ when $\partial_z f=0$ at every point of $U$. Thus its differential is conjugate-linear at every point; no complex differentiability is asserted unless the other Wirtinger derivative also vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]). Read $f$ as a map into $\mathbb R^2$; continuity makes its components locally square integrable. Recall that $W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) means that the components of $f$ admit weak first partial derivatives ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]) in $L^2_{\rm loc}$; equivalently, their almost-everywhere classes have ACL representatives in both coordinate directions whose measurable classical coordinate derivatives belong to $L^2_{\rm loc}$ ([[def-absolute-continuity-on-almost-every-coordinate-line]], [[thm-acl-characterisation-of-w-one-p]]). ACL alone does not assert this derivative integrability. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is included in AC for the completed-product Fubini interfaces. On almost every coordinate line the continuous map $f$ agrees almost everywhere with its ACL representative, hence everywhere by continuity of both restrictions; its classical line derivatives then represent its weak derivatives.

Let $K\ge1$ and put $k=(K-1)/(K+1)\in[0,1)$. The homeomorphism $f$ is **$K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense** when

(A1) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$; and

(A2) its weak Wirtinger derivatives $\partial_zf,\partial_{\bar z}f$ ([[def-wirtinger-derivatives]]) lie in $L^2_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ and satisfy
$$|\partial_{\bar z}f(z)|\le k|\partial_zf(z)|\qquad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$

The inequality is a statement about $L^2_{\rm loc}$ classes: it is independent of the choice of representative of $f$ and of the Borel representatives of its weak Wirtinger derivatives, since each such representative agrees almost everywhere with its class ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]]). The map is **analytically quasiconformal** if it is $K$-analytically quasiconformal for some finite $K$. Its minimal constant is recovered from the Beltrami coefficient defined later on this page.

**Orientation and the regularity requirement.** Inequality (A2) gives $J_f=|\partial_zf|^2-|\partial_{\bar z}f|^2\ge(1-k^2)|\partial_zf|^2\ge0$ almost everywhere, with respect to planar Lebesgue measure ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). A classical derivative inequality alone does not replace (A1): on $(0,1)^2$, the map $f(x+iy)=x+g(x)+iy$, where $g$ is the Cantor function, is a homeomorphism onto $(0,2)\times(0,1)$ ([[lem-x-plus-the-cantor-function-is-a-homeomorphism-from-zero-one-onto-zero-two]]). The Cantor function is continuous, nonconstant, and locally constant off the null Cantor set, so $g'=0$ almost everywhere ([[thm-cantor-function-properties]], [[cor-cantor-set-is-an-uncountable-lebesgue-null-set]]). Thus the classical Wirtinger derivatives are $\partial_zf=1$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere. But $g$ cannot be absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $(0,1)$: the fundamental theorem would make it constant there, and then continuity would contradict $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=1$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]). Subtracting the identity shows that $f$ fails ACL on every horizontal line and therefore fails (A1). Its classical inequality is not the weak-derivative assertion (A2). Orientation preservation follows from (A1) together with (A2), as proved by the equivalence theorem on this page.

derivations.claim: Define the locally finite Borel measure $\omega(E)=\operatorname{area}(h(E))$. This is a measure because a homeomorphism maps disjoint Borel sets to disjoint Borel sets and respects unions. It is Radon because it is the pushforward of planar area by the homeomorphism $h^{-1}$; compact and open approximation transport through that homeomorphism. The open image $h(B(x,r))$ contains $B(h(x),l(x,r))$: otherwise a segment from $h(x)$ to a point of that smaller disk outside the image would first meet the boundary $h(\partial B(x,r))$, contradicting the definition of $l$. The maximum distance from $h(x)$ in $h(\overline{B(x,r)})$ occurs on its boundary, because distance from a fixed point has no maximum in a nonempty open set. Hence $|h(y)-h(x)|\le L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for $y\in\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\pi l(x,r)^2\le\omega(B(x,r))$.

For $x\in V$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, use step 1.1 with radius $2|t|$ to obtain $|h(x+te_i)-h(x)|^2\le(H^2/\pi)\omega(B(x,2|t|))$. These balls lie in $U$. Tonelli, applied to their incidence indicator, gives $\int_V\omega(B(x,2|t|))\,dx=\int_U|V\cap B(y,2|t|)|\,d\omega(y)\le4\pi t^2\omega(U)$. Combining the two inequalities proves the explicit difference-quotient estimate. All measures in this calculation are locally finite Radon measures and the incidence set is open, so no absolute continuity or null-set preservation of $h$ has been presumed.

Continuity makes $h$ square integrable on every relatively compact $U$. The uniform estimate in step 2.1 and [F1], with $p=2$ and complex-valued functions, give $h\in W^{1,2}(V)$. Exhausting the plane proves local Sobolev regularity. Apply [F2] on a countable collection of rectangles. On almost every coordinate line, its ACL representative agrees with the continuous representative almost everywhere by Fubini, hence everywhere on each compact line interval because both are continuous there. Thus the actual map $h$ is ACL and has finite coordinate partial derivatives almost everywhere, agreeing with the weak derivatives.

By the general-homeomorphism interface [F3], $h$ is totally differentiable almost everywhere. At such a point $x$, write $h(x+v)=h(x)+Av+o(|v|)$; the remainder is uniform over $|v|=r$ after division by $r$. If $A$ has rank one, there are unit vectors $u,v$ with $Au=0$ and $|Av|>0$. Then $l(x,r)=o(r)$ whereas $L(x,r)\ge r|Av|+o(r)$, contradicting the finite circular bound. If $A$ is nonsingular with singular values $s_1\ge s_2>0$, the same uniform expansion gives $L(x,r)/r\to s_1$ and $l(x,r)/r\to s_2$, so $s_1/s_2\le H$. Its determinant is positive by [F3], since $h$ preserves orientation. The remaining possibility is $A=0$.

At almost every point the classical partials of the total derivative equal the weak derivatives by step 3.1. At the nonsingular points, [F5] and step 4.1 give $|h_{\bar z}|/|h_z|\le(H-1)/(H+1)$; at zero derivatives the asserted inequality also holds. Together with $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and ACL regularity, this is exactly analytic $H$-quasiconformality. The proof uses only the locally proved total-differentiability interface [F3]; it does not invoke an infinitesimal metric-to-quasiconformal criterion.

boundaries.evidence: Zero cusp ends are permitted: compact quotients have no rank-two abelian subgroup because a proper horocusp cannot embed into a compact space. Proof, step 1.1: Each supplied cusp group $P_i$ is the full stabilizer of its ideal point. By [F1] the full stabilizer is a translation lattice $Q_i$ containing $P_i$. Every translation in $Q_i$ preserves the entire source horoball. If some were outside $P_i$, two points of that horoball distinct modulo $P_i$ would have the same image in $M$, contradicting the supplied cusp embedding. Thus $P_i=Q_i$, and [F1] makes it maximal abelian. Conversely, let $A$ be any maximal abelian rank-two subgroup. Its proper embedded horocusp from [F1] has a connected tail missing the given compact core: properness makes its inverse image of that core compact. That tail lies in one of the finitely many supplied cusp components. Its inclusion on fundamental groups therefore puts $A$, up to conjugacy, inside that component's $P_i$. Maximality gives equality. In the compact case such a proper horocusp is impossible, so no rank-two abelian subgroup occurs. An isomorphism preserves abelianness, rank two and maximality, proving the peripheral assertion in both directions. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

On sufficiently deep tails the composite displacement is exactly zero, not merely asymptotically bounded. Proof, step 4.1: The composites $GF$ and $FG$ are the identity on all sufficiently deep cusp tails. On the remaining compact quotient cores their displacement functions $d(GF(x),x)$ and $d(FG(y),y)$ are invariant under the respective deck groups and continuous, so have finite global bounds $D,D'$. If $L_G,L_F\ge1$ are Lipschitz constants, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,x')\le2D+L_Gd(Fx,Fx')$, and similarly in the other direction. Thus $F$ is a quasi-isometric embedding, and $d(FGy,y)\le D'$ proves coarse surjectivity. This proves the quasi-isometry assertion with explicit finite constants obtained from the constructed maps. On the quotients the maps are proper, since on each tail they preserve the depth coordinate and permute the finitely many cusp ends, and their remaining domains lie in compact cores. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

A single cusp is a special case of the same finite permutation and affine lattice construction. Proof, step 2.1: For each matched cusp, choose upper half-space coordinates in source and target so that $\theta(P_i)$ is the corresponding target translation lattice, with any necessary conjugacy included in the choice of its lift. A group isomorphism of the two lattices extends uniquely to an invertible real-linear map $B_i:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$: prescribe its values on a lattice basis. The map $C_i(z,y)=(B_i z,c_i y)$, $c_i=R_i'/R_i>0$, is equivariant and preserves depth $r=\log(y/R_i)$. Its differential and inverse have uniformly bounded hyperbolic operator norms, because horizontal tangent vectors are changed by $B_i/c_i$ and vertical logarithmic tangent vectors are unchanged. Propagate this map to every translate of the chosen horoball by $C_i(\gamma x)=\theta(\gamma)C_i(x)$. Equivariance under $P_i$ makes this independent of the representative of the coset. Disjointness of the lifted cusp interiors makes the resulting map well defined there. These maps for $\theta^{-1}$ can be chosen to be exact inverses on corresponding cusps. The cutoff equals0 below depth1/2 and1 above1; constant endpoint collars make the pasted map smooth. Proof, step 3.1: On each cusp take one fixed smooth function $\chi(r)$ equal to zero for $r\le1/2$ and one for $r\ge1$. AC covers chosen lifted charts and target points; only a finite base cover is used and its deck translates are locally finite. On the remaining compact quotient cores their displacement functions $d(GF(x),x)$ and $d(FG(y),y)$ are invariant under the respective deck groups and continuous, so have finite global bounds $D,D'$. On the quotients the maps are proper, since on each tail they preserve the depth coordinate and permute the finitely many cusp ends, and their remaining domains lie in compact cores. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

No converse says arbitrary quasi-isometries induce an isomorphism of the deck groups; proper homotopy inverses are constructed for this supplied isomorphism. On the quotients these homotopies are proper: the inverse image of a compact target set is contained in the closed $D$ or $D'$ neighborhood of that set in the proper complete hyperbolic quotient, crossed with $[0,1]$. Completeness follows by lifting and extending geodesics in $\mathbb H^3$, and properness is Hopf–Rinow as in [F1]'s proof. Hence the descended maps are proper homotopy equivalences. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Use the upper half-space model $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,y):z\in\mathbb C,y>0\}$ with metric $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free, and suppose that it contains a subgroup $A\cong\mathbb Z^2$. Then $A$ fixes a unique ideal point. After conjugating that point to infinity, its full stabilizer $P=\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\infty)$ consists of translations by a lattice $\Lambda\le\mathbb C$ of rank two. It is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$.

For a sufficiently large $R$, the quotient of the closed horoball $\{y\ge R\}$ by $P$ embeds properly in $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$. Its boundary is a compact torus, its interior is a cusp, and its volume is $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. If $M$ has exactly one topological end, the complement of the open cusp has compact closure.

No finite-volume thin decomposition, abstract peripheral recognition, or rigidity theorem is assumed or concluded here. The rank-two subgroup and the quotient presentation of $M$ are hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Each supplied cusp group $P_i$ is the full stabilizer of its ideal point. By [F1] the full stabilizer is a translation lattice $Q_i$ containing $P_i$. Thus $P_i=Q_i$, and [F1] makes it maximal abelian. Conversely, let $A$ be any maximal abelian rank-two subgroup. We construct a smooth equivariant map on a neighborhood of the lifted compact core, without assuming a homotopy realization theorem. Enlarge the core to include cusp depths $r\le2$. Cover this compact set by finitely many evenly covered coordinate neighborhoods $U_j$ and choose smooth nonnegative bumps $\psi_j$ compactly supported in them whose positive sets cover the enlarged core. Such bumps are obtained by the ordinary explicit Euclidean bump function in smaller chart balls and a finite subcover. Choose one lift $\widetilde U_j$ of each chart. On its translate $\gamma\widetilde U_j$ put $\phi_{\gamma j}(x)=\psi_j(\pi x)$, and extend it by zero. This is smooth, since the bump support stays inside the chart. The family is locally finite: for a fixed $j$ the lifted chart components are disjoint, and over the compact support a sufficiently small evenly covered base neighborhood meets only the corresponding local component near each point. There are only finitely many $j$. Their sum is positive on a neighborhood of the lifted enlarged core.

For each matched cusp, choose upper half-space coordinates in source and target so that $\theta(P_i)$ is the corresponding target translation lattice, with any necessary conjugacy included in the choice of its lift. A group isomorphism of the two lattices extends uniquely to an invertible real-linear map $B_i:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$: prescribe its values on a lattice basis. The map $C_i(z,y)=(B_i z,c_i y)$, $c_i=R_i'/R_i>0$, is equivariant and preserves depth $r=\log(y/R_i)$. Its differential and inverse have uniformly bounded hyperbolic operator norms, because horizontal tangent vectors are changed by $B_i/c_i$ and vertical logarithmic tangent vectors are unchanged. Disjointness of the lifted cusp interiors makes the resulting map well defined there. These maps for $\theta^{-1}$ can be chosen to be exact inverses on corresponding cusps.

Use the hyperboloid model $\{v\in\mathbb R^{3,1}:\langle v,v\rangle=-1,v_0>0\}$ for the target. The usual upper half-space identification is $$ (z,y)\longmapsto \left(\frac{|z|^2+y^2+1}{2y},\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{y},\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{y},\frac{|z|^2+y^2-1}{2y}\right). $$ Its pullback metric is $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$ by differentiation. Hyperbolic isometries act by Lorentz-linear maps: the upper half-space translations, rotations, dilations and inversion give Lorentz maps in this formula by substitution, and generate the Möbius group by matrix fraction division. Fix target points $p_j$ and put $S(x)=\sum_{\gamma,j}\phi_{\gamma j}(x)\theta(\gamma)p_j$. This sum is locally finite and future timelike. Indeed, for future unit vectors $v,w$, $-\langle v,w\rangle\ge1$ by the distance formula, so for nonnegative weights $a_j$ with positive sum one has $-\langle\sum a_jv_j,\sum a_jv_j\rangle\ge(\sum a_j)^2>0$. Thus $F_0(x)=S(x)/\sqrt{-\langle S(x),S(x)\rangle}$ is smooth. Reindexing the sum gives $F_0(\gamma x)=\theta(\gamma)F_0(x)$.

On each cusp take one fixed smooth function $\chi(r)$ equal to zero for $r\le1/2$ and one for $r\ge1$. Where both $F_0$ and $C_i$ are defined, normalize their future-timelike linear combination $(1-\chi)F_0+\chi C_i$ as in step 2.2. Use $F_0$ below that overlap and $C_i$ above it. Constancy of the cutoff near its endpoints gives a smooth global map $F$, and all formulas are equivariant. On the compact quotient of the region outside the deep cusp tails, its derivative norm has a finite maximum by continuity. On the tails it is bounded by the finitely many affine constants in step 2.1. Integrating the derivative bound along hyperbolic segments proves that $F$ is globally Lipschitz. Repeating the construction for $\theta^{-1}$, with the inverse affine cusp maps, gives a globally Lipschitz map $G$.

The composites $GF$ and $FG$ are the identity on all sufficiently deep cusp tails. On the remaining compact quotient cores their displacement functions $d(GF(x),x)$ and $d(FG(y),y)$ are invariant under the respective deck groups and continuous, so have finite global bounds $D,D'$. If $L_G,L_F\ge1$ are Lipschitz constants, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,x')\le2D+L_Gd(Fx,Fx')$, and similarly in the other direction. Thus $F$ is a quasi-isometric embedding, and $d(FGy,y)\le D'$ proves coarse surjectivity. This proves the quasi-isometry assertion with explicit finite constants obtained from the constructed maps. On the quotients the maps are proper, since on each tail they preserve the depth coordinate and permute the finitely many cusp ends, and their remaining domains lie in compact cores.

Unique hyperbolic geodesics give an equivariant homotopy from $GF$ to the identity and from $FG$ to the identity. Their tracks have length at most $D,D'$. On the quotients these homotopies are proper: the inverse image of a compact target set is contained in the closed $D$ or $D'$ neighborhood of that set in the proper complete hyperbolic quotient, crossed with $[0,1]$. Completeness follows by lifting and extending geodesics in $\mathbb H^3$, and properness is Hopf–Rinow as in [F1]'s proof. Hence the descended maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

Propagate this map to every translate of the chosen horoball by $C_i(\gamma x)=\theta(\gamma)C_i(x)$. Equivariance under $P_i$ makes this independent of the representative of the coset. Disjointness of the lifted cusp interiors makes the resulting map well defined there. These maps for $\theta^{-1}$ can be chosen to be exact inverses on corresponding cusps. [A1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The lattice isomorphism has an invertible real-linear extension; a singular horizontal map is excluded by the group-isomorphism hypothesis. Proof, step 2.1: For each matched cusp, choose upper half-space coordinates in source and target so that $\theta(P_i)$ is the corresponding target translation lattice, with any necessary conjugacy included in the choice of its lift. A group isomorphism of the two lattices extends uniquely to an invertible real-linear map $B_i:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$: prescribe its values on a lattice basis. The map $C_i(z,y)=(B_i z,c_i y)$, $c_i=R_i'/R_i>0$, is equivariant and preserves depth $r=\log(y/R_i)$. Its differential and inverse have uniformly bounded hyperbolic operator norms, because horizontal tangent vectors are changed by $B_i/c_i$ and vertical logarithmic tangent vectors are unchanged. Propagate this map to every translate of the chosen horoball by $C_i(\gamma x)=\theta(\gamma)C_i(x)$. Equivariance under $P_i$ makes this independent of the representative of the coset. Disjointness of the lifted cusp interiors makes the resulting map well defined there. These maps for $\theta^{-1}$ can be chosen to be exact inverses on corresponding cusps. [A1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The cutoff equals0 below depth1/2 and1 above1; constant endpoint collars make the pasted map smooth. Proof, step 3.1: On each cusp take one fixed smooth function $\chi(r)$ equal to zero for $r\le1/2$ and one for $r\ge1$. Where both $F_0$ and $C_i$ are defined, normalize their future-timelike linear combination $(1-\chi)F_0+\chi C_i$ as in step 2.2. Use $F_0$ below that overlap and $C_i$ above it. Constancy of the cutoff near its endpoints gives a smooth global map $F$, and all formulas are equivariant. On the compact quotient of the region outside the deep cusp tails, its derivative norm has a finite maximum by continuity. On the tails it is bounded by the finitely many affine constants in step 2.1. Integrating the derivative bound along hyperbolic segments proves that $F$ is globally Lipschitz. Repeating the construction for $\theta^{-1}$, with the inverse affine cusp maps, gives a globally Lipschitz map $G$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

AC covers chosen lifted charts and target points; only a finite base cover is used and its deck translates are locally finite. Proof, step 1.2: We construct a smooth equivariant map on a neighborhood of the lifted compact core, without assuming a homotopy realization theorem. Enlarge the core to include cusp depths $r\le2$. Cover this compact set by finitely many evenly covered coordinate neighborhoods $U_j$ and choose smooth nonnegative bumps $\psi_j$ compactly supported in them whose positive sets cover the enlarged core. Such bumps are obtained by the ordinary explicit Euclidean bump function in smaller chart balls and a finite subcover. Choose one lift $\widetilde U_j$ of each chart. On its translate $\gamma\widetilde U_j$ put $\phi_{\gamma j}(x)=\psi_j(\pi x)$, and extend it by zero. This is smooth, since the bump support stays inside the chart. The family is locally finite: for a fixed $j$ the lifted chart components are disjoint, and over the compact support a sufficiently small evenly covered base neighborhood meets only the corresponding local component near each point. There are only finitely many $j$. Their sum is positive on a neighborhood of the lifted enlarged core. [A1, given, construct]

A group isomorphism gives peripheral preservation, explicit affine ends and an equivariant quasi-isometry. Proof, step 4.1: The composites $GF$ and $FG$ are the identity on all sufficiently deep cusp tails. On the remaining compact quotient cores their displacement functions $d(GF(x),x)$ and $d(FG(y),y)$ are invariant under the respective deck groups and continuous, so have finite global bounds $D,D'$. If $L_G,L_F\ge1$ are Lipschitz constants, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,x')\le2D+L_Gd(Fx,Fx')$, and similarly in the other direction. Thus $F$ is a quasi-isometric embedding, and $d(FGy,y)\le D'$ proves coarse surjectivity. This proves the quasi-isometry assertion with explicit finite constants obtained from the constructed maps. On the quotients the maps are proper, since on each tail they preserve the depth coordinate and permute the finitely many cusp ends, and their remaining domains lie in compact cores. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

No converse says arbitrary quasi-isometries induce an isomorphism of the deck groups; proper homotopy inverses are constructed for this supplied isomorphism. Proof, step 5.1: Unique hyperbolic geodesics give an equivariant homotopy from $GF$ to the identity and from $FG$ to the identity. Their tracks have length at most $D,D'$. On the quotients these homotopies are proper: the inverse image of a compact target set is contained in the closed $D$ or $D'$ neighborhood of that set in the proper complete hyperbolic quotient, crossed with $[0,1]$. Completeness follows by lifting and extending geodesics in $\mathbb H^3$, and properness is Hopf–Rinow as in [F1]'s proof. Hence the descended maps are proper homotopy equivalences. [F1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Use the upper half-space model $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,y):z\in\mathbb C,y>0\}$ with metric $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free, and suppose that it contains a subgroup $A\cong\mathbb Z^2$. Then $A$ fixes a unique ideal point. After conjugating that point to infinity, its full stabilizer $P=\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\infty)$ consists of translations by a lattice $\Lambda\le\mathbb C$ of rank two. It is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$.

For a sufficiently large $R$, the quotient of the closed horoball $\{y\ge R\}$ by $P$ embeds properly in $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$. Its boundary is a compact torus, its interior is a cusp, and its volume is $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. If $M$ has exactly one topological end, the complement of the open cusp has compact closure.

No finite-volume thin decomposition, abstract peripheral recognition, or rigidity theorem is assumed or concluded here. The rank-two subgroup and the quotient presentation of $M$ are hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Each supplied cusp group $P_i$ is the full stabilizer of its ideal point. By [F1] the full stabilizer is a translation lattice $Q_i$ containing $P_i$. Every translation in $Q_i$ preserves the entire source horoball. If some were outside $P_i$, two points of that horoball distinct modulo $P_i$ would have the same image in $M$, contradicting the supplied cusp embedding. Thus $P_i=Q_i$, and [F1] makes it maximal abelian. Conversely, let $A$ be any maximal abelian rank-two subgroup. Its proper embedded horocusp from [F1] has a connected tail missing the given compact core: properness makes its inverse image of that core compact. That tail lies in one of the finitely many supplied cusp components. Its inclusion on fundamental groups therefore puts $A$, up to conjugacy, inside that component's $P_i$. Maximality gives equality. In the compact case such a proper horocusp is impossible, so no rank-two abelian subgroup occurs. An isomorphism preserves abelianness, rank two and maximality, proving the peripheral assertion in both directions.

We construct a smooth equivariant map on a neighborhood of the lifted compact core, without assuming a homotopy realization theorem. Enlarge the core to include cusp depths $r\le2$. Cover this compact set by finitely many evenly covered coordinate neighborhoods $U_j$ and choose smooth nonnegative bumps $\psi_j$ compactly supported in them whose positive sets cover the enlarged core. The family is locally finite: for a fixed $j$ the lifted chart components are disjoint, and over the compact support a sufficiently small evenly covered base neighborhood meets only the corresponding local component near each point. There are only finitely many $j$. Their sum is positive on a neighborhood of the lifted enlarged core.

For each matched cusp, choose upper half-space coordinates in source and target so that $\theta(P_i)$ is the corresponding target translation lattice, with any necessary conjugacy included in the choice of its lift. A group isomorphism of the two lattices extends uniquely to an invertible real-linear map $B_i:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$: prescribe its values on a lattice basis. The map $C_i(z,y)=(B_i z,c_i y)$, $c_i=R_i'/R_i>0$, is equivariant and preserves depth $r=\log(y/R_i)$. Its differential and inverse have uniformly bounded hyperbolic operator norms, because horizontal tangent vectors are changed by $B_i/c_i$ and vertical logarithmic tangent vectors are unchanged. Propagate this map to every translate of the chosen horoball by $C_i(\gamma x)=\theta(\gamma)C_i(x)$. Equivariance under $P_i$ makes this independent of the representative of the coset. Disjointness of the lifted cusp interiors makes the resulting map well defined there. These maps for $\theta^{-1}$ can be chosen to be exact inverses on corresponding cusps.

Use the hyperboloid model $\{v\in\mathbb R^{3,1}:\langle v,v\rangle=-1,v_0>0\}$ for the target. The usual upper half-space identification is $$ (z,y)\longmapsto \left(\frac{|z|^2+y^2+1}{2y},\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{y},\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{y},\frac{|z|^2+y^2-1}{2y}\right). $$ Its pullback metric is $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$ by differentiation. Hyperbolic isometries act by Lorentz-linear maps: the upper half-space translations, rotations, dilations and inversion give Lorentz maps in this formula by substitution, and generate the Möbius group by matrix fraction division. Fix target points $p_j$ and put $S(x)=\sum_{\gamma,j}\phi_{\gamma j}(x)\theta(\gamma)p_j$. This sum is locally finite and future timelike. Indeed, for future unit vectors $v,w$, $-\langle v,w\rangle\ge1$ by the distance formula, so for nonnegative weights $a_j$ with positive sum one has $-\langle\sum a_jv_j,\sum a_jv_j\rangle\ge(\sum a_j)^2>0$. Thus $F_0(x)=S(x)/\sqrt{-\langle S(x),S(x)\rangle}$ is smooth. Reindexing the sum gives $F_0(\gamma x)=\theta(\gamma)F_0(x)$.

On each cusp take one fixed smooth function $\chi(r)$ equal to zero for $r\le1/2$ and one for $r\ge1$. Where both $F_0$ and $C_i$ are defined, normalize their future-timelike linear combination $(1-\chi)F_0+\chi C_i$ as in step 2.2. Use $F_0$ below that overlap and $C_i$ above it. Constancy of the cutoff near its endpoints gives a smooth global map $F$, and all formulas are equivariant. On the compact quotient of the region outside the deep cusp tails, its derivative norm has a finite maximum by continuity. On the tails it is bounded by the finitely many affine constants in step 2.1. Integrating the derivative bound along hyperbolic segments proves that $F$ is globally Lipschitz. Repeating the construction for $\theta^{-1}$, with the inverse affine cusp maps, gives a globally Lipschitz map $G$.

The composites $GF$ and $FG$ are the identity on all sufficiently deep cusp tails. On the remaining compact quotient cores their displacement functions $d(GF(x),x)$ and $d(FG(y),y)$ are invariant under the respective deck groups and continuous, so have finite global bounds $D,D'$. If $L_G,L_F\ge1$ are Lipschitz constants, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,x')\le2D+L_Gd(Fx,Fx')$, and similarly in the other direction. Thus $F$ is a quasi-isometric embedding, and $d(FGy,y)\le D'$ proves coarse surjectivity. This proves the quasi-isometry assertion with explicit finite constants obtained from the constructed maps. On the quotients the maps are proper, since on each tail they preserve the depth coordinate and permute the finitely many cusp ends, and their remaining domains lie in compact cores.

Unique hyperbolic geodesics give an equivariant homotopy from $GF$ to the identity and from $FG$ to the identity. Their tracks have length at most $D,D'$. On the quotients these homotopies are proper: the inverse image of a compact target set is contained in the closed $D$ or $D'$ neighborhood of that set in the proper complete hyperbolic quotient, crossed with $[0,1]$. Completeness follows by lifting and extending geodesics in $\mathbb H^3$, and properness is Hopf–Rinow as in [F1]'s proof. Hence the descended maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

boundaries.evidence: The source and target are nonemptyH3; the induced boundary is the full ideal sphere, not an assumed ray subspace. Proof, step 3.1: By [F2] and step 2.1, $f$ induces a homeomorphism of sequence boundaries. In this model that boundary is the ordinary ideal sphere. For precision, in the ball every geodesic ray from the origin is radial by step 1.1 and is parameterized as $u(r)=\tanh(r/2)\omega$, $|\omega|=1$. Substitution in the distance formula gives the product limit $(\omega|\omega')_0=-\log(|\omega-\omega'|/2)$ for distinct unit vectors and infinity for equal ones. Thus its product topology is the ordinary sphere topology, and finite-distance asymptotic rays have the same endpoint. By properness and [F2], every sequence-boundary class has a ray representative, and the uniform-on-bounded-interval topology of the radial rays is the ordinary topology of their unit endpoints. Consequently [F2]'s extension is exactly the ideal-boundary homeomorphism, and $x_n\to a$ ideally implies $f(x_n)\to h(a)$ whenever $(x_n)$ runs to infinity along a geodesic ray. [A1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

An isometry with identity boundary action fixes intersections of complete geodesics and is the identity. Proof, step 1.1: We first give the model geometry used below. Translations, complex rotations and positive dilations act by $(z,s)\mapsto(az+b,|a|s)$ and preserve the metric by substitution. Euclidean inversion in the unit sphere, followed by reflection in a vertical plane, is $(z,s)\mapsto(-\overline z/(|z|^2+s^2),s/(|z|^2+s^2))$ and extends $z\mapsto-1/z$. Its Euclidean differential scales lengths by $(|z|^2+s^2)^{-1}$, while its height scales by the same factor, so it also preserves the hyperbolic metric. These maps generate all Möbius transformations: a matrix with nonzero lower-left entry gives a translation, an inversion, a complex dilation and a translation by elementary fraction division; a zero lower-left entry gives an affine map. Thus every boundary Möbius transformation extends to an isometry. The Cayley map $T(z,s)=(2\operatorname{Re}z,2\operatorname{Im}z,|z|^2+s^2-1)/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ is a bijection onto the unit ball, with inverse $z=2(u_1+iu_2)/Q$, $s=(1-|u|^2)/Q$, $Q=u_1^2+u_2^2+(1-u_3)^2$. It carries $(0,1)$ to the origin and gives metric $4|du|^2/(1-|u|^2)^2$: its Euclidean length factor is $2/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ and $1-|T|^2=4s/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$. Radial integration in the ball, together with $|(|u|)'|\le|u'|$ on every competing path, gives distance $2\operatorname{artanh}|u|$ from the origin. Applying the affine normalization of a general basepoint yields $\cosh d((z,s),(w,t))=\frac{|z-w|^2+s^2+t^2}{2st}.$ Equality in that radial length argument characterizes the radial segment. Its inverse Cayley image shows that geodesics are the vertical lines and the Euclidean semicircles orthogonal to the boundary. In particular geodesics are unique, closed bounded hyperbolic balls are compact by the displayed formula, and the ideal endpoints of a complete geodesic are its distinct Euclidean boundary endpoints. A complete geodesic is uniquely determined by those endpoints. Consequently an isometry with identity boundary action preserves every complete geodesic and fixes the intersection of two distinct complete geodesics through each point; it is the identity. Thus the Möbius extension constructed above is unique. [given, algebra]

The exact equal-circle source-center comparison uses arcosh(5/3)=log3 and includes all positive radii. Proof, step 7.1: Postcompose $f$ by the isometry extending a Möbius transformation that sends $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$; its quasi-isometry constants do not change. The normalized boundary map restricts to a plane homeomorphism. For distinct finite $z,a$, the center of $(z,a,\infty)$ is $c(z,a)=((z+a)/2,\sqrt3|a-z|/2),$ by the affine isometry in step 1.1. If $|a-z|=|b-z|=r$, these two source centers have equal height $\sqrt3r/2$ and horizontal separation at most $r$. Their distance is at most $\operatorname{arcosh}(5/3)=\log3$ by the distance formula. Step 6.1 and the quasi-isometry inequality give $d(c(hz,ha),c(hz,hb))\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon$. Height logarithms differ by at most hyperbolic distance, so $\left|\log\frac{|h(a)-h(z)|}{|h(b)-h(z)|}\right|\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon.$ The compact source circle maps injectively to a compact curve missing $h(z)$, so its maximum and positive minimum exist. Taking them in this inequality proves the claimed all-circle bound with $H=\exp(2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon)$. This establishes a bounded equal-radius distortion, not merely a Hölder bound. [step 1.1, step 6.1, algebra]

Degenerate finite triangles are0-slim; nondegenerate triangles use their positive half-disk area. Proof, step 2.1: Every geodesic triangle lies in a totally geodesic hyperbolic plane. To see this, send one vertex to the center of the ball by the isometries in step 1.1; the two other vertices and that center lie in a Euclidean plane through the center. Reflection in that plane is a ball isometry, and uniqueness of geodesics makes its fixed plane totally geodesic. In its upper-half-plane coordinates $(x,y)$, the Christoffel formula [F3] gives $\Gamma^x_{xy}=\Gamma^x_{yx}=-1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{xx}=1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{yy}=-1/y$, and all other symbols zero. Thus for the global positive orthonormal frame $e_1=y\partial_x$, $e_2=y\partial_y$, one has $
abla_{e_1}e_1=e_2$, $
abla_{e_1}e_2=-e_1$, $
abla_{e_2}e_1=
abla_{e_2}e_2=0$ and $[e_1,e_2]=-e_1$. Consequently $R(e_1,e_2)e_2=-e_1$ and $K=-1$. A noncollinear finite triangle bounds a compact regular disk with three embedded geodesic edges and ordinary corners: its sides are the unique segments in the three geodesic half-planes, and distinct sides meet transversely at their vertices. The global frame supplies the neighbourhood required by [F3]. Gauss–Bonnet therefore gives its area $A=\pi-(\alpha+ eta+\gamma)<\pi$, since all three interior angles are positive. The area density of the displayed metric is $y^{-2}dx\,dy$. On this plane a radius-$r$ hyperbolic disk has area $2\pi(\cosh r-1)$: in the disk metric the Euclidean radius is $R=	anh(r/2)$, and integrating $4ho(1-ho^2)^{-2}\,dho\,d	heta$ gives $4\pi R^2/(1-R^2)=2\pi(\cosh r-1)$. Fix a point $p$ on one side of a nondegenerate finite triangle, and let $d_0$ be its distance to the union of the other sides. If $r<d_0$, the half-disk of radius $r$ on the interior side of the first edge is contained in the triangle. Indeed, a radial geodesic from $p$ to a point of that half-disk stays in the interior edge half-plane and would otherwise first exit across one of the other two actual edges at distance less than $d_0$. Its area is $\pi(\cosh r-1)$, while the triangle has area less than $\pi$ by [F3]. Hence $r\le\operatorname{arcosh}2$ for every $r<d_0$, giving $d_0\le\delta:=\operatorname{arcosh}2$. Degenerate triangles are $0$-slim. This proves uniform $\delta$-slimness of $\mathbb H^3$ locally, without using an external hyperbolicity assertion. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Two normalized plane charts cover the omitted ideal point as well; orientation reversal is handled by a reflection. Proof, step 8.1: If $h$ preserves orientation, apply [F4] to the plane map in step 7.1 to obtain analytic $H$-quasiconformality. To cover the omitted source point as well, choose a different omitted point $q$ and choose Möbius transformations $S,T$ taking $q,h(q)$ respectively to $\infty$, and replace $f$ by $T\circ f\circ S^{-1}$. The isometries in step 1.1 preserve the same quasi-isometry constants, so steps 4.1–7.1 and [F4] apply in this second plane chart with the same $H$. The two charts cover the sphere. If $h$ reverses orientation, postcompose by complex conjugation; its upper-half-space extension is a reflection isometry, and its composition with $h$ preserves orientation, so the same argument applies. Finally equivariance follows either by taking ideal limits along rays or by the composition property in [F2]; the exact equality $f\gamma=\theta(\gamma)f$ implies $h\gamma=\theta(\gamma)h$. [A1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

The center uses a unique Mobius map of an ordered ideal triple; AC is retained for the Morse/boundary suppliers. Proof, step 5.1: For an ordered ideal triangle $\tau=(a,b,c)$ define $c_\tau$ by applying the unique boundary Möbius transformation taking $(0,1,\infty)$ to $(a,b,c)$ to $c_0=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$ in the real vertical plane; use its isometric extension from step 1.1. Existence and uniqueness follow explicitly from the fractional linear expression sending $a,b,c$ to $0,1,\infty$. The center $c_0$ is at distance $r_0=\log\sqrt3$ from each of its three complete sides: for the vertical lines the distance formula minimizes to $\operatorname{arsinh}((1/2)/(\sqrt3/2))=\log\sqrt3$, and for the semicircle with endpoints $0,1$ the normal is the vertical line through $1/2$, giving $\log((\sqrt3/2)/(1/2))=\log\sqrt3$. Thus every $c_\tau$ has distance $r_0$ from each side. By step 4.1 and the upper quasi-isometry bound, $f(c_\tau)$ is within $D=\max\{1,\lambda r_0+\varepsilon+M\}$ of each side of the target triangle $h\tau$. [step 1.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

The quasi-isometry gives a uniform all-circle distortion bound, then the proved planar lemma yields analytic quasiconformality. Proof, step 7.1: Postcompose $f$ by the isometry extending a Möbius transformation that sends $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$; its quasi-isometry constants do not change. The normalized boundary map restricts to a plane homeomorphism. For distinct finite $z,a$, the center of $(z,a,\infty)$ is $c(z,a)=((z+a)/2,\sqrt3|a-z|/2),$ by the affine isometry in step 1.1. If $|a-z|=|b-z|=r$, these two source centers have equal height $\sqrt3r/2$ and horizontal separation at most $r$. Their distance is at most $\operatorname{arcosh}(5/3)=\log3$ by the distance formula. Step 6.1 and the quasi-isometry inequality give $d(c(hz,ha),c(hz,hb))\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon$. Height logarithms differ by at most hyperbolic distance, so $\left|\log\frac{|h(a)-h(z)|}{|h(b)-h(z)|}\right|\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon.$ The compact source circle maps injectively to a compact curve missing $h(z)$, so its maximum and positive minimum exist. Taking them in this inequality proves the claimed all-circle bound with $H=\exp(2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon)$. This establishes a bounded equal-radius distortion, not merely a Hölder bound. [step 1.1, step 6.1, algebra]

No converse extension theorem for an arbitrary boundary quasiconformal map is asserted. Proof, step 8.1: If $h$ preserves orientation, apply [F4] to the plane map in step 7.1 to obtain analytic $H$-quasiconformality. To cover the omitted source point as well, choose a different omitted point $q$ and choose Möbius transformations $S,T$ taking $q,h(q)$ respectively to $\infty$, and replace $f$ by $T\circ f\circ S^{-1}$. The isometries in step 1.1 preserve the same quasi-isometry constants, so steps 4.1–7.1 and [F4] apply in this second plane chart with the same $H$. The two charts cover the sphere. If $h$ reverses orientation, postcompose by complex conjugation; its upper-half-space extension is a reflection isometry, and its composition with $h$ preserves orientation, so the same argument applies. Finally equivariance follows either by taking ideal limits along rays or by the composition property in [F2]; the exact equality $f\gamma=\theta(\gamma)f$ implies $h\gamma=\theta(\gamma)h$. [A1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the projection-family proof below. For $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\delta\ge0$, the image of every possibly discontinuous $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic map of a nonempty compact real interval into a geodesic $\delta$-slim space has Hausdorff distance at most
$$M=92\lambda^2(\varepsilon+3\delta)$$
from every geodesic with the same endpoints. No properness is assumed.

Assume AC for the Morse/coarse-inverse proof. A quasi-isometry between geodesic hyperbolic spaces induces a homeomorphism of their Gromov-sequence boundaries; bounded-distance maps induce the same map and extensions respect composition. Properness is needed for the compact ray-boundary package, not imposed on this sequence statement.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty proper geodesic space with a product hyperbolicity constant $\kappa\ge0$, and fix $o\in X$. Proper means every closed ball of positive finite radius is compact. Every Gromov-sequence class has a geodesic ray representative $r:[0,\infty)\to X$ with $r(0)=o$, represented by $(r(n))_{n\ge1}$. The quotient of these rays by finite Hausdorff distance, with the topology induced from uniform convergence on bounded parameter intervals, is homeomorphic to the Gromov-sequence boundary with its product topology. In particular the boundary is compact, including when it is empty.

In coordinates for a Riemannian metric with matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, its Levi–Civita symbols are
$$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_\ell g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij}).$$

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $(M,g,J)$ be an oriented Riemannian surface and let $T\subseteq M$ be a
compact regular oriented disk region with exactly three vertices whose boundary
is the cyclic concatenation of three regular $C^2$ embedded geodesic segments
of the interior metric; at each vertex the incoming and outgoing one-sided unit
tangents are not antipodal. Suppose that a neighbourhood of $T$ carries a
smooth positive orthonormal frame and that $T$ is positively oriented as a disk
region. If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in(0,2\pi)$ are the interior sector angles at
the three vertices, then

$$\int_TK\,dA=\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\pi .$$

The boundary orientation is the outward-normal-first orientation of
[[def-regular-oriented-surface-region-with-piecewise-smooth-boundary]], and no
claim is made about the existence of such a triangle on a general surface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $h:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism. For $x\in\mathbb C$ and $r>0$, put $L(x,r)=\max_{|y-x|=r}|h(y)-h(x)|$ and $l(x,r)=\min_{|y-x|=r}|h(y)-h(x)|$. Suppose $L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for every $x,r$, with one fixed $1\le H<\infty$. Then $h\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, its continuous representative is ACL, and it is analytically $H$-quasiconformal:
$$|h_{\bar z}|\le\frac{H-1}{H+1}|h_z|\quad\hbox{almost everywhere}.$$
For relatively compact open sets $V\Subset U\Subset\mathbb C$, a coordinate unit vector $e_i$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, one has the explicit estimate
$$\int_V\left|\frac{h(x+te_i)-h(x)}t\right|^2\,dx\le4H^2\operatorname{area}(h(U)).$$

derivations.claim: We first give the model geometry used below. Translations, complex rotations and positive dilations act by $(z,s)\mapsto(az+b,|a|s)$ and preserve the metric by substitution. Euclidean inversion in the unit sphere, followed by reflection in a vertical plane, is $(z,s)\mapsto(-\overline z/(|z|^2+s^2),s/(|z|^2+s^2))$ and extends $z\mapsto-1/z$. Its Euclidean differential scales lengths by $(|z|^2+s^2)^{-1}$, while its height scales by the same factor, so it also preserves the hyperbolic metric. These maps generate all Möbius transformations: a matrix with nonzero lower-left entry gives a translation, an inversion, a complex dilation and a translation by elementary fraction division; a zero lower-left entry gives an affine map. Thus every boundary Möbius transformation extends to an isometry. The Cayley map $T(z,s)=(2\operatorname{Re}z,2\operatorname{Im}z,|z|^2+s^2-1)/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ is a bijection onto the unit ball, with inverse $z=2(u_1+iu_2)/Q$, $s=(1-|u|^2)/Q$, $Q=u_1^2+u_2^2+(1-u_3)^2$. It carries $(0,1)$ to the origin and gives metric $4|du|^2/(1-|u|^2)^2$: its Euclidean length factor is $2/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ and $1-|T|^2=4s/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$. Radial integration in the ball, together with $|(|u|)'|\le|u'|$ on every competing path, gives distance $2\operatorname{artanh}|u|$ from the origin. Applying the affine normalization of a general basepoint yields $\cosh d((z,s),(w,t))=\frac{|z-w|^2+s^2+t^2}{2st}.$ Equality in that radial length argument characterizes the radial segment. Its inverse Cayley image shows that geodesics are the vertical lines and the Euclidean semicircles orthogonal to the boundary. In particular geodesics are unique, closed bounded hyperbolic balls are compact by the displayed formula, and the ideal endpoints of a complete geodesic are its distinct Euclidean boundary endpoints. A complete geodesic is uniquely determined by those endpoints. Consequently an isometry with identity boundary action preserves every complete geodesic and fixes the intersection of two distinct complete geodesics through each point; it is the identity. Thus the Möbius extension constructed above is unique.

Every geodesic triangle lies in a totally geodesic hyperbolic plane. To see this, send one vertex to the center of the ball by the isometries in step 1.1; the two other vertices and that center lie in a Euclidean plane through the center. Reflection in that plane is a ball isometry, and uniqueness of geodesics makes its fixed plane totally geodesic. In its upper-half-plane coordinates $(x,y)$, the Christoffel formula [F3] gives $\Gamma^x_{xy}=\Gamma^x_{yx}=-1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{xx}=1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{yy}=-1/y$, and all other symbols zero. Thus for the global positive orthonormal frame $e_1=y\partial_x$, $e_2=y\partial_y$, one has $
abla_{e_1}e_1=e_2$, $
abla_{e_1}e_2=-e_1$, $
abla_{e_2}e_1=
abla_{e_2}e_2=0$ and $[e_1,e_2]=-e_1$. Consequently $R(e_1,e_2)e_2=-e_1$ and $K=-1$. A noncollinear finite triangle bounds a compact regular disk with three embedded geodesic edges and ordinary corners: its sides are the unique segments in the three geodesic half-planes, and distinct sides meet transversely at their vertices. The global frame supplies the neighbourhood required by [F3]. Gauss–Bonnet therefore gives its area $A=\pi-(\alpha+ eta+\gamma)<\pi$, since all three interior angles are positive. The area density of the displayed metric is $y^{-2}dx\,dy$. On this plane a radius-$r$ hyperbolic disk has area $2\pi(\cosh r-1)$: in the disk metric the Euclidean radius is $R=	anh(r/2)$, and integrating $4ho(1-ho^2)^{-2}\,dho\,d	heta$ gives $4\pi R^2/(1-R^2)=2\pi(\cosh r-1)$. Fix a point $p$ on one side of a nondegenerate finite triangle, and let $d_0$ be its distance to the union of the other sides. If $r<d_0$, the half-disk of radius $r$ on the interior side of the first edge is contained in the triangle. Indeed, a radial geodesic from $p$ to a point of that half-disk stays in the interior edge half-plane and would otherwise first exit across one of the other two actual edges at distance less than $d_0$. Its area is $\pi(\cosh r-1)$, while the triangle has area less than $\pi$ by [F3]. Hence $r\le\operatorname{arcosh}2$ for every $r<d_0$, giving $d_0\le\delta:=\operatorname{arcosh}2$. Degenerate triangles are $0$-slim. This proves uniform $\delta$-slimness of $\mathbb H^3$ locally, without using an external hyperbolicity assertion.

By [F2] and step 2.1, $f$ induces a homeomorphism of sequence boundaries. In this model that boundary is the ordinary ideal sphere. For precision, in the ball every geodesic ray from the origin is radial by step 1.1 and is parameterized as $u(r)=\tanh(r/2)\omega$, $|\omega|=1$. Substitution in the distance formula gives the product limit $(\omega|\omega')_0=-\log(|\omega-\omega'|/2)$ for distinct unit vectors and infinity for equal ones. Thus its product topology is the ordinary sphere topology, and finite-distance asymptotic rays have the same endpoint. By properness and [F2], every sequence-boundary class has a ray representative, and the uniform-on-bounded-interval topology of the radial rays is the ordinary topology of their unit endpoints. Consequently [F2]'s extension is exactly the ideal-boundary homeomorphism, and $x_n\to a$ ideally implies $f(x_n)\to h(a)$ whenever $(x_n)$ runs to infinity along a geodesic ray.

Put $M=92\lambda^2(\varepsilon+3\delta)$. If $\ell$ is a complete source geodesic with endpoints $a,b$, then $f(\ell)$ lies within distance $M$ of the target complete geodesic $\ell'$ with endpoints $h(a),h(b)$. Fix a point $x=\ell(0)$ and apply [F1] to $f\circ\ell$ on $[-n,n]$. There is a point $y_n$ of the target endpoint segment within $M+1/n$ of $f(x)$. Properness from step 1.1 gives a convergent subsequence of these witnesses. By step 3.1, the segment endpoints tend ideally to $h(a),h(b)$. The orthogonal-circle or vertical-line formulas from step 1.1 show that these segments converge on compact subsets to $\ell'$: an orthogonal circle is determined continuously by its two endpoints and its Euclidean plane, with a vertical line the limit when one endpoint is infinite. Equivalently normalize the two limiting endpoints to $0,\infty$ and use their orthogonal-circle formulas there. The witness limit therefore belongs to $\ell'$, proving the distance bound. The same argument applies to every fixed $x\in\ell$.

For an ordered ideal triangle $\tau=(a,b,c)$ define $c_\tau$ by applying the unique boundary Möbius transformation taking $(0,1,\infty)$ to $(a,b,c)$ to $c_0=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$ in the real vertical plane; use its isometric extension from step 1.1. Existence and uniqueness follow explicitly from the fractional linear expression sending $a,b,c$ to $0,1,\infty$. The center $c_0$ is at distance $r_0=\log\sqrt3$ from each of its three complete sides: for the vertical lines the distance formula minimizes to $\operatorname{arsinh}((1/2)/(\sqrt3/2))=\log\sqrt3$, and for the semicircle with endpoints $0,1$ the normal is the vertical line through $1/2$, giving $\log((\sqrt3/2)/(1/2))=\log\sqrt3$. Thus every $c_\tau$ has distance $r_0$ from each side. By step 4.1 and the upper quasi-isometry bound, $f(c_\tau)$ is within $D=\max\{1,\lambda r_0+\varepsilon+M\}$ of each side of the target triangle $h\tau$.

There is $C(D)<\infty$ such that every point within $D$ of all three complete sides of an ideal triangle is within $C(D)$ of its specified center. Normalize to $(0,1,\infty)$ by an isometry. For a point $(w,s)$, the distances to the vertical sides over $0$ and $1$ are $\operatorname{arsinh}(|w|/s)$ and $\operatorname{arsinh}(|w-1|/s)$: minimize the distance formula over the target height. Hence $1\le|w|+|w-1|\le2s\sinh D$ and $s\ge(2\sinh D)^{-1}$. The remaining side is the semicircle with endpoints $0,1$, whose height is at most $1/2$. Along every path, change in $\log s$ has absolute value at most path length, directly from the metric. Its distance bound therefore gives $s\le e^D/2$. Also $|w|\le s\sinh D\le e^D\sinh D/2$. These inequalities place $(w,s)$ in a fixed Euclidean compact subset of upper half-space. The distance formula in step 1.1 is continuous there, so its maximum distance to $c_0$ is a finite number $C(D)$. By normalization this number works for every ordered ideal triangle. Step 5.1 now gives $d(f(c_\tau),c_{h\tau})\le C(D)$.

Postcompose $f$ by the isometry extending a Möbius transformation that sends $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$; its quasi-isometry constants do not change. The normalized boundary map restricts to a plane homeomorphism. For distinct finite $z,a$, the center of $(z,a,\infty)$ is $c(z,a)=((z+a)/2,\sqrt3|a-z|/2),$ by the affine isometry in step 1.1. Step 6.1 and the quasi-isometry inequality give $d(c(hz,ha),c(hz,hb))\le2C(D)+\lambda\log3+\varepsilon$. If $h$ preserves orientation, apply [F4] to the plane map in step 7.1 to obtain analytic $H$-quasiconformality. To cover the omitted source point as well, choose a different omitted point $q$ and choose Möbius transformations $S,T$ taking $q,h(q)$ respectively to $\infty$, and replace $f$ by $T\circ f\circ S^{-1}$. Finally equivariance follows either by taking ideal limits along rays or by the composition property in [F2]; the exact equality $f\gamma=\theta(\gamma)f$ implies $h\gamma=\theta(\gamma)h$.
