citations.quote:
Use the upper half-space model
$$
\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad
ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),
$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$
z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},
$$
each assigned to one pair of opposite edges; the parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. For an oriented path $\gamma$ in a triangulated torus link of ideal vertices, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters encountered along $\gamma$, using the parameter when the path cuts off that corner on its left and its reciprocal when it cuts off the corner on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$
v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3)
=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

Integrating this probability measure on each frame fiber against hyperbolic volume defines a smooth positive measure on $G$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume AC. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be connected orientable hyperbolic manifolds, with discrete torsion-free groups. Suppose each is a compact core together with finitely many disjoint standard torus cusp ends: an end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of the union of these ends is compact. Zero ends are allowed, in which case the manifold is compact.

Every group isomorphism $\theta:\Gamma\to\Gamma'$ permutes the conjugacy classes of the peripheral cusp groups. There is a smooth $\theta$-equivariant quasi-isometry $F:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ which on every sufficiently deep lifted cusp is affine in its horizontal coordinates and preserves cusp depth after a constant height rescaling. It has a smooth equivariant quasi-inverse with inverse affine cusp maps. On quotient manifolds these maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

The standard cusp decomposition is a supplied hypothesis here; this lemma does not derive it merely from finite volume.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ act on the Riemann sphere by Möbius transformations. Let $\Gamma\le G$ be discrete, with finite nonzero Haar quotient measure $\nu$ on $X=\Gamma\backslash G$. Here Haar quotient measure means the right invariant Radon measure obtained by locally transporting Haar measure through the covering projection $G\to X$; its normalization is immaterial. Let $\theta:\Gamma\to G$ be a homomorphism, and let $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism satisfying $h\circ\gamma=\theta(\gamma)\circ h$ for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Then $h$ is Möbius.

This statement assumes the existence of the quasiconformal boundary conjugacy. It does not assert that an abstract group isomorphism or a quasi-isometry produces one.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds, and let $f:M\to N$ be an isometry. Then
$$
\int_M d\operatorname{vol}_M=\int_N d\operatorname{vol}_N.
$$
In particular, if either volume is finite, then both are finite and the values agree.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume AC. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be connected orientable hyperbolic manifolds, with discrete torsion-free groups. Suppose each is a compact core together with finitely many disjoint standard torus cusp ends: an end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of the union of these ends is compact. Zero ends are allowed, in which case the manifold is compact.

Every group isomorphism $\theta:\Gamma\to\Gamma'$ permutes the conjugacy classes of the peripheral cusp groups. There is a smooth $\theta$-equivariant quasi-isometry $F:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ which on every sufficiently deep lifted cusp is affine in its horizontal coordinates and preserves cusp depth after a constant height rescaling. It has a smooth equivariant quasi-inverse with inverse affine cusp maps. On quotient manifolds these maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

The standard cusp decomposition is a supplied hypothesis here; this lemma does not derive it merely from finite volume.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ act on the Riemann sphere by Möbius transformations. Let $\Gamma\le G$ be discrete, with finite nonzero Haar quotient measure $\nu$ on $X=\Gamma\backslash G$. Here Haar quotient measure means the right invariant Radon measure obtained by locally transporting Haar measure through the covering projection $G\to X$; its normalization is immaterial. Let $\theta:\Gamma\to G$ be a homomorphism, and let $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism satisfying $h\circ\gamma=\theta(\gamma)\circ h$ for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Then $h$ is Möbius.

This statement assumes the existence of the quasiconformal boundary conjugacy. It does not assert that an abstract group isomorphism or a quasi-isometry produces one.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds, and let $f:M\to N$ be an isometry. Then
$$
\int_M d\operatorname{vol}_M=\int_N d\operatorname{vol}_N.
$$
In particular, if either volume is finite, then both are finite and the values agree.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)$, and set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and $T_K=\partial E_K$. If $K$ is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot, then every smoothly embedded $2$-sphere in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $E_K$, and there is no smoothly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose interior misses $T_K$ and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in $T_K$.

derivations.claim: Full AC supplies the countable-choice premise in [F1] by [L1]. The supplied atoroidality and non-Seifert assumptions have the exact meanings in [F1]; they impose additional hypotheses on the exterior and do not remove either conclusion of [F2].

Apply [F2] to the stated nontrivial knot and its chosen compact exterior. It gives irreducibility and absence of a compressing disk on the boundary; by [F1], these are exactly the two conclusions asserted here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)$, and set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and $T_K=\partial E_K$. Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E_K$ be the compact connected orientable exterior of a smooth knot in $S^3$, with one torus boundary component. If $E_K$ is irreducible, its boundary is incompressible, $E_K$ is atoroidal, and $E_K$ is not Seifert-fibered, then $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ admits a complete finite-volume Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ with one torus cusp. No conclusion is asserted for a torus or satellite knot unless its exterior satisfies all four topological hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The action preserves $|z|^2+|w|^2$, so it acts smoothly on $S^3$. The orbit of $(2^{-1/2},2^{-1/2})$ is exactly $K$. A group element stabilizes this point only if $3\theta$ and $2\theta$ are both multiples of $2\pi$; coprimality of $2$ and $3$ makes the stabilizer trivial. The regions $|z|\le|w|$ and $|w|\le|z|$ are solid tori, parametrized respectively by $(z,w)=(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\eta)$ and $(z,w)=(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}\eta,w)$ with the disk coordinate bounded by $2^{-1/2}$ and $\eta\in S^1$. The $w$ coordinate is the core direction of the first solid torus and winds twice along $K$; the $z$ coordinate is the core direction of the second and winds three times. This proves the claimed $(3,2)$ torus-knot type. On the axis $z=0$ the stabilizer has order $2$, and on the axis $w=0$ it has order $3$.

On $zw\ne0$, write $\alpha=\arg z$ and $\beta=\arg w$ modulo $2\pi$. The integer coordinate change $\theta=\alpha-\beta$, $\phi=2\alpha-3\beta$ has determinant $-1$ and is invertible on the phase torus. The circle action changes $\theta$ by its parameter and fixes $\phi$, while $r=|z|\in(0,1)$ is fixed; thus the quotient of this open set is the cylinder with coordinates $(r,\phi)$, and the inverse image of any disk $D$ around $q(K)$ in it is explicitly $S^1_\theta\times D$. At $r=0$ and $r=1$ the phase circle collapses to one point at each end, so the full orbit space is a sphere; the two axis orbits have stabilizer orders $2$ and $3$. The complement of $D$ is a disk with those two cone points. Its orbits give the fibers of $E_K$, and [F2] identifies the axis fibers as exceptional of orders $2$ and $3$.

Choose a basepoint $x$ on a regular fiber, let $h$ be that fiber loop, and let $\gamma$ be any loop in $E_K$ based at $x$. The map $F:[0,1]^2\to E_K$ defined by $F(s,t)=g_{2\pi s}(\gamma(t))$ is well-defined because the tube is invariant. Its boundary represents $h\gamma h^{-1}\gamma^{-1}$: the two vertical sides are $\gamma$ and $\gamma^{-1}$ since $g_0=g_{2\pi}=\operatorname{id}$, and the horizontal sides are the fiber loop and its reverse. The square contracts its boundary, so $h$ commutes with $[\gamma]$. Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, the regular fiber class is central in $\pi_1(E_K)$.

By [F3], a Seifert-fibered exterior does not satisfy the required non-Seifert-fibered hypothesis. Step 2.1 establishes that $E_K$ is Seifert-fibered, so this example refutes the statement that every knot exterior is non-Seifert-fibered and also fails that hypothesis of the hyperbolization contract.

A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. derivations.claim: The action preserves $|z|^2+|w|^2$, so it acts smoothly on $S^3$. The orbit of $(2^{-1/2},2^{-1/2})$ is exactly $K$. A group element stabilizes this point only if $3\theta$ and $2\theta$ are both multiples of $2\pi$; coprimality of $2$ and $3$ makes the stabilizer trivial. The regions $|z|\le|w|$ and $|w|\le|z|$ are solid tori, parametrized respectively by $(z,w)=(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\eta)$ and $(z,w)=(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}\eta,w)$ with the disk coordinate bounded by $2^{-1/2}$ and $\eta\in S^1$. The integer coordinate change $\theta=\alpha-\beta$, $\phi=2\alpha-3\beta$ has determinant $-1$ and is invertible on the phase torus. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

These $Y_j$ are an orthonormal tangent basis for curvature $-1$ hyperbolic space; for example $\exp(tY_1)$ moves the basepoint distance $|t|$, and the $K$ action rotates this basis. The matrix commutators give $[X_i,X_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ and $[Y_i,Y_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}Y_k$. On $V$ let $R_j=\operatorname{ad}Y_j$. Each $Y_j$ is Hermitian, so $R_j$ is self-adjoint for $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)$, by cyclicity of trace. The $K$ action is unitary for this product.

Indeed a frame $g$ identifies the fiber over $gK$ with $V$ by $\operatorname{Ad}g$, and replacing $g$ by $gk$ changes these coefficients by $\operatorname{Ad}k^{-1}$ and rotates the tangent indices. In these coefficients write $\varepsilon_j$ for exterior multiplication by the dual of $Y_j$ and $\iota_j$ for contraction by $Y_j$. The ordinary covariant differential of the $K$ connection is $D=\sum_j\varepsilon_jY_j$, because the horizontal part of $[Y_i,Y_j]$ is zero. Differentiating the fiber change $\operatorname{Ad}g$ gives $d_E=D+T$, where $T=\sum_j\varepsilon_jR_j$. These are actual coefficient formulas on all degrees, not definitions of a different connection.

The invariant volume on $Q$ is the product of hyperbolic volume and normalized compact-fiber volume. Integration in a local bundle chart and then a partition of unity shows that integration of a $K$-invariant coefficient norm on $Q$ equals its integration on $M$. The left invariant fields $Y_j$ have zero divergence for this volume: $G$ is unimodular, since $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}Z)=0$ for the displayed Lie algebra basis, hence for all $Z$, and $\det\operatorname{Ad}(\exp Z)=1$. Right translation therefore preserves its Haar volume. Integration by parts on compact supports now gives $D^*=-\sum_j\iota_jY_j$ and $T^*=\sum_j\iota_jR_j$. The relations $\varepsilon_i\iota_j+\iota_j\varepsilon_i=\delta_{ij}$ show that $DT^*+T^*D+TD^*+D^*T=0$: the two anticommutator sums are respectively $\sum_jR_jY_j$ and its negative, since coefficient differentiation commutes with the constant matrices $R_j$. Thus $d_E\delta_E+\delta_Ed_E=DD^*+D^*D+H$, where $H=TT^*+T^*T$. All statements are $K$-equivariant and descend from $Q$ to $M$.

On one-form coefficients $a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in V^3$, the exterior-contraction relations give $(Ha)_i=\sum_jR_j^2a_i+\sum_j[R_i,R_j]a_j$. This finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator is positive definite. If $Ha=0$, positivity of $TT^*+T^*T$ gives $Ta=0$, namely $R_ia_j=R_ja_i$ for all $i,j$. Since $[R_i,R_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, the commutator sum in the displayed formula is a multiple of $R_ka_j-R_ja_k$ and vanishes. Consequently $0=\langle Ha,a\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\|R_ja_i\|^2$. Each $a_i$ commutes with all $Y_j$, which span $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ over $\mathbb C$. A matrix commuting with all traceless matrices is scalar, and a traceless scalar is zero. Thus $a=0$. Compactness of the unit sphere in $V^3$ supplies $c>0$ with $H\ge cI$.

For a compactly supported smooth one-form, integration by parts in step 3.1 and step 4.1 give $\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2=\|D\alpha\|_2^2+\|D^*\alpha\|_2^2+(H\alpha,\alpha)\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2$. We next extend this inequality to the joint weak graph domain. On each cusp choose a smooth cutoff equal to one for $t\le R$, zero for $t\ge2R$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set it equal to one on the compact core. These cutoffs $\chi_R$ have compact support and $|d\chi_R|\le C/R$. For a weak graph-domain form $v$, the product formulas $d_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_Rd_Ev+d\chi_R\wedge v$ and $\delta_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\delta_Ev-\iota_{\nabla\chi_R}v$ show convergence to $v$ in the joint graph norm. The same conclusion holds separately for each differential and codifferential and for forms of every degree. In the compact case take the cutoff identically one.

Here are the local smoothing details needed to finish that graph-density argument. In a finite collection of trivializing charts around the support of $\chi_Rv$, every differential or codifferential is a first-order matrix operator $P=\sum_jA_j(x)\partial_j+B(x)$ with smooth coefficients. Multiplication by a subordinate smooth partition reduces to forms supported inside individual charts. For convolution with a smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho_\epsilon$, the difference $P(v*\rho_\epsilon)-(Pv)*\rho_\epsilon$ is a sum of integral operators with kernels $(A_j(x)-A_j(y))\partial_j\rho_\epsilon(x-y)+(\partial_jA_j)(y)\rho_\epsilon(x-y)$ and a zero-order coefficient commutator. The $L^1$ kernel bounds are uniform on the compact chart, by the mean-value bound for $A_j$ and scaling of $\rho_\epsilon$; thus these commutators are uniformly bounded on $L^2$. They tend to zero on smooth functions by differentiation of convolutions, hence on all $L^2$ functions by smooth approximation and the uniform bound. Therefore local mollification converges in each asserted graph norm, also for the direct sum operator $(d_E,\delta_E)$. The partition contributes only fixed zero-order commutators, so a finite sum completes the approximation by compactly supported smooth forms. Together with step 5.1 this proves the coercive inequality on the maximal joint graph domain. It also proves that maximal differentials are the adjoints of maximal formal codifferentials, since their compact-support integration-by-parts identities extend by this graph density.

Let $\mathcal H_p=L^2(\Lambda^pT^*M\otimes E)$ and let $d_p$ be the maximal weak differential. It is closed: convergence of a form and its differential in $L^2$ preserves the weak test-function identity. Flatness gives $d_1d_0=0$ distributionally. Put $Z=\ker d_1$, a closed subspace of $\mathcal H_1$, and $\delta=d_0^*$. Every $w\in Z^\perp$ belongs to $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ with $\delta w=0$, because it is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}d_0\subseteq Z$. Hence the orthogonal projection $P_Z$ maps $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ into itself and $\delta P_Zv=\delta v$. On $Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, steps 5.1 and 6.1 give $\|v\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\delta v\|_2$. In particular $A=\delta|_{Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta}$ is injective with closed range: a Cauchy sequence of its images is, by this estimate, the image under the closed operator $\delta$ of a convergent sequence in $Z$.

Fix a weakly closed $\alpha\in\mathcal H_1$, so $\alpha\in Z$. On the closed range of $A$ define $\ell(Av)=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$. It is well defined and bounded, with norm at most $c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$, by step 7.1. Extend it to $\mathcal H_0$ by zero on the orthogonal complement of that range and use [F1] to obtain $b\in\mathcal H_0$ with $\langle Av,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$. For arbitrary $v\in\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, replace $v$ by $P_Zv$; its $\delta$ image is unchanged and its pairing with $\alpha$ is unchanged. Thus $\langle\delta v,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ on the full domain of $\delta$. By the adjoint definition and the graph-density conclusion of step 6.1, $b\in\operatorname{Dom}d_0$ and $d_0b=\alpha$. This proves the primitive assertion in the weak sense without an external closed-range or harmonic-representative theorem.

If $\alpha$ is smooth, the primitive $b$ is smooth. In a flat parallel frame on a coordinate ball, $d_Eb=\alpha$ is the ordinary componentwise distributional equation $db=\alpha$. A smooth closed one-form on a smaller star-shaped coordinate ball has a smooth primitive $b_0$, given by integrating along straight radial segments; differentiating the integral and using closedness verifies $db_0=\alpha$. Then $d(b-b_0)=0$ distributionally. Mollification on still smaller balls makes this difference a sequence of constants, so its distributional limit is constant as well. Thus $b=b_0+\text{constant}$ is smooth locally and hence globally. Its $L^2$ norm and the bound from step 8.1 remain unchanged.

By the adjoint definition and the graph-density conclusion of step 6.1, $b\in\operatorname{Dom}d_0$ and $d_0b=\alpha$. This proves the primitive assertion in the weak sense without an external closed-range or harmonic-representative theorem.

A smooth closed one-form on a smaller star-shaped coordinate ball has a smooth primitive $b_0$, given by integrating along straight radial segments; differentiating the integral and using closedness verifies $db_0=\alpha$. Then $d(b-b_0)=0$ distributionally. Mollification on still smaller balls makes this difference a sequence of constants, so its distributional limit is constant as well. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

derivations.claim: Shrink to a closed convex polydisc $B_\epsilon=\{\|u\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ inside the holomorphy domain. Its compactness and continuity of the derivatives give a common Lipschitz constant $L$ for all $\tau_i$ there, by integrating their derivatives along line segments. Put $A=\max_i|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)|^{-1}$ and shrink $\epsilon$ so that $AL\epsilon\le1/4$ and every $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)$ stays nonzero on $B_\epsilon$. For any nonzero real pair $(p,q)$, $p+q\tau_i(0)\ne0$ and $|q/(p+q\tau_i(0))|\le A$. Moreover $|p+q\tau_i(0)|\ge c\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$ for one common $c>0$: the real-linear maps $(p,q)\mapsto p+q\tau_i(0)$ are invertible, and their moduli have a positive minimum on the unit circle.

For a parameter tuple with finite pairs outside a sufficiently large radius $R$, define $a_i=q_i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ and the $w_i$ in the Statement. At an infinite coordinate put $a_i=w_i=0$. On $B_\epsilon$ define $T_i(u)=w_i/[1+a_i(\tau_i(u)-\tau_i(0))]$. Step 1.1 makes every denominator have modulus at least $3/4$, hence $\|T(u)\|_\infty\le(4/3)\|w\|_\infty$. Also $\|T(u)-T(u')\|_\infty\le(16/9)AL\|w\|_\infty\|u-u'\|_\infty$. Since step 1.1 makes $\|w\|_\infty\le2\pi/(cR)$, choose $R$ so large that $\|w\|_\infty\le\epsilon/2$ and $(16/9)AL\|w\|_\infty\le1/2$. The closed polydisc is nonempty and complete, and $T$ maps it into itself, so [F1] supplies its unique fixed point. Its defining equations are exactly the simultaneous full-turn equations at finite coordinates, and $u_i=0$ at infinite ones. At a finite coordinate $w_i\ne0$, so its solution $u_i$ cannot vanish. Every solution in $B_\epsilon$ is such a fixed point and is therefore this one.

The fixed-point bound in step 2.1 gives $\|u\|_\infty\le(4/3)\|w\|_\infty$. Its coordinate equation also gives $|u_i-w_i|\le(4/3)A|w_i|\,|\tau_i(u)-\tau_i(0)|\le(16/9)AL|w_i|\|w\|_\infty$. This proves the stated uniform expansion, including every $w_i=0$ coordinate exactly.

Define the coefficient map $\Phi$ on the open polydisc by the equations in the Statement. If $u_i\ne0$, the real-linear equation $p_i+q_i\tau_i(u)=2\pi i/u_i$ has a unique real pair, continuously depending on $u$. If $u_i\to0$, the norms of these pairs tend to infinity uniformly with the other coordinates in $B_\epsilon$: boundedness of $\tau_i$ gives $2\pi/|u_i|=|p_i+q_i\tau_i(u)|\le C\sqrt{p_i^2+q_i^2}$. Thus $\Phi$ is continuous also at its infinite coordinates, with $\Phi(0)=(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$. Let $V$ be the product neighborhood specified using $R$ in step 2.1, and put $U=\Phi^{-1}(V)$ inside the open polydisc. This is an open neighborhood of $0$. Every parameter in $V$ has its unique solution in the interior by step 2.1, so $\Phi:U\to V$ is bijective.

Its inverse is continuous on the whole product neighborhood, including partially unfilled tuples. If parameter tuples converge, their fixed-point maps $T$ from step 2.1 converge uniformly on $B_\epsilon$. For a finite limiting coordinate, $a_i,w_i$ converge in the displayed rational formulas. For an infinite limiting coordinate, $w_i\to0$ while $|a_i|\le A$, so the corresponding $T_i$ tends uniformly to zero by the $3/4$ denominator bound, regardless of the directions of the real pairs. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: In $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$, the standard Hopf link is $H=\{z_1z_2=0\}$. On its complement, $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2/|z_1z_2|$ is a submersion to $S^1$. Writing $r=|z_1|^2$, $\theta=\arg z_1$, and $\phi=\arg z_2$, a fiber is $0<r<1$, $\phi=-\theta+\text{constant}$, hence an annulus. For base angle $s\in[0,2\pi]$, transport by $\theta_s=\theta+\chi(r)s$, $\phi_s=\phi+(1-\chi(r))s$, where $\chi=1$ near $r=0$ and $\chi=0$ near $r=1$, fixes both boundary circles at $s=2\pi$ and makes one full annular twist between them. The sign is determined by the signed linking of the positive normal push-off of the core with the core: changing the handedness of the Hopf band reverses the twist. With $a\cdot_F b=+1$, the positive twist about $a$ acts by $b\mapsto a+b$, while the negative twist about $b$ acts by $a\mapsto a+b$. Hence the two band monodromies have the stated actions $R_a$ and $L_b$.

Cutting a fibered exterior open along its page gives page $\times[0,1]$, with the two ends reidentified by the monodromy. In the square plumbing, the two annulus pages meet in the plumbing square $D$ and their product collars meet in $D\times[0,1]$. The interval coordinates agree on this product, so gluing the cut-open product pieces gives $(A\mathbin{\natural_D}B)\times[0,1]=F\times[0,1]$, where $A\mathbin{\natural_D}B$ denotes the surface obtained by gluing the two annuli along $D$. Reidentifying the interval ends extends each band map by the identity outside its annulus. The first return map is the composition in the stipulated plumbing order; choosing the positive band first gives $R_a\circ L_b$. The boundary knot is the standard figure-eight isotopy class by the specified plumbing presentation and [F2], and the chosen exterior is formed by deleting the binding neighborhood as in [F1]. Thus the exterior is the mapping torus of $F$ with that monodromy.

Each annulus has Euler characteristic $0$, and the plumbing square has Euler characteristic $1$, so $\chi(F)=0+0-1=-1$. The plumbing is connected, oriented, and has one boundary component by the stated gluing; hence $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ gives $g(F)=1$. Thus $F$ is a once-punctured torus.

In the ordered basis $([a],[b])$, the columns of $R_a$ are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, while the columns of $L_b$ are $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$. Their product is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Inclusion of the once-punctured torus into the torus obtained by capping its sole boundary induces an isomorphism on $H_1$, since attaching a disk along the boundary adds no 1-cycle or 2-cycle relation in degree one. Extending the boundary-fixing monodromy by the identity on that disk therefore has the same displayed action.

[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: In $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$, the standard Hopf link is $H=\{z_1z_2=0\}$. On its complement, $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2/|z_1z_2|$ is a submersion to $S^1$. Writing $r=|z_1|^2$, $\theta=\arg z_1$, and $\phi=\arg z_2$, a fiber is $0<r<1$, $\phi=-\theta+\text{constant}$, hence an annulus. For base angle $s\in[0,2\pi]$, transport by $\theta_s=\theta+\chi(r)s$, $\phi_s=\phi+(1-\chi(r))s$, where $\chi=1$ near $r=0$ and $\chi=0$ near $r=1$, fixes both boundary circles at $s=2\pi$ and makes one full annular twist between them. The sign is determined by the signed linking of the positive normal push-off of the core with the core: changing the handedness of the Hopf band reverses the twist. With $a\cdot_F b=+1$, the positive twist about $a$ acts by $b\mapsto a+b$, while the negative twist about $b$ acts by $a\mapsto a+b$. Hence the two band monodromies have the stated actions $R_a$ and $L_b$.

Cutting a fibered exterior open along its page gives page $\times[0,1]$, with the two ends reidentified by the monodromy. In the square plumbing, the two annulus pages meet in the plumbing square $D$ and their product collars meet in $D\times[0,1]$. The interval coordinates agree on this product, so gluing the cut-open product pieces gives $(A\mathbin{\natural_D}B)\times[0,1]=F\times[0,1]$, where $A\mathbin{\natural_D}B$ denotes the surface obtained by gluing the two annuli along $D$. Reidentifying the interval ends extends each band map by the identity outside its annulus. The first return map is the composition in the stipulated plumbing order; choosing the positive band first gives $R_a\circ L_b$. The boundary knot is the standard figure-eight isotopy class by the specified plumbing presentation and [F2], and the chosen exterior is formed by deleting the binding neighborhood as in [F1]. Thus the exterior is the mapping torus of $F$ with that monodromy.

Each annulus has Euler characteristic $0$, and the plumbing square has Euler characteristic $1$, so $\chi(F)=0+0-1=-1$. The plumbing is connected, oriented, and has one boundary component by the stated gluing; hence $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ gives $g(F)=1$. Thus $F$ is a once-punctured torus.

In the ordered basis $([a],[b])$, the columns of $R_a$ are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, while the columns of $L_b$ are $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$. Their product is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Inclusion of the once-punctured torus into the torus obtained by capping its sole boundary induces an isomorphism on $H_1$, since attaching a disk along the boundary adds no 1-cycle or 2-cycle relation in degree one. Extending the boundary-fixing monodromy by the identity on that disk therefore has the same displayed action.
