citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.

Assume AC. Let $k\ge1$ and let $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^k$, with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)\ne0$. Put $v_i(u)=u_i\tau_i(u)$. At a coordinate with $u_i\ne0$, define real coefficients $(p_i,q_i)$ by
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i;$$
at $u_i=0$ define its parameter to be $\infty$ in the one-point compactification $S_i=\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$.

One may take $V=\prod_i(\{(p,q):p^2+q^2>R^2\}\cup\{\infty\})$ for a sufficiently large $R$. Every such tuple has a unique small simultaneous solution, with $u_i=0$ exactly at the unfilled coordinates. Uniformly as the tuple tends to the complete point, writing $w_i=2\pi i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ for finite coordinates and $w_i=0$ at $\infty$, one has
$$u_i=w_i+O(|w_i|\|w\|_\infty),\qquad \|u\|_\infty\le\tfrac43\|w\|_\infty.$$
This analytic assertion allows real coefficients of either orientation. Primitive integral coefficients are included, but no geometric completion is asserted by the equations alone.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold with a compact smooth core and $k\ge1$ disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Choose positively oriented peripheral bases $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$. Let $\rho_u$, for $u$ near $0$ in $\mathbb C^k$, be the augmented holonomy family supplied by the augmented holonomy-coordinate theorem, based at the complete holonomy $\rho_0$. Thus the logarithms satisfy $v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$.

After shrinking this neighborhood, there are smooth hyperbolic metrics $g_u$ on $M$, possibly incomplete, with holonomy $\rho_u$. They depend smoothly on the real and imaginary parts of $u$ on every compact subset, and $g_0$ is the given complete metric. Each end with $u_i=0$ is a complete finite-volume translation cusp. Each end with $u_i\ne0$ has an explicit developing map onto the punctured tube about its peripheral axis, with the angular and axial periods specified by $u_i,v_i$.

$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i,$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.

Assume AC. Let $k\ge1$ and let $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^k$, with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)\ne0$. Put $v_i(u)=u_i\tau_i(u)$. At a coordinate with $u_i\ne0$, define real coefficients $(p_i,q_i)$ by
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i;$$
at $u_i=0$ define its parameter to be $\infty$ in the one-point compactification $S_i=\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$.

There are neighborhoods $U$ of $0$ and $V$ of $(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$ in $\prod_iS_i$ for which this parameter map is a homeomorphism $U\to V$. One may take $V=\prod_i(\{(p,q):p^2+q^2>R^2\}\cup\{\infty\})$ for a sufficiently large $R$. Every such tuple has a unique small simultaneous solution, with $u_i=0$ exactly at the unfilled coordinates. Uniformly as the tuple tends to the complete point, writing $w_i=2\pi i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ for finite coordinates and $w_i=0$ at $\infty$, one has
$$u_i=w_i+O(|w_i|\|w\|_\infty),\qquad \|u\|_\infty\le\tfrac43\|w\|_\infty.$$
This analytic assertion allows real coefficients of either orientation. Primitive integral coefficients are included, but no geometric completion is asserted by the equations alone.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold with a compact smooth core and $k\ge1$ disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Choose positively oriented peripheral bases $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$. Let $\rho_u$, for $u$ near $0$ in $\mathbb C^k$, be the augmented holonomy family supplied by the augmented holonomy-coordinate theorem, based at the complete holonomy $\rho_0$. Thus the logarithms satisfy $v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$.

After shrinking this neighborhood, there are smooth hyperbolic metrics $g_u$ on $M$, possibly incomplete, with holonomy $\rho_u$. They depend smoothly on the real and imaginary parts of $u$ on every compact subset, and $g_0$ is the given complete metric. Each end with $u_i=0$ is a complete finite-volume translation cusp. Each end with $u_i\ne0$ has an explicit developing map onto the punctured tube about its peripheral axis, with the angular and axial periods specified by $u_i,v_i$.

Suppose $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and, for every $i\in J$, a primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ satisfies
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i,$$
while $u_i=0$ for $i\notin J$. Then $g_u$ extends across all ends in $J$ to a smooth complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the ordinary Dehn filling whose meridians are $p_i\mu_i+q_i\lambda_i$. For arbitrary supplied orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphisms realizing these same slopes, the resulting topological filling is orientation-preservingly and core-preservingly homeomorphic to this realization, by a homeomorphism equal to the identity on the truncated original manifold. Transporting the realization's smooth structure and metric through this homeomorphism gives the asserted smooth hyperbolic metric on that supplied filling. No assertion is made about a separately prescribed smooth structure for an arbitrary topological gluing. The added cores are ordinary smooth geodesics, with no cone or orbifold singularity. Their lengths are
$$\ell_i=\frac{|u_i|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)}{2\pi}>0.$$
Along such filling parameters tending to zero, the metrics converge smoothly to $g_0$ on every compact subset of $M$, the core lengths tend to zero, and the filled volumes tend to $\operatorname{Vol}(M,g_0)$. No ideal triangulation is assumed. This theorem realizes given small holonomy solutions; it does not assert their existence for specified slopes.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric and torus cusps $C_1,\ldots,C_k$. For a chosen cusp $C_i$, choose a horospherical section $T_i$ and identify its Euclidean universal cover with $\mathbb R^2$ so its deck group is a rank-two translation lattice. A slope on $T_i$ is represented by a primitive lattice vector $v$ modulo sign. Its **Euclidean slope length on the chosen section** is $\ell_{T_i}(v)=\lVert v\rVert$ in the induced Euclidean metric. In upper half-space coordinates, if the section is the quotient of the horosphere of height $h>0$ by lattice $\Lambda$, then $\ell_{T_i}(p,q)=|p u+q w|/h$, where $u,w$ are the translation vectors representing the chosen basis. Replacing height $h$ by $h'>0$ multiplies every slope length by $h/h'$; therefore the length depends on the chosen section and is not an intrinsic number until that section is fixed.

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

Define the standard figure-eight knot $K_8$ to be the oriented closure of the three-strand geometric braid $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$. Its endpoint permutation is a $3$-cycle, so this closure has one component.

Let $\Delta_0=[0,1,2,3]$ and $\Delta_1=[0',1',2',3']$ be oriented ideal tetrahedra with orientation-reversing affine face maps
$$
[0,1,2]\to[3',1',2'],\quad
[0,1,3]\to[0',1',2'],\quad
[0,2,3]\to[0',1',3'],\quad
[1,2,3]\to[0',2',3'].
$$
This is the two-tetrahedron ideal triangulation obtained from the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram by cutting along crossing arcs, identifying upper and lower polyhedron faces with equal region labels, and collapsing the two bigon faces. Its edge classes are
$$
\{01,02,23,0'1',1'3',2'3'\},\qquad
\{12,03,13,1'2',0'2',0'3'\};
$$
each has valence six, and the unique ideal vertex link is a torus. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$
H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.
$$

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.
For a covering $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$, the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_1(E,e_0)\to\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is injective.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F2], the countable-choice premise [F1] holds. The face gluing and regular-shape assignment in [F3] give the complete finite-volume metric and its two-tetrahedron volume. By [F4] and [F6], the zero filling along the preferred longitude is the stated torus bundle.

Write the bundle as the mapping torus of its torus monodromy. Pull it back along the explicit universal cover $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ of $S^1$; its total space is $T^2\times\mathbb R$, and the pullback projection is a covering because it is trivial over each lifted bundle chart. Its fundamental group is $\pi_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z^2$. By [F8], this subgroup injects into the fundamental group of the filled manifold.

If the filled manifold admitted a complete hyperbolic metric, it would be a closed connected three-manifold with curvature $-1$. By [F5] its fundamental group could contain no $\mathbb Z^2$ subgroup, contradicting step 2.1. Hence the zero filling is nonhyperbolic. The original complete structure has volume $2v_3=6\Lambda(\pi/3)$ by step 1.1.

Unfold the eight cusp-link triangles by the face maps into the standard rectangular strip, and label them $a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h$ from left to right; identify the strip boundary sides as prescribed by those same maps. Let $\alpha$ be the edge path across the strip from the left side of $a$ on the left boundary to the left side of $a$ on the right boundary, and let $\beta$ be the edge path on the left boundary from the base of $a$ to the top of $h$. Their ordered corner factors are respectively $z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1},z_3,w_2^{-1},z_2,w_3^{-1}$ and $z_2^{-1},w_1$. The face-pairing incidence check gives one positive transverse intersection, so their homology classes form a basis of $H_1$ and the loops form a basis of $\pi_1$ of the torus link. The two edge products are $z_1^2z_3w_1^2w_3$ and $z_2^2z_3w_2^2w_3$, while
$$
H(\alpha)=\left(\frac{z_2z_3}{w_2w_3}\right)^2,\qquad H(\beta)=\frac{w_1}{z_2}.
$$
For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, assigning $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ makes both edge products and both cusp multipliers equal to $1$ and gives total angle $2\pi$ around each edge. The gluing therefore gives the figure-eight complement a complete finite-volume curvature $-1$ metric with one peripheral torus cusp.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot with compact exterior obtained by deleting the binding neighborhood from its open-book presentation and peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$, where $\mu$ is the positive meridian and $\lambda$ is the preferred zero-homology longitude. The exterior fibers over $S^1$ with fiber a once-punctured torus and monodromy fixing its boundary pointwise. Filling along the slope $\lambda$ produces a torus bundle over $S^1$. For the fiber and ordered core basis in the figure-eight plumbing convention, the induced action on the capped torus homology is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $M$ is a closed connected orientable three-manifold with a complete Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$, then its fundamental group contains no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$.

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.
For a covering $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$, the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_1(E,e_0)\to\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is injective.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the chosen smooth knot-exterior data. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, with one boundary component. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose positive normal push-off of its core has linking number $+1$ with the core; a negative Hopf band has linking number $-1$. A square plumbing identifies a square in the boundary collars of the annuli with the four boundary edges alternating between the annuli, then smooths corners. Let $F$ be this plumbed surface, and choose the compact exterior by deleting the interior of the binding neighborhood $N(K_8)\cong\partial F\times D^2$ supplied by the open book; on every page this neighborhood meets the page in an annular collar of $\partial F$. Let $a,b$ be the core curves, ordered so that $a$ is the positive-band core and $a\cdot_F b=+1$. The exterior $E_{K_8}$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $F$. With the twist convention that the positive twist $R_a$ sends $a\mapsto a$, $b\mapsto a+b$, and the negative twist $L_b$ sends $a\mapsto a+b$, $b\mapsto b$, the monodromy is $R_a\circ L_b$. After capping $\partial F$ by a disk, its action on the ordered homology basis $([a],[b])$ is represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

derivations.claim: First identify the two figure-eight models used here. In [F3], $K_8$ is the closure of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$, the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram. In [F9], the same standard figure-eight knot is presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of a positive and a negative Hopf band; Calegari's Example 5.39 identifies the boundary of the opposite-handed Hopf-band Murasugi sum as the figure-eight knot. Thus both are the same oriented $4_1$ knot class, and an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy identifies the braid closure with the plumbing boundary. Choose the binding and tubular neighborhoods compatibly under this isotopy. It identifies the compact exteriors and carries the positive meridian and preferred longitude to the corresponding peripheral classes (up to simultaneous reversal, which does not change the unoriented zero slope). The hyperbolic exterior from [F3] and the fibered exterior from [F9] are therefore the same marked exterior for this example. By [A1] and [F2], the countable-choice premise [F1] holds. The face gluing and regular-shape assignment in [F3] give the complete finite-volume metric and its two-tetrahedron volume. By [F4] and [F6], the zero filling along the preferred longitude is the stated torus bundle.

Write the bundle as the mapping torus of its torus monodromy. Pull it back along the explicit universal cover $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ of $S^1$; its total space is $T^2\times\mathbb R$, and the pullback projection is a covering because it is trivial over each lifted bundle chart. Its fundamental group is $\pi_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z^2$. By [F8], this subgroup injects into the fundamental group of the filled manifold.

If the filled manifold admitted a complete hyperbolic metric, it would be a closed connected three-manifold with curvature $-1$. By [F5] its fundamental group could contain no $\mathbb Z^2$ subgroup, contradicting step 2.1. Hence the zero filling is nonhyperbolic. The original complete structure has volume $2v_3=6\Lambda(\pi/3)$ by step 1.1.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.

- The function $f$ is a **Morse function** when every critical point of $f$ is
  nondegenerate
  ([[def-critical-point-and-critical-value-of-a-smooth-function]],
  [[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex]]).
- The function $f$ is an **excellent Morse function** when it is Morse and any
  two distinct critical points have distinct critical values.

Thus excellence is stronger than the Morse condition: it excludes repeated
critical values, not repeated indices.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and let $p$ be a critical point of $f$. The
Hessian $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the
finite-dimensional real vector space $T_pM$
([[def-hessian-of-a-function-at-a-critical-point]]).

- The **nullity** of $p$ for $f$ is
  $$\operatorname{null}_p(f):=\dim\ker\bigl(\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)\bigr).$$
- The critical point $p$ is **nondegenerate** when
  $\operatorname{null}_p(f)=0$.
- The **index** of $p$ for $f$ is the largest dimension of a subspace of $T_pM$
  on which $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is negative definite.
- The **coindex** of $p$ for $f$ is the largest dimension of a subspace of
  $T_pM$ on which $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is positive definite.

The positivity and negativity conventions are those of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Cut a short trivial arc from $K$ inside a small ball. Identify its complementary ball with the unit ball $B^3\subset\mathbb R^3$ so that the remaining arc is a smooth embedding $a:[0,1]\to B^3$, its endpoints lie on $S^2$, and its interior lies in the open ball. Straighten its endpoint collars to be radial and transverse to $S^2$. A small perturbation supported away from the endpoints makes $a$ avoid the origin; compactness and the fact that a one-dimensional embedded arc has empty interior allow the perturbation to be chosen arbitrarily small in $C^1$, so it remains embedded and fixed on the endpoint collars. Put $f(s)=\lVert a(s)\rVert^2$. Then $f>0$ on $[0,1]$, $f(0)=f(1)=1$, $f<1$ on $(0,1)$, and transversality gives $f'(0)<0<f'(1)$.

The zeros of $f'$ lie in a compact subinterval of $(0,1)$ because $f'$ is nonzero on the endpoint collars. Cover the zero set by finitely many intervals carrying smooth functions $\phi_i$ supported in $(0,1)$ whose derivatives equal $1$ on smaller intervals still covering the zero set. For $u=(u_i)$ define $f_u=f+\sum_i u_i\phi_i$. On a neighborhood of every zero of $f'$ the total family $\mathcal F(s,u)=f'_u(s)$ is a submersion in the parameter direction, since some $\partial\mathcal F/\partial u_i=\phi_i'(s)=1$. On the compact complement of that neighborhood, $|f'|$ has a positive lower bound, so for all sufficiently small $u$ no new zeros occur there. Thus the total map is transverse to $0$ for parameters in a sufficiently small ball. By [F3], choose a parameter in that ball for which $0$ is a regular value of $f'_u$. The critical points of $f_u$ are then nondegenerate and finite. Shrink the parameter ball so $0<f_u<1$ on the perturbation support. The radial arcs $a_\lambda(s)=\sqrt{f_{\lambda u}(s)/f(s)}\,a(s)$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, form a smooth isotopy of embeddings fixed near the endpoints: the formula is smooth since $f>0$, and sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations preserve immersion and injectivity on the compact source. By [F4], extend this isotopy in an ambient isotopy supported away from the removed trivial arc, so replacing $a$ by $a_u$ preserves the knot type of its closure. Rename $a_u$ as $a$ and $f_u$ as $f$.

In the unit ball $B^4=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:\lVert x\rVert^2+t^2\le1\}$ define $\Omega=\{(s,t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le1-f(s)\}$ and $D=\{(a(s),t):(s,t)\in\Omega\}$. The map $(s,t)\mapsto(a(s),t)$ is an injective immersion, hence an embedding because $\Omega$ is compact. The function $q(s)=(1-f(s))/(s(1-s))$ extends smoothly and positively to $s=0,1$, with $q(0)=-f'(0)>0$ and $q(1)=f'(1)>0$. Consequently $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from the round disk $v^2\le s(1-s)$ onto $\Omega$. The boundary of $\Omega$ is regular: at an interior boundary point $t\ne0$, and at its two endpoints $f'(s)\ne0$, so the differential of $f(s)+t^2$ is nonzero. Thus $D$ is a smooth disk, its boundary lies in $S^3$, and its interior lies in the open four-ball. By [F6], its boundary is exactly the boundary knot specified by properness.

The two boundary arcs of $D$ are the lifts $(a(s),\pm\sqrt{1-f(s)})$ and meet the equatorial $S^2=\{t=0\}\cap S^3$ only at their endpoints. Each hemisphere of $S^3$ is a standard three-ball. Away from a small collar of its equator, projection $(x,t)\mapsto x$ is a smooth diffeomorphism onto the corresponding truncated ball and identifies the lifted arc with $a$. At an endpoint, use the equator collar coordinate $t\ge0$ (or $-t\ge0$ in the lower hemisphere). Since $f'(0)\ne0$ and $f'(1)\ne0$, the implicit function theorem writes the lifted arc near each endpoint as $s=\sigma(t^2)$, with $\sigma$ smooth; in a chart $y$ on the equator its tangential coordinates are $y(t)=y_0+O(t^2)$, while $t$ is the inward collar coordinate. Choose a cutoff $\chi(y,t)$ supported in this chart and equal to $1$ near the arc, and use $(y,t)\mapsto(y-\chi(y,t)(y(t)-y_0),t)$. Its derivative is the identity plus $O(t)$, so after shrinking the collar it is a diffeomorphism and straightens the arc to $\{y_0\}\times[0,\epsilon)$. This is the same standard ball-arc collar as the radial endpoint collar of $a$. Thus the lifted upper arc is the original ball-arc tangle and the lower one is its image under $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$, up to collar-supported isotopy. The boundary orientation traverses one lifted arc in the direction of $a$ and the other in the reverse direction. By [F2] and [F5], closing these two arcs with the fixed connected-sum gluing gives precisely the oriented type $K\#K^\dagger$. Therefore $\partial D$ has the required oriented knot type.

On $D$, the squared radial function is $\rho(s,t)=f(s)+t^2$. Its interior critical points are exactly $(s,0)$ where $f'(s)=0$. At each such point the Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(f''(s),2)$, which is nondegenerate and has index $0$ when $f''(s)>0$ and index $1$ when $f''(s)<0$ by [F7]. Thus there are no index-$2$ critical points, and step 4.1 identifies the boundary knot as $K\#K^\dagger$. This proves the statement.

**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.

- The function $f$ is a **Morse function** when every critical point of $f$ is
  nondegenerate
  ([[def-critical-point-and-critical-value-of-a-smooth-function]],
  [[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex]]).
- The function $f$ is an **excellent Morse function** when it is Morse and any
  two distinct critical points have distinct critical values.

Thus excellence is stronger than the Morse condition: it excludes repeated
critical values, not repeated indices.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and let $p$ be a critical point of $f$. The
Hessian $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the
finite-dimensional real vector space $T_pM$
([[def-hessian-of-a-function-at-a-critical-point]]).

- The **nullity** of $p$ for $f$ is
  $$\operatorname{null}_p(f):=\dim\ker\bigl(\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)\bigr).$$
- The critical point $p$ is **nondegenerate** when
  $\operatorname{null}_p(f)=0$.
- The **index** of $p$ for $f$ is the largest dimension of a subspace of $T_pM$
  on which $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is negative definite.
- The **coindex** of $p$ for $f$ is the largest dimension of a subspace of
  $T_pM$ on which $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is positive definite.

The positivity and negativity conventions are those of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Cut a short trivial arc from $K$ inside a small ball. Identify its complementary ball with the unit ball $B^3\subset\mathbb R^3$ so that the remaining arc is a smooth embedding $a:[0,1]\to B^3$, its endpoints lie on $S^2$, and its interior lies in the open ball. Straighten its endpoint collars to be radial and transverse to $S^2$. A small perturbation supported away from the endpoints makes $a$ avoid the origin; compactness and the fact that a one-dimensional embedded arc has empty interior allow the perturbation to be chosen arbitrarily small in $C^1$, so it remains embedded and fixed on the endpoint collars. Put $f(s)=\lVert a(s)\rVert^2$. Then $f>0$ on $[0,1]$, $f(0)=f(1)=1$, $f<1$ on $(0,1)$, and transversality gives $f'(0)<0<f'(1)$.

The zeros of $f'$ lie in a compact subinterval of $(0,1)$ because $f'$ is nonzero on the endpoint collars. Cover the zero set by finitely many intervals carrying smooth functions $\phi_i$ supported in $(0,1)$ whose derivatives equal $1$ on smaller intervals still covering the zero set. For $u=(u_i)$ define $f_u=f+\sum_i u_i\phi_i$. On a neighborhood of every zero of $f'$ the total family $\mathcal F(s,u)=f'_u(s)$ is a submersion in the parameter direction, since some $\partial\mathcal F/\partial u_i=\phi_i'(s)=1$. On the compact complement of that neighborhood, $|f'|$ has a positive lower bound, so for all sufficiently small $u$ no new zeros occur there. Thus the total map is transverse to $0$ for parameters in a sufficiently small ball. By [F3], choose a parameter in that ball for which $0$ is a regular value of $f'_u$. The critical points of $f_u$ are then nondegenerate and finite. Shrink the parameter ball so $0<f_u<1$ on the perturbation support. The radial arcs $a_\lambda(s)=\sqrt{f_{\lambda u}(s)/f(s)}\,a(s)$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, form a smooth isotopy of embeddings fixed near the endpoints: the formula is smooth since $f>0$, and sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations preserve immersion and injectivity on the compact source. By [F4], extend this isotopy in an ambient isotopy supported away from the removed trivial arc, so replacing $a$ by $a_u$ preserves the knot type of its closure. Rename $a_u$ as $a$ and $f_u$ as $f$.

In the unit ball $B^4=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:\lVert x\rVert^2+t^2\le1\}$ define $\Omega=\{(s,t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le1-f(s)\}$ and $D=\{(a(s),t):(s,t)\in\Omega\}$. The map $(s,t)\mapsto(a(s),t)$ is an injective immersion, hence an embedding because $\Omega$ is compact. The function $q(s)=(1-f(s))/(s(1-s))$ extends smoothly and positively to $s=0,1$, with $q(0)=-f'(0)>0$ and $q(1)=f'(1)>0$. Consequently $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from the round disk $v^2\le s(1-s)$ onto $\Omega$. The boundary of $\Omega$ is regular: at an interior boundary point $t\ne0$, and at its two endpoints $f'(s)\ne0$, so the differential of $f(s)+t^2$ is nonzero. Thus $D$ is a smooth disk, its boundary lies in $S^3$, and its interior lies in the open four-ball. By [F6], its boundary is exactly the boundary knot specified by properness.

The two boundary arcs of $D$ are the lifts $(a(s),\pm\sqrt{1-f(s)})$ and meet the equatorial $S^2=\{t=0\}\cap S^3$ only at their endpoints. Each hemisphere of $S^3$ is a standard three-ball. Away from a small collar of its equator, projection $(x,t)\mapsto x$ is a smooth diffeomorphism onto the corresponding truncated ball and identifies the lifted arc with $a$. At an endpoint, use the equator collar coordinate $t\ge0$ (or $-t\ge0$ in the lower hemisphere). Since $f'(0)\ne0$ and $f'(1)\ne0$, the implicit function theorem writes the lifted arc near each endpoint as $s=\sigma(t^2)$, with $\sigma$ smooth; in a chart $y$ on the equator its tangential coordinates are $y(t)=y_0+O(t^2)$, while $t$ is the inward collar coordinate. Choose a cutoff $\chi(y,t)$ supported in this chart and equal to $1$ near the arc, and use $(y,t)\mapsto(y-\chi(y,t)(y(t)-y_0),t)$. Its derivative is the identity plus $O(t)$, so after shrinking the collar it is a diffeomorphism and straightens the arc to $\{y_0\}\times[0,\epsilon)$. This is the same standard ball-arc collar as the radial endpoint collar of $a$. Thus the lifted upper arc is the original ball-arc tangle and the lower one is its image under $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$, up to collar-supported isotopy. The boundary orientation traverses one lifted arc in the direction of $a$ and the other in the reverse direction. By [F2] and [F5], closing these two arcs with the fixed connected-sum gluing gives precisely the oriented type $K\#K^\dagger$. Therefore $\partial D$ has the required oriented knot type.

On $D$, the squared radial function is $\rho(s,t)=f(s)+t^2$. Its interior critical points are exactly $(s,0)$ where $f'(s)=0$. At each such point the Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(f''(s),2)$, which is nondegenerate and has index $0$ when $f''(s)>0$ and index $1$ when $f''(s)<0$ by [F7]. Thus there are no index-$2$ critical points, and step 4.1 identifies the boundary knot as $K\#K^\dagger$. This proves the statement.

derivations.claim: Suppose first that a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$ has boundary $K$. Choose an interior point $p\in D$ and a sufficiently small round four-ball $E$ about $p$ contained in $\operatorname{int}B^4$. In orthonormal coordinates at $p$, the local graph theorem writes $D$ as $z=g(u)$ over a disk in its tangent plane, with $g(0)=0$ and $Dg(0)=0$. For small radius $R$, the function $r\mapsto r^2+g(r\theta)^2$ has derivative $2r+O(r^3)>0$ for every unit direction $\theta$ and $0<r\le R$. Hence $D\cap\partial E$ is one radial graph over the tangent circle. Replacing $g$ by $\lambda g$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, and solving the same strictly increasing radial equation gives an isotopy on $\partial E$ to the equatorial circle. Thus $D\cap\partial E$ is the unknot. The family of round balls moving the center of $E$ to $0$ along a path in $\operatorname{int}B^4$ is an isotopy of compact embeddings supported in $\operatorname{int}B^4$; apply [F4] to extend it. Hence $B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}E$ is diffeomorphic, with boundary collars, to the standard shell $S^3\times I$. Removing $\operatorname{int}(D\cap E)$ from $D$ gives an annulus in that shell with boundary $K$ and an unknot.

Conversely, suppose $K$ is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot. Reverse the interval coordinate if needed so the unknot is the lower boundary. Glue a standard four-ball along the lower $S^3$ end of $S^3\times I$. The union is a standard four-ball with an added boundary collar: explicitly, the collar extends the radial coordinate of the unit ball from radius $1$ to radius $2$, and radial rescaling identifies it with the unit ball. Cap the lower unknot boundary of the annulus by the standard disk from [F3]. The annulus and cap meet in matching product collars, so their union is a smooth properly embedded disk with boundary $K$.

The product collars at the two boundary circles identify the annulus from step 1.1 with a smooth concordance, after orienting it so the lower boundary is the negative of its induced knot orientation and the upper boundary is positive. If necessary, reverse the interval coordinate to place the unknot at the lower end; a half-turn of the standard round circle about a diameter is an orientation-preserving ambient rotation that reverses its circle orientation, so the endpoint still has the standard oriented unknot type. Reversing the annulus orientation when required gives the boundary convention in [F1]. Therefore $K$ is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove that a smooth slice disk gives smooth concordance to the unknot, and step 1.2 proves the converse.

derivations.claim: Suppose first that a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$ has boundary $K$. Choose an interior point $p\in D$ and a sufficiently small round four-ball $E$ about $p$ contained in $\operatorname{int}B^4$. In orthonormal coordinates at $p$, the local graph theorem writes $D$ as $z=g(u)$ over a disk in its tangent plane, with $g(0)=0$ and $Dg(0)=0$. For small radius $R$, the function $r\mapsto r^2+g(r\theta)^2$ has derivative $2r+O(r^3)>0$ for every unit direction $\theta$ and $0<r\le R$. Hence $D\cap\partial E$ is one radial graph over the tangent circle. Replacing $g$ by $\lambda g$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, and solving the same strictly increasing radial equation gives an isotopy through smooth embeddings of $S^1$ in $\partial E\cong S^3$ to the equatorial circle. By [F4], with target $\partial E\cong S^3$, this isotopy extends to an ambient isotopy of $S^3$; hence $D\cap\partial E$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot. The family of round balls moving the center of $E$ to $0$ along a path in $\operatorname{int}B^4$ is an isotopy of compact embeddings supported in $\operatorname{int}B^4$; apply [F4] with target $\mathbb R^4$ to extend it. Hence $B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}E$ is diffeomorphic, with boundary collars, to the standard shell $S^3\times I$. Removing $\operatorname{int}(D\cap E)$ from $D$ gives an annulus in that shell with boundary $K$ and a standard unknot.

Conversely, suppose $K$ is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot. Reverse the interval coordinate if needed so the unknot is the lower boundary. Glue a standard four-ball along the lower $S^3$ end of $S^3\times I$. The union is a standard four-ball with an added boundary collar: explicitly, the collar extends the radial coordinate of the unit ball from radius $1$ to radius $2$, and radial rescaling identifies it with the unit ball. Cap the lower unknot boundary of the annulus by the standard disk from [F3]. The annulus and cap meet in matching product collars, so their union is a smooth properly embedded disk with boundary $K$.

The product collars at the two boundary circles identify the annulus from step 1.1 with a smooth concordance, after orienting it so the lower boundary is the negative of its induced knot orientation and the upper boundary is positive. If necessary, reverse the interval coordinate to place the unknot at the lower end; a half-turn of the standard round circle about a diameter is an orientation-preserving ambient rotation that reverses its circle orientation, so the endpoint still has the standard oriented unknot type. Reversing the annulus orientation when required gives the boundary convention in [F1]. Therefore $K$ is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot.

A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].
