citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ over $I$. For every $(s,p)\in I\times M$
there exist an open interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$, open
neighbourhoods $U_r$ of the evolving points, and a smooth map

$$ \Psi:\{(t,s,q): t,s\in J,\ q\in U_s\}\to M $$

such that $t\mapsto \Psi_{t,s}(q)$ is the unique solution of
$\dot\gamma(t)=X_t(\gamma(t))$ with $\Psi_{s,s}(q)=q$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous, where $M$ is a smooth manifold, and let $\varepsilon:M\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive continuous error function. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$\|\widetilde F(p)-F(p)\|<\varepsilon(p)\qquad\text{for all }p\in M.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Let $H$ be a free abelian group of rank $2g$ and let $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ be a bilinear form. Write $H_{\mathbb Q}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and extend $V$ $\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to $H_{\mathbb Q}$. If $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of dimension $g$ and $V(x,y)=0$ for all $x,y\in L$, then $M=H\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand of $H$ and $V|_{M\times M}=0$.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. After matching product collars and pushing the interior of $F$ slightly into $B^4$, the closed locally flat surface $\Sigma=F\cup_KD$ bounds a compact connected oriented locally flat three-manifold $R\subset B^4$. The conclusion includes an oriented ambient product neighborhood of $R$ on both sides, with the positive normal push-off along the $F$ portion of $\partial R=\Sigma$ lying on the complementary side of $R$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, the inclusion of smooth into continuous real singular chains induces an isomorphism
$$H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$$
in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. 4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. $$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

derivations.claim: If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. Since $J:H\to\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism, the functional $J(e,-)$ is primitive, so Bezout's identity gives $f\in H$ with $J(e,f)=1$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$.

Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$.

For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$.

For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$.

The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

derivations.claim: In $(H,V)\oplus(H,-V)$, the diagonal subgroup $\Delta H=\{(x,x):x\in H\}$ is a direct summand: it is the kernel of the surjection $(x,y)\mapsto x-y$ and that surjection has section $z\mapsto(z,0)$. Its rank is $\operatorname{rank}H$, half the rank of $H\oplus H$. For $x,y\in H$, $(V\oplus(-V))((x,x),(y,y))=V(x,y)-V(x,y)=0$, so $\Delta H$ is a metabolizer.
By [F1], the metabolic direct sum in step 1.1 represents zero, while the direct-sum relation identifies its class with $[V]+[-V]$. Hence $[-V]=-[V]$.

Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$.

Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose core has self-linking $+1$ in the positive-push convention. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. The graph $M=\{(x,Px):x\in\mathbb Z^2\}$ is spanned by $e_1+e_4$ and $e_2+e_3$; projection onto the first factor identifies it with $\mathbb Z^2$, so it is a rank-$2$ direct summand. citations.quote:
Let $C_\bullet$ and $D_\bullet$ be chain complexes. A **chain map**
$f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a family of morphisms
$$f_n:C_n\to D_n$$
such that for every $n\in\mathbb Z$,
$$d^D_n\circ f_n=f_{n-1}\circ d^C_n.$$

Equivalently, each square
$$\begin{matrix} C_n&\xrightarrow{f_n}&D_n\\ d^C_n\downarrow&&\downarrow d^D_n\\ C_{n-1}&\xrightarrow{f_{n-1}}&D_{n-1} \end{matrix}$$
commutes.

Let $C_\bullet,D_\bullet$ be chain complexes in an abelian category
$\mathcal A$, and let $f,g:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be chain maps. A **chain homotopy**
$s:f\simeq g$ is a graded morphism of degree $1$,
$$s_n:C_n\to D_{n+1},$$
such that for every $n\in\mathbb Z$,
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n.$$

Equivalently, $f-g$ is the degree-$0$ boundary of the degree-$1$ family $s$ in
[[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]].

A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a **chain homotopy equivalence** if
there exists a chain map $g:D_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ such that
$$g\circ f\simeq1_C,\qquad f\circ g\simeq1_D.$$

Such a map $g$ is called a **homotopy inverse** of $f$.

A left $R$-module $P$ is **projective** if it has the lifting property for epimorphisms: whenever $q:E\to M$ is a surjective module homomorphism and $f:P\to M$ is a module homomorphism, there exists a module homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to E$ such that $q\circ\tilde f=f$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

The lift need not be unique. Projectivity asks for a lift in every such square.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F$ be a function with domain $n$ all of whose
values are nonempty sets. Then the family of its values,
$\mathcal{F} = F[n] = \{\, F(i) : i \in n \,\}$, has a choice function
([[def-choice-function]]).

This is a theorem of ZF: its proof uses no form of the Axiom of Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$. The
natural number $n$ serves as the index set in the von Neumann sense,
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "$F$ has domain $n$"
says precisely that the members of $\mathcal{F}$ are listed as
$F(0), \dots, F(n-1)$. The listing need not be injective, and $\mathcal{F}$ is the
set of values, so repetitions are harmless and are not counted.

The displayed statement and its proof use only a natural-number-indexed
function. They do not identify an arbitrary finite family with a particular
enumeration.

Multiplying the formula on the right by $h$ and substituting $dh$ in its first term proves the next case: the identity coefficient changes from $\epsilon_s$ to $\epsilon_s+(-1)^s=\epsilon_{s+1}$ and the last summand acquires index $s$. These are specified finite formulas in every degree. We next verify that $D$ is a chain complex and that the named maps have all claimed properties; these are not assumed from a matrix citation.

The final column of $\delta_n$ has only its final block $+\partial_n$. Therefore $\delta_n\alpha_n=\alpha_{n-1}d_n$, using $\partial f=fd$. To check $\beta_{n-1}\delta_n=d_n\beta_n$, consider column $j$. If $j=n$, the assertion is $g_{n-1}\partial_n=d_ng_n$. Otherwise put $t=n-j\ge1$. The superdiagonal contribution is $(-1)^t h^tdg_j$ (zero if $j=0$); the diagonal contribution is $\epsilon_t h^{t-1}g_j-(-1)^{t-1}h^{t-1}ug_j$. Reindexing the lower contributions by $\ell=n-1-k$ gives $-\sum_{\ell=0}^{t-2}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{t-1-\ell}g_j$. The total is exactly $dh^tg_j$ by step 1.1. Thus both intertwining identities hold, without yet assuming $\delta^2=0$.

Directly in the blocks, $$\delta_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}\delta_n=1_{D_n}-\alpha_n\beta_n.$$ Indeed for rows $k<n$ the off-diagonal blocks cancel when $n$ is replaced by $n+1$, and the two diagonal blocks sum to $1$. In row $n$ only the first term is present: its blocks are $-f_nh^{n-j}g_j$ for $j<n$ and $1-f_ng_n$ for $j=n$. They are exactly the final row of $1-\alpha\beta$. For $n=0$ this is simply $\delta_1s_0=1-f_0g_0$. Also $\beta_n\alpha_n=g_nf_n$.

We prove $\delta_{n-1}\delta_n=0$ by induction on $n$. It holds at $n=1$ since $D_{-1}=0$. On the first $n$ summands of $D_n$, identified with $s_{n-1}D_{n-1}$, step 2.2 and the two intertwining identities give $$\begin{aligned} \delta_{n-1}\delta_ns_{n-1} &=\delta_{n-1}(1-\alpha\beta-s_{n-2}\delta_{n-1})\\ &=(1-\alpha\beta)\delta_{n-1}-\delta_{n-1}s_{n-2}\delta_{n-1}\\ &=s_{n-3}\delta_{n-2}\delta_{n-1}=0. \end{aligned}$$ The final equality uses the induction hypothesis, and negative-index terms mean zero. On the remaining summand $F_n$, the two final-column observations give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Thus the composite vanishes on every summand. This proves $\delta^2=0$. Now step 2.1 says that $\alpha,\beta$ are chain maps, and step 2.2 together with $1-\beta\alpha=dh+hd$ gives a chain homotopy equivalence $C\simeq D$.

Set $T=\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$. For all $n\ge m$, $D_n$ is canonically $T$, because all subsequent summands are zero. For $n\ge m+1$, the square matrix $\delta_n:T\to T$ depends only on the parity of $n$. Write $p$ for its value when $n$ is even. The formulas show that its value when $n$ is odd is $1-p$: the off-diagonal blocks change sign and the diagonal blocks are complementary. Taking two consecutive such degrees in $\delta^2=0$ gives $p(1-p)=0=(1-p)p$, hence $p^2=p$. No assertion that the homotopy idempotent $fg$ itself is strictly idempotent has been made.

Choose the explicit even integer $N=2(m+1)$, and let $q=p:T\to T$. Define $E_n=D_n$ for $0\le n<N$, $E_N=qT\subseteq T=D_N$, and $E_n=0$ otherwise. Restrict $\delta_N$ to $qT$ at the top, and keep $\delta_n$ below it. The square-zero identities remain valid by step 3.1. The maps $J:E\to D$ are the evident inclusions. Define $I:D\to E$ to be identity below $N$, $q$ in degree $N$ and zero above $N$. At degree $N$, $\delta_Nq=\delta_N$ because $1-q=\delta_{N+1}$ and $\delta_N\delta_{N+1}=0$. At degree $N+1$, $q\delta_{N+1}=q(1-q)=0$. These are the only boundary degrees in checking that $I$ is a chain map; $J$ is a chain map by restriction, and $IJ=1_E$.

Define $t_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ to be zero for $n<N$ and the canonical identity $T\to T$ for $n\ge N$. Then $$1_D-JI=\delta t+t\delta.$$ Below $N$ both sides are zero. In degree $N$ the right side is $\delta_{N+1}=1-q$, which is the left side. Above $N$ it is the sum of the two complementary matrices $p$ and $1-p$, hence identity, as is the left side. Thus $I,J$ give a specified chain homotopy equivalence between $D$ and the bounded complex $E$.

The modules $E_n$ below $N$ are finite direct sums of the supplied finite free modules, so their concatenated bases are finite. The module $qT$ is generated by the finitely many vectors $q(e_i)$, where $(e_i)$ is that concatenated basis of $T$, and $T=qT\oplus(1-q)T$: write $x=qx+(1-q)x$, and apply $q$ to an element in the intersection to show it is zero. For completeness its projectivity is choice-free. Given a surjection $v:U\to V$ and a right-linear $w:qT\to V$, take, for each of the finitely many $e_i$, a lift in $U$ of $w(qe_i)$. Their simultaneous existence is [F3]. Extend this finite assignment right-linearly to a map $\widetilde w:T\to U$. Then $v\widetilde w=wq$, and restriction to $qT$ is the requested lift. The same proof with $q=1$ gives projectivity of the lower finite free modules. This verifies the actual lifting property, not the general claim that arbitrary free modules are projective in ZF.

Set $a=I\alpha$, $b=\beta J$. These are chain maps and $$1_C-ba=d(h+\beta t\alpha)+(h+\beta t\alpha)d,$$ since $1_C-\beta JI\alpha=(1_C-\beta\alpha)+\beta(1_D-JI)\alpha$. Similarly, using $IJ=1_E$ and step 2.2, $$1_E-ab=\delta_E(IsJ)+(IsJ)\delta_E.$$ Indeed $I(1_D-\alpha\beta)J=1_E-I\alpha\beta J$. These are the explicit required homotopies $H=h+\beta t\alpha$ and $L=IsJ$.

Every degree of $D$, every matrix product used to define its maps, and each component of the homotopies uses a finite sum and finitely many compositions of supplied maps. The single family indexed by all nonnegative degrees is defined by these formulas; it is not obtained by independently selecting a lift or basis in each degree. The only lifts selected in the entire projectivity verification are a finite list for one supplied lifting problem. If the two input complexes vanish below a common integer $b$, reindex $C'_n=C_{n+b}$, $F'_n=F_{n+b}$ with the same differentials and domination equations, apply the construction, and reindex the result back. No infinite recursion of choices and no unbounded-below input is involved. The proof therefore establishes exactly the stated ZF conclusion for the required bounded-below setting.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). A complex-linear functional $\tau:M\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if $\tau(P)\in[0,+\infty)$ for every positive operator $P\in M$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), a **state** if it is positive and $\tau(I_H)=1$, **normal** if its restriction to the operator-norm unit ball of $M$ is continuous for the relative weak-operator topology ([[def-strong-and-weak-operator-topologies]], [[def-operator-norm]]), **tracial** if $\tau(ST)=\tau(TS)$ for all $S,T\in M$, and **faithful** if $\tau(T^*T)=0$ implies $T=0$. A **faithful normal tracial state** is a positive normalized trace that is both normal and faithful. In particular, $(M,\tau)$ is a **finite tracial von Neumann algebra** when $\tau$ is a faithful normal tracial state. If $H=\{0\}$ then $M=\{0\}$ and has no state, since $I_H=0$.

For a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $K$, the normalized matrix trace $\operatorname{tr}_K/\dim K$ is a faithful normal tracial state on $\mathcal B(K)$, and it is the unique tracial state.

For a discrete group $\Gamma$ equipped with the discrete topology, let $H_\Gamma=\ell^2(\Gamma,\mathbb C)$, whose Hilbert-space structure under AC is established in the proof. Define the left and right regular operators by
$$
(\lambda_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(g^{-1}h),\qquad (\rho_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(hg)\qquad(g,h\in\Gamma).
$$
Put $L(\Gamma):=W^*(\lambda_\Gamma(\Gamma))$ using the concrete generated von Neumann algebra of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. Then
$$
\tau_\Gamma(T):=\langle T\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle\qquad(T\in L(\Gamma))
$$
is a faithful normal tracial state on $L(\Gamma)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, with operator spectrum $\sigma(T)$
([[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then:

1. there is a unique regular projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
   $\sigma$-algebra of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb C$
   such that $\int z\,dE(z)=T$ and, equivalently,
   $$\Phi_E(f)=f(T)\qquad\text{for every continuous }f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C,$$
   where $f(T)$ is the continuous functional calculus of
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]] and
   $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel integral of the projection valued measure $E$;
   this $E$ is the **spectral projection valued measure** of $T$;

   a regular projection valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: A spectral projection of a self-adjoint matrix over $A$ belongs to the same matrix von Neumann algebra: it commutes with every element of that algebra's commutant by [F3], so belongs to its double commutant by [F2]. In the rectangular case apply this observation to $B^*B$ and $BB^*$; the polar partial isometry is the strong limit of $B(B^*B+\varepsilon I)^{-1/2}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and belongs to the rectangular matrix algebra by [F2]–[F4]. Thus kernel, initial and final projections are matrices over $A$. The equality $\tau_s(v^*v)=\tau_r(vv^*)$, obtained by summing the trace identity for the matrix entries of $v$, gives the displayed rank-nullity formula. The algebraic kernel is exactly $P_{\ker B}A^s$, and $B$ maps $(I-P_{\ker B})A^s$ bijectively onto its algebraic image.

Every finite projective module has the form $eA^r$ for an idempotent $e$. Its Hilbert range is closed because $e^2=e$. Let $p$ be its orthogonal range projection, which lies in $M_r(A)$ by step 1.1. Since $ep=p$ and $pe=e$, one has $eA^r=pA^r$. Every module map between two such projection modules is given by a rectangular matrix: extend it to the ambient finite free module by composing with the source projection. If the algebraic map is injective, its Hilbert kernel projection is zero, since a nonzero kernel projection has a nonzero column in the algebraic kernel. Polar decomposition then implies that the source projection trace is at most the target projection trace. Applying this to an isomorphism and its inverse proves invariance of projective dimension.

For finitely many vectors of $L$, let $B$ have those vectors as columns. The corresponding range projection $q_B$ lies in $M_r(A)$ by step 1.1. As the finite subsets increase, the ranges increase, and their union has Hilbert closure equal to the closure of $L$: a vector $x\in A^r$ gives its Hilbert representative by applying its entries to $\delta_e$, while right translates of those representatives are also representatives of vectors of $L$. Their closed span contains the range of each column operator, because the coordinate vectors span $\ell^2(G)$ densely. The increasing projections converge strongly to their supremum $q\in M_r(A)$ by [F2]. Their ranges lie in the range of $p$, so $q\le p$.

For each such $B$, let $q_{B,\varepsilon}=\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(BB^*)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Then $q_{B,\varepsilon}\le q_B$ and $q_{B,\varepsilon}\uparrow q_B$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The bounded Borel function $f_\varepsilon(t)=t^{-1}\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(t)$ gives $q_{B,\varepsilon}=BB^*f_\varepsilon(BB^*)$. Hence every column of $q_{B,\varepsilon}$ is a right $A$-linear combination of columns of $B$, and $q_{B,\varepsilon}A^r\subseteq L$. Normality of the trace first lets these traces approach $\tau_r(q_B)$ and then, over finite subsets, $\tau_r(q)$. Conversely any finite projective submodule of $L$ embeds in $qA^r$, so step 2.1 bounds its dimension by $\tau_r(q)$. Taking suprema proves $\dim_A L=\tau_r(q)$.

The module $(p-q)A^r$ embeds in $pA^r/L$, giving lower dimension bound $\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q)$. For the reverse bound let a finite projective $P$ embed in that quotient. Projectivity lifts this map to a map $f:P\to pA^r$. For each projection $q_{B,\varepsilon}$ from step 3.1, the map $(p-q_{B,\varepsilon})f$ is injective: its kernel maps under $f$ into $q_{B,\varepsilon}A^r\subseteq L$, and therefore has zero image under the given embedding of $P$ into the quotient. Step 2.1 yields $\dim_A P\le\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q_{B,\varepsilon})$. Taking the projection traces arbitrarily close to $\tau_r(q)$ proves the quotient formula.

Submodules of a zero-dimensional module are zero-dimensional by the defining supremum. If a finite projective embeds in a quotient of a zero-dimensional module, projectivity lifts it to an injective map into the original module; hence its dimension is zero, proving quotient closure. For an exact sequence $0\to U\to V\to W\to0$ with $U,W$ zero-dimensional, take any finite projective $P\subseteq V$. Its kernel $K=P\cap U$ and its image $P/K\subseteq W$ are zero-dimensional. Apply steps 3.1 and 4.1 inside a projection representation of $P$: those formulas give $\dim_A P=\dim_A K+\dim_A(P/K)=0$. Thus $V$ is zero-dimensional. Finally, each image of a zero-dimensional module in a filtered colimit is zero-dimensional by quotient closure; these images form a directed family. Every finite set of generators of a finite projective submodule of the colimit lies in one member, so that projective has dimension zero. This proves filtered-colimit closure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $A$ and $C$ be groups, and let

$$\alpha,\beta:C\to A$$

be injective group homomorphisms ([[def-group-homomorphism]]). Let $F(\{t\})$
be the free group on one generator and form the free product
$A\ast F(\{t\})$ ([[def-free-product-of-a-family-of-groups]],
[[def-free-group]]). The **HNN extension** of $A$ with associated edge maps
$\alpha,\beta$ is

$$\frac{A\ast F(\{t\})}{\left\langle\!\left\langle t\alpha(c)t^{-1}\beta(c)^{-1}:c\in C\right\rangle\!\right\rangle}.$$

Equivalently, in **relative-presentation notation**, it is

$$\left\langle A,t\ \middle|\ t\alpha(c)t^{-1}=\beta(c)\text{ for every }c\in C\right\rangle.$$

Thus the conjugacy relations are

$$t\,\alpha(c)\,t^{-1}=\beta(c)\qquad(c\in C).$$

If $A=\langle X\mid R\rangle$ is presented as in
[[def-group-presentation]], choose words $u_c,v_c\in F(X)$ representing
$\alpha(c),\beta(c)$ for each $c\in C$. The corresponding ordinary group
presentation is

$$\left\langle X,t \,\middle|\, R,\ t u_c t^{-1}v_c^{-1}\text{ for every }c\in C\right\rangle.$$

Different choices of $u_c,v_c$ differ by consequences of $R$, so they give
the same quotient. The relative notation avoids making any word-lift choice.

The new generator $t$ is the **stable letter**.

In an HNN extension, the canonical map from the base group $A$ to the presented
group is injective. Equivalently, a base-group element represents the identity
in the HNN extension only when it is already the identity in $A$.

Let

$$G=\left\langle A,t \,\middle|\, t\,\alpha(c)\,t^{-1}=\beta(c)\text{ for }c\in C\right\rangle$$

be an HNN extension. Let $H$ be a group, let $f:A\to H$ be a group
homomorphism, and let $h\in H$ satisfy

$$h\,f(\alpha(c))\,h^{-1}=f(\beta(c))\qquad(c\in C).$$

Then there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline f:G\to H$$

whose restriction to $A$ is $f$ and whose value on the stable letter is
$\overline f(t)=h$.

For $n\ge0$, let $B_n(G)$ be the free abelian group on
$(g_0,\ldots,g_n)\in G^{n+1}$, with diagonal left action
$h(g_0,\ldots,g_n)=(hg_0,\ldots,hg_n)$. For $n\ge1$, put
$$d_n=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i:B_n(G)\longrightarrow B_{n-1}(G),$$
where $d_i$ deletes the $i$th vertex. In degree zero use the augmentation
$\varepsilon:B_0(G)\to\mathbb Z$, $\varepsilon(g_0)=1$, with trivial action
on $\mathbb Z$. Thus the augmented complex is
$\cdots\to B_1(G)\to B_0(G)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\mathbb Z\to0$; no
undefined object $B_{-1}$ or differential $d_0$ is used.

Assume DC and the supplied projective-resolution convention for derived group homology. For every left $G$-module $M$, $H_n(G;M)$ is naturally the homology of $C_n(G;M)=(\overline B_n(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)_G$, with diagonal left action and alternating vertex-deletion differential. Equivalently it is computed by $\overline B^{\rm right}(G)\otimes_{\mathbb ZG}M$, where $b\cdot g=g^{-1}b$.

derivations.claim: Put $B=K\times K$. First adjoin $u$ with $u(g,1)u^{-1}=(1,g)$, an HNN extension between the two injective copies of $K$ in $B$. Next adjoin $t$ with $t(g,1)t^{-1}=(g,g)$; these associated maps remain injective after the first extension. By [F1], $B$ embeds after both adjunctions. Eliminating $(1,g)$ using the first relation leaves precisely the displayed presentation of $m(K)$: commutation between the two factors gives $[h,ugu^{-1}]=1$, and the diagonal relation becomes $tgt^{-1}=gugu^{-1}$. Conversely those relations define the commuting homomorphisms $(g,h)\mapsto g uhu^{-1}$ and satisfy both HNN relations, so the two presentation maps are inverse on generators. Thus $k_K:K\to m(K)$ is injective.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $A$ and $C$ be groups, and let

$$\alpha,\beta:C\to A$$

be injective group homomorphisms ([[def-group-homomorphism]]). Let $F(\{t\})$
be the free group on one generator and form the free product
$A\ast F(\{t\})$ ([[def-free-product-of-a-family-of-groups]],
[[def-free-group]]). The **HNN extension** of $A$ with associated edge maps
$\alpha,\beta$ is

$$\frac{A\ast F(\{t\})}{\left\langle\!\left\langle t\alpha(c)t^{-1}\beta(c)^{-1}:c\in C\right\rangle\!\right\rangle}.$$

Equivalently, in **relative-presentation notation**, it is

$$\left\langle A,t\ \middle|\ t\alpha(c)t^{-1}=\beta(c)\text{ for every }c\in C\right\rangle.$$

Thus the conjugacy relations are

$$t\,\alpha(c)\,t^{-1}=\beta(c)\qquad(c\in C).$$

If $A=\langle X\mid R\rangle$ is presented as in
[[def-group-presentation]], choose words $u_c,v_c\in F(X)$ representing
$\alpha(c),\beta(c)$ for each $c\in C$. The corresponding ordinary group
presentation is

$$\left\langle X,t \,\middle|\, R,\ t u_c t^{-1}v_c^{-1}\text{ for every }c\in C\right\rangle.$$

Different choices of $u_c,v_c$ differ by consequences of $R$, so they give
the same quotient. The relative notation avoids making any word-lift choice.

The new generator $t$ is the **stable letter**.

In an HNN extension, the canonical map from the base group $A$ to the presented
group is injective. Equivalently, a base-group element represents the identity
in the HNN extension only when it is already the identity in $A$.

Let

$$G=\left\langle A,t \,\middle|\, t\,\alpha(c)\,t^{-1}=\beta(c)\text{ for }c\in C\right\rangle$$

be an HNN extension. Let $H$ be a group, let $f:A\to H$ be a group
homomorphism, and let $h\in H$ satisfy

$$h\,f(\alpha(c))\,h^{-1}=f(\beta(c))\qquad(c\in C).$$

Then there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline f:G\to H$$

whose restriction to $A$ is $f$ and whose value on the stable letter is
$\overline f(t)=h$.

For $n\ge0$, let $B_n(G)$ be the free abelian group on
$(g_0,\ldots,g_n)\in G^{n+1}$, with diagonal left action

$$d_n=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i:B_n(G)\longrightarrow B_{n-1}(G),$$
where $d_i$ deletes the $i$th vertex. In degree zero use the augmentation
$\varepsilon:B_0(G)\to\mathbb Z$, $\varepsilon(g_0)=1$, with trivial action
on $\mathbb Z$. Thus the augmented complex is
$\cdots\to B_1(G)\to B_0(G)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\mathbb Z\to0$; no
undefined object $B_{-1}$ or differential $d_0$ is used.

Assume DC and the supplied projective-resolution convention for derived group homology. For every left $G$-module $M$, $H_n(G;M)$ is naturally the homology of $C_n(G;M)=(\overline B_n(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)_G$, with diagonal left action and alternating vertex-deletion differential. Equivalently it is computed by $\overline B^{\rm right}(G)\otimes_{\mathbb ZG}M$, where $b\cdot g=g^{-1}b$.

We first fix the intersection sign and verify independence directly. For transverse oriented $2$-chains $C,T$ in an oriented $3$-manifold, orient their intersection so that
$$\partial(C\cap T)=(\partial C)\cap T-C\cap(\partial T).$$
This sign follows by the outward-normal-first boundary convention in an oriented coordinate ball: taking a boundary in the second sheet passes its outward normal past the one normal direction of the first sheet. Consequently, the total signed endpoint count gives
$$C\cdot\partial T=(\partial C)\cdot T.$$
These identities extend linearly to chains; the terms on paired interior faces cancel. For a closed $2$-chain $E$ and torsion cycle $y$, choose $m>0$ and $\partial T=my$. Then $m(E\cdot y)=E\cdot\partial T=0$, so $E\cdot y=0$. Thus if $\partial C=nx$ and $\partial C'=n'x$, the closed chain $n'C-nC'$ has zero intersection with $y$, giving $(C\cdot y)/n=(C'\cdot y)/n'$. Replacing $x$ by $x+\partial S$ permits replacing $C$ by $C+nS$ and changes the quotient by the integer $S\cdot y$. Replacing $y$ by $y+\partial T$ changes it by $(C\cdot\partial T)/n=x\cdot T$, also an integer. A change of transverse position is a chain homotopy: its prism has the moved-chain difference as boundary, so these same boundary identities apply. Hence the expression defines a pairing on the stated homology classes, independent of all these choices modulo $\mathbb Z$.

To identify that pairing with the Bockstein, use [F4] and [F5] and represent $x$ by a primal cellular $1$-cycle $a$, and $y$ by a dual cellular $1$-cycle $b$. Since $n[a]=0$, there is an integral primal cellular $2$-chain $C$ with $\partial C=na$. The dual-cell pairing gives the rational cellular $1$-cochain
$$u(e)=\frac{C\cdot e}{n}$$
on every oriented dual edge $e$. Let $z_a$ be the integral cellular $2$-cochain on the dual complex defined by $z_a(\sigma)=a\cdot\sigma$. The sign convention in step 2.1 gives, for every dual $2$-cell $\sigma$,
$$(\delta u)(\sigma)=\frac{C\cdot\partial\sigma}{n} =\frac{(\partial C)\cdot\sigma}{n} =a\cdot\sigma=z_a(\sigma).$$
There is no extra minus sign: in an oriented chart with $a$ tangent to the first coordinate and its dual $2$-cell tangent to the second and third coordinates, $a\cdot\sigma=+1$. A primal $2$-cell followed by its positive transverse dual edge likewise has intersection $+1$. These are precisely the oriented dual-cell representatives of inverse cap duality, so $[z_a]=\operatorname{PD}(x)$.

Reducing $u$ modulo $\mathbb Z$ gives a cocycle $\bar u$, because $\delta u=z_a$ is integral. Under the natural comparison [F5], the connecting map in [F3] is constructed by lifting this cocycle to a rational cochain and taking its coboundary; therefore
$$\beta[\bar u]=[\delta u]=\operatorname{PD}(x),\qquad \langle[\bar u],y\rangle=u(b)\bmod\mathbb Z =\frac{C\cdot b}{n}\bmod\mathbb Z.$$

Cellular representatives cause no restriction by [F5]: cellular and singular chain models represent the same classes, and changes of representatives and transverse positions have already been accounted for. Thus the precise identity is
$$\lambda_Y(x,y)=\bigl\langle\beta^{-1}\operatorname{PD}(x),y\bigr\rangle.$$
The evaluation is on the homology class $y$, not on a cohomology class called its Poincaré dual; equivalently it is the corresponding degree-$3$ cup-product evaluation on $[Y]$.

Under [F2], evaluation identifies $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with the entire character group $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. The displayed identity in step 2.3 identifies the adjoint of the bounding-chain pairing with the composite of this isomorphism, $\beta^{-1}$, and $\operatorname{PD}$. All three are isomorphisms, so the pairing is nonsingular. In particular its bilinearity also follows from these homomorphisms and evaluation.

For torsion classes $x,y$, choose transverse representatives and chains $C,D$ with $\partial C=nx$ and $\partial D=my$. The boundary identity of step 2.1 applied to $C\cap D$ gives $n(x\cdot D)=m(C\cdot y)$. Interchanging a $1$-cycle and a $2$-chain in an oriented $3$-manifold changes the intersection sign by $(-1)^{(3-1)(3-2)}=+1$, so $x\cdot D=D\cdot x$. citations.quote: Let $X$ be a path-connected CW space. The oriented bordism set $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ consists of classes of pairs $(M,f)$, where $M$ is a closed smooth oriented $n$-manifold and $f:M\to X$. Two pairs are bordant when there is a compact oriented $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M_0\sqcup(-M_1)$ and a map $F:W\to X$ restricting to $f_0$ and $f_1$ on the boundary. Disjoint union defines the operation. For a group $G$, $K(G,1)$ denotes a connected CW space with fundamental group $G$ and contractible universal cover.

derivations.claim: The sum is well-defined: if $F_i:W_i\to X$ are bordisms witnessing equivalences of pairs for $i=0,1$, then $W_0\sqcup W_1$ with map $F_0\sqcup F_1$ is a bordism witnessing the equivalence of the disjoint unions. Boundary orientations are inherited componentwise.

Disjoint union is associative and commutative up to the orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that rebracket or permute its components; composing the maps with these diffeomorphisms preserves the bordism classes. The empty manifold with its unique map is a two-sided identity.

The cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ with map $f\circ\operatorname{pr}_M$ has boundary $(M,f)\sqcup(-M,f)$ under the product orientation convention. Thus $(-M,f)$ is a two-sided inverse of $(M,f)$, so the operation is an abelian group operation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk with boundary $K\subset S^3$. Choose a closed tubular neighborhood $N(D)\cong D^2\times D^2$ meeting $S^3$ in $\partial D\times D^2$, and let $X_D$ be the closure of $B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}N(D)$, with corners rounded. The positive meridian is the oriented circle $\{x\}\times\partial D^2$ in the overlap $D^2\times S^1$, oriented by the ambient and disk orientations.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Both $B^4$ and $N(D)$ are contractible, and $N(D)\cap X_D$ is connected and homotopy equivalent to $S^1$ by [F1]. The reduced degree-zero part of Mayer–Vietoris [F2] therefore gives $\widetilde H_0(X_D;\mathbb Z)=0$, so $X_D$ is connected.

In degree one, the sequence has $H_2(B^4)=0$, then $H_1(N(D)\cap X_D)\cong\mathbb Z$, then $H_1(N(D))\oplus H_1(X_D)$, then $H_1(B^4)=0$. Since $H_1(N(D))=0$, the inclusion of the overlap induces an isomorphism $H_1(N(D)\cap X_D)\to H_1(X_D)$. Its generator is the positive meridian by [F1].
For every $i\ge2$, the adjacent groups $H_i(N(D)\cap X_D)$, $H_i(N(D))$, and $H_i(B^4)$ vanish. Exactness of [F2] then forces $H_i(X_D)=0$. This proves the asserted homology in all degrees.

Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $S_0,S_1$ be compact connected oriented smooth surfaces with nonempty smooth boundary. Supply finite smooth triangle presentations: face-to-face triangular disks, with circular interior vertex links and interval boundary links, whose parametrizations are smooth nonsingular maps in surface charts through each closed triangle. Suppose the two presentations have the same Euler characteristic and the same positive number $b$ of boundary components.

For any bijection of their boundary components, any orientation-preserving smooth circle maps on the paired components, and any prescribed inward collar germs, there is an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $B:S_0\to S_1$ realizing those circle maps and their collar identifications. In particular one may prescribe one marked point on each boundary circle. The diffeomorphism can additionally agree with finitely many prescribed orientation-preserving interior diffeomorphism germs at distinct points with distinct target points, while retaining the boundary collars.

All surface presentations are supplied finite data. No triangulation-existence, arbitrary topological smoothing, three-dimensional smoothing or unproved smooth classification result is assumed.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$

derivations.claim: Work in an inward collar $S^3\times[0,\epsilon)$ of the standard ball. Push $F$ to the graph of a smooth positive interior depth function, zero on its boundary and with positive inward derivative there. Such a function is obtained from the supplied finite band and disk charts and positive finite bump sums, retaining the prescribed boundary collar. Round its finitely many seams in those charts. Denote this neat pushed surface by $F'$, and remove the interior of a small product normal disk neighborhood. The result $V_F$ is a compact smooth manifold after the displayed corner roundings. Its boundary is the knot exterior $E_K$ glued to $F\times S^1$ along their common torus: a normal disk to $F'$ has boundary the positive meridian, and the surface boundary direction is the preferred zero-linking longitude. This already fixes the peripheral marking, before any new handle is attached.

Here is a useful cut model, including why its chamber is a ball. The trace of the inward push gives a three-dimensional sheet from $F'$ back to its original position in $S^3$. Cut $V_F$ open along the portion of this sheet outside the removed normal neighborhood. The two banks are copies of a thickening of $F$, and the resulting chamber $Q$ is a ball with these marked banks. This last assertion has a collar construction. In each normal two-plane the removed disk and the cut trace are a rounded slit reaching the outside boundary. Cutting the slit opens it into an indentation attached to that boundary. Over a small three-dimensional neighborhood of $F$ in $S^3$, straighten that indentation to a depth graph $s=h(x)$; the graph has support in that neighborhood. The straightening in a normal section is the increasing reparametrization between two rounded intervals, and agrees with the identity at the outer section endpoints. The product coordinates along $F$ paste these reparametrizations; at its boundary use the supplied half-disk collar, so the slit endpoint is the same rounded half-section on both sides. All widths can be chosen common over the finitely many compact disk/band pieces. For a collar of depth $L>\max h$, the formula $(x,s)\mapsto(x,h(x)+(L-h(x))s/L)$ is a diffeomorphism from the original collar onto the graph indentation, agrees with the unchanged interior along a smaller interpolated collar, and has strictly positive normal derivative. It is identity outside the graph support. Undoing this indentation identifies $Q$ with the standard ball. The banks retain precisely the positive and negative normal push copies of $F$ in its boundary. This is a cut-and-collar parameterization, not a claim that an arbitrary smooth four-ball is standard.

We now change the boundary to actual zero surgery. Let $H$ be a smooth genus-$g$ handlebody whose oriented boundary is the union of a copy of $F$ and a disk along $\partial F$. Such a marked handlebody is supplied by the finite standard disk with $2g$ bands on the boundary of the standard genus-$g$ three-dimensional handlebody. The given disk-band surface has a finite smooth triangle presentation by subdividing its finitely many rectangles and disks in their coordinates. Both surfaces have Euler characteristic $1-2g$ and one boundary, so [F2] matches them with the exact given boundary map and collar. This transfers the handlebody parameter to the given $F$. Glue $H\times S^1$ to $V_F$ along $F\times S^1$, using the normal circle as the second factor and opposite boundary orientations. Round the product corners in those same collars, and call the result $W_F$. The remaining boundary is exactly $E_K\cup(D^2\times S^1)$, where the disk meridian is the actual preferred longitude and the circle core is the actual positive meridian. Its orientation restricts to the original oriented exterior. Therefore the boundary identification is the oriented [F1] zero surgery, rather than a homology-equivalent substitute. Equivalently, this gluing attaches the $g$ round handles which compress $F$ to the displayed disk. It is not the simply connected two-handle trace of zero surgery.

Form the infinite cyclic cut space by taking chambers $Q_k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and identifying the positive bank of $Q_k$ with the negative bank of $Q_{k-1}$. Fix the indexing so the positive meridian crosses to the next chamber; its deck motion is $T$. Finite consecutive unions of chambers are simply connected by [F3]: each chamber is a ball and each joining thickened $F$ is connected, so the tree of trivial vertex groups has trivial pushout. A compact loop or homotopy meets only finitely many chambers, since the chamber pattern is locally finite. Hence the full cut space is simply connected and is the universal cover, with deck group generated by $T$. Thus $\pi_1(V_F)=\mathbb Z$, generated by the actual positive meridian. The cover's Mayer–Vietoris sequence, or its degreewise short exact small-chain sequence, has the form of the mapping cone of the difference of the two bank inclusions, from $C_*(F)\otimes\Lambda$ to $C_*(Q)\otimes\Lambda$. The same assertion holds directly with a specified character in place of $\Lambda$: coefficients are trivial within each bank and chamber, and the second bank map has the character factor. Since $Q$ is a ball and $F$ has one boundary component, it gives $$H_2(V_F;\Lambda)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda,\qquad H_3(V_F;\Lambda)=0.$$ On degree-zero homology the difference map is $1-t$ up to its invertible sign/deck factor. For every $z\ne1$ this factor is invertible, while the degree-one chamber homology is zero. Directly using the character small-chain sequence therefore gives $H_2(V_F;\mathbb C_z)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb C)$, without a possibly nonflat specialization argument.

The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $S_0,S_1$ be compact connected oriented smooth surfaces with nonempty smooth boundary. Supply finite smooth triangle presentations: face-to-face triangular disks, with circular interior vertex links and interval boundary links, whose parametrizations are smooth nonsingular maps in surface charts through each closed triangle. Suppose the two presentations have the same Euler characteristic and the same positive number $b$ of boundary components.

For any bijection of their boundary components, any orientation-preserving smooth circle maps on the paired components, and any prescribed inward collar germs, there is an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $B:S_0\to S_1$ realizing those circle maps and their collar identifications. In particular one may prescribe one marked point on each boundary circle. The diffeomorphism can additionally agree with finitely many prescribed orientation-preserving interior diffeomorphism germs at distinct points with distinct target points, while retaining the boundary collars.

All surface presentations are supplied finite data. No triangulation-existence, arbitrary topological smoothing, three-dimensional smoothing or unproved smooth classification result is assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk and let $X_D$ be its compact exterior. Then $X_D$ is connected, $H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by the positive meridian, and $H_i(X_D;\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $i\ge2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
right $R$-modules, and $G$ a left $R$-module. Then naturally in $C,G$,
$0\to H_n(C)\otimes_RG\to H_n(C\otimes_RG)\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(H_{n-1}(C),G)\to0$
is exact.

Assume AC. Let $X_D$ be the exterior of a smooth proper disk, with positive-meridian isomorphism $H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Let $X_{D,\infty}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, and let $t$ denote the deck transformation represented by the positive meridian. For $q\ge2$, define $X_{D,q}=X_{D,\infty}/\langle t^q\rangle$.

Let
$$0\to A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\to C_\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of complexes in an abelian category. Then there is an
exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A)\to H_n(B)\to H_n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial_n}H_{n-1}(A)\to H_{n-1}(B)\to H_{n-1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

derivations.claim: The deck transformation acts trivially on $H_0(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$ because the cover is connected. From the first sequence in [F2], its homology exact sequence and [F1] show that $t-1$ is an isomorphism on $H_i(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)$ for every $i\ge1$: for $i\ge2$ both neighboring homology groups of $X_D$ vanish, while in degree one exactness uses $H_2(X_D)=0$, $H_1(X_D)=\mathbb F_p$, and the zero map $t-1$ on $H_0(X_{D,\infty})$. Thus the degree-one quotient and kernel both vanish.

In characteristic $p$, repeated Frobenius gives $t^{p^k}-1=(t-1)^{p^k}$. Therefore $t^q-1$ is an isomorphism on every positive-degree homology group of $X_{D,\infty}$ and is zero on its degree-zero homology. The long exact sequence of the second sequence in [F2] now gives $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong H_0(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$, while the quotient cover is connected and hence $H_0(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$.

For each $i\ge2$, both the cokernel on $H_i(X_{D,\infty})$ and the kernel on $H_{i-1}(X_{D,\infty})$ of $t^q-1$ vanish by step 2.1 and the isomorphisms of step 1.1. Exactness therefore gives $H_i(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$. This includes all higher degrees and completes the calculation.
