**Section13: The good-group input and the geometric-dual correction.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

There is a real additional issue in applying the old tower argument to controlled handle cancellation. The arbitrary accessory nullhomotopies in Section6 may meet the old geometric dual spheres. Pushing those accessories down and tubing over the duals clears the BODY but does not clear their intersections with the duals themselves. Thus Sections6–12, by themselves, give standard disk cores but do not prove that the original dual spheres remain geometrically dual to the completed towers. The following collar-controlled preparation supplies the missing operation and also uses the ORIGINAL good-group Definition directly, without replacing arbitrary good groups by cyclic groups.

The smooth relative filling used in these finite operations has a concrete justification under Countable Choice. A continuous disk filling with its supplied smooth boundary collar first admits a smooth approximation. To keep the collar fixed, use the Euclidean embedding and smooth neighborhood retraction constructed in the actual Whitney-approximation proof: interpolate in the ambient Euclidean coordinates between the old map and its smooth approximation with a cutoff which is zero on a smaller boundary collar and one outside the region where the old map is already smooth, then apply that retraction. Its pointwise approximation bound keeps the whole interpolation inside the retraction neighborhood. This gives a smooth filling and homotopy fixed on the smaller collar. In a target with boundary, first push any unwanted interior boundary contacts into the target collar's positive side, fixed on the prescribed source collar; double the target only for the approximation, and choose its error smaller than half the positive target-boundary distance on the remaining interior. Thus the final filling stays in the intended manifold with its prescribed proper collar.

For genericity, cover the remaining compact disk interior by finitely many coordinate patches and add small affine coordinate polynomials times cutoffs. Their parameters independently vary values and first derivatives on smaller patches. The evaluation into first-jet coordinates is therefore submersive, for parameters in a sufficiently small common ball. The rank-one derivative stratum has codimension(2−1)(4−1)=3 and the rank-zero stratum codimension8, both exceeding the domain dimension2. Parametric transversality consequently makes the perturbed map an immersion. Compactness gives a common local-injectivity scale for this immersion and for sufficiently small subsequent C1 perturbations. Off that scale the pair configurations form a compact set. At two distinct points choose disjoint bump patches, so the two-value evaluation is submersive. Transversality to the diagonal in V times V makes its double locus zero-dimensional and compact, hence finite. At three distinct points use three disjoint bumps; the three-value diagonal has codimension8>6, so triple points are absent. Interior-point/boundary-point coincidences likewise have expected dimension2+1−4<0 and are removed while the boundary collar is fixed. The finite products of parameter balls have dense sets of good parameters by the actual parametric-transversality theorem. No assertion that ordinary pointwise transversality alone proves a jet statement is being used: the independent affine-jet parameters supply the required submersion explicitly.

These finite operations also apply to Whitney and accessory fillings with their fixed local corner models: perform the perturbations off those closed collars and keep their prescribed normal directions. The same finite multi-evaluation argument gives pairwise transversality of the different new disks and the old sheets.

The given maps and collars here are smooth in the supplied neighborhood. The TOP-generic interpretation of the broader disk-data Definition requires a later relative smoothing bridge and is not inferred from ambient smoothness. First record the finite geometric Casson move. Let two immersed surfaces F,G have an opposite-sign pair p,q with a framed Whitney disk W. For every interior point of G intersection W choose an arc in W from its preimage to the interior of the G Whitney boundary arc. Choose these arcs away from the finite preimages of F intersection W and from the double-point preimages of W, and use separate parallel widths where they share an endpoint region. Push the G sheet along that arc and past the G boundary arc. This removes the selected G intersection W and introduces only G self-intersections near that boundary arc. It misses F, since the interior of the G Whitney arc misses F and all arcs avoided the F preimages. After the finite pushes, the interior of W misses G. Perform the immersed Whitney move on F across W. It removes p,q; its only new intersections are F self-intersections coming from W self-points or F intersection W. No F–G points remain from the operation. It is a regular homotopy supported in a neighborhood of W, so all algebraic intersection and self-intersection numbers and boundary framings are preserved. For a finite family, exclude the other prescribed body sheets from the support by first clearing W using their geometric duals whenever that is stipulated below. This is the actual finite separation move, not a smooth embedded-Whitney-disk assertion.

Apply it to the input disks f_i and framed spheres g_i. The excess f_i–g_j points can be paired by framed immersed Whitney disks because their group-ring coefficients cancel. The required boundary circle is null: equal group labels, with the sheet choices matched, are exactly the equality making that Whitney loop trivial. A relative smooth generic filling supplies the disk; boundary twisting corrects its Whitney framing. Use the preceding move on the two collections, so it creates only self-intersections within either collection and removes all excess mutual points. This makes g_i geometrically dual to f_i. Since the original f_i already have zero mutual lambda and mu, no spherical tubing which changes their homotopy classes is required. They have only undergone regular homotopies.

The inclusion M'=M minus an open framed plumbing neighborhood of the f_i into M induces a pi1 isomorphism. Surjectivity follows by moving loops off a finite two-dimensional image. For injectivity, put a nullhomotopy in general position with respect to that image; after deleting small disks at its finitely many intersections, its extra boundary circles are meridians of the f_i sheets. Each meridian is null in the complement using the punctured immersed geometric dual g_i. This fills all punctures and gives the nullhomotopy in M'. The same argument handles both sheets at a double point. Hence M' has the given good fundamental group.

Choose framed Whitney disks D_j for all intersections within and among the f_i, and tube their interiors over separate parallels of g_i to remove their intersections with every f_i. Thus D_j are immersed proper disks in M'. At one paired double point take its Clifford torus T_j in the local product normal chart. Its two meridional caps each intersect exactly one f sheet; tube each cap at that point to a punctured parallel g_i. This gives capped tori T_j^c entirely in M'. Their bodies lie arbitrarily close to the corresponding component of the boundary of the plumbing neighborhood, and are geometrically dual to D_j. Their caps have zero mutual lambda and mu: the local meridional interiors are disjoint, their attaching collars meet only in their prescribed boundary crossing, and the remaining points are exactly those among the framed g_i parallels, with the same cancelling group labels. The input zero Wall numbers therefore give zero coefficients before augmentation. Contract separate parallel capped tori to get geometric dual spheres for D_j, push D_j off these contractions, and tube intersections of the ORIGINAL torus caps with D_j into those parallel spheres. The resulting T_j^c are genuinely dual capped surfaces, meaning their caps also miss D_j. This cleanup preserves the cap Wall hypotheses: the contraction sphere is built from two oppositely oriented parallels of each cap and the torus body, so its intersection with any old cap is a signed sum of the old cap–cap coefficients, hence zero; its self-number is a sum of the same zero self/cross coefficients. The sesquilinear and quadratic sphere-sum formulas therefore leave all cap lambda/mu numbers zero when a cap is tubed to those spheres. The bodies stay in their chosen boundary collar.

Here is the collar reservation which prevents the old gap. Parameterize the actual boundary collar by t in [0,1], with boundary t=0, and put the initial T_j bodies in5/6<t<1. Only attaching collars of D_j and of the torus caps enter this collar otherwise. Tube all D_j mutual/self-points over full parallels of T_j^c in this outermost slab. The resulting bottom surfaces D'_j are embedded, mutually disjoint, and have the same framed boundaries; their caps C' are the two appropriate torus-cap parallels at every tube. If C denotes the torus caps, lambda(C,C')=mu(C)=0 by the preceding coefficient calculation and parallel-copy identities. Take a fresh family of capped-torus parallels with bodies in4/6<t<5/6 and contract it, pushing nothing off, to obtain spheres S_j geometrically dual to D'_j.

Pair the C–C' points by framed immersed Whitney disks. Their boundaries lie above t=4/6, and their nullhomotopies can be chosen there: deleting t<4/6 from a boundary collar is a homotopy equivalence with an explicit collar-push inverse. Tube these disks over S_j to make their interiors disjoint from all D'_j. The tube paths and spheres stay above the fresh lower collar slabs. Apply the geometric Casson move to C and C'. Its supports miss D'_j and all unused torus BODIES below4/6. Thus the new caps miss each other as the two collections, while arbitrary self/intersections within each cap collection are still allowed and remain algebraically cancelling.

Push the C' self/mutual points down D'_j and tube full capped-torus parallels with bodies in3/6<t<4/6. This adds the second surface stages, producing height-two capped gropes D''_j. Their body is embedded by the same scorecard as Section3. Separate their new caps C'' from C exactly as before, now using contracted parallels in2/6<t<3/6 and Whitney nullhomotopies outside t<2/6. All remaining torus bodies may now be taken in0<t<2/6. They and their caps are geometrically dual to the entire height-two gropes, including their caps. Raise the latter to any required finite height, keeping their first two stages, and successively contract one extra top stage to make their caps pairwise disjoint, with their self-points in canonical cancelling pairs. These neighborhood operations miss the dual capped surfaces because those were made disjoint from the whole starting grope except at the bottom transverse point.

Now the actual good-group Definition applies in its exact place. Choose grope height n+2.5. Each disjoint top height-1.5 component is a supplied disk-like framed grope. Apply goodness to its homomorphism into pi1(M') to obtain the framed null disk in that canonical model. Section14 smooths it within a neighborhood with trivial group image while retaining its attaching frame; thus it supplies the smooth immersed disk required here, with double-point loops null in M'. Distinct replacement disks lie in disjoint component neighborhoods. The retained grope has height n+1. Contract one top stage symmetrically: the new cap double loops are parallel copies or differences of the null loops, hence null; the cap self-points come in algebraically cancelling finger pairs. The first n stages have been kept EXACTLY. Taking n≥4 is sufficient for Sections7–12.

Fill those double-point loops by framed immersed accessory disks. Their boundaries miss t<2/6, so their fillings may be pushed off that collar. Hence they miss the torus BODIES reserved there, although they may intersect its caps and the grope arbitrarily. Contract fresh dual capped surfaces with bodies in1/6<t<2/6 to get spheres S''_j. Correct the accessory framings, push their body intersections down, and tube over S''_j to clear the whole grope body. The resulting accessories are the proper tower top caps. Finally take the LAST capped-torus parallels with bodies in0<t<1/6 and contract them, pushing every tower-cap sheet off the contraction. Their bodies already miss the accessories by the collar choice. The resulting spheres R_j therefore miss the ENTIRE tower except for their prescribed bottom transverse point. This final contraction/push-off is the step which the uncontrolled use of the original spheres in Section6 could not provide.

The R_j are nullhomotopic in the ORIGINAL M. Indeed symmetric contraction of a fixed capped surface is independent up to homotopy of its caps: it is regularly homotopic to surgery on only the first cap of each pair; switch the unused second caps; it is also homotopic to surgery on only the second caps; then switch the first caps. Thus in M replace the caps built from g_i by the original small meridional caps. The contracted Clifford torus is now contained in the original double-point four-ball, and is null there. This proves [R_j]=0 in pi2(M), despite its being a useful nonzero class in pi2(M').

Remove intersections of the original g_i with the towers by pushing them down the tower to the bottom and tubing over R_j. They still meet the f_i only at their one original dual point, since all these changes lie in M'. They now miss the entire tower. The changes of g_i are homotopies and additions of whiskered R_j, which are null in M, so preserve their original homotopy classes. Perform Sections7–12 inside neighborhoods of the towers disjoint from these g_i, with their one dual intersection moved into the protected attaching collar. The resulting embedded framed Whitney disks are disjoint from every g_i. Their Whitney moves on the f_i give disjoint properly locally flat embedded disks, regularly homotopic rel boundary/framing to the original f_i, and with the g_i still geometrically dual. They also provide the product normal charts required in the final surface-compression application: on the untouched pieces keep the old smooth disk frames; on each Whitney replacement use the pulled-back standard two-handle frame, glued by the Whitney framing along its two boundary arcs. This is a finite construction of a normal disk bundle over the resulting disk, trivialized by those compatible frames. Compactness permits sufficiently small widths so different patches overlap only by their prescribed bundle transitions and the resulting total-space map is injective. Thus the constructed disks have their OWN product tubes, without using the later general TOP normal-bundle theorem. Thus the original disk theorem's homotopy conclusion is supplied by WHITNEY MOVES, rather than assumed from an arbitrary standard-core choice.
**Section14: Smoothing a framed null disk inside a canonical grope neighborhood.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit.

This operation addresses the category of the disk obtained from GOODNESS, whose boundary is the canonical smooth attaching region of the framed model grope. It does not smooth an arbitrary original boundary knot or a TOP-generic disk in an unrelated ambient manifold. Its input is a generic immersed disk with the supplied extending framing/product germs which make its boundary the model attaching region. If 'framed boundary' were read as an arbitrary external integer without an extending framed immersion, the following parity argument would not apply; that is not the framed-disk convention used here.

Let Q be the smooth framed model neighborhood, phi:pi1(Q)→Gamma, and d:D^2→Q the supplied generic framed disk with phi-null double-point loops. Its compact image A is homeomorphic to a finite polyhedron P: subdivide the parameter disk with the finitely many paired double-point preimages as vertices and with their stars disjoint, identify those vertex pairs, and subdivide once more. The resulting finite quotient complex maps continuously bijectively onto A and hence homeomorphically, by compactness and the Hausdorff target. Its fundamental group is generated by the finitely many double-point loops, since the disk before identifying the pairs is simply connected. Thus phi kills the entire image of pi1(A).

Here is an explicit neighborhood-retraction argument, avoiding a general normal-bundle theorem. Realize P as a finite subcomplex of a standard simplex, subdivide barycentrically, and note that its subdivision is FULL: a simplex whose chain of face-vertices all belong to P belongs to P. On the open star of P in that subdivided simplex, delete the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside P and normalize the remaining positive sum. Fullness makes this a continuous retraction onto P. A small neighborhood in Euclidean space first retracts to the simplex, by taking nonnegative coordinates and normalizing their sum. Composing gives a Euclidean neighborhood retraction onto P.

Extend the finitely many coordinates of the inverse homeomorphism A→P continuously to Q as follows. For a residual continuous scalar function r_n on compact A with sup norm at most c_n, choose the least positive integer L_n such that
|r_n(a)−r_n(b)| ≤ c_n/2 + L_n dist(a,b)   for all a,b in A.

Uniform continuity and boundedness give such an integer. Put h_n(x)=inf_(a in A)(r_n(a)+L_n dist(x,a)), clamped to[−c_n,c_n]. It is bounded and L_n-Lipschitz; on A its error from r_n lies between0 and c_n/2. Define r_(n+1)=r_n−h_n|A and c_(n+1)=c_n/2. The uniformly convergent sum of the h_n extends the original coordinate function exactly. All constants are suprema/infima or least integers, so this is a definable recursion. For a zero starting function use the zero extension. The finite coordinate extensions give a map Psi:Q→R^N. On the inverse image of the preceding Euclidean retraction neighborhood, compose with its retraction and P→A. This gives a continuous retraction r:U→A from an actual open neighborhood U of A.

Form the smooth double $Q^{\mathrm{dbl}}$ from the two copies of the supplied smooth grope neighborhood, using its given product boundary collar, as in Section13. Use the proper Euclidean embedding j of this BOUNDARYLESS double and its smooth neighborhood retraction R supplied by the actual Whitney-approximation proof. There is a continuous fold c:Q^{dbl}→Q: it is the identity on the first copy, identifies the second copy with the first by the doubling identification, and in the shared collar is (x,t)→(x,|t|). For x in a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood U' of compact A in U⊂Q, the segment between j(x) and j(r(x)) stays in the domain of R. Indeed r fixes A, and compact j(A) has positive distance from the closed complement of that domain. The formula c(R((1−t)j(x)+t j(r(x)))) is a continuous homotopy IN Q from the inclusion U'→Q to r|U', fixed on A. Hence every loop in U' has phi-trivial image in Q. No smooth retraction onto the boundary of Q is used, and no smoothness of the fold is claimed.

Carry out the smooth relative approximation and finite jet perturbation of d in the DOUBLE, fixing its supplied smooth attaching collar pointwise. Choose a smaller closed source boundary collar inside the collar where d is already smooth; keep a neighborhood of that smaller collar fixed by the cutoff. The complement of that neighborhood in the compact parameter disk is a compact set mapped into IntQ, since d is proper. Its image therefore has positive distance from the boundary of Q in the doubled metric. It also has a positive tolerance for remaining in U', by relative openness and compactness. Choose the approximation and subsequent finite perturbations below both tolerances. On the fixed collar the map remains d; everywhere else it stays in IntQ∩U'. Thus the resulting map is a smooth proper generic disk IN Q, with the original attaching collar and framing, and all its double-point loops lie in U'. The continuous fold used in1.127 is NOT applied to this smooth approximation. For the framing, take the supplied framed parallel of the original d with its disjoint boundary parallel. Its ordinary relative intersection with d is twice the signed self-point count, and is therefore even; the normal-zero term is absent because that frame extends. The relative intersection number is unchanged under homotopy fixing these boundary parallels. For the smooth approximation it equals2mu+e, by the local parallel-sheet count and the zeros of a generic normal section. Thus its relative Euler number e is even. Interior cusps change e by2, so finitely many restore e=0 and the required frame. Their new loops are trivial in the same small coordinate balls, so phi-nullness survives. The resulting SMOOTH framed generic null disk has the original attaching region.

This operation shows why the goodness step can be consumed in the canonical smooth grope model with the framed-disk convention, without using arbitrary TOP neighborhood smoothing, stable5 integration, or the full boundary/collar smoothing needed for an unrelated original TOP-generic input. That boundary/collar bootstrap is not claimed here.
**Section15: Countable Choice versus the successive tower choices.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit.

Countable Choice is not being identified with Dependent Choice. Saying 'choose a next tower at each stage' would not justify this foundation claim. The geometric selections in this particular smooth-model construction can instead be made by a single-valued least-code rule, after fixing the Euclidean embedding/retraction of the smooth neighborhood once.

For a new disk with a specified smooth boundary collar, list pairs consisting of a dyadic collar width and a finite tuple of rational polynomials on the standard parameter disk. Use its supplied boundary-collar map b and a fixed smooth radial cutoff alpha, equal to1 on a smaller collar and0 off that collar. Form the Euclidean candidate alpha j(b)+(1−alpha)P and apply the fixed neighborhood retraction R. The term alpha j(b) is extended by zero only where alpha already vanishes; it is smooth there. Candidates are retained only when the Euclidean values lie in the retraction domain and the resulting map has the required proper boundary collar, genericity, support and finite intersection conditions. Framed candidates are listed simultaneously: project rational polynomial vector fields to the smooth normal plane of the candidate disk, blend them with the prescribed boundary frame on the same collar, and retain those with oriented linearly independent normal vectors everywhere. Orthogonal projection is computed from the ambient embedding metric and the derivative matrix, so is part of the fixed formula.

Whenever an admissible smooth framed filling exists, some listed candidate exists. Choose the dyadic collar inside a collar on which that filling agrees with b. Rational polynomials approximate its Euclidean coordinates and its normal frame uniformly with the required first derivatives. Here is the needed C1 density calculation. Extend each smooth coordinate function slightly past the compact disk, using its finitely many local extensions and a finite smooth partition, and restrict to a containing square rescaled to[0,1]^2. Its Bernstein polynomial is the finite sum of f(k/n,l/n) times the two binomial basis polynomials. Uniform convergence follows from uniform continuity: the binomial weights are probabilities, and the weight outside a fixed distance eta of(x,y) is at most1/(2n eta^2) by the sum of their variances. Its x derivative is the analogous degree(n−1,n) sum of n(f((k+1)/n,l/n)−f(k/n,l/n)), each an average of the x derivative on an interval of length1/n; uniform continuity of that derivative and the same variance bound give uniform derivative convergence. The y derivative is identical. Approximate the finitely many coefficients by rationals with error smaller than the desired C1 tolerance divided by4n: the basis sums to1 and the derivative difference has bound2n times that error. Restrict back to the disk. This proves the claimed rational-polynomial C1 density rather than assuming an analytic power series for an arbitrary smooth function. The values stay in the open retraction domain; properness away from the fixed collar, the normal-frame determinant and the finite transversality angles have positive compact lower bounds. Thus sufficiently close candidates preserve them. Near a generic immersion the double points and their labels persist in disjoint coordinate balls and no new double points occur outside them, by compactness off the local-injectivity diagonal. For a group-null filling use Section14's open neighborhood with null group image: sufficiently close candidates lie there, so retain all null-loop conditions. Candidates which are required to lie in a prescribed relative homotopy class do so for sufficiently close approximations, by the straight retraction homotopy fixed on the boundary collar.

The least natural-number code satisfying these actual predicates therefore specifies the disk and its frame uniquely. Decidability of the predicates is not asserted or needed for set-theoretic definability. This is not a choice function on arbitrary subsets of a mapping space: it is minimization in a specified COUNTABLE list which has just been proved nonempty for each geometric step.

The other choices have the same form. Paths and finger arcs are finite polygonal/rational smooth approximations in the already specified charts, with endpoint templates and finite disjointness conditions. Parallel widths and modification balls use the first dyadic radius meeting the strict compact separation conditions. Finite orderings of double points can be obtained lexicographically from their distinct parameter preimage coordinate tuples, and every finite tree or interval subdivision is chosen in that ordering. The local shrinking Baire step of Section5 has its own explicit countable rational bump rule, preserving every earlier finite avoidance margin. The successive approximations of Sections9–12 use least cofinal story levels and least integer tolerances. No choice is made over an uncountable family of possible future branches.

Thus each next finite stage is a uniquely defined function of the previous finite stage, the original input and the fixed embedding/retraction. Ordinary recursion on the natural numbers constructs the entire sequence. The single fixed smooth embedding/retraction and the actual transversality/approximation suppliers use their stated Countable Choice hypothesis; once those are fixed, no additional Dependent Choice principle is introduced by the tower or shrinking recursion. This is the precise foundation claim of the current smooth-input candidate. It does not turn the open unrestricted problem into a theorem and does not supply a TOP smoothing theorem.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed generic immersions $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. A topological generic immersion has the local models of a smooth generic immersion: at a point with one inverse image its image sheet is locally flat, with a proper half-space chart at boundary points in which the disk is a half-plane and its boundary lies on the ambient boundary, and each of its finitely many self-double points has exactly two preimages and the coordinate-plane model $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$. All mutual intersections among the disk and sphere maps are also required to be finite and transverse, so the equivariant intersection sums below are finite. Proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary. Each disk $f_i$ is supplied with a specified normal framing along $S^1$, equivalently the framing of its boundary attaching solid torus; this boundary framing is part of the datum and need not extend over $D^2$. Each sphere $g_i$ is supplied with a trivialization of its normal microbundle over $S^2$. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces. Each transverse intersection $p$ of two surfaces contributes $\epsilon(p)g_p$ to $\lambda$, where $\epsilon(p)\in\{1,-1\}$ compares their induced local orientation with the chosen orientation of $X$, and $g_p\in G$ is the loop that travels along the chosen path to the first surface, then to $p$, and returns along the second surface and its chosen path. Thus $\lambda$ is a signed equivariant intersection sum in $\mathbb Z[G]$. Wall's self-intersection sum $\mu$ is the signed sum over self-double points in $\mathbb Z[G]/\langle g-g^{-1}:g\in G\rangle$, because interchanging the two sheets replaces a label by its inverse. The relative normal Euler (boundary-framing) obstruction of $f_i$ is zero precisely when its specified boundary framing extends over $D^2$; the datum does not assume that it vanishes. The spheres are **algebraically dual** when $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$ for every $i,j$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$ for every $i$. The disk data are **algebraically unobstructed** when also $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for every $i$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is a proper framed generic immersion $d:D^2\looparrowright G^c$ of a disk into the grope's actual four-dimensional framed block. Its boundary is the core attaching circle, with the normal framing specified by the attaching solid-torus neighborhood, and each double-point loop of $d$, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

Use the framed four-dimensional block and stage conventions for gropes in the cited definitions. A **capped grope** is a staged thickening whose bottom surface stage is joined along curves in a symplectic basis to higher surface stages, with the final tip circles capped by framed immersed disks. A **disk-like capped grope** has one connected bottom surface stage with exactly one attaching circle. Its **height** is the number of successive surface stages on each side of the symplectic basis, with caps terminating the stages. A disk-like capped grope has **height one and one-half**, written $1.5$, when its two sides have heights $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$ in the asymmetric convention; equivalently, one half of the first-stage basis has one additional surface stage and the other half is capped immediately. The **attaching region** is the framed solid-torus neighborhood of the single attaching circle. For an immersed disk, a **double-point loop** is the image of a path in the domain disk joining the two preimages of a transverse self-intersection. In the disk-embedding property for an input capped grope, this loop is read as the corresponding element of the grope's fundamental group; choosing a basing path from the grope basepoint fixes that based element.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be a continuous map between smooth manifolds. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ homotopic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

derivations.claim: **Section1: Finite contraction and cyclic-label cancellation.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

A finite framed four-dimensional capped-grope neighborhood is supplied, with its usual product collars and self-plumbing charts. Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input.

Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Consequently, if all designated labels lie in an interval [a,b], every new label has absolute value at most b−a.

Cut the top surface at each pair of symplectic attaching curves. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. **Section2: The finite asymmetric bootstrap.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Start with one symplectic pair above the bottom surface: on the positive side a framed capped surface R of positive genus, on the negative side a framed immersed cap W. Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. Thus they may create cap intersections but no body intersections. Their original intersections with R or the body of F are empty, and sufficiently small parallel copies retain that property. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W.

For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections.

This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections.
**Section3: Finite bootstrap to height three.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section2 gives (1,0) to (1,1). Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All choices involve finite paths, parallels and normal widths in supplied framed blocks. Use the move first with p=q=1, then exchange the two sides and use p=1,q=2. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap.
**Section4: Efficient symmetric raising and the word bound.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Once both sides have height at least two, there is an efficient variant which contracts only the TOP stage of a transverse grope. For the side P to be extended, form the transverse grope from the opposite side Q. Its height is that of Q. Contract its top stage and push the old caps off that contraction by Section1. The transverse grope now has height one less and its caps are disjoint from all old caps. Push each intersection on a P cap down the P stages, and at the bottom tube off over this transverse grope. The same body/cap scorecard as Section3 applies: new bodies consist of separate parallel copies of the old embedded opposite-side bodies, and all cap intersections have been removed from the new body before it is declared a body. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope with the height of the contracted transverse grope. In terms of full path heights a,b INCLUDING the shared bottom, the updated path height is a+b−2. Alternate the sides. Starting with a_{−1}=a_0=3, the successive updated path heights obey a_n=a_{n−1}+a_{n−2}−2. The uniform height is the smaller of the two current path heights. Writing a_n−2 as a Fibonacci recursion gives, after 2k steps, uniform height at least 2^k: consecutive pairs increase the smaller Fibonacci term by at least a factor two. Additional initial height only improves the bound.

For clarity, the required estimate concerns WORDS, not numbers of double points. Base every old cap-point loop by a path in the old grope. Body-stage paths contribute no new plumbing generator. Contraction copies an old point without changing its generator. A push off a contraction creates the difference loop of Section1, a word of length at most two in the OLD cap-point generators. A new intersection among caps of the parallel transverse grope has length one, since its sheets are old parallel sheets. The only remaining type is a loop using a newly pushed-down finger: follow its first sheet across at most two old cap-point loops to the parallel transverse copy, cross its new cap intersection (one old generator), and return across at most two old loops on the other finger. The two bottom-stage paths cancel, as do the parallel collar paths. This is a concatenation of at most 2+1+2 old generators or inverses. These exhaust the new intersections: they occur on unchanged parallels, on a contraction push, or between two inserted fingers. Thus each step sends every NEW generator to a word of length at most five in the PRECEDING generators. Induction gives length at most 5^(2k) after 2k steps, and absolute Z label at most 5^(2k)B. No count of the possibly much larger number of points is substituted for this word bound.
**Section5: The special relative disk-to-disk operation in standardness.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

This is the operation of FQ4.6, with the actual relative data made explicit. Let f:B^4→B^4 be continuous and onto, with a homeomorphic boundary restriction. Its point-inverse collection is null (only finitely many fibres have diameter at least any positive epsilon), its singular IMAGE is nowhere dense, and E is a closed subset of the target containing the whole boundary. Suppose f:f^−1(E)→E is a homeomorphism. Then there is a homeomorphism h:B^4→B^4 equal to f on f^−1(E). Here E CONTAINS the boundary; it is not merely a subset of that boundary. The latter misreading would make the relative assertion too weak for the collared-tower application.

Use the following intermediate configuration. W is compact metrizable; e,f:B^4→W and g:W→B^4 are onto. The composites ge,gf are identity on the boundary. The fibres of g,ge,gf are null; their relevant singular images Sigma_g, g(Sigma_e),g(Sigma_f) are nowhere dense and pairwise well separated: neither set meets the closure of another. A protected closed set E_0 containing the boundary is disjoint from all three, and the relation e^−1 f is fixed there. Nullity makes each singular image countable (group the nontrivial fibres by diameter at least1/m). We will decrease both e- and f-fibre diameters while controlling the relations e^−1 f and f^−1 e between the TWO fixed domain balls.

Here is the local replacement. Choose a closed round ball B in the TARGET of g, disjoint from E_0,Sigma_g,g(Sigma_f), and a smaller concentric ball B_0 whose boundary misses g(Sigma_e). The restrictions over B for g and over the sphere boundary of B_0 for ge are homeomorphisms: they are continuous bijections of compact spaces to Hausdorff spaces. We require no open neighborhood of that sphere free of e singular values, which may accumulate on it. Replace g^−1(int B_0) in W by (ge)^−1(B_0), gluing their boundaries by e. The result is W'. On the inserted piece define e' to be the identity and g' to be ge; outside use the old e,g. These maps match at the gluing and satisfy g'e'=ge. The map e' is a homeomorphism over the inserted piece, so every e-fibre with g-image in B_0 has been eliminated. This is a finite compact adjunction, not a claim that W' is already a manifold.

To transfer f, take a homeomorphism w:B→B^4 fixed on B_0. Such a map exists by radial extension from the center of these convex balls. On g^−1 B define
H=g^−1 w^−1 g e w g,

where g^−1 is single-valued on B because B misses Sigma_g. Outside use the identity. On the boundary of B the definitions agree because ge is identity on the outer sphere. In the part whose image lies in g^−1 B_0, the first g^−1 w^−1 cancels the g before e; the remaining map e w g lifts to the inserted piece as w g. Thus H has a continuous lift H':W→W', and put f'=H'f. This gives f'=f outside the region with gf-image in B. On the inserted piece its formula is wgf. On the remaining annular region its fibres are the transported fibres of ge. Since gf is a homeomorphism over B, these new fibres are coordinate copies of a null family, so they remain null. The other fibres are unchanged. For g' the outside fibres are subsets of old g fibres, and the inside fibres are old ge fibres in the inserted compact piece. Both coordinate inclusions are uniformly continuous on their compact domains; a finite union of the corresponding null collections is null. For g'f', outside B nothing changes; in the inner piece it equals ge composed with the homeomorphism wgf, and in the annular piece it equals w^−1 ge wgf. Thus its nontrivial fibres are homeomorphic coordinate images of ge fibres. This is the actual nullity argument; composition of arbitrary null maps is not being asserted to preserve nullity.

The only possible failure of the separation condition is between the transported countable singular image and the retained image of ge. Choose w so these are well separated off B_0. This choice needs no unproved Baire assertion under the original countable-choice branch. Fix one radial reference map w_0:B→B^4. Enumerate the two countable singular sets. For each point condition require that its image avoid the CLOSED closure of the other singular set, and for each inverse-point condition require the analogous inverse avoidance. Each requirement is open and dense among homeomorphisms with the fixed inner/outer boundary data: a small coordinate ball around the free point lies off those fixed boundaries, and a compactly supported translation moves that point off the prescribed nowhere-dense closed set. Explicitly use x→x+rho(x)v with |v|Lip(rho)<1; the contraction inverse proves it is a homeomorphism. The required target complement is open dense, so a least satisfactory rational v in a fixed enumeration exists. Choose supports and rational radii from a fixed coordinate enumeration. The forward and inverse maps converge uniformly, and their limits are inverse by uniform continuity. The limit homeomorphism meets every avoidance requirement. This is a definable countable recursion with explicit finite rational searches, not dependent choice for arbitrary nonempty sets of homeomorphisms. It gives the required local configuration e',f',g'.

All conditions hold; the other singular sets are empty. Rescale the two fixed source metrics initially to diameter<1. Suppose all e_n- and f_n-fibres have diameter less than2^−n. This proves the needed relative disk-to-disk replacement operation. It does NOT by itself prove that a tower is a disk: that application still needs the actual dual-handle/design/common-quotient construction, including the other approximation whose fibres are explicit disk-with-boundary-neighborhood pieces. No general4D cell-like approximation theorem is imported.
**Section6: From a null grope to the first actual tower story.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

This step has an exact input which the cyclic construction must supply: an actual properly immersed framed disk-like capped grope A of height at least three, whose entire image has trivial fundamental-group image in the smooth ambient four-manifold, together with framed geometric transverse spheres, each missing A except for its one prescribed bottom-stage point. It does not start with vanishing algebraic intersections alone. All modifications below take place in supplied plumbing charts and finitely many immersed disk charts; the ambient manifold is smooth at this stage.

First raise the height as far as needed by Section4, reserving one more full stage than the desired number of stages in the story. Because the raising maps factor through the previous grope neighborhood, its image remains group-null. Order the finitely many components of the extra top stage. Contract the first one, and push the cap sheets of every other component off that contraction by the ribbon Whitney disks of Section1. Contract the second and push all still uncontracted cap sheets off it; continue. The resulting grope caps are pairwise disjoint. They need not be embedded, but every self-intersection is part of the finger-pair model, with a specified Whitney disk. Here is the local pairing check: pushing a sheet off a contraction replaces its old cap intersection by the two parallel intersections with the opposite cap through the central square. Their signs are opposite, and the ribbon between the two parallel cap copies, continued along the chosen arc on the dual cap, is the Whitney disk. At an old cap self-intersection the four parallel-sheet intersections split into two such opposite-sign pairs. Order the pushes so each newly contracted component is protected from all later cap sheets. Distinct ribbon arcs are disjoint except at their prescribed central-square crossings; any interior crossings are among the disks which will be declared top caps, rather than intersections among the remaining grope caps. This is the actual disk-with-finger-pairs model, not the assertion that zero algebraic self-intersection supplies embedded Whitney disks.

For each finger pair choose an accessory circle: start at its chosen double point, follow one sheet to the Whitney arc and return on the other sheet. It is a loop in the image of the contracted grope. It is therefore nullhomotopic in the ambient manifold by the input nullness; no conclusion about the fundamental group of the complement is needed. A nullhomotopy relative to this fixed embedded boundary arc can be put in general position as an immersed disk with its prescribed boundary collar. The boundary collar is the accessory collar in the standard finger model. Its extending normal framing is corrected, if necessary, by interior twists in that disk together with boundary twists in the model collar; interior twists change the relative Euler number by two, and one boundary twist changes its parity. The latter creates an intersection with the grope cap, which is permitted temporarily. The boundary-circle germ itself and the original bottom attaching framing are fixed. The accessory disks and the previously specified ribbon Whitney disks are now the TOP caps. All finger pairs and their accessory boundary collars have the same finite plumbing model as an ordinary disk finger move followed by its Whitney and accessory disks. Thus the thickening is a one-story tower model before properness is imposed.

Only top-cap intersections with the lower grope remain to be removed. At such an intersection, modify the TOP-cap sheet, pushing it along the lower grope sheet through its successive attaching collars down to the first stage. At one attaching collar the two sides of the push produce two points on the preceding stage; after finitely many stages this produces finitely many points on the bottom. All paths avoid the other finitely many preimages. Remove each resulting bottom point by tubing the top cap over a separate parallel of the corresponding geometric transverse sphere, choosing its orientation to cancel the point. The punctured transverse sphere has no other intersection with the grope. Hence this operation changes only top caps, makes them disjoint from every grope stage including the grope caps, and may create intersections only among top caps. Tubing to a sphere preserves the top-cap disk topology. Its framing extends by the untwisted tube and the supplied sphere framing. Top caps are allowed to have mutual and self-plumbings. The bottom attaching circle, all its framing data, and every reserved lower stage are fixed.

We have obtained an ACTUAL proper one-story capped tower of the chosen finite grope height. Its model has an embedded lower body, grope caps with the prescribed finger-pair singularities, and arbitrary plumbings only among the top Whitney/accessory caps. The finite framed neighborhoods glue by their stipulated product collars, so the conclusion is a framed neighborhood of that tower, not only a map of its underlying two-complex. This is the first-story operation needed before replication and convergence. It has not constructed additional stories or identified any tower neighborhood with a standard two-handle.
**Section7: Replication of a tower, with the body and top caps kept distinct.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Write G for a story's grope body, C for its grope caps with their paired finger points, and D for the top Whitney/accessory caps. Thus G union C is the story body; intersections among D are allowed, whereas D misses G union C. When another story replaces D, the new story bodies, and not their eventual top caps, must be disjoint and embedded in the stipulated plumbing model. This distinction is essential in the following replication.

First describe the transverse grope operation in the actual finite model. A surface attached at a positive curve of a symplectic pair has a sphere-like transverse capped grope formed from two parallels of the negative branch and the annulus joining their boundaries. Its bottom meets that positive surface once. Its caps are parallels of the original grope caps. At their intersections with the original grope caps, the two parallel sheets give the ribbon Whitney pairs of Section1. If a further story is present, the corresponding Whitney disk is the bottom of the next story's disk-like grope. Replace the affected band of the transverse grope by two parallels of that Whitney grope and the boundary band along its Whitney arc. This is the grope version of the ordinary Whitney move: cutting the band removes the two old intersection points, and all new intersections lie in the top caps of the inserted Whitney grope. Its body misses every lower story, since that next-story body does. Repeat through the finite list of stories. Stop with its caps parallel to the LAST GROPE caps C, so their possible intersections with the original tower are only with its top caps D. Do not take the additional contraction through the final Whitney/accessory caps: that would give geometric transverse gropes whose nullness is no longer guaranteed. The transverse grope then meets the original tower only at its single specified transverse body point and at the TOP caps D. Its body AND caps use only parallels of pieces of the original tower BODY strictly above the first surface stage.

The group-nullness used here is a direct model calculation. Collapse each surface stage to its symplectic attaching curves and connecting arcs, and each paired-finger grope cap to its double-point graph. The stage-curve generators bound the next stages after contraction. The double-point graph generators bound the specified accessory disks; the Whitney disk identifies the generator at the mate point with the same generator or its inverse according to the sheet orientation. Accordingly every loop in the body strictly above the first stage is null in the entire tower neighborhood. Only the plumbing generators among the TOP caps can remain in that neighborhood's fundamental group. Thus the transverse grope just constructed has trivial group image there. This calculation concerns its actual body and cap paths through the model; it makes no assertion that arbitrary top-cap plumbings are null.

Suppose now a proper tower has first-story grope height at least four. Apply the preceding operation to the second-stage surfaces, contract parallel transverse gropes, and push the old top-cap sheets off those contractions. This supplies framed geometric transverse spheres for the disk-like components remaining after the first surface stage and its fixed collar are removed. Work in that complement. The first-stage collar will be fixed throughout what follows.

Choose the positive side of the top story to be replicated. For its second-stage surfaces construct transverse gropes from the opposite, negative branches. Arrange their caps to meet only the negative-side top caps, as in the preceding Whitney-grope procedure. Contract one top surface stage of the transverse gropes and push the negative-side top caps off those contractions. The resulting transverse gropes and the changed negative cap sheets still have trivial group image whenever that assertion is made of the new BODY: their new body loops run in the old body neighborhood just analyzed, and contraction/push-off changes a loop only by a product of old body loops. Top-cap plumbing generators have not been declared trivial. The negative lower body is unchanged. The height-four hypothesis leaves enough height to raise these transverse gropes to any prescribed finite height by Section4.

Make the needed transverse gropes disjoint near-parallels by ordering their constructions. Contract a parallel, then push all still unused cap sheets off it, using separate ribbon arcs. Repeat for the finite number of copies needed. This is why merely taking many geometric parallels of an immersed capped grope would not suffice: their caps could intersect the old body to be added. The ordered contraction/push-off produces copies whose bodies are disjoint and whose caps miss those old body sheets. Each copy is still null by the model calculation.

At every mutual or self-intersection of POSITIVE top caps, push one sheet down that positive branch to its second-stage surface. A push through one stage doubles the number of points; there are finitely many stages, so only finitely many points result. At every resulting point tube over a separate full transverse grope, not its contraction. The punctured transverse bottom surface removes the point; its higher stages and caps become the higher stages and caps on the changed positive top sheet. The original positive top caps are now properly immersed capped gropes of the chosen height. Their new bodies are disjoint: all their former mutual/self-points were treated, the transverse bodies are disjoint near-parallels, and their caps were cleared off the former top sheets before the tubing. Intersections which remain are among the new caps. The negative branch body has stayed fixed.

There is also the necessary group check for the NEW body. A double-point loop in a changed cap comes from a single selected transverse-grope copy and from the fingers used for that one former top-cap point. The two paths down the original positive branch are parallel, so their whisker words cancel. What remains is a loop in that transverse copy, which is null by the preceding model calculation. Copies used for DIFFERENT former points are distinct near-parallels; their body pieces do not meet and cannot create additional body generators. Thus the new positive body has trivial group image in the complement being used. The retained negative body already has that property, since all its generators are killed by its old Whitney/accessory scaffold. No conclusion is taken about either collection's as-yet-unassigned top-cap plumbing loops.

Raise the new top grope by one extra stage, contract its top components successively and push all the later caps off each contraction. As in Section6, this gives mutually disjoint grope caps with canonical finger-pair Whitney disks. Their accessory loops lie in the just verified null BODY, so they admit immersed accessory disks in the working complement. This produces legitimate new top caps disjoint from the full body. The positive side now has one additional story. Interchange positive and negative and repeat. The original lower body and its framed attaching product are fixed, and both sides now have one additional story, with any prescribed finite height in the new top story.

This is a finite replication inside an arbitrarily small supplied neighborhood of the old tower together with the required accessory-disk images. The latter are not automatically small from the word estimate; localization is exactly the issue separated in the additional localization hypotheses for a controlled application. **Section8: Squeezing and convergence, retaining only a pinched neighborhood.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Replicate twice by Section7, obtaining three stories with as many stages as desired in the second story. Delete the top caps and contract each component of the third-story grope completely. The contractions supply caps for the second story. Distinct such caps are disjoint, since the distinct third-story BODIES were disjoint; the discarded top-cap intersections have not been retained. The old top caps give nullhomotopies of the generators of each upper-story body, in the complement of the retained first-story body.
