Thus the upper-story regular neighborhoods are group-null there. We need to move their finite spines, rather than assert that an arbitrary embedded two-complex can be shrunk by isotopy.

For each upper-story component collapse its regular neighborhood to a finite graph K. One can see the collapse directly: cut a surface stage to its attaching curves and arcs joining the curves; repeat upward; a cap with self-plumbings collapses to its double-point graph and connecting arcs. The disks of the preceding first story which enter this neighborhood consist of strips ending on K. More precisely, relative to their portions C outside the neighborhood, they are a mapping cylinder L times I whose inner ends are mapped into K. This description is obtained in the same finite surface cuts and normal disk blocks. It provides the regular neighborhood of the PAIR C union (L times I) union K, not a claim that the first-story cap disks are fixed pointwise while their attaching ends move.

Choose distinct small smooth coordinate balls, one for each upper-story component, in the complement of the retained first-story body. The null graph map is homotopic there to an embedding of the same abstract graph in the chosen ball: collapse a maximal tree and use the actual generator nullhomotopies, then reverse a contraction of a tiny standard graph in the ball. Perturb this graph homotopy relative to its initial end and its final small-ball end to a one-parameter family of embeddings. The dimension calculation is useful here: two nonincident moving graph points and their common time form a three-dimensional parameter space, less than four, so general position removes equal-image pairs at the SAME time. Preserve the finite vertex stars by translations in small vertex charts, and perturb edge interiors with the endpoints fixed. This gives an isotopy of the graph. Intersections of its TRACE at different times need not disappear; they do not obstruct a graph isotopy and are not being used as a Whitney-disk theorem.

The first-story grope body is avoided by the whole homotopy. Arrange its finitely many intersections with the remaining cap sheets C and the mapping-cylinder strips transversely. Push those sheet intersections along the homotopy toward its free final end and past the final graph. In a normal coordinate ball this is the ordinary finger push of a two-sheet off a terminal one-dimensional arc; its support is a narrow neighborhood of the chosen trace path. Each push modifies only a grope-cap sheet, not the retained grope body. Intersections it creates are among those cap sheets. At their finitely many crossings choose different narrow parallel paths, so the changes do not meet the initial graph or the retained body. The result is an isotopy of K disjoint from C and from the interiors of the mapping-cylinder strips, with their prescribed common inner endpoints allowed in the pair model. The outer ends of those strips on C are fixed. No claim of an embedded homotopy TRACE of a graph in four-space is required.

An isotopy of this finite smooth graph extends to an ambient isotopy of a sufficiently small regular neighborhood, fixed outside a neighborhood of its track and fixed on C and the retained grope body. Here is the elementary extension in the present setting. Near each moving vertex use its small translated coordinate ball. Subdivide time so the vertex balls remain disjoint and each moving edge segment lies in a fixed product chart. On the interior of such an edge, extend its velocity by a cutoff in the normal three-disk, agreeing with the chosen vertex translations at its ends. A finite partition of unity along the edge pieces gives a compactly supported smooth vector field agreeing with the velocity on the graph. Integrate for that short time interval; in the compact support the solution exists throughout the interval. Compose the finitely many intervals. The supports avoid the fixed pair pieces just cleared from the track. Transport the graph regular neighborhood by this isotopy; make its final normal widths small enough that the ENTIRE upper-story neighborhood, not just its spine, lies in the selected small ball. Transport the attaching mapping cylinders at the same time, retaining their outer ends. This proves the required squeezing without using a topological half-space unknotting assertion or a general TOP smoothing theorem.

Now iterate within the resulting upper-story neighborhoods. At stage n choose disjoint closed coordinate four-balls B_(n,j), of diameter<2^−n, containing precisely the next replacement components; choose their closures in the interiors of their parent balls. The old body and its marked attaching product lie outside their interiors. All subsequent modifications for a descendant are required to lie in that same ball. Section7 supplies the next finite story and the preceding squeezing supplies such balls of the next diameter, so the induction uses only the finite operations already specified. Heights can be prescribed in advance at every story; in particular the first story retains height at least four, sufficient for the standardness construction.

We spell out why this gives an embedded LIMIT OBJECT and why it gives less than an ordinary open neighborhood at its ends. Away from the nested balls every point is fixed after finitely many stages, so its map is the finite-stage framed embedding there. An infinite descending branch of balls has a unique intersection point: the balls are nested nonempty compact sets in a compact first-stage neighborhood and their diameters tend to zero. Distinct branches separate in disjoint balls at some finite level, so their points are distinct. Such a limit point cannot equal an old finite-stage body point: a deeper descendant closure lies in the interior of its parent, whereas that finite body point is excluded from all sufficiently deep replacement interiors. The topology at a branch is given by the descendant balls. These observations show injectivity and continuity of the natural map from the end-compactified model to the ambient space. Its domain is compact: an open cover first covers the compact set of branches by finitely many cylinder neighborhoods in the finite-branching tree, then covers the remaining finite-stage compact body by finitely many sets. A continuous injection from that compact domain to the Hausdorff ambient manifold is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For the NEIGHBORHOOD make the same construction with the framed four-dimensional model blocks, not just their spines. At each stage modify the previous block so it meets each chosen ball in the ordinary neighborhood of the disk being replaced; later replacement blocks are contained in that ball. Repeat the preceding compactness and shrinking-ball argument for these blocks and their ends. The result is an embedded PINCHED regular neighborhood, with the prescribed attaching solid torus and framing unchanged. At an end it may have no ambient interior and no locally flat boundary. Nothing in the argument identifies it with a two-handle or supplies a TOP normal bundle there. That identification is exactly the separate parameterization obligation. The construction can be supported in any prescribed open neighborhood containing the actual input tower and the finite nullhomotopies used in the replication, by choosing all balls and normal widths with closures in that open set. This is the support guarantee needed by the additional localization hypotheses for a controlled application once its localized inputs are supplied.
**Section9: The explicit radial collapse used on the model side.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

The model-side shrinking needs more than the assertion that a compact set is contractible. Its nontrivial fibers have supplied neighborhood coordinates of two particular kinds: a closed ball, or an embedded framed disk together with a regular neighborhood of its boundary circle. In the second case that regular neighborhood overlaps the disk in an ANNULAR COLLAR. Treating the overlap as just the core circle would give the wrong quotient model. We describe the collapse in those coordinates.

First let E be a closed starlike subset in the interior of a Euclidean ball, with center0. Its radial extent e(u)=max{r:ru is in E} is upper semicontinuous: if u_j→u and r_j≤e(u_j) converge to r, closedness gives ru in E. Given an open neighborhood U of E, compactness permits a continuous positive radial function v(u)>e(u) whose radial closed ball V lies in U. To construct v, take for each direction a small angular neighborhood on which e is below a chosen strict radial bound; take finitely many of these neighborhoods and a partition of unity, and use their strict upper bounds. Refine the angular cover enough that the resulting radial set stays in U. A sequence of such V_i can therefore be chosen with V_(i+1) in int V_i and intersection E.

Let {T_j} be a null collection of closed sets disjoint from E, and fix delta>0. Choose V_0 so any T_j meeting V_0 has diameter<delta/2; only finitely many exceptions must be avoided. Choose positive radii b_i decreasing to0, with b_0 the radius of the ambient ball and b_i−b_(i+1)<delta/8. Inductively choose V_i in int V_(i−1), within distance2^−i of E, so any T_j meeting V_i misses the complement of V_(i−1). This is possible: any T_j meeting arbitrarily close to E and also outside the fixed V_(i−1) has diameter bounded below by half the positive distance from E to that complement. There are only finitely many such T_j, all disjoint from E. Avoid them in V_i. Put W_i=V_i union the centered ball B_(b_i). These remain starlike with continuous positive radius functions, are nested, and intersect in E.

On each ray map the interval W_i minus int W_(i+1) affinely to the interval B_(b_i) minus int B_(b_(i+1)), and send E to0. Adjacent formulas agree at their endpoints; continuous radial functions give continuity away from E, and b_i→0 gives continuity at E. The result k is identity on the outer boundary, collapses exactly E, and is a homeomorphism off E. One must check its effect on the OTHER T_j, not merely the distinguished collapse. If x is outside V_i in the shell between W_i and W_(i+1), then k moves x by at most b_i−b_(i+1)<delta/8. Any T_j meeting V_i is contained in V_(i−1), so the whole part which may be moved a large distance lies at most one such radial level apart. If both x,y in T_j lie outside all relevant V levels, their displacements are<delta/8. Otherwise take the deepest level met by T_j and project x,y radially to the corresponding small sphere. Radial projection from points outside that sphere does not increase their distance; the two interpolation intervals change their distances by at most2delta/8 each. Hence, when diam T_j<delta/2, diam k(T_j)<delta. A T_j not meeting V_0 is unchanged except for the small radial displacements. Thus for every j either all its points move by<delta, or its entire image has diameter<delta. This is the control required for later null fibers.

Here is a concrete verification for the second fiber type. In its supplied framed disk chart write x=r exp(i theta) for the disk coordinate and y=s exp(i phi) for its normal coordinate. After a small radial adjustment of the boundary tube, the pair is
D={0≤r≤1,s=0},
E=D union {(r−1)^2+s^2≤a^2},   0<a<1,

with the angular identifications at r=0 and s=0. The neighborhood is rotational in both angles. Its two-dimensional orbit quadrant has a boundary interval [0,1] on s=0 representing D, and a half-disk about (1,0) representing the boundary tube. Collapse [0,1]. The quotient quadrant is again a quadrant, and the tube half-disk becomes a half-disk meeting the corner: this is an elementary planar construction, not a four-dimensional quotient theorem. To see it explicitly, first replace the two circular arcs by polygonal arcs using radial interpolation in disjoint annular neighborhoods. Triangulate the finite region between the arcs and the quadrant boundary. Collapsing the boundary interval merges its consecutive boundary vertices; the remaining region has the same cyclic boundary order as the quadrant with a half-disk based at its corner. Match these boundary orders, cut the remaining region along an arc joining its two boundary components, and extend the boundary maps by coning the resulting polygons from interior points. The maps agree on the two copies of the cut. Use the identity outside the chosen orbit neighborhood. This is a homeomorphism of the QUOTIENT quadrant to the ordinary quadrant, preserving its two distinguished axes.

Choose its target tube half-disk to be {(r−1)^2+s^2≤1,r≥0,s≥0}. Lift the orbit map by keeping theta and phi. Preservation of the axes ensures continuity across the angular collapses; its inverse has the same property. It is therefore an ambient homeomorphism from the four-dimensional disk quotient by D to the standard disk, supported in the supplied normal chart. The image of E is
E'={ (x,y): |x|^2+|y|^2≤2|x| }.

It is starlike about0: for 0≤t≤1, the displayed left side at (tx,ty) is t^2 times the old left side, whereas the right side is t times the old right side. The image contains0 and has precisely the intended overlapping-boundary-tube quotient topology. Thus E is EVENTUALLY starlike by two explicit collapses: first the framed disk D, then E'. This uses the supplied disk and boundary-tube coordinates, not a normal-bundle existence theorem for an arbitrary locally flat disk.

Apply the preceding starlike collapse first to D and then to E'. The other disjoint null sets still form a null collection after the first collapse, by uniform continuity on the compact source; the quotient images remain disjoint from the distinguished set. Choose the first collapse's control small enough for the second step's coordinate uniform-continuity tolerances. Finite sets whose coordinate diameters exceed the chosen tolerance can be excluded from the collapse neighborhoods because they are disjoint from the distinguished set. Pulling the radial operations back through the supplied coordinate maps proves the same movement-or-small-image conclusion in the original metric. The maps are identity on the boundary of the local ball throughout.

Finally suppose alpha:B^4→Q is an onto quotient with a null collection of nontrivial fibers, each of one of these two SUPPLIED coordinate types, Q compact metric, and alpha a homeomorphism on the outer boundary. We give the iteration with the correct inverse CONTROL MAP, rather than claiming the raw inverse relations converge to a function. A raw inverse fiber may remain large permanently when that original alpha fiber is collapsed.

Start with f_0 the identity. Maintain a continuous onto f_n:B^4→B^4 whose only nontrivial fibers are finitely many original alpha fibers, and such that every set f_n(alpha^−1(q)) has diameter<epsilon_n, where epsilon_n decreases summably to0. Because alpha is constant on every f_n fiber, it descends to a continuous map u_n:B^4→Q with u_n f_n=alpha. Continuity follows from the compact quotient property of f_n. Every current image E_q=f_n(alpha^−1(q)) is therefore a set on which u_n is constant. The uncollapsed E_q retain their original supplied neighborhood type, since f_n is a homeomorphism near each such compact set, disjoint from the finite already collapsed fibers.

There are finitely many current E_q of diameter at least epsilon_(n+1)/2: nullity follows from uniform continuity of f_n on the original null family. Choose mutually disjoint small coordinate neighborhoods U_q of these E_q so diam U_q<2epsilon_n and diam u_n(U_q)<epsilon_n in the chosen metric of Q. The first bound follows from diam E_q<epsilon_n and a small neighborhood; the second follows from continuity of u_n and its constancy on E_q. Choose a closed coordinate ball in each U_q carrying the prescribed fiber model. If there are N selected sets, apply each local collapse with the movement-or-small-image tolerance d=epsilon_(n+1)/(4N+4), treating the other current E sets as the null family. Other selected sets are outside its support. Every unselected set starts with diameter<epsilon_(n+1)/2. Over the N collapses its diameter either increases by at most2Nd, or, after the last small-image outcome, is at most d+2Nd. Both bounds are strictly below epsilon_(n+1). Thus no untreated current fiber image crosses the next size threshold. Compose these finitely many collapses to get g_n and put f_(n+1)=g_n f_n. Its newly nontrivial fibers are exactly the selected entire original alpha fibers, so u_n is constant on each g_n fiber. Hence it descends to a continuous u_(n+1) with u_(n+1)g_n=u_n and u_(n+1)f_(n+1)=alpha.

The changes of f_n occur in the coordinate U_q, so their uniform size is<2epsilon_n. For the inverse control maps, if y=g_n(z) is in such a neighborhood, then u_(n+1)(y)=u_n(z) and both z,y lie in U_q. Consequently d_Q(u_(n+1)(y),u_n(y))<epsilon_n. Outside those neighborhoods there is no change. Thus both f_n and u_n are uniformly Cauchy; write their continuous limits f_infinity and u. Passing to u_n f_n=alpha gives u f_infinity=alpha. Uniform convergence also implies that f_infinity is constant on every alpha fiber, since diam f_n(alpha^−1(q))→0.

To prove u injective, let u(y)=q and choose x_n with f_n(x_n)=y. Then alpha(x_n)=u_n(y)→q. A subsequence converges to x in the compact original ball. Uniform convergence gives f_infinity(x)=y and alpha(x)=q. Therefore EVERY y with u(y)=q lies in the singleton f_infinity(alpha^−1(q)). Conversely this singleton maps to q by u f_infinity=alpha. Thus u is bijective. It is a homeomorphism from compact B^4 to Hausdorff Q, agreeing with alpha on the outer boundary. This proves the model-side approximation without any assertion that the raw f_n inverse fibers shrink or that a uniform limit of set-valued inverses is automatically a homeomorphism.
**Section10: Why the collared singular model is an actual ball.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

There is a necessary reduction before Section5 can be applied to the tower model: its DOMAIN must be a standard ball. A map beta:C'→B^4 by itself does not prove that hypothesis. The special singular parameterization supplies extra structure which gives the reduction explicitly.

Suppose a surjection q:B^4→C' has exactly the following nontrivial fibers: for a closed K in S^3 they are the full intervals c({s} times [0,1]), s in K, in a supplied embedded collar c:S^3 times [0,1]→B^4 with c(s,1)=s. Every other fiber is a point. The inner collar boundary may be wild on its inner side; the formula below requires only the GIVEN collar embedding. Suppose q on the OUTER boundary S^3 is a homeomorphism to the specified boundary of C'. Attach an exterior boundary collar S^3 times [1,2] to both domain and quotient, using that boundary homeomorphism. The enlarged domain is still the literal standard ball with an exterior product collar.

Choose j:S^3→[0,1] with zero set K, for example j(s)=min(1,dist(s,K)), with the empty-K case j=1. On the combined collar S^3 times [0,2] define
F(s,t)=(s,j(s)t)                         for 0≤t≤1,
F(s,t)=(s,j(s)+(t−1)(2−j(s)))            for 1≤t≤2.

On the complement of that collar use the identity, identifying its t=0 boundary by c. The formulas agree at t=1, fix t=0 and t=2, and vary continuously with s. If j(s)>0 they give a strictly increasing interval homeomorphism. If j(s)=0 their only nontrivial point inverse is [0,1], sent to0; the remainder maps strictly increasingly to[0,2]. Thus F is onto the same standard enlarged ball and has EXACTLY the fibers of the quotient q with the added collar. The induced bijection from C' union its added collar to that enlarged ball is a homeomorphism by compactness and the Hausdorff target. In particular this is not an invocation of a four-dimensional Schoenflies theorem or a conclusion that the wild inner boundary is locally flat.

Now assume the actual common quotient construction has supplied beta:C'→Q with null fibers and nowhere-dense singular image, and Section9 has given a homeomorphism a:B^4→Q matching alpha on the boundary. Extend a^−1 beta over the added collar by its boundary product to the ordinary B^4 union exterior collar. Use the explicit homeomorphism just constructed to identify the DOMAIN with a standard ball. The extended map is an onto ball-to-ball map with null fibers and nowhere-dense singular image. Its restriction over the ENTIRE target exterior collar is a homeomorphism. Apply Section5 with that closed collar as protected E. The resulting homeomorphism agrees with the extended map on the whole preimage collar, so it takes its complementary inner C' exactly onto the complementary inner standard B^4, with the required boundary map. Its attaching solid torus inherits the specified original framing because that boundary map was protected, not subsequently adjusted by an arbitrary sphere homeomorphism.

This is the full reduction made in FQ4.6 printed80, including its paragraph between the proposition and the proof. That paragraph is indispensable: applying the ball-to-ball proposition directly to an unparameterized pinched neighborhood C' would be circular. It uses the special wild-COLLAR arc fibers, not merely arbitrary arc fibers. The actual dual-handle construction must therefore provide that precise singular parameterization, in addition to providing beta and its common quotient; those are still the geometric design obligations before the present operation can be used on the original disk problem.
**Section11: Dual model and the singular collar parameterization.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Fix a FINITE model tower, before its extra plumbings are mapped into the ambient manifold. The entire disk-like capped model has regular neighborhood D^2 times D^2. Deleting the caps instead leaves the complement of disjoint dual two-handles H_m=(D^2 times D^2,D^2 times S^1). The latter convention for their attaching solid torus is the dual one; it is not the original attaching S^1 times D^2. This statement is checked at one elementary surface move: replace the disk by its self-tube along a short arc. Its complement acquires a one-handle, and the two caps supply its cancelling dual two-handle pair. Slice the tube by a normal three-disk. The two cap dual disks run on opposite sides of that slice; outside the tube they are two parallel strips, while inside it their strips pass once on opposite normal sides. Gluing the slice back gives the two linked solid tori in the original D^2 times S^1. Replacing one cap by another capped surface repeats exactly this operation INSIDE its own dual handle. Multiple handles on a surface give disjoint stacks of this pair. Finger moves on a cap, and its added Whitney/accessory disks, give further dual handles contained in those already present. Thus successive finite stories give nested finite families H_(n,m), and the neighborhood of their body is
(D^2 times D^2) minus union_m int H_(n,m).
The elementary pair of linked tori just described is the Bing pair in this argument; its specified strips, rather than a link name alone, determine the relevant pattern.

Here is the finite shortening operation on that pattern. Cut the longitude of the parent solid torus at a small box. After the first doubling each core has a long forward-and-return pair of strands, monotone in the longitude coordinate, with the remaining clasp confined to the cut box. A 'monotone loop of length r' means one strand runs monotonically through an interval of length r and the other returns through that same interval; the rest has longitude diameter<a. If r>a, place a doubling clasp a short distance a along the forward strand and its mate a short distance a from the far turn on the return strand. On either child the two middle opposite parallel runs bound an empty ribbon: they are the two sides of the same normal strip, with its clasp endpoints outside that ribbon. Cancel these two runs by pushing across this ribbon. The remaining child has one forward-and-return pair of longitude length at most r−a; its two short joining pieces and clasp have longitude diameter<a. Perform the cancellation for the two children in different normal levels of the parent strip. Their supports are disjoint, and the old single linked passage between the children stays in their short clasp boxes. This is an isotopy of the doubled pair inside the parent torus: the moving ribbon is in its product normal disk, its endpoints are fixed on the two clasp boxes, and at each intermediate time the strands remain in their prescribed separate normal levels. It does not cut a linked component or pass it through the other one.

Iterate the shortening. The initial forward-and-return length is less than the circumference of the longitude circle, say2pi. After more than2pi/a steps every child core has longitude diameter<a. Compress the transverse disk widths as well, with an isotopy in the solid-torus product coordinates. Hence sufficiently many grope stages put every boundary solid torus of the dual handles in a ball of arbitrarily small prescribed diameter about a point of the longitude core. Further Whitney/accessory handles lie inside the preceding dual handles, so also satisfy that bound. All moves are in the finite MODEL, with its actual normal strips; no assertion is made that an arbitrary linked family can be made small componentwise without that iterated pattern.

Apply this to the convergent tower of Section8. At the n-th step use replication and squeezing to add two stories: choose the grope height of the first high enough for the preceding dual-boundary shortening to the next required model tolerance, and put the ambient next-story pieces in balls of diameter<2^−n. For each dual handle H_(n,m):D^2 times D^2→D^2 times D^2, choose its collar on the attaching D^2 times S^1. The precise two model bounds are diam H_(n,m)(D^2 times S^1)<2^−n and diam H_(n,m)(D^2 times ((1/2+2^−n)D^2))<2^−n. The former follows from the boundary shortening; the latter is arranged by compressing the radial disk factor toward the center, leaving the attaching collar fixed. Arrange the new collars to agree with the old collar on the outer interval [2^−n,1]; this is accomplished by product interpolation inside the old dual handle. The changes at step n are supported over the part of the old collar below height2^−n. All attaching parts and their ambient images have the same shrinking bounds.

For precision, let d:(D^2 times S^1) times [0,1]→D^2 times D^2 be the initial radial collar. Let c_n be its successive modifications. Require: c_(n+1)=c_n outside the new dual handles times [0,2^−n]; inside them it has the just specified product attaching collar; its complete descendant collar lies inside the parent handle; and each modified handle's central region H_(n,m)(D^2 times ((1/2+2^−n)D^2)) has diameter<2^−n. Nested dual-handle branches then give a limit collar c. If a point of the collar parameter lies in only finitely many modified pieces, its image stabilizes in a finite embedded collar chart. If it lies in an infinite branch, the corresponding nested transverse regions have diameters tending to zero, so define its unique limit image. Distinct branches are disjoint at a finite level; their limit points cannot coincide. A branch point and a finite-stage point also separate at a finite level. This proves injectivity. The same diameter bounds give continuity at branch points and local finite-chart continuity elsewhere. Compactness gives an embedding of the whole collar.

The complement of the body in the finite dual model is the union of the interiors of the H_(n,m). Its endpoint compactification is obtained by collapsing each connected component of their nested intersection to a point. For a fixed descending handle branch the attaching tori have diameters tending to zero, so their intersection is a unique z in the boundary collar parameter space. The descendant-collar containment puts the full c({z} times [0,1]) in every handle of the branch. Conversely each handle is covered by its attaching radial collar and its specified central region. Points of its collar approach c({z} times [0,1]) by uniform continuity of the embedded limit collar as its attaching torus shrinks; points in its central region approach c(z,0) by that region's diameter bound. Thus any point in the nested handle intersection lies on that full fiber. That component is EXACTLY c({z} times [0,1]), for z in the closed intersection K of the nested attaching solid tori. Conversely every such fiber is one component of the intersection. The finite model identifications with the actual convergent tower neighborhoods, followed by the nested-ball limiting identification in Section8, therefore give an onto parameterization
q:D^2 times D^2 → C'

whose nontrivial fibers are precisely those wild-collar intervals. It is identity on the marked S^1 times D^2, and its restriction on the complementary boundary D^2 times S^1 is a homeomorphism to the frontier of C'. Its boundary collar is the one needed in Section10. It does not assert q itself is a homeomorphism; distinct points along a nontrivial collar interval have deliberately been identified.

Repeating after any common finite prefix separates every pair of different infinite words. The shrinking diameters then distinguish a limit point from every finite-stage point. This proves the extension q:E→C' is a homeomorphism onto its image, by compactness. It remains identity on the original attaching solid torus. This is the part of the construction that really uses additional STORIES; extra stages alone would not give the uncapped gap tower in which the new parameterizations are inserted.

For the common quotient we also need the finite disk data on each model block. The boundary tori T_(s,m) are regular neighborhoods of boundaries of framed immersed disks D_(s,m) in the parent solid torus. They come from the actual dual-disk strips of Section11, separated at the next cofinal story levels. Their double curves are disjoint arcs with no triple points: in one elementary dual strip block the two sheets meet in one strip arc, and stacking uses disjoint blocks; later fingers are placed in distinct normal strips. This verifies that property for THESE disks, without inferring it for an arbitrary link of immersed disks in a three-manifold.

Assign a height function e_(s,m) to each such disk. On its collar inside its OWN T_(s,m) use the middle height of J_s. On its intersections with earlier tori use constant nonendpoint Cantor heights. Inductively choose the remaining height interval (a,b) inside the permitted parent Cantor interval, avoiding the finitely many earlier constant heights. The new disks lie inside those parent tori, so this separates their graphs from all earlier graphs. At the present finite level, the double arcs have disjoint preimage neighborhoods and no triple points. On one preimage strip of each double arc add a small positive height bump and on the other add a negative one, supported off the fixed boundary collars. The finitely many arcs have disjoint strip neighborhoods, so these changes are compatible and can be made in (a,b). The graphs are embedded and mutually disjoint. Their boundary collars still lie in their own solid-torus blocks, and all graphs avoid every other collapsed block: on an intersected descendant torus their height is the chosen nonendpoint Cantor value, never a middle-third height. This is why arbitrary constant-height spanning disks would not have worked.

In the model ball collapse the closure of B and, for every s,m, the compact set
A_(s,m)=(T_(s,m) times J_s) union graph(e_(s,m))

to a point. The sets are pairwise disjoint by the preceding height choices. Each is the framed embedded disk plus its boundary solid-torus neighborhood of Section9; the overlap is its boundary annular collar. Their diameters tend to zero with depth, since their disks lie in the preceding small parent torus and their heights lie in its small Cantor interval. There are finitely many at each depth. Thus this is a null family. Let alpha be the quotient map to Q.

We verify that this quotient has the topological properties actually needed by Section5 and Section9. Its equivalence relation is closed: for converging pairs of equivalent points, either a single closed collapsed set occurs on a subsequence, or infinitely many distinct sets occur, in which case their diameters tend to zero and the two limits coincide. A closed equivalence relation on a compact metric space has Hausdorff quotient: separate two compact equivalence classes by disjoint neighborhoods, then shrink to saturated neighborhoods using closedness of the relation's projections. It also has a countable basis here. If a class lies in a saturated open set, choose a finite union V of rational basic balls containing that compact class with closure in the saturated open set. The open quotient set Q minus alpha(B^4 minus V) contains the class and lies in the required open set. Countably many finite unions V suffice. Hence the compact Hausdorff quotient is metrizable. Nullity of its nontrivial alpha fibers is exactly the construction, and their supplied local shapes are exactly those of Section9.

On q(E) define beta=alpha q^−1. Each component of the complement of q(E) is one of the nested omitted gap regions or the initial interior region. Its frontier corresponds to the boundary of B or of one T_(s,m) times J_s, together with the spanning graph collar inserted there; alpha is constant on that whole frontier. Extend beta constantly across the closure of the component. The extensions agree on their frontiers. Away from a branch they are finite compact gluings and hence continuous. At a branch both the containing model block and its entire ambient gap region have diameters tending to zero, giving continuity by the neighborhood criterion. They produce no additional unintended identifications, since distinct gap frontiers correspond to distinct collapsed sets, and different branches separate in disjoint finite-level blocks. Thus beta:C'→Q is continuous and onto. Its nontrivial fibers are a null collection: beyond any fixed depth they lie in the specified small ambient gap regions, and only finitely many shallower fibers remain. No particular manifold type is required of those beta fibers.

The singular images are nowhere dense, not just countable. Every neighborhood of a branch image contains a sufficiently deep parent block. Within that block retain a collar slab between its next child tori and away from the finite disk graphs. This is a nonempty open four-dimensional piece missed by all collapsed sets. At a finite collapsed-set image the same construction is made in an arbitrarily small neighboring deeper block; at an uncollapsed point it is immediate from the retained open pieces. Therefore every open subset of Q meets an open set of singleton fibers, for both alpha and beta. Both maps are homeomorphisms on the protected outer boundary, with the same prescribed attaching product.

Section9 now gives a boundary-matching homeomorphism from the model ball to Q. Section10 identifies the collared C' with a literal standard ball by the explicit singular-collar interval formula. The extended beta then satisfies Section5 with the exterior collar protected. Its resulting homeomorphism restricts to C'→B^4 with the prescribed attaching solid torus/framing. Pulling back the standard core gives the locally flat disk with its OWN product normal chart, which is exactly the standard-handle output stipulated in Section11. The construction remains in the prescribed component neighborhood: every descendant tower, gap insertion and limiting block was chosen there, and all standardness maps are maps of that embedded pinched neighborhood rather than changes of the ambient manifold outside it.
**Section13: The good-group input and the geometric-dual correction.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

There is a real additional issue in applying the old tower argument to controlled handle cancellation. The arbitrary accessory nullhomotopies in Section6 may meet the old geometric dual spheres. Pushing those accessories down and tubing over the duals clears the BODY but does not clear their intersections with the duals themselves. Thus Sections6–12, by themselves, give standard disk cores but do not prove that the original dual spheres remain geometrically dual to the completed towers. The following collar-controlled preparation supplies the missing operation and also uses the ORIGINAL good-group Definition directly, without replacing arbitrary good groups by cyclic groups.

The smooth relative filling used in these finite operations has a concrete justification under Countable Choice. A continuous disk filling with its supplied smooth boundary collar first admits a smooth approximation. To keep the collar fixed, use the Euclidean embedding and smooth neighborhood retraction constructed in the actual Whitney-approximation proof: interpolate in the ambient Euclidean coordinates between the old map and its smooth approximation with a cutoff which is zero on a smaller boundary collar and one outside the region where the old map is already smooth, then apply that retraction. Its pointwise approximation bound keeps the whole interpolation inside the retraction neighborhood. This gives a smooth filling and homotopy fixed on the smaller collar. In a target with boundary, first push any unwanted interior boundary contacts into the target collar's positive side, fixed on the prescribed source collar; double the target only for the approximation, and choose its error smaller than half the positive target-boundary distance on the remaining interior. Thus the final filling stays in the intended manifold with its prescribed proper collar.

For genericity, cover the remaining compact disk interior by finitely many coordinate patches and add small affine coordinate polynomials times cutoffs. Their parameters independently vary values and first derivatives on smaller patches. The evaluation into first-jet coordinates is therefore submersive, for parameters in a sufficiently small common ball. The rank-one derivative stratum has codimension(2−1)(4−1)=3 and the rank-zero stratum codimension8, both exceeding the domain dimension2. Parametric transversality consequently makes the perturbed map an immersion. Compactness gives a common local-injectivity scale for this immersion and for sufficiently small subsequent C1 perturbations. Off that scale the pair configurations form a compact set. At two distinct points choose disjoint bump patches, so the two-value evaluation is submersive. Transversality to the diagonal in V times V makes its double locus zero-dimensional and compact, hence finite. At three distinct points use three disjoint bumps; the three-value diagonal has codimension8>6, so triple points are absent. Interior-point/boundary-point coincidences likewise have expected dimension2+1−4<0 and are removed while the boundary collar is fixed. The finite products of parameter balls have dense sets of good parameters by the actual parametric-transversality theorem. No assertion that ordinary pointwise transversality alone proves a jet statement is being used: the independent affine-jet parameters supply the required submersion explicitly.

These finite operations also apply to Whitney and accessory fillings with their fixed local corner models: perform the perturbations off those closed collars and keep their prescribed normal directions. The same finite multi-evaluation argument gives pairwise transversality of the different new disks and the old sheets.

The given maps and collars here are smooth in the supplied neighborhood. The TOP-generic interpretation of the broader disk-data Definition requires a later relative smoothing bridge and is not inferred from ambient smoothness. First record the finite geometric Casson move. Let two immersed surfaces F,G have an opposite-sign pair p,q with a framed Whitney disk W. For every interior point of G intersection W choose an arc in W from its preimage to the interior of the G Whitney boundary arc. Choose these arcs away from the finite preimages of F intersection W and from the double-point preimages of W, and use separate parallel widths where they share an endpoint region. Push the G sheet along that arc and past the G boundary arc. This removes the selected G intersection W and introduces only G self-intersections near that boundary arc. It misses F, since the interior of the G Whitney arc misses F and all arcs avoided the F preimages. After the finite pushes, the interior of W misses G. Perform the immersed Whitney move on F across W. It removes p,q; its only new intersections are F self-intersections coming from W self-points or F intersection W. No F–G points remain from the operation. It is a regular homotopy supported in a neighborhood of W, so all algebraic intersection and self-intersection numbers and boundary framings are preserved. For a finite family, exclude the other prescribed body sheets from the support by first clearing W using their geometric duals whenever that is stipulated below. This is the actual finite separation move, not a smooth embedded-Whitney-disk assertion.

Apply it to the input disks f_i and framed spheres g_i. The excess f_i–g_j points can be paired by framed immersed Whitney disks because their group-ring coefficients cancel. The required boundary circle is null: equal group labels, with the sheet choices matched, are exactly the equality making that Whitney loop trivial. A relative smooth generic filling supplies the disk; boundary twisting corrects its Whitney framing. Use the preceding move on the two collections, so it creates only self-intersections within either collection and removes all excess mutual points. This makes g_i geometrically dual to f_i. Since the original f_i already have zero mutual lambda and mu, no spherical tubing which changes their homotopy classes is required. They have only undergone regular homotopies.

The inclusion M'=M minus an open framed plumbing neighborhood of the f_i into M induces a pi1 isomorphism. Surjectivity follows by moving loops off a finite two-dimensional image. For injectivity, put a nullhomotopy in general position with respect to that image; after deleting small disks at its finitely many intersections, its extra boundary circles are meridians of the f_i sheets. Each meridian is null in the complement using the punctured immersed geometric dual g_i. This fills all punctures and gives the nullhomotopy in M'. The same argument handles both sheets at a double point. Hence M' has the given good fundamental group.

Choose framed Whitney disks D_j for all intersections within and among the f_i, and tube their interiors over separate parallels of g_i to remove their intersections with every f_i. Thus D_j are immersed proper disks in M'. At one paired double point take its Clifford torus T_j in the local product normal chart. Its two meridional caps each intersect exactly one f sheet; tube each cap at that point to a punctured parallel g_i. This gives capped tori T_j^c entirely in M'. Their bodies lie arbitrarily close to the corresponding component of the boundary of the plumbing neighborhood, and are geometrically dual to D_j. Their caps have zero mutual lambda and mu: the local meridional interiors are disjoint, their attaching collars meet only in their prescribed boundary crossing, and the remaining points are exactly those among the framed g_i parallels, with the same cancelling group labels. The input zero Wall numbers therefore give zero coefficients before augmentation. Contract separate parallel capped tori to get geometric dual spheres for D_j, push D_j off these contractions, and tube intersections of the ORIGINAL torus caps with D_j into those parallel spheres. The resulting T_j^c are genuinely dual capped surfaces, meaning their caps also miss D_j. This cleanup preserves the cap Wall hypotheses: the contraction sphere is built from two oppositely oriented parallels of each cap and the torus body, so its intersection with any old cap is a signed sum of the old cap–cap coefficients, hence zero; its self-number is a sum of the same zero self/cross coefficients. The sesquilinear and quadratic sphere-sum formulas therefore leave all cap lambda/mu numbers zero when a cap is tubed to those spheres. The bodies stay in their chosen boundary collar.

Here is the collar reservation which prevents the old gap. Parameterize the actual boundary collar by t in [0,1], with boundary t=0, and put the initial T_j bodies in5/6<t<1. Only attaching collars of D_j and of the torus caps enter this collar otherwise. Tube all D_j mutual/self-points over full parallels of T_j^c in this outermost slab. The resulting bottom surfaces D'_j are embedded, mutually disjoint, and have the same framed boundaries; their caps C' are the two appropriate torus-cap parallels at every tube. If C denotes the torus caps, lambda(C,C')=mu(C)=0 by the preceding coefficient calculation and parallel-copy identities. Take a fresh family of capped-torus parallels with bodies in4/6<t<5/6 and contract it, pushing nothing off, to obtain spheres S_j geometrically dual to D'_j.

Pair the C–C' points by framed immersed Whitney disks. Their boundaries lie above t=4/6, and their nullhomotopies can be chosen there: deleting t<4/6 from a boundary collar is a homotopy equivalence with an explicit collar-push inverse. Tube these disks over S_j to make their interiors disjoint from all D'_j. The tube paths and spheres stay above the fresh lower collar slabs. Apply the geometric Casson move to C and C'. Its supports miss D'_j and all unused torus BODIES below4/6. Thus the new caps miss each other as the two collections, while arbitrary self/intersections within each cap collection are still allowed and remain algebraically cancelling.

Push the C' self/mutual points down D'_j and tube full capped-torus parallels with bodies in3/6<t<4/6. This adds the second surface stages, producing height-two capped gropes D''_j. Their body is embedded by the same scorecard as Section3. Separate their new caps C'' from C exactly as before, now using contracted parallels in2/6<t<3/6 and Whitney nullhomotopies outside t<2/6. All remaining torus bodies may now be taken in0<t<2/6. They and their caps are geometrically dual to the entire height-two gropes, including their caps. Raise the latter to any required finite height, keeping their first two stages, and successively contract one extra top stage to make their caps pairwise disjoint, with their self-points in canonical cancelling pairs. These neighborhood operations miss the dual capped surfaces because those were made disjoint from the whole starting grope except at the bottom transverse point.

Now the actual good-group Definition applies in its exact place. Choose grope height n+2.5. Each disjoint top height-1.5 component is a supplied disk-like framed grope. Apply goodness to its homomorphism into pi1(M') to obtain the framed null disk in that canonical model. Section14 smooths it within a neighborhood with trivial group image while retaining its attaching frame; thus it supplies the smooth immersed disk required here, with double-point loops null in M'. Distinct replacement disks lie in disjoint component neighborhoods. The retained grope has height n+1. Contract one top stage symmetrically: the new cap double loops are parallel copies or differences of the null loops, hence null; the cap self-points come in algebraically cancelling finger pairs. The first n stages have been kept EXACTLY. Taking n≥4 is sufficient for Sections7–12.

Fill those double-point loops by framed immersed accessory disks. Their boundaries miss t<2/6, so their fillings may be pushed off that collar. Hence they miss the torus BODIES reserved there, although they may intersect its caps and the grope arbitrarily. Contract fresh dual capped surfaces with bodies in1/6<t<2/6 to get spheres S''_j. Correct the accessory framings, push their body intersections down, and tube over S''_j to clear the whole grope body. The resulting accessories are the proper tower top caps. Finally take the LAST capped-torus parallels with bodies in0<t<1/6 and contract them, pushing every tower-cap sheet off the contraction. Their bodies already miss the accessories by the collar choice. The resulting spheres R_j therefore miss the ENTIRE tower except for their prescribed bottom transverse point. This final contraction/push-off is the step which the uncontrolled use of the original spheres in Section6 could not provide.

The R_j are nullhomotopic in the ORIGINAL M. Indeed symmetric contraction of a fixed capped surface is independent up to homotopy of its caps: it is regularly homotopic to surgery on only the first cap of each pair; switch the unused second caps; it is also homotopic to surgery on only the second caps; then switch the first caps. Thus in M replace the caps built from g_i by the original small meridional caps. The contracted Clifford torus is now contained in the original double-point four-ball, and is null there. This proves [R_j]=0 in pi2(M), despite its being a useful nonzero class in pi2(M').

Remove intersections of the original g_i with the towers by pushing them down the tower to the bottom and tubing over R_j. They still meet the f_i only at their one original dual point, since all these changes lie in M'. They now miss the entire tower. The changes of g_i are homotopies and additions of whiskered R_j, which are null in M, so preserve their original homotopy classes. Perform Sections7–12 inside neighborhoods of the towers disjoint from these g_i, with their one dual intersection moved into the protected attaching collar. The resulting embedded framed Whitney disks are disjoint from every g_i. Their Whitney moves on the f_i give disjoint properly locally flat embedded disks, regularly homotopic rel boundary/framing to the original f_i, and with the g_i still geometrically dual. They also provide the product normal charts required in the final surface-compression application: on the untouched pieces keep the old smooth disk frames; on each Whitney replacement use the pulled-back standard two-handle frame, glued by the Whitney framing along its two boundary arcs. This is a finite construction of a normal disk bundle over the resulting disk, trivialized by those compatible frames. Compactness permits sufficiently small widths so different patches overlap only by their prescribed bundle transitions and the resulting total-space map is injective. Thus the constructed disks have their OWN product tubes, without using the later general TOP normal-bundle theorem. Thus the original disk theorem's homotopy conclusion is supplied by WHITNEY MOVES, rather than assumed from an arbitrary standard-core choice.
**Section14: Smoothing a framed null disk inside a canonical grope neighborhood.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit.

This operation addresses the category of the disk obtained from GOODNESS, whose boundary is the canonical smooth attaching region of the framed model grope. It does not smooth an arbitrary original boundary knot or a TOP-generic disk in an unrelated ambient manifold. Its input is a generic immersed disk with the supplied extending framing/product germs which make its boundary the model attaching region. If 'framed boundary' were read as an arbitrary external integer without an extending framed immersion, the following parity argument would not apply; that is not the framed-disk convention used here.

Let Q be the smooth framed model neighborhood, phi:pi1(Q)→Gamma, and d:D^2→Q the supplied generic framed disk with phi-null double-point loops. Its compact image A is homeomorphic to a finite polyhedron P: subdivide the parameter disk with the finitely many paired double-point preimages as vertices and with their stars disjoint, identify those vertex pairs, and subdivide once more. The resulting finite quotient complex maps continuously bijectively onto A and hence homeomorphically, by compactness and the Hausdorff target. Its fundamental group is generated by the finitely many double-point loops, since the disk before identifying the pairs is simply connected. Thus phi kills the entire image of pi1(A).

Here is an explicit neighborhood-retraction argument, avoiding a general normal-bundle theorem. Realize P as a finite subcomplex of a standard simplex, subdivide barycentrically, and note that its subdivision is FULL: a simplex whose chain of face-vertices all belong to P belongs to P. On the open star of P in that subdivided simplex, delete the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside P and normalize the remaining positive sum. Fullness makes this a continuous retraction onto P. A small neighborhood in Euclidean space first retracts to the simplex, by taking nonnegative coordinates and normalizing their sum. Composing gives a Euclidean neighborhood retraction onto P.

Extend the finitely many coordinates of the inverse homeomorphism A→P continuously to Q as follows. For a residual continuous scalar function r_n on compact A with sup norm at most c_n, choose the least positive integer L_n such that
|r_n(a)−r_n(b)| ≤ c_n/2 + L_n dist(a,b)   for all a,b in A.

Uniform continuity and boundedness give such an integer. Put h_n(x)=inf_(a in A)(r_n(a)+L_n dist(x,a)), clamped to[−c_n,c_n]. It is bounded and L_n-Lipschitz; on A its error from r_n lies between0 and c_n/2. Define r_(n+1)=r_n−h_n|A and c_(n+1)=c_n/2. The uniformly convergent sum of the h_n extends the original coordinate function exactly. All constants are suprema/infima or least integers, so this is a definable recursion. For a zero starting function use the zero extension. The finite coordinate extensions give a map Psi:Q→R^N. On the inverse image of the preceding Euclidean retraction neighborhood, compose with its retraction and P→A. This gives a continuous retraction r:U→A from an actual open neighborhood U of A.

Form the smooth double $Q^{\mathrm{dbl}}$ from the two copies of the supplied smooth grope neighborhood, using its given product boundary collar, as in Section13. Use the proper Euclidean embedding j of this BOUNDARYLESS double and its smooth neighborhood retraction R supplied by the actual Whitney-approximation proof. There is a continuous fold c:Q^{dbl}→Q: it is the identity on the first copy, identifies the second copy with the first by the doubling identification, and in the shared collar is (x,t)→(x,|t|). For x in a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood U' of compact A in U⊂Q, the segment between j(x) and j(r(x)) stays in the domain of R. Indeed r fixes A, and compact j(A) has positive distance from the closed complement of that domain. The formula c(R((1−t)j(x)+t j(r(x)))) is a continuous homotopy IN Q from the inclusion U'→Q to r|U', fixed on A. Hence every loop in U' has phi-trivial image in Q. No smooth retraction onto the boundary of Q is used, and no smoothness of the fold is claimed.

Carry out the smooth relative approximation and finite jet perturbation of d in the DOUBLE, fixing its supplied smooth attaching collar pointwise. Choose a smaller closed source boundary collar inside the collar where d is already smooth; keep a neighborhood of that smaller collar fixed by the cutoff. The complement of that neighborhood in the compact parameter disk is a compact set mapped into IntQ, since d is proper. Its image therefore has positive distance from the boundary of Q in the doubled metric. It also has a positive tolerance for remaining in U', by relative openness and compactness. Choose the approximation and subsequent finite perturbations below both tolerances. On the fixed collar the map remains d; everywhere else it stays in IntQ∩U'. Thus the resulting map is a smooth proper generic disk IN Q, with the original attaching collar and framing, and all its double-point loops lie in U'. The continuous fold used in1.127 is NOT applied to this smooth approximation. For the framing, take the supplied framed parallel of the original d with its disjoint boundary parallel. Its ordinary relative intersection with d is twice the signed self-point count, and is therefore even; the normal-zero term is absent because that frame extends. The relative intersection number is unchanged under homotopy fixing these boundary parallels. For the smooth approximation it equals2mu+e, by the local parallel-sheet count and the zeros of a generic normal section. Thus its relative Euler number e is even. Interior cusps change e by2, so finitely many restore e=0 and the required frame. Their new loops are trivial in the same small coordinate balls, so phi-nullness survives. The resulting SMOOTH framed generic null disk has the original attaching region.

This operation shows why the goodness step can be consumed in the canonical smooth grope model with the framed-disk convention, without using arbitrary TOP neighborhood smoothing, stable5 integration, or the full boundary/collar smoothing needed for an unrelated original TOP-generic input. That boundary/collar bootstrap is not claimed here.
**Section15: Countable Choice versus the successive tower choices.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit.

Countable Choice is not being identified with Dependent Choice. Saying 'choose a next tower at each stage' would not justify this foundation claim. The geometric selections in this particular smooth-model construction can instead be made by a single-valued least-code rule, after fixing the Euclidean embedding/retraction of the smooth neighborhood once.

For a new disk with a specified smooth boundary collar, list pairs consisting of a dyadic collar width and a finite tuple of rational polynomials on the standard parameter disk. Use its supplied boundary-collar map b and a fixed smooth radial cutoff alpha, equal to1 on a smaller collar and0 off that collar. Form the Euclidean candidate alpha j(b)+(1−alpha)P and apply the fixed neighborhood retraction R. The term alpha j(b) is extended by zero only where alpha already vanishes; it is smooth there. Candidates are retained only when the Euclidean values lie in the retraction domain and the resulting map has the required proper boundary collar, genericity, support and finite intersection conditions. Framed candidates are listed simultaneously: project rational polynomial vector fields to the smooth normal plane of the candidate disk, blend them with the prescribed boundary frame on the same collar, and retain those with oriented linearly independent normal vectors everywhere. Orthogonal projection is computed from the ambient embedding metric and the derivative matrix, so is part of the fixed formula.

Whenever an admissible smooth framed filling exists, some listed candidate exists. Choose the dyadic collar inside a collar on which that filling agrees with b. Rational polynomials approximate its Euclidean coordinates and its normal frame uniformly with the required first derivatives. Here is the needed C1 density calculation. Extend each smooth coordinate function slightly past the compact disk, using its finitely many local extensions and a finite smooth partition, and restrict to a containing square rescaled to[0,1]^2. Its Bernstein polynomial is the finite sum of f(k/n,l/n) times the two binomial basis polynomials. Uniform convergence follows from uniform continuity: the binomial weights are probabilities, and the weight outside a fixed distance eta of(x,y) is at most1/(2n eta^2) by the sum of their variances. Its x derivative is the analogous degree(n−1,n) sum of n(f((k+1)/n,l/n)−f(k/n,l/n)), each an average of the x derivative on an interval of length1/n; uniform continuity of that derivative and the same variance bound give uniform derivative convergence. The y derivative is identical. Approximate the finitely many coefficients by rationals with error smaller than the desired C1 tolerance divided by4n: the basis sums to1 and the derivative difference has bound2n times that error. Restrict back to the disk. This proves the claimed rational-polynomial C1 density rather than assuming an analytic power series for an arbitrary smooth function. The values stay in the open retraction domain; properness away from the fixed collar, the normal-frame determinant and the finite transversality angles have positive compact lower bounds. Thus sufficiently close candidates preserve them. Near a generic immersion the double points and their labels persist in disjoint coordinate balls and no new double points occur outside them, by compactness off the local-injectivity diagonal. For a group-null filling use Section14's open neighborhood with null group image: sufficiently close candidates lie there, so retain all null-loop conditions. Candidates which are required to lie in a prescribed relative homotopy class do so for sufficiently close approximations, by the straight retraction homotopy fixed on the boundary collar.

The least natural-number code satisfying these actual predicates therefore specifies the disk and its frame uniquely. Decidability of the predicates is not asserted or needed for set-theoretic definability. This is not a choice function on arbitrary subsets of a mapping space: it is minimization in a specified COUNTABLE list which has just been proved nonempty for each geometric step.

The other choices have the same form. Paths and finger arcs are finite polygonal/rational smooth approximations in the already specified charts, with endpoint templates and finite disjointness conditions. Parallel widths and modification balls use the first dyadic radius meeting the strict compact separation conditions. Finite orderings of double points can be obtained lexicographically from their distinct parameter preimage coordinate tuples, and every finite tree or interval subdivision is chosen in that ordering. The local shrinking Baire step of Section5 has its own explicit countable rational bump rule, preserving every earlier finite avoidance margin. The successive approximations of Sections9–12 use least cofinal story levels and least integer tolerances. No choice is made over an uncountable family of possible future branches.

Thus each next finite stage is a uniquely defined function of the previous finite stage, the original input and the fixed embedding/retraction. Ordinary recursion on the natural numbers constructs the entire sequence. The single fixed smooth embedding/retraction and the actual transversality/approximation suppliers use their stated Countable Choice hypothesis; once those are fixed, no additional Dependent Choice principle is introduced by the tower or shrinking recursion. This is the precise foundation claim of the current smooth-input candidate. It does not turn the open unrestricted problem into a theorem and does not supply a TOP smoothing theorem.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed immersed spheres $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. Here a generic immersion is locally a topological embedding except at finitely many double points, each with exactly two preimages whose image sheets are the coordinate planes $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$; proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary; and framed means that the normal microbundle has a chosen trivialization extending the specified boundary framing. citations.quote: Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is an immersed disk whose framed boundary is the attaching region of $G^c$, such that each double-point loop of the disk, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input.

**Operation.** Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. Cutting a genus-g one-boundary surface along its complete symplectic system leaves the disk region with paired edges; the four parallel cap sectors and this square fill each pair of edges. Thus this replaces the surface with its contracted disk. All replacements take place in the supplied framed block. Parallel copies are made in its chosen normal coordinate; the central square uses the untwisted product collar, so the external attaching framing is unchanged. The result may be immersed, which is allowed.

For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. Finitely many paths on one cap can be chosen with disjoint interiors by an embedded finite tree and small parallel offsets. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. In a product rectangle around the path, this is just the rectangle between the two parallel copies, closed by the boundary square. Its interior is disjoint from the old body and all unmodified sheets. A generic sufficiently small choice of the finitely many product widths is possible because their unwanted incidences are finitely many closed disjoint compact sets. No appeal to a normal bundle over an arbitrary TOP surface occurs.

Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Ribbons on the same cap have been chosen parallel and disjoint, and ribbons belonging to different handles have disjoint block neighborhoods. Therefore every new intersection has exactly the stated two designated ancestors. Repeating for all parallel descendants removes the designated old point altogether. This is a finite sequence of ordinary finger/Whitney operations in explicit smooth block charts; a small relative perturbation makes the resulting intersections transverse.

Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. A path to the new intersection follows the first pushed sheet along the ribbon to its second-sheet cap, crosses the common central square, and returns along the other ribbon in reverse. Cancel the common paths in the old body. The resulting word is g h^{-1}; changing starting path conjugates it and exchanging the two resulting sheets inverts it. This is a calculation in the original supplied neighborhood, since every ribbon and push lies there. Its Z label is consequently ±(phi(g)−phi(h)). An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. The construction, classification of new intersections and claimed bound follow.

**Section2: Halving and the finite stopping bound.** Suppose there are h top surface stages available for contraction and the absolute labels of all the actual cap-point generators are at most an integer N. The unmodified old positive labels are less than N/2; old negative labels may still range to −N. Contract the next top stage and designate the labels in [−N,−N/2]. Again new labels have absolute value at most N/2. Old labels outside this interval already have absolute value at most N/2. Thus two contractions reduce the bound to N/2. The same construction works when N is odd, since inequalities refer to real bounds and labels remain integers.

After q pairs of contractions the bound is N/2^q. Choose the least integer q with 2^q>N; if N=0 take q=0. This is a finite integer algorithm. At that point every cap-point generator has label zero. The neighborhood group is generated by these loops: the abstract disk-like capped grope is simply connected (its symplectic basis loops are killed by its attached higher stages/caps), and each self-plumbing identifies two small simply connected sheet neighborhoods, adding its one double-point loop. Cutting the finite plumbing neighborhoods restores the abstract source. Van Kampen, adding them back one at a time, gives precisely these generators, with no assertion that an arbitrary ambient group is free. Hence the entire neighborhood image has zero Z label.

Contract the remaining body stages to a disk. Every operation stays in this neighborhood, so all double-point loops of the final framed immersed disk have zero image under the original homomorphism. Its boundary and framing are unchanged. This proves null-disk production **when sufficiently many actual stages have been constructed**; it does not yet manufacture those stages from height1.5.

In the symmetric height-raising construction, the precise quantitative target can be stated without the harmless factor-of-two compression in FQ2.9. If 2k raising steps give height at least 2^k and each resulting cap-point loop has word length at most 5^{2k} in the original finite cap-point generators, their absolute labels are at most 5^{2k}B. It suffices that
2^(−floor((2^k−1)/2)) · 5^(2k) · B < 1.

Reserve one bottom surface stage; the other stages supply the indicated number of contraction pairs. The displayed quantity tends to zero because its base-two logarithm is at most −2^(k−1)+O(k)+log2 B. Thus a least successful k is obtained by a terminating integer search. No infinite choice or convergence theorem is hidden in this numerical step. Sections3–4 prove the required height and word-length estimates starting from the asymmetric height1.5 input.

The same construction is repeated for the finitely many pairs; their body blocks are disjoint, and interactions between cap systems are allowed. All operations fix a neighborhood of the original bottom surface and its attaching region.

Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. The annulus and the single crossing are read in the supplied symplectic handle block, not in a hypothetical neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface.

Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. This includes the original caps of F, the caps of R and the remaining parts of W. All intersections newly produced by those pushes are between those cap sheets. The sphere T is therefore disjoint from both R and the body/caps of F, and from the caps of R, and meets W at its one prescribed point only. Self-intersections of T are allowed. The ribbons have support near cap arcs and their central squares, away from the lower body, so they do not alter any of the displayed body intersections.

Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W.

For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections.

This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections.

**Section4: Height raising and word length.** Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section3 gives (1,0) to (1,1). The following side extension, used only finitely often in this bootstrap, supplies (1,1) to (2,1) to (2,3). Let P be the side to be raised and Q its other side, of heights p,q at least one. Construct F transverse to the bottom surface of P by taking two normal parallels of Q and closing their rims with the normal annulus. It is sphere-like of height q. Its body is embedded, meets P only at the specified first-stage point, and misses all other body stages; intersections of its caps with the old caps are allowed.

Its only body intersection is that prescribed transverse point. To make the caps of F disjoint from the old P caps, push an F-cap sheet at each intersection down the old P cap to its attaching stage and then down successive P stages to its bottom. A finger across one attaching collar replaces one intersection with two on the immediately lower stage; this is two parallel paths around the two ends of that collar. After p stages there are finitely many points on the bottom of P. Tube them off over parallel copies of T. These changes affect only caps of F. They cannot reintroduce intersections with old P caps because T misses those caps and the finger paths on the old caps avoid the other finitely many double-point preimages. The new intersections are among caps of F and possibly the old Q caps, which are still caps. All old body stages are fixed.

It may acquire self/intersections with other caps, which are allowed. It remains disjoint from the old P caps and all body stages: the punctured T used in the tubing has had its unique bottom-P intersection removed. Crucially T is also disjoint from the body of F, so the Q caps miss every body piece to be added in the next step.

Finally treat every self/mutual intersection among the old P caps by pushing one of its P sheets down the P stages and tubing it off over copies of the full F, rather than T. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope: its first added stage is the old disk with punctured bodies of F attached, followed by the higher stages of those copies of F. Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All old P-cap intersections have been removed; the added bodies are embedded and disjoint from each other because distinct body parallels of F are disjoint, and the tube paths avoid all other old preimages. The new caps are copies of F's caps. Those were made disjoint from ALL old P caps before this step, and properness makes them disjoint from F's parallel bodies. Consequently every new intersection is among caps, not on a new body. A cap with no intersections may be regarded as a genus-zero stage with no attached higher surface, as in the disk-like model. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap.
