Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal C$ be a ribbon category with chosen left duals and tensor unit $\mathbf 1$. A **finite oriented framed link colored in $\mathcal C$** is a finite disjoint union $L$ of oriented smoothly embedded circles in $S^3$, a homotopy class of nowhere-zero normal vector field on each component, and an assignment of an object of $\mathcal C$ to each component. A framed colored isotopy carries orientations, framings, and component colors. If $F_{\mathcal C}$ is the ribbon-tangle evaluation functor, define
$$\operatorname{RT}_{\mathcal C}(L):=F_{\mathcal C}(L)\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1).$$
This value depends only on the framed colored isotopy class. It is not automatically a field scalar; if $\mathcal C$ is $k$-linear and $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1)=k$, it is a scalar in $k$. The empty link is assigned $1_{\mathbf 1}$.

An **effective field** is a field whose elements have finite encodings and whose exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, equality test, and inversion of nonzero elements are terminating procedures. Input a finite-dimensional strict matrix realization of a $k$-linear ribbon category with $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=k$, finite-dimensional color objects with fixed bases, exact matrices for every braiding and inverse braiding used, duality and twist data, and the induced pivotal matrix $J_W$ for the tensor word $W=V_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{a_n}$. Also input a finite braid word $\beta$ on $n\ge1$ strands and the top color tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$. The matrices are assumed to satisfy the stated ribbon-category axioms; an implementation does not infer those axioms from arbitrary matrices.

Use the strand-position permutation homomorphism $\pi:B_n\to\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$ given by $\pi(\sigma_i)=(i\ i+1)$. Read the braid letters in composition order, updating the current color tuple at each crossing by swapping its adjacent colors. For a positive letter $\sigma_i$, use the matrix of
$$1\otimes\cdots\otimes c_{V_{a_i},V_{a_{i+1}}}\otimes\cdots\otimes1,$$
and for a negative letter use its inverse. Let the blackboard-framed closure join the bottom and top endpoint at each position by the identity pairing. Reject the input if the final color tuple differs from the initial tuple: the tuple records the colors at the paired endpoints, so equality is exactly the condition that the closure carries a consistent color on every component. Starting with the identity matrix, multiply the typed crossing matrices in word order to obtain $M_\beta:W\to W$, then return
$$\operatorname{Tr}(J_WM_\beta)\in k.$$
This is the exact ribbon evaluation of the blackboard-framed colored braid closure in the given matrix realization. No algorithm is asserted for arbitrary abstract ribbon categories without effective finite matrix data.

For every valid input of the colored-braid evaluation algorithm, where the braid word has $m$ letters and the total tensor-product dimension is $D$, the procedure terminates after exactly $m$ crossing-matrix updates and one finite pivotal-trace contraction. It returns the ribbon-category evaluation of that framed colored braid closure in the given matrix realization. The stated bound concerns the number of matrix updates; each update is a finite exact matrix multiplication over the effective field.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

In a braided rigid monoidal category there is a natural isomorphism

$$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

called the **Drinfeld morphism** (or **Drinfeld isomorphism**), defined by

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

Write

$$d_{X,Y}:X^{\vee\vee}\otimes Y^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}(X\otimes Y)^{\vee\vee}$$

for the monoidal comparison of the double-dual functor. Then

$$d_{X,Y}\circ(u_X\otimes u_Y)=u_{X\otimes Y}\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}.$$

Thus $u$ need not be monoidal: the double braiding is precisely its
monoidality obstruction.

Every permutation of a finite set is a product of pairwise disjoint cycles,
uniquely up to reordering the factors and cyclically rotating the entries within
each cycle. The identity permutation has the empty disjoint-cycle decomposition.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the closed-link value is the ribbon-tangle evaluation, and [F3] identifies the algorithm output with that value. In the flip category, each positive braid generator swaps two adjacent tensor factors and each negative generator does the same swap, so the braid action on $V^{\otimes n}$ is the permutation of factors given by $\pi(\beta)$. The twist is identity. Let $w_1,\ldots,w_{d^n}$ be the tensor basis of $W=V^{\otimes n}$ and $w_1^*,\ldots,w_{d^n}^*$ its ordinary dual basis. Substitution in [F5]'s formula gives $u_W(w_r)(w_s^*)=1$ when $r=s$ and $0$ otherwise, so the ribbon-induced pivotal map is the canonical double-dual identification. Thus [F2]–[F3] reduce the value to the ordinary matrix trace of that permutation operator.

Fix a rigid monoidal category with chosen left duals. For a morphism
$a:X\to X^{\vee\vee}$, the **left categorical trace** of $a$ is the endomorphism
of the unit

$$\operatorname{Tr}_L(a):\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_X}X\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{a\otimes1_{X^\vee}}X^{\vee\vee}\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_{X^\vee}}\mathbf 1.$$

For a morphism $b:X^{\vee\vee}\to X$, the **right categorical trace** of $b$ is

$$\operatorname{Tr}_R(b):\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{1_{X^\vee}\otimes b}X^\vee\otimes X\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X}\mathbf 1.$$

So a bare endomorphism $X\to X$ is not yet an input to categorical trace; one
first needs a comparison between $X$ and a double dual.

In a braided rigid monoidal category there is a natural isomorphism

$$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

called the **Drinfeld morphism** (or **Drinfeld isomorphism**), defined by

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

Write

$$d_{X,Y}:X^{\vee\vee}\otimes Y^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}(X\otimes Y)^{\vee\vee}$$

for the monoidal comparison of the double-dual functor. Then

$$d_{X,Y}\circ(u_X\otimes u_Y)=u_{X\otimes Y}\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}.$$

Thus $u$ need not be monoidal: the double braiding is precisely its
monoidality obstruction.

Every permutation of a finite set is a product of pairwise disjoint cycles,
uniquely up to reordering the factors and cyclically rotating the entries within
each cycle. The identity permutation has the empty disjoint-cycle decomposition.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

For $n\ge2$, the **braid group** $B_n$ is the group with generators
$\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and relations

$$\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\qquad(1\le i\le n-2),$$

$$\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\qquad(1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1).$$

Equivalently,

$$B_n=\langle \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\ \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\ (1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

interpreted in the sense of [[def-group-presentation]] and
[[def-relators-relations-and-finite-presentations]].

For $n=0$ and $n=1$, there are no generators, and $B_n$ is the trivial group
given by the empty presentation.

Let $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ be a presentation, let $H$ be a group, and let
$u:X\to H$ be a function. If the evaluation of every $r\in R$ under $u$ is
$e_H$, then there is a unique homomorphism

$$\overline u:\langle X\mid R\rangle\longrightarrow H$$

with $\overline u([x])=u(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Moreover, $\overline u$ is
surjective if and only if $u(X)$ generates $H$.

citations.quote:
The **4T relation** is
$$
D_1-D_2+D_3-D_4=0.
$$
Two chords **intersect** if their endpoints alternate around the oriented circle. A chord is **isolated** if it intersects no other chord. The **1T relation** sets every unframed diagram with an isolated chord equal to zero. The framed degree-$n$ chord-diagram module is the free $R$-module on degree-$n$ chord diagrams modulo all 4T relations. The unframed degree-$n$ chord-diagram module is the free $R$-module on degree-$n$ chord diagrams modulo 4T and 1T relations. A framed weight system is an $R$-linear functional on the framed module; an unframed weight system is an $R$-linear functional on the unframed module.

derivations.claim: A degree-$n$ chord diagram is a pairing of $2n$ cyclically ordered endpoints, so only finitely many such diagrams exist. A 4T relation is determined by a background diagram and finitely many endpoint positions, and a 1T relation by one diagram; hence there are finitely many relation vectors. By [F1], each has integer coefficients, so they form the rows of a finite integer matrix $A$. Write $A_n(F):=F^{C_n}/\operatorname{rowspan}_F(A)$ and $W_n(F):=\operatorname{Hom}_F(A_n(F),F)$. Since $k$ has characteristic zero, $\mathbb Q$ embeds in $k$. The rank of $A$ is unchanged by this field extension: a nonzero maximal minor over $\mathbb Q$ remains nonzero in $k$, while every larger minor that vanishes over $\mathbb Q$ still vanishes in $k$. Thus the row space over $k$ is the scalar extension of the rational row space, and $A_n(k)\cong A_n(\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}k$.

The quotient is finite-dimensional, so extending a rational basis and its dual basis gives $W_n(k)\cong W_n(\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}k$. If $n=0$, the sole diagram is the empty diagram and any weight system is its value $c\in k$; the constant invariant $V(K)=c$ has top symbol $c$. For $n>0$, choose a finite $\mathbb Q$-basis $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_d$ of $W_n(\mathbb Q)$; finite-dimensional row reduction chooses this basis without a choice axiom. By [F2], for each $i$ there is a rational-valued finite-type invariant $V_i$ with top symbol $\phi_i$. Write the given weight system as $W=\sum_{i=1}^d a_i\phi_i$ with $a_i\in k$, and define $V=\sum_{i=1}^d a_iV_i$, viewing each rational value in $k$. Linearity of the finite-difference operator gives top symbol $W$. If $W_n(\mathbb Q)=0$, the sum is empty and the zero invariant supplies the zero weight system.

citations.quote:
Fix the round metric and orientation on $S^3$. An **$m$-singular oriented knot** is a smooth immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$ with exactly $m$ distinct transverse double points and no other self-intersections; each double-point image has exactly two preimages with linearly independent tangent vectors, and the preimage pairs are disjoint. The knot has no framing. Choose disjoint small balls around its double points, each containing no other part of the singular knot. At each double point there are two **resolutions**, obtained by separating the two local branches in the ball; label them $+$ and $-$ so the resolved crossing signs are respectively $+1$ and $-1$ under the convention that, in a diagram whose positive viewing normal agrees with the ambient orientation, the sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\mathrm{over}},v_{\mathrm{under}})$ and the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$.

A **framed oriented knot** is a smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ together with a homotopy class through nowhere-zero smooth sections of its oriented rank-two normal bundle. For an immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$, including one with double points, define its branchwise normal bundle over the parameter circle by $\nu_K:=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$, oriented so that a positive tangent followed by a positive normal basis gives the ambient orientation. Because $dK$ has rank one at every parameter, its image is locally a smooth line subbundle and this quotient is locally a rank-two bundle. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the framed clauses below, so these normal quotient bundles have their smooth vector-bundle structures. A **framed $m$-singular knot** has finitely many transverse double points and finitely many simple zeroes of a smooth section of $\nu_K$, all disjoint; its number $m$ of singularities is the number of double points plus the number of zeroes. A simple zero is one at which the derivative of the section in an oriented local trivialization is nonzero. Resolve double points as above, extending the normal section over the local resolution balls; each resulting section determines a framing homotopy class. To resolve a framing zero at parameter $t=0$, choose the oriented normal trivialization so the section is $t e_1$ near $0$, with $e_2$ the positive quarter-turn of $e_1$; replace it by $t e_1+\delta e_2$ or $t e_1-\delta e_2$ for sufficiently small $\delta>0$. These are the $+$ and $-$ resolutions of that zero and determine the framing classes on the resolved knots.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For an $R$-valued ambient-isotopy invariant $V$ of unframed oriented knots and an $m$-singular knot $K$, its **finite difference** is
$$
D_mV(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^m}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\epsilon_i\right)V(K_\epsilon),
$$
where $K_\epsilon$ resolves singularity $i$ positively when $\epsilon_i=+1$ and negatively when $\epsilon_i=-1$. For $m=0$, set $D_0V(K)=V(K)$. The same formula defines $D_mV$ for an invariant of framed knots on framed singular knots, counting both double points and framing zeroes among the $m$ singularities. For one double point it reads $V(K_+)-V(K_-)$; the zero resolutions use the local normal-section model just specified. An invariant has **type at most $n$** if $D_{n+1}V$ vanishes on every $(n+1)$-singular object in its category. It has **exact type $n$** if it has type at most $n$ but not type at most $n-1$. Type at most $-1$ means the zero invariant, so a nonzero type-at-most-zero invariant has exact type zero. For an unframed link, replace $S^1$ by a finite disjoint union of oriented circles, allow marked self- or mixed double points, and use the same resolution sum. For a framed link, take a normal section on each component and count its simple zeroes together with all double points.

Let $D,D'$ be regular oriented diagrams of links $L,L'$. If the diagrams
differ by one oriented Reidemeister move or a planar isotopy, the links are
equivalent. The local Reidemeister replacement has a realization supported
in a ball over its move disk, after choosing lifts that agree outside that
ball. Comparing arbitrary realizing links may additionally require changing
their heights away from the move disk.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: To realize a degree-$n$ diagram, take its finite cyclic list of chord endpoints, identify each paired pair as a four-valent vertex, and join consecutive endpoints by arcs in $S^3$. Choose disjoint small vertex balls first. Place the finitely many intervening arcs successively in general position relative to those already placed; two one-dimensional arcs in a three-manifold can be separated by a small endpoint-fixed perturbation, so there are no unintended intersections. Smoothing the joins gives exactly the prescribed double points. In the framed case choose a nonzero normal section along the regular arcs and the two branches at every vertex. To close the section around the parameter circle, cut at one regular parameter; the two endpoint unit normals lie in an oriented two-plane and can be joined because its unit circle is connected. Smooth the finitely many joins. This constructs a zero-free framed representative. The framed branch uses [A1] for the normal-bundle structures.

Let $K,K'$ be representatives of the same diagram. Identify their finite marked graphs and fix matching local models in disjoint vertex balls. Join corresponding edge arcs by a homotopy relative to those balls, and homotope the normal sections over the edge strips, allowing zeroes during the homotopy. A finite relative perturbation makes the coincidence equations for two distinct curve parameters transverse: they are three scalar equations in the two curve parameters and time, so their solutions are isolated. It also makes the normal-section zero equation transverse: it is two scalar equations in the curve parameter and time, so its solutions are isolated. The parameter domains can be made compact after deleting a neighborhood of the diagonal, where each curve is locally embedded; the fixed vertex neighborhoods contain no new events. The higher-codimension loci for tangencies, triple points, degenerate section zeroes, or simultaneous events are avoided by the same finite perturbation. Hence only finitely many isolated double-point or framing-zero events occur. Passing any one event changes $D_nV$ by, up to sign, $D_{n+1}V$ on the object with that extra singularity, which vanishes by type at most $n$ in [F1]. Therefore $D_nV(K)=D_nV(K')$. These are finite-dimensional perturbations of a compact one-parameter family; the framed branch additionally uses [A1], and no countable choice is used in the unframed argument.

For a 4T generator choose the four local singular representatives with the same outside $(n-2)$ marked double points and, in the framed case, the same zero-free framing outside the move ball. Resolving the local marked double point with the positive-minus-negative convention gives $w_V(D_1)=a-b$, $w_V(D_2)=c-d$, $w_V(D_3)=c-a$, and $w_V(D_4)=d-b$, where $a,b,c,d$ are the four values of $D_{n-1}V$ on the remaining local configurations. The repeated configurations are identified by the oriented Reidemeister III isotopies in [F3]: $a$ occurs in the positive resolution of $D_1$ and negative resolution of $D_3$, $b$ in the negative resolutions of $D_1,D_4$, $c$ in the positive resolutions of $D_2,D_3$, and $d$ in the negative resolution of $D_2$ and positive resolution of $D_4$. Their resolution signs follow [F4]. Therefore $w_V(D_1)-w_V(D_2)+w_V(D_3)-w_V(D_4)=(a-b)-(c-d)+(c-a)-(d-b)=0$. The same local calculation applies to zero-free framed representatives because the framing outside the move ball is unchanged. This local calculation is choice-free once the framed objects are defined.

Fix the round metric and orientation on $S^3$. An **$m$-singular oriented knot** is a smooth immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$ with exactly $m$ distinct transverse double points and no other self-intersections; each double-point image has exactly two preimages with linearly independent tangent vectors, and the preimage pairs are disjoint. The knot has no framing. Choose disjoint small balls around its double points, each containing no other part of the singular knot. At each double point there are two **resolutions**, obtained by separating the two local branches in the ball; label them $+$ and $-$ so the resolved crossing signs are respectively $+1$ and $-1$ under the convention that, in a diagram whose positive viewing normal agrees with the ambient orientation, the sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\mathrm{over}},v_{\mathrm{under}})$ and the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$.

A **framed oriented knot** is a smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ together with a homotopy class through nowhere-zero smooth sections of its oriented rank-two normal bundle. For an immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$, including one with double points, define its branchwise normal bundle over the parameter circle by $\nu_K:=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$, oriented so that a positive tangent followed by a positive normal basis gives the ambient orientation. Because $dK$ has rank one at every parameter, its image is locally a smooth line subbundle and this quotient is locally a rank-two bundle. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the framed clauses below, so these normal quotient bundles have their smooth vector-bundle structures. A **framed $m$-singular knot** has finitely many transverse double points and finitely many simple zeroes of a smooth section of $\nu_K$, all disjoint; its number $m$ of singularities is the number of double points plus the number of zeroes. A simple zero is one at which the derivative of the section in an oriented local trivialization is nonzero. Resolve double points as above, extending the normal section over the local resolution balls; each resulting section determines a framing homotopy class. To resolve a framing zero at parameter $t=0$, choose the oriented normal trivialization so the section is $t e_1$ near $0$, with $e_2$ the positive quarter-turn of $e_1$; replace it by $t e_1+\delta e_2$ or $t e_1-\delta e_2$ for sufficiently small $\delta>0$. These are the $+$ and $-$ resolutions of that zero and determine the framing classes on the resolved knots.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For an $R$-valued ambient-isotopy invariant $V$ of unframed oriented knots and an $m$-singular knot $K$, its **finite difference** is
$$
D_mV(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^m}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\epsilon_i\right)V(K_\epsilon),
$$
where $K_\epsilon$ resolves singularity $i$ positively when $\epsilon_i=+1$ and negatively when $\epsilon_i=-1$. For $m=0$, set $D_0V(K)=V(K)$. The same formula defines $D_mV$ for an invariant of framed knots on framed singular knots, counting both double points and framing zeroes among the $m$ singularities. For one double point it reads $V(K_+)-V(K_-)$; the zero resolutions use the local normal-section model just specified. An invariant has **type at most $n$** if $D_{n+1}V$ vanishes on every $(n+1)$-singular object in its category. It has **exact type $n$** if it has type at most $n$ but not type at most $n-1$. Type at most $-1$ means the zero invariant, so a nonzero type-at-most-zero invariant has exact type zero. For an unframed link, replace $S^1$ by a finite disjoint union of oriented circles, allow marked self- or mixed double points, and use the same resolution sum. For a framed link, take a normal section on each component and count its simple zeroes together with all double points.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot
$K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, its normal bundle is
$\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, oriented so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a
positive basis of a normal fibre gives the ambient orientation. A **framing**
of $K$ is a homotopy class through smooth nowhere-zero sections of $\nu K$.
The normal bundle is made a smooth vector bundle under this axiom; a framed
knot includes the section class as data, not a choice made afterwards. For the
relative integer use the round metric transferred from the unit sphere in
$\mathbb R^4$ by the explicit diffeomorphism
$$x\longmapsto\left(\frac{2x}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2},\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2-1}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2}\right),\qquad\infty\longmapsto(0,0,0,1).$$
It induces a smooth bundle metric on $\nu K$. The resulting winding number is
independent of the metric: any two smooth fibre metrics interpolate through
positive metrics and the corresponding angle maps are homotopic.

Given a reference framing $[s_0]$ and another framing $[s_1]$, use a bundle
metric and the positive quarter-turn $J$ on each oriented normal plane to write
the normalized representative of $s_1$ as
$$s_1(x)=\cos\theta(x)s_0(x)+\sin\theta(x)Js_0(x).$$
The resulting map $S^1\to S^1$ has a continuous angle lift along a parameter
interval $[0,1]$: subdivide into finitely many intervals whose images lie in
open semicircles and choose consecutive local arguments agreeing at endpoints.
Since the map is closed, the lift changes by $2\pi m$ for some $m\in\mathbb Z$;
different lifts differ by a constant multiple of $2\pi$, and homotopies keep
$m$ fixed. This integer $m$ is the **relative framing integer** of $[s_1]$
with respect to $[s_0]$. Thus, once a reference framing is supplied, the
framing classes are an integer torsor; no absolute integer is assigned before
choosing a reference.

The **self-linking number** of a framed knot $(K,[s])$ is the linking number
of $K$ with a sufficiently small push-off along $s$, oriented parallel to $K$.
The push-off and its integer are independent of the representative section,
small radius, and normalized tubular chart by the preceding well-definedness
result.

If a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$ is supplied with boundary $K$, its
**Seifert framing relative to $\Sigma$** is the homotopy class of the inward
unit conormal to $K$ in $\Sigma$, viewed as a nonzero normal section to $K$ in
$S^3$. This definition is relative to the supplied surface; it neither asserts
that every knot bounds such a surface nor asserts the self-linking-zero result.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be an
oriented smooth embedded circle and let $s$ be a smooth nowhere-zero section of
its normal bundle. For any tubular neighbourhood chart that is the inclusion
on the zero section and identifies each vertical normal fibre with the ambient
normal quotient by the identity, the curve $K_{\varepsilon s}$ obtained by
mapping the graph of $\varepsilon s$ into $S^3$ is an embedded oriented circle
disjoint from $K$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. The integer
linking number of $K$ with $K_{\varepsilon s}$ is independent of the sufficiently
small radius, of the representative section in its homotopy class, and of the
normalized tubular chart. It therefore defines a self-linking integer of the
framing class $[s]$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a knot $K$ with blackboard framing $b_D$. The self-linking number of the
framed knot $(K,b_D)$ equals the diagram writhe:
$$\operatorname{sl}(K,b_D)=\operatorname{wr}(D).$$
For a link component $K_i$, the corresponding self-linking number is its
self-writhe $\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$. Total writhe of a link still includes
the signs of mixed crossings, while the sum of component self-linking numbers
uses only self-crossings.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $K$ be an $n$-singular knot with an isolated chord corresponding to the double point $p$. Its two preimages split the parameter circle into arcs $A$ and $B$. Isolation means no other marked double point has one preimage on each of $A$ and $B$. Choose a regular projection. There are finitely many ordinary crossings between the arcs. Switch them one at a time until every crossing has the $A$-branch over the $B$-branch. Each switch changes $D_nV$ by, up to sign, the $(n+1)$-fold difference on the knot with that ordinary crossing newly marked; this is zero by [F1]. Thus these switches preserve $D_nV(K)$.

For the framed branch, let $V$ be integer-valued self-linking. On a regular framed diagram compare a unit representative of its framing section $f$ with the unit blackboard normal section $b$. Their oriented fibrewise angle defines a map $S^1\to S^1$; let $\tau(f,b)\in\mathbb Z$ be its degree. A full turn of $f$ relative to $b$ adds one local clasp to the push-off: the two mixed crossings in that clasp have the same sign, so [F7]–[F8] give a linking-number change of one. Thus [F4]–[F8] give $\operatorname{sl}(K,f)=\operatorname{wr}(D)+\tau(f,b)$. For a framed singular knot with two disjoint singularities, all changes outside their local balls are fixed. Inside each ball, resolving a double point changes only that crossing's writhe contribution and local angle path; resolving a framing zero changes only the local angle path. Winding degrees add under concatenation, so the four self-linking values have the form $C+c_1\epsilon_1+c_2\epsilon_2$ for constants independent of $(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)$. Their alternating second difference is $(C+c_1+c_2)-(C+c_1-c_2)-(C-c_1+c_2)+(C-c_1-c_2)=0$. This covers any pair of double-point or framing-zero singularities, so self-linking has type at most $1$. On a one-chord diagram with blackboard framing, the two crossing resolutions have writhes $+1$ and $-1$ and zero relative twist; their derivative is $1-(-1)=2$ by [F3] and [F6]. This is nonzero over $\mathbb Z$, so no universal framed 1T vanishing law is valid. The $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumption enters only through [F4]–[F8] and [A1].

The consistent over-under assignment lets the lifts of the interiors of $A$ and $B$ lie in opposite open half-spaces bounded by a plane through $p$. Cap each arc on its own side by a short boundary-parallel arc to obtain oriented singular knots $A^\circ$ and $B^\circ$ carrying the remaining marked double points. The two resolutions at $p$ are the connected sums $A^\circ\#B^\circ$ and $B^\circ\#A^\circ$. An orientation-preserving half-turn of the round $S^3$ that exchanges the two balls of the connected-sum decomposition carries the first knot, with its orientation, to the second; the path of rotations through angles from $0$ to $\pi$ is an ambient isotopy. Hence the two resolutions are ambient-isotopic, so their $V$-values agree and $D_nV(K)=0$.

derivations.claim: Let $C$ be half the signed sum of all mixed crossings except the marked one. Under [A1], [F4] identifies the diagram half-sum with the integer linking number and [F5] makes it an ambient-isotopy invariant. By [F2] and [F3], the positive and negative resolutions contribute respectively $+\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac12$ to this linking number, so $\operatorname{lk}(L_1,L_2)_+-\operatorname{lk}(L_1,L_2)_-=(C+\tfrac12)-(C-\tfrac12)=1$. This is the stated positive-minus-negative derivative under [F1]; reversing that subtraction changes its sign.
A knot has one component and therefore no unordered pair of distinct components; the total pairwise linking sum contains no terms and equals $0$.

If both marked crossings are mixed, write their resolution signs as $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\in\{+1,-1\}$ and absorb every other mixed crossing into $C$. By [F2]–[F4], $\operatorname{lk}(L_{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2})=C+\tfrac12(\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2)$. The alternating second difference is zero: the constant has coefficient $1-1-1+1=0$, and each term linear in one $\epsilon_i$ cancels when the other sign is summed. If either marked crossing is a self-crossing, the link formula [F3] is independent of that resolution, so the alternating sum over its two choices cancels term by term. Thus $D_2=0$ for every pair of marked crossings by [F1].

Use coordinates $(z,t)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ on oriented $\mathbb R^3$, with $t$ increasing upward. A knot is a smooth embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ with the orientation of $S^1$. A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Put $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{fr/un}}_{\mathbb C}:=\prod_{n\ge0}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr/un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$, with multiplication induced by connected sum of diagrams and unit the empty diagram. For $q$ ordered upward strands, let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ be the completion of the associative algebra generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$ for $1\le i<j\le q$, with relations $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ when $i,j,k,l$ are distinct and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ when $i,j,k$ are distinct. The generator $t_{ij}$ is a horizontal chord joining strands $i$ and $j$; multiplication stacks diagrams from bottom to top.

More generally, a compact strict Morse tangle $T$ is a compact oriented smooth one-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, with distinct boundary points on the planes $t=a$ and $t=b$, transverse to those planes, and with nondegenerate interior critical points of height having distinct critical values. A tangle chord diagram is a finite set of unordered pairs of distinct interior points on the oriented tangle skeleton. Its 4T relation is the same local alternating relation as above on the skeleton. The unframed tangle quotient also sets to zero any chord whose endpoints are consecutive in the order along the same skeleton component; for a circle the order is cyclic and for an arc it is linear. The completed degreewise tangle diagram space is denoted $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}(T)$.

The unframed configuration series of a strict Morse presentation $K$ is the formal degreewise series
$$
Z(K):=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{t_{\min}<t_m<\cdots<t_1<t_{\max}}\ \sum_{P}(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]_{\mathrm{un}}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\frac{dz_j-dz'_j}{z_j-z'_j}\ \in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}.
$$
The ordered simplex is divided into chambers by the critical values of $t|_K$. In each chamber, $P$ ranges over choices, at each level $t_j$, of an unordered pair of distinct points $(z_j,t_j),(z'_j,t_j)$ of $K$. The diagram $D_P$ joins the corresponding preimages on the oriented parameter circle. The integer $\downarrow(P)$ counts endpoints at which $t$ decreases along the orientation of $K$. The differential form is pulled back to the chamber by the selected local branches. The degree-zero term is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$; the displayed integrals are interpreted as improper integrals on each chamber.

For a compact strict Morse tangle $T$, $Z(T)$ is given by the same formula with $T$ in place of $K$, the interval $(a,b)$ in place of $(t_{\min},t_{\max})$, the chord diagrams on the tangle skeleton in place of circle diagrams, and the corresponding unframed tangle quotient in place of $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}$. A parenthesized braid is a special case with no interior critical points.

For a parenthesized braid path $\gamma$ in the configuration space of $q$ distinct complex points, define its Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (KZ) series by the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy of
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j).$$
Explicitly, if $\gamma:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ is an ordinary path with noncolliding endpoints, its holonomy is
$$1+\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{0<t_m<\cdots<t_1<1}\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_1)\cdots\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_m).$$
A tangential endpoint is a limiting collision configuration together with a specified nonzero first-order direction of approach for each colliding cluster. When endpoints have such clusters prescribed by the parenthesizations, the holonomy is the constant term after removing the local logarithmic factors $\exp(t_{ij}\log\varepsilon/(2\pi i))$ at each tangential endpoint. A change between the two parenthesizations of three consecutive strands is encoded by the regularized transport $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}$.

For parenthesized braids the KZ holonomy takes values in the framed strand algebra, where only tangled 4T is imposed; passing from a closed framed strand diagram to an unframed knot applies the quotient by isolated-chord 1T. Fix a standard hump $H$ by starting with the two-critical-point unknot and inserting one local birth of a maximum-minimum pair; thus $H$ has two local maxima. The normalized unframed Kontsevich series of $K$ is
$$
I(K):=Z(K)\,Z(H)^{-r(K)}\in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C},
$$
The normalization uses one copy of $Z(H)$ for each local maximum; its degree-zero term is $1$, so its inverse is interpreted in the product completion. This definition makes no assertion that the unnormalized KZ coefficients are rational or that equal Kontsevich series separate knot types.

Height increases upward, the right-bottom strand is the overstrand under the determinant crossing convention, and the labels at the ends record the ordered parenthesizations; no proof below relies on the drawing.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without
boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold, and let
$F\colon M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy such that $F_t:=F(\cdot,t)$ is an
embedding for every $t\in I$. Suppose $F$ is constant near the ends of $I$:
there is $\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ with $F(x,t)=F(x,0)$ for $t\le\varepsilon$
and $F(x,t)=F(x,1)$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon$ and all $x\in M$. Then for every
open neighbourhood $W$ of the image $F(M\times I)$ there is an ambient isotopy
$H\colon N\times I\to N$ such that

$$H_t\circ F_0=F_t\quad\text{for every }t\in I,$$

$H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, each $H_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $N$, and $H_t$ is the
identity outside $W$ for every $t$. Moreover $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\in[0,\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}]$ and
$H_t=H_1$ for $t\in[1-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},1]$.

derivations.claim: The set of embeddings of the compact circle into $\mathbb R^3$ is open in the $C^1$ topology. To verify this for the given compact family, cover $S^1$ by finitely many parameter intervals on which the derivative of each $K_s$ has a uniform positive lower bound; a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation remains an immersion there. On the compact complement of a neighborhood of the diagonal in $S^1\times S^1$, injectivity has a uniform positive separation because $(s,x,y)\mapsto\|K_s(x)-K_s(y)\|$ is continuous and positive. A sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbation preserves that separation. Thus a small perturbation of $h$ alone keeps every slice embedded and fixed at the two endpoint collars. The straight interpolation between $h$ and its perturbation is also $C^1$-small, hence stays embedded; [F6] extends this path to ambient isotopy.

For a smooth height family $h$ on $S^1\times[0,1]$, use finitely many coordinate intervals and smooth bump functions supported away from the endpoint collars to form a finite-dimensional perturbation family $h_a=h+\sum_j a_j\phi_j$. Cutoff multiples of $x$, $x^2/2$, $x^3/6$, and $(s-s_0)x$ prescribe, independently, $h_x,h_{xx},h_{xxx},h_{xs}$ at a point; finitely many smaller intervals cover the compact cylinder. The universal maps for $h_x$, $(h_x,h_{xx})$, $(h_x,h_{xx},h_{xxx})$, and $(h_x,h_{xx},h_{xs})$ are transverse to zero because the parameter derivatives span the corresponding target coordinates. By [F4], choose one arbitrarily small parameter for which all four slices are transverse. The zero set of $h_x$ is then a one-manifold; the zero set of $(h_x,h_{xx})$ is zero-dimensional; and the two three-coordinate maps have no zeros because their two-dimensional source has smaller dimension than their target. Thus every degeneracy has $h_x=h_{xx}=0$, $h_{xxx}\ne0$, and $h_{xs}\ne0$. The fold condition is open, so later perturbations can be chosen small enough to preserve it.

Remove small disjoint fold neighborhoods and endpoint collars from the parameter cylinder. On the remaining compact set, distinct critical points have a positive separation in the circle coordinate. Cover it by finitely many charts and add bump functions with disjoint small supports so that, at any two distinct critical points, the parameter derivatives independently span the two derivative values and the difference of the function values. For a pair $(x,y)$, the event map $(s,x,y)\mapsto(h_x(s,x),h_x(s,y),h(s,x)-h(s,y))$ is therefore transverse to zero for generic coefficients by [F4]. Its source and target both have dimension three, so its zeros are isolated. At a zero the derivative matrix has determinant $h_{xx}(s,x)h_{xx}(s,y)(h_s(s,x)-h_s(s,y))$. The first two factors are nonzero because the fold neighborhoods were removed; transversality makes the third nonzero. Thus the two critical values cross transversely. These zeros stay away from the removed diagonal neighborhoods by the fold model of step 2.1, so they form a compact zero-dimensional set and are finite.

Use further bump functions supported near mutually distinct critical points, so their value and derivative jets can be changed independently. For three distinct critical points, the event map with their three $x$-derivatives and two value differences has five scalar components on a four-dimensional parameter-and-point domain; [F4] makes its zero set empty. For two disjoint value crossings, four critical-point equations and two value differences give six components on a five-dimensional domain, so simultaneous crossings are absent. A birth/death coinciding in height with another critical point imposes $h_x=h_{xx}=0$ at the fold, $h_x=0$ at the other point, and equality of their values: four independent conditions on a three-dimensional domain, so this event is absent. A fold simultaneous with a value crossing at two other critical points imposes five independent conditions on a four-dimensional domain and is absent. Two folds at the same parameter impose four equations on a three-dimensional domain and are absent as well. The same finite-dimensional bump family can impose all these conditions simultaneously: the bad parameter set for each map is null by [F4], their finite union is null, and every coefficient ball contains a point outside that union.

Outside the finite fold and crossing parameters, every critical point is nondegenerate and the critical values are pairwise distinct, so each height slice is strict Morse. Steps 2.1–4.1 show that the only exceptional events are isolated max-min births or deaths and transverse crossings of two distinct critical values; the imposed three-point, four-point, and fold-pair conditions exclude simultaneous events and triple values. The total perturbation can be chosen arbitrarily small, so step 1.1 keeps every slice embedded and in the same oriented knot class. The perturbation vanishes near $s=0,1$, hence leaves the specified endpoint presentations fixed.

Use coordinates $(z,t)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ on oriented $\mathbb R^3$, with $t$ increasing upward. A knot is a smooth embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ with the orientation of $S^1$. A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Put $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{fr/un}}_{\mathbb C}:=\prod_{n\ge0}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr/un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$, with multiplication induced by connected sum of diagrams and unit the empty diagram. For $q$ ordered upward strands, let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ be the completion of the associative algebra generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$ for $1\le i<j\le q$, with relations $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ when $i,j,k,l$ are distinct and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ when $i,j,k$ are distinct. The generator $t_{ij}$ is a horizontal chord joining strands $i$ and $j$; multiplication stacks diagrams from bottom to top.

More generally, a compact strict Morse tangle $T$ is a compact oriented smooth one-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, with distinct boundary points on the planes $t=a$ and $t=b$, transverse to those planes, and with nondegenerate interior critical points of height having distinct critical values. A tangle chord diagram is a finite set of unordered pairs of distinct interior points on the oriented tangle skeleton. Its 4T relation is the same local alternating relation as above on the skeleton. The unframed tangle quotient also sets to zero any chord whose endpoints are consecutive in the order along the same skeleton component; for a circle the order is cyclic and for an arc it is linear. The completed degreewise tangle diagram space is denoted $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}(T)$.

The unframed configuration series of a strict Morse presentation $K$ is the formal degreewise series
$$
Z(K):=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{t_{\min}<t_m<\cdots<t_1<t_{\max}}\ \sum_{P}(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]_{\mathrm{un}}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\frac{dz_j-dz'_j}{z_j-z'_j}\ \in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}.
$$
The ordered simplex is divided into chambers by the critical values of $t|_K$. In each chamber, $P$ ranges over choices, at each level $t_j$, of an unordered pair of distinct points $(z_j,t_j),(z'_j,t_j)$ of $K$. The diagram $D_P$ joins the corresponding preimages on the oriented parameter circle. The integer $\downarrow(P)$ counts endpoints at which $t$ decreases along the orientation of $K$. The differential form is pulled back to the chamber by the selected local branches. The degree-zero term is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$; the displayed integrals are interpreted as improper integrals on each chamber.

For a compact strict Morse tangle $T$, $Z(T)$ is given by the same formula with $T$ in place of $K$, the interval $(a,b)$ in place of $(t_{\min},t_{\max})$, the chord diagrams on the tangle skeleton in place of circle diagrams, and the corresponding unframed tangle quotient in place of $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}$. A parenthesized braid is a special case with no interior critical points.

For a parenthesized braid path $\gamma$ in the configuration space of $q$ distinct complex points, define its Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (KZ) series by the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy of
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j).$$
Explicitly, if $\gamma:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ is an ordinary path with noncolliding endpoints, its holonomy is
$$1+\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{0<t_m<\cdots<t_1<1}\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_1)\cdots\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_m).$$
A tangential endpoint is a limiting collision configuration together with a specified nonzero first-order direction of approach for each colliding cluster. When endpoints have such clusters prescribed by the parenthesizations, the holonomy is the constant term after removing the local logarithmic factors $\exp(t_{ij}\log\varepsilon/(2\pi i))$ at each tangential endpoint. A change between the two parenthesizations of three consecutive strands is encoded by the regularized transport $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}$.

For parenthesized braids the KZ holonomy takes values in the framed strand algebra, where only tangled 4T is imposed; passing from a closed framed strand diagram to an unframed knot applies the quotient by isolated-chord 1T. Fix a standard hump $H$ by starting with the two-critical-point unknot and inserting one local birth of a maximum-minimum pair; thus $H$ has two local maxima. The normalized unframed Kontsevich series of $K$ is
$$
I(K):=Z(K)\,Z(H)^{-r(K)}\in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C},
$$
The normalization uses one copy of $Z(H)$ for each local maximum; its degree-zero term is $1$, so its inverse is interpreted in the product completion. This definition makes no assertion that the unnormalized KZ coefficients are rational or that equal Kontsevich series separate knot types.

The following figure illustrates the positive Artin generator $\sigma_1$ and parenthesization conventions. Height increases upward, the right-bottom strand is the overstrand under the determinant crossing convention, and the labels at the ends record the ordered parenthesizations; no proof below relies on the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.82,thick]

  \draw[very thick] (1,0) -- (0.5,1.5) -- (0,3);
  \draw (0,0) -- (0.48,1.44);

  \node at (1.2,2.55) {$\sigma_1$};

\end{tikzpicture}
```

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: Choose pairwise disjoint balls around the $n$ singular points so each resolved pair of branches is monotone in height inside its ball. The same height function is used on every resolution, so $r(K_\epsilon)=r$ for all $\epsilon$. If necessary, move the singular knot by an isotopy supported in the balls to separate the singular heights and make the crossings monotone; each corresponding resolution is carried by the same ambient isotopy, so [F6] leaves $\Delta^n I(K)$ unchanged.

Expand the degree-$m$ part of $\Delta^n I(K)$ as a finite sum of pairing integrals over the resolution choices. If a pairing has no chord endpoint in the $i$th crossing ball, its integrand and diagram are independent of the sign $\epsilon_i$, because the two resolved knots agree outside that ball. Summing over $\epsilon_i=+1,-1$ therefore cancels that term. Hence every nonzero contribution to the $n$-fold difference must meet each of the $n$ balls.

A chord joining endpoints in two different crossing balls, or one crossing ball and the complement, has denominator bounded away from zero: the balls are disjoint, and the singular immersion has no other intersections. Its endpoint-level interval in the shrinking local ball is $O(\varepsilon)$, so the mean-value bound for $d\log(z-z')$ makes its integral $O(\varepsilon)$. The other factors remain absolutely integrable by [F5], and there are finitely many degree-$m$ pairing types. Since the alternating resolution sum is unchanged when each crossing ball is shrunk by [F6], every term containing such a chord has zero limiting contribution and therefore vanishes in the finite difference. If $m<n$, a surviving pairing must touch all $n$ balls with only $m$ chords, so at least one chord joins distinct regions; its contribution vanishes by this estimate. Thus every homogeneous component of degree $m<n$ is zero.

For one singular point, let $w_\pm(t)=z_{1,\pm}(t)-z_{2,\pm}(t)$ be the relative complex coordinate of its two monotone branches in the positive and negative resolutions. The loop obtained by following $w_+$ and then the reverse of $w_-$ winds once positively around $0$: the two resolutions are the opposite half-turns of the relative vector. Hence $\frac1{2\pi i}\left(\int d\log w_+-\int d\log w_-\right)=1$. For two upward branches this is the difference of angular changes $+\pi-(-\pi)=2\pi$. The $n$ local level variables range independently over their crossing slabs. The global ordered simplex partitions into the finitely many possible orders of these variables; on each part the coordinate-permutation sign is canceled by the same wedge-permutation sign, so summing the regions is the product integral by Fubini. For $n=0$, the alternating sum is $I(K)$ and its degree-zero coefficient is $1$ by [F2]. Thus $\Delta^n I(K)=D+\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{>n}$ in every case.

The knot has no framing. Choose disjoint small balls around its double points, each containing no other part of the singular knot. At each double point there are two **resolutions**, obtained by separating the two local branches in the ball; label them $+$ and $-$ so the resolved crossing signs are respectively $+1$ and $-1$ under the convention that, in a diagram whose positive viewing normal agrees with the ambient orientation, the sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\mathrm{over}},v_{\mathrm{under}})$ and the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$.

A **framed oriented knot** is a smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ together with a homotopy class through nowhere-zero smooth sections of its oriented rank-two normal bundle. Because $dK$ has rank one at every parameter, its image is locally a smooth line subbundle and this quotient is locally a rank-two bundle. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the framed clauses below, so these normal quotient bundles have their smooth vector-bundle structures. A **framed $m$-singular knot** has finitely many transverse double points and finitely many simple zeroes of a smooth section of $\nu_K$, all disjoint; its number $m$ of singularities is the number of double points plus the number of zeroes. A simple zero is one at which the derivative of the section in an oriented local trivialization is nonzero. Resolve double points as above, extending the normal section over the local resolution balls; each resulting section determines a framing homotopy class. To resolve a framing zero at parameter $t=0$, choose the oriented normal trivialization so the section is $t e_1$ near $0$, with $e_2$ the positive quarter-turn of $e_1$; replace it by $t e_1+\delta e_2$ or $t e_1-\delta e_2$ for sufficiently small $\delta>0$. These are the $+$ and $-$ resolutions of that zero and determine the framing classes on the resolved knots.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For an $R$-valued ambient-isotopy invariant $V$ of unframed oriented knots and an $m$-singular knot $K$, its **finite difference** is
$$
D_mV(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^m}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\epsilon_i\right)V(K_\epsilon),
$$
where $K_\epsilon$ resolves singularity $i$ positively when $\epsilon_i=+1$ and negatively when $\epsilon_i=-1$. For $m=0$, set $D_0V(K)=V(K)$. The same formula defines $D_mV$ for an invariant of framed knots on framed singular knots, counting both double points and framing zeroes among the $m$ singularities. For one double point it reads $V(K_+)-V(K_-)$; the zero resolutions use the local normal-section model just specified. An invariant has **type at most $n$** if $D_{n+1}V$ vanishes on every $(n+1)$-singular object in its category. It has **exact type $n$** if it has type at most $n$ but not type at most $n-1$. For an unframed link, replace $S^1$ by a finite disjoint union of oriented circles, allow marked self- or mixed double points, and use the same resolution sum. A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Fix the round metric and orientation on $S^3$. An **$m$-singular oriented knot** is a smooth immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$ with exactly $m$ distinct transverse double points and no other self-intersections; each double-point image has exactly two preimages with linearly independent tangent vectors, and the preimage pairs are disjoint. At each double point there are two **resolutions**, obtained by separating the two local branches in the ball; label them $+$ and $-$ so the resolved crossing signs are respectively $+1$ and $-1$ under the convention that, in a diagram whose positive viewing normal agrees with the ambient orientation, the sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\mathrm{over}},v_{\mathrm{under}})$ and the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$.

A **framed oriented knot** is a smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ together with a homotopy class through nowhere-zero smooth sections of its oriented rank-two normal bundle. For an immersion $K:S^1\to S^3$, including one with double points, define its branchwise normal bundle over the parameter circle by $\nu_K:=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$, oriented so that a positive tangent followed by a positive normal basis gives the ambient orientation.
