The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X A$, inclusion induces an isomorphism
$$H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z;G)$$
for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

Assume AC.  Every $R$-oriented rank-$n$ numerable vector bundle over a CW
complex, or over a paracompact Hausdorff base of CW type, has a unique
normalized Thom class $u_\xi$, and
$$a\longmapsto\pi^*a\smile u_\xi:H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$
for every $k$.  Without a supplied orientation, the canonical twisted form is
$$H^k(B;\mathcal O_R(\xi))\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R).$$
The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ be closed oriented embedded submanifolds with $a+b=n$. Using the oriented intersection number of [[def-oriented-intersection-number]] (whose source is the compact submanifold and whose target is the closed submanifold, first factor first), set $$\langle A,B\rangle_M:=I(A,B)=I(i_A,B)\in\mathbb Z,$$ where $i_A:A\hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion and $I(i_A,B)$ is evaluated on any smooth map homotopic to $i_A$ and transverse to $B$; when $A$ and $B$ are transverse this is the finite signed count $\sum_{p\in A\cap B}\varepsilon(p)$ of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]. For non-transverse $A,B$ the value is the common value on all such transverse representatives, by [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]]. With $\mathbb F_2$ coefficients the same construction with the mod 2 intersection number [[def-mod-two-intersection-number]] defines $\langle A,B\rangle_{2}\in\mathbb F_2$ without orientability of $A,B$ or $M$; there [[thm-mod-two-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]] supplies the same independence. The number depends only on the homotopy classes of the two inclusions, so replacing a factor by a homotopic submanifold, or by a homotopic embedding of the same manifold, leaves it unchanged. The factor order is part of the definition: [[thm-intersection-number-under-factor-interchange]] gives $\langle B,A\rangle=(-1)^{ab}\langle A,B\rangle$ and $\langle B,A\rangle_2=\langle A,B\rangle_2$. No claim is made yet that the number depends only on the homology classes of $A$ and $B$ (homology invariance is proved in [[thm-geometric-intersection-equals-the-poincare-dual-cup-pairing]]; [[lem-geometric-intersection-descends-through-oriented-cobordism-of-cycles]] separately proves bordism invariance), nor that every homology class has an embedded representative (see [[rem-not-every-homology-class-is-represented-by-an-embedded-submanifold-integrally]]). statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The map $[s:t]\mapsto[s^2:st:t^2]$ is an embedding: on $s\ne0$ its affine coordinates are $(1,u,u^2)$ with $u=t/s$, and on $t\ne0$ they are $(v^2,v,1)$ with $v=s/t$, so each chart recovers the source coordinate and has nonzero derivative. Its image is the smooth zero set $xz-y^2=0$, hence is a complex-oriented sphere. A generic projective line, for example $x+z=0$, meets it at the two simple roots of $s^2+t^2=0$, both positively. Two distinct projective lines meet once positively and represent the generator $h$ from [F1], so the intersection pairing gives $[Q]=2[\mathbb{CP}^1]$ and $[Q]\cdot[Q]=4$.

The normal Euler number of $Q$ is therefore $4$ by [F3]. The boundary of its oriented normal disk bundle is the oriented circle bundle with Euler number $4$. The disk bundle is the $+4$-framed 2-handlebody on the unknot, so its boundary is $L(4,1)$ under [F4]. Reversing the orientation of the complement reverses the boundary orientation if needed to match the convention in the Statement.

By [F2], the relative cohomology groups of $(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)$ are $\mathbb Z$ in degrees $2$ and $4$ and zero otherwise, since $Q\cong S^2$. The map $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)\to H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2)$ sends the Thom generator to the Poincare dual of $Q$, which is $2h$ by step 1.1 and [F1]; hence it is multiplication by $2$. The map $H^4(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)\to H^4(\mathbb{CP}^2)$ is an isomorphism: under the Thom identification it sends the positive generator of $H^2(Q)$ to its push-forward, whose evaluation on $[\mathbb{CP}^2]$ is its evaluation on $[Q]$, namely $1$.

The cohomology long exact sequence of the pair gives $H^1(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$, $H^2(B_2;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/2$, and $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $j\ge3$: in degree one the map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ is injective multiplication by $2$, in degree two its cokernel is $\mathbb Z/2$ and the next relative group is zero, and in degree four the relative-to-absolute map is an isomorphism. In degree zero, the relative group vanishes, so $H^0(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)\to H^0(B_2;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism; hence $B_2$ is connected. Repeat the relative calculation over $\mathbb Q$: the degree-two map is multiplication by $2$ and the degree-four map is the identity, both isomorphisms, so the pair sequence gives $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $j>0$ and $H^0(B_2;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. The UCT over $\mathbb Q$ then gives the rational homology of a point. Together with step 2.1 this proves that $B_2$ is a rational homology ball bounded by $L(4,1)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X A$, inclusion induces an isomorphism
$$H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z;G)$$
for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

Assume AC.  Every $R$-oriented rank-$n$ numerable vector bundle over a CW
complex, or over a paracompact Hausdorff base of CW type, has a unique
normalized Thom class $u_\xi$, and
$$a\longmapsto\pi^*a\smile u_\xi:H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$
for every $k$.  Without a supplied orientation, the canonical twisted form is
$$H^k(B;\mathcal O_R(\xi))\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R).$$
The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

Let $\xi\to B$ be an $R$-oriented metric rank-$n$ bundle with orientation
section $o=(o_b)$.  For the inclusion of pairs
$$i_b:(D(\xi_b),S(\xi_b))\longrightarrow(D(\xi),S(\xi)),$$
a **Thom class normalized by $o$** is a class
$$u_\xi\in H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$
such that $i_b^*u_\xi=o_b$ for every $b\in B$.

Relative singular cochains make every restriction $i_b^*$ well typed.  This
is a normalization condition only: the definition asserts neither existence
nor uniqueness, which are proved later.  For $B=\varnothing$ the condition is
vacuous and the unique class in the zero relative group is normalized.  In
rank zero, $D(\xi)=B$, $S(\xi)=\varnothing$, and normalization says that the
degree-zero class restricts to the chosen unit on every point.  The zero ring,
one-point bases, identity inclusions, and empty sphere fibers cause no
exception.  No representative or family of classes is selected, so the
definition is choice-free.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed $R$-oriented smooth $n$-manifold, where $R=\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2$, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed $R$-oriented embedded $z$-submanifold. Put $r=n-z$ and orient $
u_Z=TM|_Z/TZ$ in tangent-first order: $\det TM|_Z=\det TZ\otimes\det
u_Z$. Choose a smooth metric and a tubular chart whose differential induces the identity on this normal quotient; restrict to a sufficiently small closed disk bundle. Such normalized charts exist by the construction in [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]].

The normalized Thom class $u_
u\in H^r(D(
u),S(
u);R)$ corresponds to a class $\alpha\in H^r(M,M\setminus Z;R)$ by the punctured-fibre comparison and tubular excision. Write $ ar\alpha\in H^r(M;R)$ for its relative-to-absolute image. Then
$$ ar\alpha\cap[M]=(-1)^{rz}(i_Z)_*[Z]\in H_z(M;R).$$
Equivalently, $ ar\alpha=(-1)^{rz}D_M^{-1}((i_Z)_*[Z])$. The sign is the shuffle from tangent-first coordinates to normal-first cap evaluation. Over $\mathbb F_2$ all orientations are canonical and the sign disappears. A relative class capped directly with the absolute $[M]$ instead has relative homology as target; the displayed formula uses $ ar\alpha$.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ be closed oriented embedded submanifolds with $a+b=n$. Write $[A]=(i_A)_*[A]_A$, $[B]=(i_B)_*[B]_B$, and $\mathrm{PD}[A]=D_M^{-1}([A])$, $\mathrm{PD}[B]=D_M^{-1}([B])$. In the cohomology-first, front-evaluation cap and cup conventions,
$$I(A,B)=\langle\mathrm{PD}[A]\smile\mathrm{PD}[B],[M]\rangle.$$
For nontransverse submanifolds $I(A,B)$ is computed by a transverse map homotopic to $i_A$; no embedded representative for that map is required. Over $\mathbb F_2$ the same formula holds without orientability. Consequently this geometric number depends only on the represented homology classes, with the factor order of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]].

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $f:X^x\to M$ and $g:Z^z\to M$ be smooth maps from oriented smooth manifolds, with $x+z=n$ and $f,g$ transverse in the sense of [[def-transverse-smooth-maps]]. Let $a\in X$, $b\in Z$ satisfy $f(a)=g(b)=y$. Then $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ and $T_yM$ have the same dimension, and transversality says that

$$(df_a,dg_b):T_aX\oplus T_bZ\longrightarrow T_yM,\qquad (v,w)\mapsto df_a(v)+dg_b(w),$$

is surjective, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-transverse-linear-subspaces]]); the sum is direct because the dimensions add up. The ordered direct sum $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ carries the product orientation with the first factor $T_aX$ and the second factor $T_bZ$ ([[def-product-orientation]]), and the three tangent spaces carry their manifold orientations ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

The **local oriented intersection sign** $\varepsilon(a,b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is $+1$ when this isomorphism carries the product orientation of $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ to the orientation of $T_yM$, and $-1$ otherwise; equivalently it is the orientation sign of the induced isomorphism of determinant lines ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

For transverse oriented embedded submanifolds $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ with $a+b=n$ one takes $f$ and $g$ to be the inclusion maps ([[def-transverse-embedded-submanifolds]]); the sign at $p\in A\cap B$ then compares $T_pA\oplus T_pB\to T_pM$ with $A$ first. The empty intersection is allowed and carries no signs. In dimension zero the sign compares the two orientation rays directly, and for $x=z=n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_X(a)\varepsilon_Z(b)\varepsilon_M(y)$, the product of the two source point signs and the ambient point sign. The factor order is part of the definition: with the two factors exchanged the signs are multiplied by $(-1)^{ab}$, exactly the graded-commutativity sign measured later on this page by the factor-interchange theorem. No compactness, closedness hypothesis or choice axiom is used in this local definition.

Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ be closed oriented embedded submanifolds with $a+b=n$. Using the oriented intersection number of [[def-oriented-intersection-number]] (whose source is the compact submanifold and whose target is the closed submanifold, first factor first), set $$\langle A,B\rangle_M:=I(A,B)=I(i_A,B)\in\mathbb Z,$$ where $i_A:A\hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion and $I(i_A,B)$ is evaluated on any smooth map homotopic to $i_A$ and transverse to $B$; when $A$ and $B$ are transverse this is the finite signed count $\sum_{p\in A\cap B}\varepsilon(p)$ of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]. For non-transverse $A,B$ the value is the common value on all such transverse representatives, by [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]]. With $\mathbb F_2$ coefficients the same construction with the mod 2 intersection number [[def-mod-two-intersection-number]] defines $\langle A,B\rangle_{2}\in\mathbb F_2$ without orientability of $A,B$ or $M$; there [[thm-mod-two-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]] supplies the same independence. The number depends only on the homotopy classes of the two inclusions, so replacing a factor by a homotopic submanifold, or by a homotopic embedding of the same manifold, leaves it unchanged. The factor order is part of the definition: [[thm-intersection-number-under-factor-interchange]] gives $\langle B,A\rangle=(-1)^{ab}\langle A,B\rangle$ and $\langle B,A\rangle_2=\langle A,B\rangle_2$. No claim is made yet that the number depends only on the homology classes of $A$ and $B$ (homology invariance is proved in [[thm-geometric-intersection-equals-the-poincare-dual-cup-pairing]]; [[lem-geometric-intersection-descends-through-oriented-cobordism-of-cycles]] separately proves bordism invariance), nor that every homology class has an embedded representative (see [[rem-not-every-homology-class-is-represented-by-an-embedded-submanifold-integrally]]). Countable Choice is inherited from the transverse-representative selection in [[def-countable-choice]]; the finite signed counts themselves are choice-free.

Let $X$ be a compact oriented smooth $x$-manifold without boundary, let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed oriented embedded $z$-submanifold with $x+z=n$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). For a smooth $f:X\to M$ transverse to $Z$, the **oriented intersection number** is the finite sum

$$I(f,Z):=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(Z)}\varepsilon(p)\in\mathbb Z,$$

with the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]; the sum is finite by [[lem-compact-transverse-complementary-intersections-are-finite]]. For an arbitrary smooth $g:X\to M$, choose a transverse $f$ homotopic to $g$ ([[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], under Countable Choice; the homotopy is a smooth family in the sense of [[def-smooth-family-of-maps-and-evaluation-map]]) and set $I(g,Z):=I(f,Z)$; independence of the choice is [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], not assumed here. For compact oriented complementary-dimensional submanifolds $A,B\subseteq M$, where one is compact and the other closed, one sets $I(A,B):=I(i_A,B)$ with $i_A$ the inclusion, so the first factor is the submanifold $A$. If the source is not compact, or the target submanifold is not closed, the sum may fail to be finite or invariant; the safe extension by properness with compact trace is recorded in the remark on properness later on this page. Countable Choice is assumed for selecting transverse representatives and for the classification used to prove independence of that selection; the signs, the finite sum and the empty case (which contributes $0$) are choice-free.

For transverse maps $f:X^x\to M$, $g:Z^z\to M$ with compact oriented boundaryless sources and $x+z=\dim M$, define $I(f,g)$ as the sum of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]] over $X\times_MZ$. This set is closed in the compact product because $M$ is Hausdorff, and discrete by [[def-transverse-complementary-dimensional-intersection-set]], so the sum is finite. If $g$ is an inclusion this recovers $I(f,Z)$. Ambient compactness is unnecessary in either construction.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold and let $A^a\subseteq M$ be a compact boundaryless oriented embedded submanifold with $2a=n$. Orient $\nu_A=TM|_A/TA$ by the tangent-first rule. Choose a smooth bundle metric and a tubular chart $\varphi$ whose normal differential along the zero section is the identity, as constructed in [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]]. Compactness of $A$ permits a uniform small disk bundle inside the tube. For any small smooth section $s$ transverse to the zero section, let $A_s=\varphi(s(A))$, oriented by the parametrization $\varphi\circ s:A\to A_s$. The **self-intersection number** is
$$A\cdot A:=I(A,A_s),$$
with $A$ first and $A_s$ second.

Every section is an embedding into its total space: projection is a left inverse, its differential is injective, and projection restricted to its graph is its continuous inverse. Composing with the tube therefore gives an embedding. The homotopy $\varphi(ts)$ consists of embeddings and joins the inclusion to the push-off. Compactness makes $A_s$ closed and the transverse count finite. Small transverse sections exist: extend local frame vectors to compactly supported sections by [[lem-every-vector-in-a-fibre-extends-to-a-compactly-supported-smooth-section]], take finitely many which span every fibre by compactness, and apply [[thm-parametric-transversality]] to their parameter-linear sum. The full evaluation is transverse because the parameter directions span every fibre. A good parameter can be chosen arbitrarily small, including the rank-zero case where every section is already transverse.

The same definition using [[def-mod-two-intersection-number]] gives $A\cdot_2A$ for any boundaryless ambient $M$ and any compact boundaryless embedded $A$ with $2a=n$, using no orientations. The numerical value is independent of the tube and small section: each push-off map is homotopic to the inclusion, and the two-map diagonal construction underlying [[thm-intersection-number-under-factor-interchange]] and [[thm-mod-two-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]] makes the ordered count invariant under that homotopy. This argument requires no assertion that the tube-germ comparison is an isotopy. Under AC the integral Euler evaluation is proved in [[thm-self-intersection-is-the-euler-number-of-the-normal-bundle]]. The local signs and finite counts themselves require no choice.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an oriented boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold, $A^a\subseteq M$ a compact boundaryless oriented embedded submanifold with $2a=n$, and let $
u_A=TM|_A/TA$ carry the orientation induced by $M$ and $A$ ([[prop-a-transverse-oriented-normal-bundle-orients-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Then the self-intersection number of [[def-self-intersection-number-of-an-oriented-submanifold]] is well defined and $$A\cdot A=\langle e(
u_A),[A]angle\in\mathbb Z,$$ where $e(
u_A)\in H^{a}(A;\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of [[def-euler-class-by-zero-section-pullback-of-the-thom-class]] and $[A]\in H_a(A;\mathbb Z)$ is the fundamental class. In particular the self-intersection number is independent of the tubular embedding and of the transverse push-off, and it is an invariant of the pair $(A,
u_A)$. For a rank-$r$ oriented bundle $E	o M$ with $M$ closed oriented of dimension $n=r$ and a transverse section $s$, the signed zero count equals $\langle e(E),[M]angle$; this is the form in which the theorem is applied below.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An oriented lens space is an oriented closed $3$-manifold obtained by gluing two solid tori by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism. For coprime integers $p>0$ and $q$, let $L(p,q)$ denote the oriented union of the exterior of the unknot in the oriented $3$-sphere and a solid torus whose meridian is identified with the slope $p[\mu_U]+q[\lambda_U]$ on the unknot exterior. Thus this library uses the convention $L(p,q)=E_U(p/q)$; no symbol $L(0,q)$ is assigned.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $J=J_1\cup\cdots\cup J_n$ be an oriented link of $n\ge1$ smooth components in $S^3$. Choose pairwise disjoint closed tubular neighborhoods $N(J_i)$, let $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_iN(J_i))$, and let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian of $J_i$. Let $\lambda_i$ be the longitude parallel to $J_i$ with zero self-linking. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^n$ on the meridian basis $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$; for $i\ne j$, define $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ to be the $j$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$, the usual oriented linking number. Use the boundary-torus intersection convention $\mu_i\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda_i=+1$. Give $J_i$ an integer framing $f_i$ and fill along $\delta_i=\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i$. Let $A$ be the symmetric integer matrix with $A_{ii}=f_i$ and $A_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ for $i\ne j$. Assume $\det A\ne0$, and let $Y$ be the resulting oriented surgery manifold, oriented as the boundary of the 4-dimensional surgery handlebody with outward normal first. Then $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. For torsion classes $[C],[D]\in H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ represented by oriented 1-cycles, choose $m>0$ and an integral 2-chain $F$ with $\partial F=mC$ and define $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\mathbin{\cdot}D)/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}$, where the intersection is signed by the orientation of $Y$. If $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ are meridian-coordinate representatives of $[C],[D]$, then
$$
\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}.
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For every subspace $A\subseteq X$ and abelian group $G$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{j}H^n(X;G)\xrightarrow{r}H^n(A;G)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{n+1}(X,A;G)\to\cdots.$$
Here $j$ comes from including the relative cochains, $r$ is restriction, and the connector sends a cocycle class $[a]$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, for any cochain extension $\widetilde a$ of $a$ to $X$. Negative groups are zero, so the sequence begins $0\to H^0(X,A;G)\to H^0(X;G)\to H^0(A;G)$.

Choose the filtration $\mathbb{CP}^0\subset P\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ with $P=\{y=0\}\cong\mathbb{CP}^1$ and $\mathbb{CP}^0=[1:0:0]$. Its successive complements are $\mathbb C$ and $\mathbb C^2$, so the cellular boundary maps vanish for degree reasons and $H_2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[P]$, $H_4(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mathbb{CP}^2]$; UCT gives free cohomology, and put $h=\mathrm{PD}[P]$. The projective maps $T_t([x:y:z])=[x:y+tx:z]$ ($0\le t\le1$) give a homotopy from the inclusion of $P$ to that of $P'=\{y=x\}$. The two lines meet transversely at $[0:0:1]$ with positive sign, since a complex-linear isomorphism between their tangent complex lines and the ambient complex plane has positive real determinant. By [F3], $[P]^2=1$. On the charts $s
e0$ and $t
e0$, the conic map $[s:t]\mapsto[s^2:st:t^2]$ has target coordinates $(u,u^2)$ with $u=t/s$ and $(v^2,v)$ with $v=s/t$, respectively; these recover the source coordinate and have injective derivatives. Its image is exactly $xz-y^2=0$: if $x
e0$ the point is $[1:y/x:(y/x)^2]$, and if $x=0$ then $y=0$ and the point is $[0:0:1]$. The same chart descriptions show the zero set is a smooth complex-oriented sphere and the map is an embedding. The line $P$ meets it at the two simple roots $st=0$, both transversely and positively in the complex orientations. Thus [F3] gives $[Q]\cdot[P]=2$; because $[P]$ generates $H_2$, this implies $[Q]=2[P]$, hence $[Q]\cdot[Q]=4$.

The normal Euler number of $Q$ is therefore $4$ by [F4]. Its unit normal circle bundle is the boundary of its tubular disk bundle. Compute its genus-one gluing directly from the conic charts, without assuming an Euler-to-surgery identification. In the chart $x=1$ write the surface as $(y,z)=(u,u^2)$ and use normal coordinate $n=z-y^2$. In the chart $z=1$ use normal coordinate $n'=x-y^2$. Their change is $n'=(z-y^2)/z^2$; differentiating in the normal direction on the conic gives $n'=u^{-4}n$ in the normal line bundle. On the equator $u=e^{i\varphi}$ its unit normal circle transition is therefore $\theta_N=\theta_S-4\varphi$. Each closed hemisphere has its actual displayed complex normal frame, so its unit circle bundle is $D^2\times S^1$, a solid torus. On their common torus let $m$ be the equator loop at fixed $\theta_S$, and $l$ the fiber loop. The southern solid-torus meridian is $m$, and the northern meridian is $m+4l$, since holding $\theta_N$ fixed gives that exact slope. Identify the southern solid torus with the standard unknot exterior by $l=\mu_U$, $m=\lambda_U$: its fiber is the core circle, while its base disk is the exterior meridian disk. The second filling slope is therefore $4\mu_U+\lambda_U$, with the global boundary orientation determined by the product identifications. If those identifications reverse the desired global orientation, reverse the orientation of the total space; the statement permits exactly that choice. Thus [F5] identifies the total circle bundle with $L(4,1)$ up to orientation, by an actual meridian calculation. The complement has the opposite boundary orientation to its tubular neighborhood in the complex-oriented projective plane; choose the orientation of $B_2$ as allowed in the Statement so its boundary agrees with the declared lens-space convention.

By [F2], the relative cohomology groups of $(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)$ are $\mathbb Z$ in degrees $2$ and $4$ and zero otherwise, since $Q\cong S^2$. The relative-to-absolute map in degree two sends the Thom generator to $\mathrm{PD}[Q]$: the normal-Thom sign is $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$ by [F2]. By step 1.1, $[Q]=2[P]$, so this map is multiplication by $2$ under $h=\mathrm{PD}[P]$. For degree four, let $a$ be the positive generator of $H^2(Q;\mathbb Z)$, with $\langle a,[Q]\rangle=1$. The Thom image of $a$ evaluates on $[\mathbb{CP}^2]$ as $\langle a,[Q]\rangle$: excision reduces the evaluation to the normal disk fibers, and the normalized Thom class evaluates $+1$ on each such fiber by [F2]. Thus the degree-four relative-to-absolute map sends a generator to a generator and is an isomorphism.

By [F6], the cohomology long exact sequence of the pair gives $H^1(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$, $H^2(B_2;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/2$, and $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $j\ge3$: in degree one the map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ is injective multiplication by $2$, in degree two its cokernel is $\mathbb Z/2$ and the next relative group is zero, and in degree four the relative-to-absolute map is an isomorphism. In degree zero, the relative group vanishes, so $H^0(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)\to H^0(B_2;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism; hence $B_2$ is connected. Repeat the relative calculation over $\mathbb Q$: the degree-two map is multiplication by $2$ and the degree-four map is the identity, both isomorphisms, so the pair sequence gives $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $j>0$ and $H^0(B_2;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. The UCT over $\mathbb Q$ then gives the rational homology of a point. Together with step 2.1 this proves that $B_2$ is a rational homology ball bounded by $L(4,1)$.

citations.quote: Let $B$ be a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and oriented boundary the rational homology sphere $Y$, where $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. Let $\mathfrak t$ be a boundary Spin$^c$ structure extending over $B$. Removing an open four-ball from the interior gives a Spin$^c$ cobordism $W$ with boundary $-S^3\sqcup Y$, and each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism on rational homology. In both orientations, the induced Heegaard Floer infinity map is an isomorphism of degree zero and the corresponding plus-map inequality gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge0$ and $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le0$.

The reversed punctured cobordism gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le0$ by [F1]. A rational number satisfying both inequalities is zero, so $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. The argument applies only to the Spin$^c$ structure that extends.

Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and connected rational homology sphere boundary $Y$. If a boundary Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$ extends over $B$, then its Heegaard Floer correction term vanishes: $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $Q\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ be the nonsingular complex conic parametrized by $[s:t]\mapsto[s^2:st:t^2]$, let $N(Q)$ be a closed tubular disk bundle, and let $B_2=\overline{\mathbb{CP}^2\setminus\operatorname{int}N(Q)}$. Then $B_2$ is a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B_2;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$. Its boundary is the circle bundle of Euler number $4$ over $S^2$, hence is the lens space $L(4,1)$ up to orientation; orient $B_2$ so that the boundary agrees with the stated lens-space convention.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $J=J_1\cup\cdots\cup J_n$ be an oriented link of $n\ge1$ smooth components in $S^3$. Choose pairwise disjoint closed tubular neighborhoods $N(J_i)$, let $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_iN(J_i))$, and let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian of $J_i$. Let $\lambda_i$ be the longitude parallel to $J_i$ with zero self-linking. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^n$ on the meridian basis $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$; for $i\ne j$, define $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ to be the $j$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$, the usual oriented linking number. Use the boundary-torus intersection convention $\mu_i\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda_i=+1$. Give $J_i$ an integer framing $f_i$ and fill along $\delta_i=\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i$. Let $A$ be the symmetric integer matrix with $A_{ii}=f_i$ and $A_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ for $i\ne j$. Assume $\det A\ne0$, and let $Y$ be the resulting oriented surgery manifold, oriented as the boundary of the 4-dimensional surgery handlebody with outward normal first. Then $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. For torsion classes $[C],[D]\in H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ represented by oriented 1-cycles, choose $m>0$ and an integral 2-chain $F$ with $\partial F=mC$ and define $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\mathbin{\cdot}D)/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}$, where the intersection is signed by the orientation of $Y$. If $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ are meridian-coordinate representatives of $[C],[D]$, then
$$
\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}.
$$

Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and connected rational homology sphere boundary $Y$. Assume $Y$ has a nonsingular framed-link surgery presentation with the boundary orientation and linking convention of the surgery linking-form result. The coefficient sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ gives an isomorphism $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. Define the cohomological linking pairing by
$$\lambda_Y(x,y)=\langle\beta^{-1}(x)\smile y,[Y]\rangle\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z.$$
Let $M$ be the image of restriction $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and $M^\perp=\{x:\lambda_Y(m,x)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. Then the boundary Spin$^c$ structures extending over $B$ form one affine coset of $M$, the pairing is nonsingular, $M=M^\perp$, and $|M|^2=|H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)|$.

Let $B$ be a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and oriented boundary the rational homology sphere $Y$, where $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. If a boundary Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$ extends over $B$, then its Heegaard Floer correction term vanishes: $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. The extension hypothesis is essential; no vanishing is asserted for Spin$^c$ structures that do not extend.

Use the Ozsvath–Szabo orientation convention $L(p,1)$ given by positive $p$-surgery on the unknot and label its Spin$^c$ structures by $i\in\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, represented by $0\le i<p$. For every integer $p\ge1$,
$$d(L(p,1),i)=\frac{(2i-p)^2-p}{4p}.$$
For the opposite orientation the correction terms are negated, with the conjugate Spin$^c$ label understood.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $B_2$ is a rational homology ball with $|H_1(L(4,1))|=4$. Therefore [F3] gives exactly $\sqrt4=2$ extending Spin$^c$ structures.

At label $i=0$, [F4] gives $d(L(4,1),0)=(16-4)/16=3/4\ne0$. Every extending structure has $d=0$ by [F3], so label $0$ is not in the two-element extension set. Thus a nonextending structure has nonzero correction term while the rational-ball filling exists, refuting the stated claim.

citations.quote:
A **plane graph** is a finite simple graph ([[def-finite-simple-graph]]) together with distinct points of $\mathbb R^2$ for its vertices and a polygonal arc ([[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]]) for each edge, joining its endpoints, such that an edge interior contains no vertex and two edge arcs meet only at a common endpoint. A finite simple graph is **planar** if it is isomorphic to the abstract graph underlying some plane graph.

A **face** is a region of the complement of the drawing ([[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]). The **boundary subgraph** of a face consists of the vertices and whole edges lying in its frontier; this is a subgraph in the sense of [[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]].
If a connected plane graph has vertex, edge and face sets $V,E,F$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]), then $$|V|-|E|+|F|=2.$$

derivations.claim: For each edge $e$ choose two distinct interior points at one-third and two-thirds of its polygonal parametrization, using the finitely many edge parametrizations in the code. Subdivide $e$ at those points into three edges and declare the two points new vertices. If $e$ is a loop at $v$, its replacement is the path $v-x_e-y_e-v$ with three distinct vertices along the loop; it has no loop edge. New vertices are unique to their original edge, so replacement edges from different original edges cannot be parallel, and the three edges replacing one original edge have different endpoint pairs. Thus the subdivided graph $G'$ is simple. Subdivision preserves connectedness and leaves the point-set drawing unchanged, so its faces are exactly those of $G$. With $E$ original edges, $V'=V+2E$ and $E'=3E$, hence $V'-E'=V-E$. If $E=0$, nonempty connectedness forces $V=1$, and the same construction leaves the one-vertex simple plane graph unchanged. By [F1], $G'$ is a connected plane graph in the library's simple-graph convention in either case.
Apply [F2] to $G'$. Since $F'=F$ and $V'-E'=V-E$ by step 1.1, the equality $V'-E'+F'=2$ gives $V-E+F=2$.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. The crossingless one-component code is a separate case: its Gauss data are one empty component word, its DT pairing and crossing-sign vector are empty at $c=0$, and its PD data are the single loop `Loop[1]`; every format also carries an orientation marker, `ccw` or `cw`, for the unit circle $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ in the oriented plane, and the outer-face marker is `outside`. Thus the crossingless code records which direction orients its circle. It has no crossing graph or face-permutation test. derivations.claim: **Necessity.** In a spherical realization, remove a point in one face and stereographically project the rest of the sphere to the plane. This gives a connected polygonal plane multigraph with the same crossing vertices, edge pairs, and faces. Tracing a face with its boundary on the same side applies the clockwise successor $\sigma$ and then the edge reversal $\alpha$; hence its face cycles are exactly those of $\phi$, so its face count is $F$. Applying [F2] gives $V-E+F=2$.

**A spanning-tree realization.** Assume $V-E+F=2$. Scan the finite edge list, retaining an edge exactly when it joins two distinct current components. Connectedness makes the retained edges a spanning tree $T$: each retained edge reduces the component count by one and cannot create a cycle, and the scan ends with one component. Root $T$ at the least crossing label. Embed that root in a small polygonal disk on the sphere. Visit the other vertices by increasing tree distance from the root, breaking ties by crossing label. For each new vertex, add its tree edge to its already embedded parent, placing the new dart in the prescribed clockwise gap among the parent darts already placed and choosing the new vertex disk in that face. The new vertex has no previously placed tree darts, so its remaining cyclic order can be completed without constraint. Each addition is a leaf edge and creates no crossing. The resulting connected polygonal tree has one face by [F2], because it has $V$ vertices and $V-1$ edges.

**Face-cycle change.** There are $r=E-(V-1)$ edges outside $T$. Add them in a fixed finite order by attaching an untwisted rectangular band at the two prescribed dart intervals of the vertex disks. The boundary components of the disk-and-band neighborhood are exactly the cycles of the current face permutation. If a band attaches to one boundary component, it cuts that component into two; if it attaches to two different components, it joins them. This follows by following the two long sides of the rectangle after the two end intervals are glued. Therefore each edge addition changes the face-cycle count by $+1$ or $-1$. The initial count is one and the final count is $F=E-V+2=r+1$, so the sum of the $r$ changes is $r$. Each change is at most $+1$, hence every change is $+1$ and the two attachment intervals lie on one current face.

**Place the remaining edges.** Maintain the invariant that each complementary cap of the regular neighbourhood is a polygonal disk with a piecewise-linear parametrization by a convex polygon, preserving its boundary port order; [F4] supplies these disk parametrizations. For the next edge, step 2.1 places both attachment intervals on one current cap. In its convex polygon model choose distinct points $p,q$ in the two intervals and an interior point $r$ not on the line through $p,q$. Convexity puts the two segments $[p,r]$ and $[r,q]$ inside the polygon except at their boundary endpoints; because $r$ is off the line $pq$, their union is a simple polygonal crosscut. It cuts the convex polygon into the two regions bounded by this crosscut and the two respective boundary arcs. Each boundary is a simple polygon, so [F4] makes each closure a polygonal disk. Pull the crosscut and the two subdisks back through the stored parametrization; the two sides of the inserted edge band follow the two boundary copies of the crosscut, so the resulting face cycles are exactly the two cycles from step 2.1. Restricting the old parametrization to the two polygonal regions supplies the next face-cap parametrizations. Thus the invariant and prescribed rotations persist at each finite insertion, producing the required spherical embedding.

**Decorate and lift.** Replace each crossing disk by the standard transverse crossing with the given opposite over/under pairs. The arrow and sign-consistent cyclic-order conditions make the oriented strands and crossing signs agree with the code. Lift the over-strand above the under-strand in each of the finitely many disjoint crossing disks, and interpolate heights along the edge bands. **Plane model and empty boundary case.** Choose a point in the distinguished face and remove it before stereographic projection; that face is then the unbounded face and all other cyclic data remain fixed. Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. Disconnected crossing graphs and disconnected crossingless links are outside this code class.

A **normalized planar-diagram code** with $c>0$ has crossing labels
$C=\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and four dart positions $0,1,2,3$ at each crossing, in
clockwise order beginning with the outgoing over-dart. The opposite pair
$(0,2)$ is over and $(1,3)$ is under. For sign $+1$, the clockwise record is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$; for sign $-1$ it is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$. Edge labels are assigned
by scanning crossings in increasing order and their four dart positions in
order, giving the next positive integer to the pair containing the first
not-yet-labelled dart. The outer face is recorded by its least dart in its
face cycle. These rules remove arbitrary edge-name and face-name choices;
different crossing labelings may still represent the same diagram. At $c=0$
a normalized code is the crossingless record with one of the two orientation
markers above.

A **Gauss code** for an oriented diagram records, in traversal order on each
oriented component, a signed crossing label: $+j$ means the component passes
over at crossing $j$, and $-j$ means it passes under. For a knot there is one
cyclic word; for a link there is one cyclic word per component. Each crossing
label must occur exactly twice in total, once positively and once negatively.
When $c>0$, every listed component word is nonempty; a separate crossingless
component is not part of this code class. The zero-crossing case is only the
one-component code specified above.
The code also carries a separate algebraic crossing-sign vector
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$, one entry for each label. Choosing a basepoint
turns the knot's cyclic word into a based word; changing the basepoint
cyclically shifts the word, and relabeling crossings changes only their names.
The visit order, over/under signs, and crossing-sign vector determine the
crossing rotation system; it is realizable in the sphere only when the
resulting code is spherical. A plane Gauss code also carries an identifier of
one cycle of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

A **signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code**, in this page's convention, encodes a
based oriented knot with $c$ crossings by numbering its $2c$ visits
$1,\ldots,2c$ in traversal order. For each odd visit $2j-1$, record the even
visit $2k$ paired with it as $d_j=+2k$ when the odd visit is over and
$d_j=-2k$ when it is under; also record the algebraic crossing sign
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$ for crossing label $j$, the pair containing odd
visit $2j-1$. Its parity conditions are that
$|d_1|,\ldots,|d_c|$ are exactly the even numbers $2,4,\ldots,2c$, each once,
and each paired crossing has one over-visit and one under-visit. The separate
$\varepsilon_j$ records the crossing sign; signed DT conventions elsewhere
may encode signs differently. The associated cyclic traversal and crossing
signs determine a rotation system, which must pass the same spherical
realizability test. A plane DT code also carries an identifier of one cycle
of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

An **oriented planar-diagram code** labels each edge segment by an integer and
lists its two incident darts at crossing records. Each crossing record lists
its four directed edge ends in clockwise order, beginning with the outgoing
over-dart, and records which opposite pair is over, the orientation of each
strand, and the crossing sign. Every edge label occurs exactly twice, once as
an incoming end and once as an outgoing end. The code must satisfy the local
crossing-order rule above; its crossing graph must be connected when nonempty;
and its rotation system must satisfy $V-E+F=2$. The record also carries an
identifier of one cycle of its face permutation as the outer face. Thus an
arbitrary word in labels, even when each label occurs twice, is not declared
realizable until all incidence, orientation, crossing, connectedness, and
face-count tests pass.

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or
oriented planar-diagram code in the conventions of this page. The crossing
count $c$ is a nonnegative integer. When $c>0$, the code includes the finite
crossing labels, edge-end incidences, strand arrows, over/under data, crossing
signs, and a distinguished outer face. When $c=0$, the only admissible input
for this procedure is the one-component crossingless code specified in the
code definition.

failed check below and `witness` identifies the offending field, label, or
crossing, or `Valid(diagram, components, faces, outerFace)`. Here `diagram` is
a finite gluing record consisting of one crossing disk per vertex, one
rectangular edge band for each pair of darts under $\alpha$, and one cap disk
per cycle of the face permutation. Each band is attached at its recorded dart ports, and each
crossing disk records its clockwise order, strand orientations, over/under
pair, and sign. `components` lists the oriented link cycles, `faces` lists the
face-permutation cycles, and `outerFace` is the selected cycle. The gluing
record represents a polygonal spherical diagram; deleting a point in its
selected face gives the plane model. The procedure tests realizability of
this code only; it does not compare the represented link with another code.

   nonnegative integer, return `invalid-header` with that field.

2. If $c=0$, accept only one empty Gauss component word, the empty signed-DT
   code, or the single `Loop[1]` PD record, each with exactly one orientation
   marker, `ccw` or `cw`. Return
   `invalid-crossingless-code` otherwise. For an accepted input return the
   standard circle with the marked orientation, one component, its two sphere
   faces, and the `outside` face selector. Do not run crossing-graph tests.

3. For a Gauss code with $c>0$, reject an empty component word. Check that
   every label lies in $\{1,\ldots,c\}$, occurs exactly twice in total, and
   occurs once with each over/under sign. Check that its separate crossing-sign
   vector has length $c$ and entries in $\{+1,-1\}$. Return
   `invalid-crossing-label` for the first out-of-range label,
   `invalid-crossing-visit-count` with the label and its over/under counts for
   any visit failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position. Turn successive visits on each component word into directed edge
   labels, including each cyclic last-to-first edge, numbering these segments
   in the listed component order and then in traversal order, and form the
   crossing records from the over/under visits and the stored crossing signs.

4. For a signed DT code, check that its pairing list and sign vector each have
   length $c$, each pairing value has absolute value in
   $\{2,4,\ldots,2c\}$, every such absolute value occurs once, and every sign
   is $+1$ or $-1$. Return `invalid-dt-pairing` with the first bad index for a
   pairing failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position for a sign failure. The odd visit $2j-1$ is crossing $j$; if
   $d_j>0$ it is the over-visit and if $d_j<0$ it is the under-visit. At the
   even visit paired with $2j-1$, use crossing label $j$ and the opposite
   over/under sign. Decode visits in order $1,\ldots,2c$ into the corresponding
   signed Gauss word and continue with step 3.

5. For a PD code, check that there are exactly $c$ crossing records and four
   dart occurrences at each record. Return `invalid-crossing-record` with the
   first bad record otherwise. Use the edge labels and arrows in the records
   to form the paired-dart involution, crossing rotations, over/under pairs,
   and crossing signs.

6. In every nonempty encoding, check that each edge label has exactly two
   occurrences, one incoming and one outgoing; each crossing has exactly four
   incident darts; the opposite pairs are exactly one over-strand and one
   under-strand; each strand has one incoming and one outgoing end; and the
   cyclic order matches the stored crossing sign. Return, in that order,
   `invalid-edge-incidence`, `invalid-crossing-valence`,
   `invalid-over-under-pair`, `invalid-strand-orientation`, or
   `invalid-crossing-sign-order`, with the first offending label or crossing.

7. Starting at each as-yet unvisited outgoing dart, cross its edge by $\alpha$
   to the incoming dart at the other endpoint and continue through the
   opposite dart of that same strand. Stop only when the starting outgoing
   dart is reached. If an end is missing, a dart repeats before that return, or
   any dart remains uncovered after all cycles are traced, return
   `invalid-component-closure` with the first such dart. Then test the crossing
   graph for connectedness; if it is disconnected, return

   disk by its prescribed transverse crossing, attach one cap disk along each
   face cycle, and lift the over-strand above the under-strand. Return this
   finite gluing record, the directed components, the face cycles, and the
   outer-face identifier.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let

derivations.claim: By validity, the code passes every finite check in [F3]. If $c=0$, [F1] gives the one-component crossingless code and its `cw` or `ccw` orientation; [F2] realizes that oriented code as the standard circle with the `outside` face selector. If $c>0$, its one component satisfies the knot-code condition, and the face-count hypothesis in [F2] yields a spherical crossing graph with the prescribed rotations and edge pairings; deleting a point in the selected face gives its plane model. In this nonempty case, replacing each crossing disk by the prescribed transverse crossing and lifting the over-strand gives the decorated regular diagram returned by the procedure.

Suppose $c>0$. At each double point the two branches are smooth and transverse. Smooth local defining functions for them have independent differentials, so together form coordinates in which the branches are the coordinate axes. Corresponding oriented branch germs and cyclic orders give orientation-preserving matching crossing charts. Take disjoint small crossing disks in these charts. Each edge left after truncation is a compact embedded interval; a strip coordinate along it can be chosen to agree with the crossing coordinates near both ends. Explicitly extend the end longitudinal parameters increasingly along the interval, and extend their transverse coordinate vector fields by finitely many convex combinations of fields pointing to the same side; these combinations stay transverse. Short flows give the strip, and compactness supplies a common width. Shrink the finitely many widths to avoid all other truncated edges and crossing disks except their assigned end collars. This construction treats different endpoint germs separately, so it applies to loops and parallel edges as well. Using the same abstract disk-and-band model in the two drawings gives a smooth diffeomorphism of their graph neighborhoods $N_0,N_1$ carrying vertices, edges, strand orientations, and crossing decorations as prescribed. Round corresponding boundary corners in the same model; the map is then smooth across all joins and carries their smooth boundary circles to the matching circles. These circles correspond to the same face cycles, even when a facial walk repeats a cut vertex.

Relabel the finite crossing set in increasing order and assign edge labels by the canonical scan in [F1]. The selected face is represented by the least dart of its face cycle. These are exactly the normalization rules used by the bounded enumerator. The resulting code has $c$ crossings, so it occurs in the enumerator's finite loops at bound $c$; [F4] then guarantees that its reconstruction is returned.

Regard the drawings and neighborhoods as subsets of the oriented sphere. Every complementary component of a connected neighborhood $N_i$ is a smooth disk. Indeed [L1] gives its bounded disk in a stereographic chart; choosing a second stereographic chart with its removed point inside that disk presents the other side as a bounded smooth Jordan region, also a disk by [L1]. The connected set $N_i$ lies on its collar side, so the other disk misses $N_i$; it contains no other boundary component, since that component's neighborhood collar would put $N_i$ on the other side. Thus it is a whole complementary component, and all components arise this way. Extend the neighborhood diffeomorphism over each pair of matching disks by [L1], using collars induced by its smooth extension across their boundary germs. Such a germ extension exists in the local smooth boundary charts, and has positive normal derivative; finitely many charts and a smaller collar retain smoothness and invertibility. Hence the extended maps agree on actual collars, and the finite gluing is a smooth orientation-preserving sphere diffeomorphism. The selected outer face matches the disks containing infinity. When extending this pair, also prescribe the identity germ at infinity using the interior clause of [L1]. To apply that lemma, view each complementary disk in a stereographic chart whose removed point lies in its own neighborhood $N_i$; for the outer pair, the prescribed coordinate germ is the expression of the sphere's identity near infinity in these two charts. The resulting sphere diffeomorphism fixes a neighborhood of infinity. Its plane restriction $H$ is therefore an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism carrying the two decorated diagrams.

If $c=0$, the two diagrams are smooth embedded circles with the same `cw` or `ccw` orientation marker. Choose an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of their bounded disks using [L1]; its boundary map carries the circle orientations because these markers agree. Extend across the exterior disks on the sphere by [L1], matching the induced boundary collars and prescribing the identity germ at infinity as in step 2.2. This again produces an orientation-preserving plane diffeomorphism $H$ carrying the oriented diagram and its selected exterior face.

Finally every orientation-preserving smooth plane diffeomorphism $H$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth path of plane diffeomorphisms. Write $b=H(0)$ and $A=DH(0)$, and set $J_t(x)=(H(tx)-b)/t$ for $t>0$, $J_0(x)=Ax$. The identity $J_t(x)=\int_0^1 DH(stx)x\,ds$ proves joint smoothness at $t=0$. For $t>0$ the map is a composition of diffeomorphisms, and $J_0$ is the invertible positive linear map $A$. Join the identity to $A$ by polar decomposition: the positive definite factor is joined linearly to the identity, and the rotation factor by interpolating its angle. Follow that path by $J_t$ from $A$ to $H-b$, then by translations from $H-b$ to $H$. Replace each crossing disk by the prescribed smooth transverse crossing, choosing the ports and collars so the edge-band centerlines join their crossing strands tangentially. Away from the crossing disks, round the finitely many polygonal bends in pairwise disjoint neighborhoods that meet no other edge portion. On each over-strand set the height to $+1$ and on each under-strand set it to $-1$ near every crossing; along each edge interval interpolate smoothly between its prescribed endpoint heights, constant near those endpoints. The resulting projection is a smooth immersion with exactly the prescribed finite transverse double points and no triple points. Its only repeated projected points are crossing pairs, and those pairs have distinct heights, so the lift is a smooth embedded link in $S^3$. Thus the procedure's plane model is a regular oriented diagram by [F3] representing the input code.

Suppose $c>0$. At each double point the two branches are smooth and transverse. Smooth local defining functions for them have independent differentials, so together form coordinates in which the branches are the coordinate axes. Corresponding oriented branch germs and cyclic orders give orientation-preserving matching crossing charts. Take disjoint small crossing disks in these charts. Each edge left after truncation is a compact embedded interval; a strip coordinate along it can be chosen to agree with the crossing coordinates near both ends. Explicitly extend the end longitudinal parameters increasingly along the interval, and extend their transverse coordinate vector fields by finitely many convex combinations of fields pointing to the same side; these combinations stay transverse. Short flows give the strip, and compactness supplies a common width. Shrink the finitely many widths to avoid all other truncated edges and crossing disks except their assigned end collars. This construction treats different endpoint germs separately, so it applies to loops and parallel edges as well. Using the same abstract disk-and-band model in the two drawings gives a smooth diffeomorphism of their graph neighborhoods $N_0,N_1$ carrying vertices, edges, strand orientations, and crossing decorations as prescribed. Round corresponding boundary corners in the same model; the map is then smooth across all joins and carries their smooth boundary circles to the matching circles. These circles correspond to the same face cycles, even when a facial walk repeats a cut vertex.

Relabel the finite crossing set in increasing order and assign edge labels by the canonical scan in [F1]. The selected face is represented by the least dart of its face cycle. These are exactly the normalization rules used by the bounded enumerator. The resulting code has $c$ crossings, so it occurs in the enumerator's finite loops at bound $c$; [F4] then guarantees that its reconstruction is returned.

Regard the drawings and neighborhoods as subsets of the oriented sphere. Every complementary component of a connected neighborhood $N_i$ is a smooth disk. Indeed [L1] gives its bounded disk in a stereographic chart; choosing a second stereographic chart with its removed point inside that disk presents the other side as a bounded smooth Jordan region, also a disk by [L1]. The connected set $N_i$ lies on its collar side, so the other disk misses $N_i$; it contains no other boundary component, since that component's neighborhood collar would put $N_i$ on the other side. Thus it is a whole complementary component, and all components arise this way. Extend the neighborhood diffeomorphism over each pair of matching disks by [L1], using collars induced by its smooth extension across their boundary germs. Such a germ extension exists in the local smooth boundary charts, and has positive normal derivative; finitely many charts and a smaller collar retain smoothness and invertibility. Hence the extended maps agree on actual collars, and the finite gluing is a smooth orientation-preserving sphere diffeomorphism. The selected outer face matches the disks containing infinity. When extending this pair, also prescribe the identity germ at infinity using the interior clause of [L1]. To apply that lemma, view each complementary disk in a stereographic chart whose removed point lies in its own neighborhood $N_i$; for the outer pair, the prescribed coordinate germ is the expression of the sphere's identity near infinity in these two charts. If $c=0$, the two diagrams are smooth embedded circles with the same `cw` or `ccw` orientation marker.
